en: Oṃ. Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Thus have I heard at one time: The Blessed One was dwelling in the pavilion of the assembly circle of inconceivable, marvelous, and wondrously arrayed bodhisattvas, situated in the expanse of the sky above the Śuddhāvāsa heaven. There, the Blessed One addressed the sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm. 1.1.

"Listen, O sons of the gods! I shall speak for the benefit of all beings the mantra-words that fulfill all desires, which provide the life-span, health, and sovereignty upon which all sentient beings depend—the inconceivable, marvelous, and wondrous display of the conduct, meditative absorptions, supernormal powers, and specific liberations of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, as well as his bodhisattva-transformations within the maṇḍala. Listen to it; attend to it well and thoroughly; I shall speak it to you. (1.2)
Then those sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm, with palms joined in reverence, spoke thus:

Therefore, may the Blessed One speak concerning the conduct of the bodhisattvas, the attainment of the specific stages of meditative concentration, the ascending to the vajra-throne, the subduing of Māra, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, the departure [from saṃsāra] of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, rebirth among gods and humans, the pacification of all suffering, the removal of poverty, disease, and affliction for the wealthy, the state of being unsurpassable in all worldly and supramundane mantra-practices, the fulfillment of all hopes, and the making of the word of all Tathāgatas unfailing. May the Blessed One, with a mind of loving-kindness and a mind of benefit, speak out of compassion for us and for all sentient beings. 1.3.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed the entire realm of the Śuddhāvāsa deities with his Buddha-eye, entered the samādhi called *Viśuddhaviṣayajyotirvikaraṇavidhvaṃsinī* (The Destruction of the Radiance of the Pure Domain). Immediately upon the Blessed One’s entry into this state, a network of light rays called *Saṃkusumitabodhisattvasañcodanī* (The Exhortation of the Saṃkusumita Bodhisattva) issued forth from the circle of hair between his eyebrows. Accompanied by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rays, they circumambulated the Blessed One three times to the right and traversed the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system. Passing beyond world systems as numerous as the sands of a hundred thousand Ganges rivers in the northeastern direction, they entered a world system named Kusumāvatī, where the Tathāgata named Saṃkusumitarājendra resides. There, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta dwells together with bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have entered their practice by the power of their former vows. Upon seeing that manifestation of light, his face breaking into a slight smile, he addressed that assembly of bodhisattvas.
"O sons of the Victorious One, this 'Impeller by Rays' of ours has arrived here. May you all prepare yourselves! 1.5

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, with eyes wide open and unblinking, stood facing the direction from which that radiance issued. Then that ray of light, having illuminated the world-system Kusumāvatī with a great radiance as an exhortation, circumambulated the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarājendra, three times to the right, and vanished into the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī.
Aphorism 1.4;
Aphorism 1.5;
Aphorism 1.6.
Ap 1.7 Ap 1.8 Ap 1.9

Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarājendra, three times, bowed his head in prostration, placed his right knee upon the ground, and addressed the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarājendra, as follows. 1.7.

The Blessed One, Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksambuddha, has taken us into his consideration. "O Blessed One, let us go from here to this Sahā world-system to see, pay homage to, and serve the Blessed One Śākyamuni; and to explain the ritual procedures for all mantra practices, sādhanas, and maṇḍalas, as well as the secret rituals of the manuals, the forms of cloth-paintings, the heart-mantras of all Tathāgatas, the secret mudrās, and the empowerments, in order to fulfill all the hopes of all sentient beings. (1.8)
When this had been said, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarājendra, spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Go, Mañjuśrī Kumāra, at whatever time you deem appropriate. Furthermore, in our name, the Blessed One Śākyamuni should be asked whether he has little affliction, little ailment, ease of movement, and a state of dwelling in comfort.
Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarājendra, spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.

Moreover, O Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as the sands of a hundred thousand Gaṅgā rivers have spoken, and will speak, of your secret chapter on the ritual procedures for the initiation, mudrās, and maṇḍala of the mantra practice—including the fulfillment of all hopes, the satisfaction of all sentient beings, the light-jewel chapter, the sovereignty of knowledge regarding the past, future, and present, the prophecy of lordship, the recitation of mantras, the finality of the place, the time of disappearance, the chapter on the expansion [of the teaching], and the culmination of the practice through the traversal of all the worldly and transcendent stages of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas. I too now rejoice in this. Go, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, at whatever time you deem appropriate; in the presence of Śākyamuni you shall hear this Dharma discourse, and you yourself shall also proclaim it. And here is the mantra: 1.10. *Oṃ mañjuśrīye svāhā* || 1.10 ||
Homage to all the Tathāgatas, whose teachings are inconceivable and unimpeded. Oṃ ra ra smara! O you who possess unimpeded teachings and assume the form of a youth, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!

Young man, this is that root mantra of Mañjuśrī; it is the heart of all Tathāgatas, spoken by all Tathāgatas, and will be spoken [by them]. You too shall now speak it, having gone to the Sahā world-system, in its detailed analysis, as the performer of all rites. It has been authorized by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni. Furthermore, the supreme heart-mantra here is: Oṃ vākyedaṃ namaḥ. 1.12.
And here is the *upahṛdaya*:
*hūṃ* at the end of the mantra. 1.13.

Then, indeed, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having been authorized by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarāja, entered the samādhi named "Attaining the Seat of Awakening, which is the Outflow of the Bodhisattva Practice and Adorned with All Arrays."
Aphorism 1.13, Aphorism 1.14, Aphorism 1.15, Aphorism 1.16.

Immediately upon Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta’s attainment of meditative absorption, that entire world-system, extending through the four directions, above, below, and across, became completely filled in every way by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. 1.14.

Excellent, excellent, O Son of the Conqueror, that you enter into this particular samādhi! It is not possible for any of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even those bodhisattvas who have entered the practice and are established on the ten stages to enter into it. || 1.15 ||

Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarājendra, having consulted together with those Blessed Buddhas, spoke this mantra of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta—the supreme heart, the supreme secret, the accomplisher of all aims, known as the "Single Syllable," which is a divine and most secret [mantra] that effects the welfare of all sentient beings and is to be accomplished by others through specific mantra practices. 1.16.

Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarājendra, remained silent for a moment. Having surveyed the entire world-system with his Buddha-eye, he brought those Blessed Buddhas to mind and, with a mind characterized by loving-kindness, uttered this mantra:
*Namaḥ sarvabuddhānām | Oṃ maṃ*.
This mantra, Mañjuśrī, is the supreme heart-mantra that accomplishes all activities.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having emerged from that samādhi, just as...

Just as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm—in a mere moment of a finger-snap, a blink, or a single instant—he entered the miraculous transformation of a specific meditative absorption called "the power, speed, and wisdom of supernatural faculties" (ṛddhibalajavabuddhi). Having done so, he arrived at this Sahā world-system. Upon arrival, he stationed himself above in the realm of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, which rests upon great maṇi-jewels in the expanse of the sky. Illuminating that entire abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods with a vast radiance of light, he entered the meditative absorption called "the illumination of the adornment of radiant jewels" (jyotiratnapratimaṇḍanodyotinī). 1.18.

Immediately upon entering that meditative absorption, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta miraculously produced for the purpose of worshiping the Blessed One Śākyamuni a divine rain of perfumes, garlands, ointments, wreaths, and powders; as well as a celestial pavilion composed of many jewels, adorned with jeweled parasols extending for hundreds of thousands of yojanas, beautified by divine visible arrays of great silk streamers, and filled with divine flowers, banners, flags, and garlands, draped with nets of jeweled bells that emitted sweet sounds proclaiming the non-retrogression of bodhisattvas and their establishment in [the path].

Having seen that wondrous and marvelous miracle, that supernatural display of the Bodhisattva, those sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host had their hair stand on end. Seeing their celestial abodes trembling, their hearts were filled with intense anxiety as they wondered, "Have we perhaps fallen away from our supernatural powers? In great haste, they began to cry out loudly, saying: "Save us, O Blessed One! Save us, Śākyamuni!"
Then the Blessed One addressed the entire assembly of the Śuddhāvāsa deities:

"Do not fear, friends; do not be afraid! This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, who has come from the presence of the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarāja in the Buddha-field Saṃkusumita, in order to see, pay homage to, and attend upon [me], and to proclaim the great mantra-words of extensive practice for the sake of others, and the marvelous words of the Dharma."
Aphorism 1.19, Aphorism 1.20, Aphorism 1.21.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having circumambulated the Blessed One Śākyamuni three times, gazed at the Blessed One with unblinking eyes, prostrated at his feet, and praised the Blessed One with these syllables, words, and phonemes: 1.22. [The Hymn of Praise]
Homage to you, the liberated one, O noble one; homage to you, the Supreme Person.
Homage to you, the best of beings, the accomplisher of the purpose of all conduct. 1.23
Homage to you, O lion among men, who wards off all misfortune! May your mind be gracious, O great hero, the destroyer of all hardships. 1.24
Homage to you, O lotus among men, whose holy fragrance is infinite! Homage to you, O lotus among men, who purifies the mire of the three realms of existence! 1.25
Homage to you, the liberated one, the deliverer from all suffering!
Homage to you, the peaceful one, the perfect tamer of all who are untamed!
Homage to you, the accomplished one, the fulfiller of the purpose of all mantra-practices! Homage to you, the auspicious one, the most auspicious among all that is auspicious!
Homage to you, the Buddha, who has awakened to all phenomena! Homage to you, the Tathāgata, the suchness of all phenomena, the teacher who has entered into the mode of non-proliferation! 1.28

Homage to you, the Omniscient One, who are established in the establishment of all knowledge, all objects of knowledge—both conditioned and unconditioned—and the paths of the three vehicles leading to nirvāṇa. Thus [ends section 1.29].
Having thus praised the Blessed One face-to-face with these syllables, words, compendia, and verses of hymn, he spoke as follows:

From here, the Blessed One, having passed through world-systems as numerous as the sands of a hundred thousand Ganges rivers, in the north-eastern direction, there was a buddha-field named Saṃkusumita. Therein is a world-system called Kusumāvatī, where the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarājendra—worthy, perfectly awakened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans—resides and teaches the Dharma that is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end; which is meaningful, well-phrased, unique, complete, pure, and radiant, revealing the conduct of a Buddha. He currently remains, stays, and maintains himself, and he teaches the Dharma—the Bodhisattva-piṭaka concerning the meaning of mantra-conduct—and the path that follows the threefold conduct, which is a protection, a shelter, a refuge, a final resort, secure, the ultimate goal, and the absolute consummation for all sentient beings. Having been granted permission by that very Blessed One, he has come here to the presence of the Blessed One’s feet. And that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarājendra, inquired after the Blessed One’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, ease of movement, and state of dwelling in comfort. And he spoke thus: 1.30. [The verse follows.]
Aphorism 1.31: "The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is that by which an object is correctly measured."

It is truly marvelous that in such a time of the five corruptions, the Buddha, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, has appeared and teaches all dharmas—complete in both words and syllables—for the sake of attaining liberation from the three paths and rebirth among gods and humans. It is marvelous, indeed, the vigor of that Blessed One Śākyamuni, in that he establishes sentient beings in nirvāṇa—the ultimate security and peace—even though they belong to a class of beings unfit for it and follow a path that leads to the arising of the three realms of existence. Only Buddhas can know the minds of the Blessed Buddhas. What am I able to do? Can I know the Buddha-transformation of the Blessed Buddhas, who possess inconceivable, wondrous, and sovereign miraculous powers? Or can I know their mental conduct, their engagement in practice, or their accomplishment of activities? Even in a hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of eons, one could not describe it even in brief. This manifestation of the Tathāgatas must be seen as the unconditioned reality of all forms, both collectively and individually, without exception. Regarding those who rely on the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through vision, only the Blessed Tathāgata knows their conduct or can describe their qualities; we do not. 1.31

Then Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince, was seated upon a great jewel-lotus created through the miraculous power of his own supernatural transformations, gazing at the Blessed One Śākyamuni. Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni addressed Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with a Brahma-like voice—resounding like the song of the kalaviṅka bird, like the roar of thunder, and like the peal of a drum—a voice endowed with the purpose of bringing forth the conduct of Bodhisattvas in accordance with the teaching of the Dharma, preceded by various discourses and introductory questions on the successive stages of the Tathāgata’s path: [1.32] Thus he spoke to Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince.

Welcome to you, Mañjuśrī! [This is] the accomplishment empowered by all Buddhas through the conduct of the Great Beings; that which brings about the welfare of all Bodhisattvas; the empowerment of the mandala, mudrās, and secret mantras along with their esoteric rites; the fulfiller of all hopes for longevity, health, and sovereignty; the means for accomplishing all sādhanas and the knowledge of the tantras regarding what is to be known; the bestower of kingdoms, fields, and the preservation of the past, future, and present; in short, the fulfiller of all hopes for all sentient beings; the manifestation of true virtues; the follower of the mantra conduct; the producer of joy in other beings; the bestower of invisibility, sky-faring, and the power of movement on foot; the maker of the wise; the attractor [of others]; the one who causes entry into the netherworld (pātāla); the performer of sorcery (ābhicāruka); the achiever of all desires; the one who gathers together yakṣas, yakṣiṇīs, servants (kiṅkara), piśācas, and all spirits; and the one who restores children, the elderly, and the young to their natural state.

In brief, it accomplishes all rites and fulfills all desires; it is employed in rites of sorcery (*ābhicāruka*), nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), and pacification (*śāntika*). In whatever manner it is applied, in that very manner is its goal accomplished. This *Mahākalparatnapaṭalavisara*, the crest-jewel of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, has been authorized by us and spoken by all the Buddhas as a treasury of the Dharma and the meaning of the practice of the mantras of pure beings, for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, and for the sake of all beings, both gods and humans. 1.34. {V5}

A person who has attained the fruit of Arhatship is one who has abandoned all defilements. This is because he has abandoned the afflictions belonging to the three realms and nine grades, which are to be abandoned through cultivation. Furthermore, he is one who has abandoned the outflows, for he has abandoned the outflows of the three realms. He is also one who has abandoned birth, for he has abandoned the birth associated with the three realms. Moreover, he is one who has abandoned old age and death, for he has abandoned the old age and death associated with the three realms. He is also one who has abandoned all suffering, for he has abandoned the suffering associated with the three realms. Furthermore, he is one who has abandoned all origination, for he has abandoned the origination associated with the three realms. He is also one who has abandoned all cessation, for he has abandoned the cessation associated with the three realms. Moreover, he is one who has abandoned all paths, for he has abandoned the paths associated with the three realms. Finally, he is one who has abandoned all phenomena, for he has abandoned the conditioned phenomena associated with the three realms. Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta entered the bodhisattva-samādhi called *Sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhānajyotiraśmivyūhālaṅkārasañcodanī* (The Illumination and Exhortation by the Array of Light-Rays of the Empowerment of All Buddhas). As soon as that pure being had entered it, he illuminated with light-rays the world-systems and buddha-fields numbering more than the sands of many Ganges rivers, from the Akaniṣṭha heaven down to the great Avīci hell. Whatever beings there were who were suffering, they all attained the pacification and cessation of their suffering. Having exhorted all the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the Blessed Buddhas, that light-ray then vanished into the crown of the head of the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. At that moment, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who were established in the buddha-fields situated in the eastern direction, were exhorted by that manifestation of the radiant circle of the sphere of light-rays. Namely: 1.35. [The names of the Buddhas follow.]

The Tathāgata named Jyotissaumyagandhāvabhāsaśrī, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaiḍūryaprabharāja, the Tathāgata named Samantāvabhāsaśrī, the Tathāgata named Samudgatarāja, the Tathāgata named Śālendrarāja, the Tathāgata named Lokendrarāja, the Tathāgata named Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarāja, the Tathāgata named Anantāvabhāsarājendra, and the Tathāgata named Jyotiraśmirājendra. || 1.36 ||

With these as their leaders, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in infinite and boundless world-systems, surrounded by hosts of bodhisattvas—gathered together in the Sahā world-system to see the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who was residing in the palace of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa) and was teaching, together with Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the extensive chapter on the meaning of the mantra-words for the exposition of the bodhisattva conduct. These Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, assembled there.

In this way, having illuminated all the Buddha-fields in the southern, western, and northern directions, as well as the intermediate directions—and thus above, below, and across—having eclipsed all the abodes of Māra in every Buddha-field, and being surrounded by hosts of bodhisattvas and preceded by the community of śrāvakas, they stood forth, desiring to manifest that abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods and the greatness of the bodhisattvas through the miraculous power of the Buddhas, and desiring to illuminate the unimpeded teaching of the Tathāgata, which consists of the extensive chapters on the specific samādhis for accomplishing the practice of mantras. It is as follows: 1.38.

Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.44,

[They were] those who enter into the enumeration of beings and non-beings through the king of jewels of *rākṣasa* mantras and gems; who follow the conduct of beings; who imitate the discipline of beings according to their inclinations; who assume forms distinguished by those [beings]; who deliver the Dharma through the realization of the instructions of the Vidyārājas; who establish the path of speech that does not transgress the samaya of entering into all mundane and supramundane [realms], which are like the lotus and vajra of the Tathāgatas; and who ensure the non-interruption of the lineage of the Three Jewels. Namely: 1.42.

The Uṣṇīṣa is most wonderful, most exalted, the white parasol, the one with infinite petals, the hundred-petaled, the victorious uṣṇīṣa, the world-transcending, the victorious uṣṇīṣa, the risen uṣṇīṣa, the lotus-rayed, the gold-rayed, the white-rayed, the arrayed uṣṇīṣa, the mass of gold, the mass of white, the mass of splendor, the mass of jewels, the mass of equality, the renowned mass, the mass of reality, the mass of truth, the mass whose intrinsic nature is non-existence, and the mass that is not false. 1.43.

By these and other Uṣṇīṣa Kings—who have entered the infinite realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), who fulfill the intentions and aspirations of sentient beings according to their inclinations, and who are endowed with the heart-essence of all Victors—it is impossible, even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, to state the limit of the enumeration of these Uṣṇīṣa Kings, nor to describe the majesty of those whose strength and prowess are inconceivable. It is described here only by way of a brief summary and in concise form. (1.44) Now, the assembly of the Vidyārājñīs shall be spoken of, as follows:
The ūrṇā, the eyebrows, the eyes, the eyelashes, the ears, and the neck; fearlessness, compassion, loving-kindness, pity, wisdom, the light-ray, consciousness, radiance, stainless, and white. 1.45.
Likewise, there were other Vidyārājñīs emitted from the infinite and boundless forms of the Tathāgatas, namely:

Together with these and others—those who know the flavor of liberation within the infinite realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), who have reached the lesser vehicle that converges into the three vehicles, who flee from *saṃsāra*, who meditate upon the three liberations and the dhyānas, who are perfected in the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) and the modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), who are well-composed, well-ordained, and have entered the way of right method to converge in the realm of nirvāṇa, characterized by equality and the absence of conceptual proliferation—they too sat down there in that great circle of the assembly, immediately following the Blessed One Śākyamuni, who is established in the station of the Three Jewels and the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

And there were many great female disciples who had entered the realm of nirvāṇa through the assembly, who relied upon the vehicle of the unconditioned path, who were pure and free from passion, who had attained universal radiance, who purified the qualities of the field worthy of offerings, who were the very essence of the circle of sentient beings, and who were sovereigns over the world. They were the supreme lords over all beings—two-footed, four-footed, many-footed, and footless—who are fields of merit for gods and humans worthy of worship. For example: 1.64.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having gazed upon that entire circle of the assembly, with pure resolve and knowing the realm of sentient beings to be of the nature of non-existence, of the nature of space, and transcending the three times, addressed Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince.

"Pay attention, Mañjuśrī, to the conduct for the benefit of sentient beings; cultivate the bodhisattva samādhi named ‘The Subduing of the Power of Māra,’ which possesses the power of the ten Tathāgatas, which brings about the attainment of the meaning of mantra practice through the endowment of faith in the desired fruits of action and the joy of one’s own inclinations, and which is the dharma-foot, the karma-foot, the peace-foot, and the liberation-foot, the extraction from conceptual construction, and the attainment of non-conceptual equality. 1.68.

Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, entered the meditative absorption immediately upon the words spoken by the Blessed One. As soon as Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, had entered that absorption, he caused this trichiliocosm—the trichiliocosm equal in number to the atoms in hundreds of thousands of many world-systems—to tremble violently; having illuminated it with a great radiance, he displayed the power of his own supernatural faculties and uttered his own mantra-syllables.

Homage to all Buddhas, who have arisen from the nature of non-existence. Homage to the Pratyekabuddhas and the noble Śrāvakas. Homage to the Bodhisattvas, the great beings, the lords established on the ten stages. It is as follows: 1.70.

Oṃ! Kha kha! Khāhi khāhi! O tamer of wicked beings, you who hold a sword, mace, axe, and noose in your hands; four-armed, four-faced, six-legged one! Go, go! O destroyer of great obstacles, you of deformed countenance, who strikes terror into all spirits, you who utter the loud laugh of *aṭṭahāsa*, you who are clothed in a tiger skin! Perform, perform all rites! Cut, cut all mantras! Break, break the supreme mudrā! Summon, summon all spirits! Churn, churn all the wicked! Cause them to enter, cause them to enter the center of the maṇḍala! O ender of the life of Yama Vaivasvata, perform, perform my task! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Do not delay, do not delay! Remember your vow! Hūṃ hūṃ! Phaṭ phaṭ! Shatter, shatter! O fulfiller of all hopes! Ho, ho, Blessed One! Why do you tarry? Accomplish all my aims! Svāhā!

This great wrathful king of the Blessed Mañjuśrī, named Yamāntaka, slays even King Yama; he brings them under his power—how much more so other beings? As soon as this great wrathful king was spoken, all beings approached the presence of the Blessed One, distressed, terrified, trembling, agitated in mind, and broken-hearted; they had no other refuge, no other protection, and no other resort, except for the Buddha, the Blessed One, and the youthful Mañjuśrī.

Then, whatever beings there may be—those moving on earth, those moving in water, those moving in the sky, both stationary and mobile; those born from a womb, from an egg, from moisture, or by spontaneous generation—even they, at that very instant and in that very moment, were established throughout infinite and boundless world-systems, situated above, below, across, in the cardinal directions, and in the intermediate directions. At that moment, having been driven away by the Great King of Wrath himself, they were led [to other realms]. And this King of Wrath [should not be placed] before one who has not yet abandoned passion.

It should be recited. For what reason? Because even he [the practitioner] might die or wither away. Having established the *samaya*, it should be recited before an image of the Buddha containing relics, or before a reliquary (*caitya*), or before a manuscript of the True Dharma, or before Mañjuśrī in his form as a youth. It must not be recited for the sake of other rites, nor anywhere else; for the reason is that [reciting it elsewhere] would lead to great calamities and great ruin, resulting in self-destruction. 1.73.

For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, are supremely compassionate. However, it is solely for the sake of establishing the guidance of the Dharma—which brings about the accomplishment of the conduct of omniscient wisdom and leads all beings to mastery—so as to bring the entire realm of sentient beings to the attainment of nirvāṇa; for the sake of their aspiration to establish the teaching, to ensure the non-interruption of the three paths, the three jewels, and the lineage of mantras; and through the outflow of the power of great compassion which illuminates the practice of mantra; with a mind that overcomes the forces of Māra, destroys great obstacles, and wards off wicked kings; that subdues one's own power, wards off the power of others, and effects paralyzing, casting down, and destroying; that teaches, dries up [afflictions], and satisfies; and that reveals the practice of one's own mantras to accomplish tasks swiftly—increasing longevity, health, and sovereignty—they abide in great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*), and great joy (*mahāmuditā*). For that reason and cause, he spoke with a mind free from all discursive thought (*tarka*) and non-discursive thought (*avitarka*). 1.74. {S17}

Thus these great mothers, with retinues of many hundreds of thousands of mothers, also remained in that great circle of the assembly, uttering the words, "Homage to the Buddha!"

In this way, from hundreds of thousands of various beings—human and non-human, sentient and non-sentient—down to the great Avīci hell and up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), the entire expanse of space became filled. Within the assembly of beings, there was no conflict among any living creature. Through the Buddha’s empowerment and the adornment of the Bodhisattva’s miraculous power, all beings beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, standing above their heads, as well as Mañjuśrī in the form of a youth.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed the entire world-system with his Buddha-eye, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Speak, speak, O Pure Being! Recite the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, which is the detailed exposition of the chapters on the meditative absorption for the definitive determination of the meaning of mantra practice, whenever you deem it to be the right time."

Then Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince, having been granted permission by the Blessed One Śākyamuni, entered the samādhi called "The Array and Ornament of the Nature of the Sky, the Hard and Continuous Array of the Vajra-Strike. Immediately upon Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince, entering that state, he empowered that abode of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa) so that it became composed of vajra, extending for many hundreds of thousands of yojanas. Therein, those many yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, maruts, and piśācas—in short, the entire realm of sentient beings—by the empowerment of the Bodhisattva, were established and seated within that celestial palace which resembled a vajra-jewel, remaining without harming one another.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having perceived that great assembly of the gathered multitude, addressed the wrathful king Yamāntaka.

O, O Great King of Wrath, you who have emerged from all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! Protect, protect this great assembly-circle (*maṇḍala*) and all sentient beings; bring them under your control! Subdue the wicked! Awaken the gentle! Inspire faith in those who are faithless! Until I have spoken this Bodhisattva-piṭaka concerning the practice of one’s own mantras—the extensive ritual procedures for the maṇḍala of mantra-practice—go outside and guard it! 1.109. {B22v}

Thus addressed, the Great Wrathful King, assuming a most hideous form, issued forth. Surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of wrathful deities, the wrathful king Yamāntaka went forth in all directions— east, west, north, south, above, below, and across— to protect and uphold the teaching for the sake of all sentient beings, letting out a terrible roar everywhere.

He remained standing. Then they all became gentle and well-disposed, and they did not transgress his command. And they heard this sound: "For whoever should violate this agreement, his head shall split into a hundred pieces like the cluster of an arjaka flower. And that was due to the empowerment of the Bodhisattva. 1.110.
Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, spoke these verses on the meaning of the dharma of his own mantra practice:

"The mantras of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with a single quality shall attain accomplishment. What is that one quality? Namely, perceiving all phenomena as being free from conceptual proliferation. (1.111)
The mantras of a bodhisattva established in two qualities shall attain accomplishment. Which two? Not abandoning the thought of awakening and equanimity toward all sentient beings. (1.112)

Through three qualities, they attain the fulfillment of the instruction on the purpose of their own mantra practice. Which three? Non-abandonment of all sentient beings by way of guarding the vow of bodhisattva ethical discipline, and non-abandonment of one’s own mantra. 1.113.

The mantras of a bodhisattva who has first generated the mind of awakening (prathamacittotpādika) will attain accomplishment when he is endowed with four qualities. What are these four? Not abandoning one’s own mantras; not interrupting the mantras of others; bringing forth loving-kindness toward all sentient beings; and having a mind cultivated by great compassion. The mantras of a bodhisattva who has first generated the mind of awakening will attain accomplishment when he is endowed with these four qualities. (1.114)

There are five qualities through which a bodhisattva’s inclusion within the scriptural collections (*piṭaka*) shall bring the accomplishment and fulfillment of the practice of mantras (*mantracaryā*). What are the five? Dwelling in secluded places; dwelling in remote forests; not harboring malice toward other beings; not looking toward worldly mantras; and being established in ethical discipline, learning, and proper conduct. These five qualities shall bring about the fulfillment of the attainment of the purpose of the practice of mantras. (1.115)

Six qualities lead to the fulfillment of the goal of mantra practice. What are the six? They are: not interrupting one’s faith in the Three Jewels; not interrupting one’s faith in the Bodhisattvas; delighting in both mundane and supramundane mantras; seeing the dharmadhātu free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*); not rejecting the Mahāyāna sūtras whose meaning is profound; having a mind free from weariness; seeking the practice of mantras; and not falling away from the side of virtue. These six qualities lead to the convergence of the accomplishment of the mantras of the *vidyā*-practice. 1.116.

Seven qualities lead to the entry into the mantra practice that is appropriate for the time of accomplishing knowledge (*vidyā*). What are the seven? 1. The profound method, which is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); 2. Devotion to the conduct of a bodhisattva through recitation, teaching, study, writing, and faith; 3. Through the observance of rules regarding time and place, the performance of *japa*, fire-offerings (*homa*), silence, austerity, and the endurance of non-haste, movement, mindfulness, wisdom, and fortitude; 4. Through the entry into the profound method of the Dharma of the Mahāyāna, which is the equipment (*saṃbhāra*) of a bodhisattva; 5. Through skill in the activities of accomplishing independent mantras, such as summoning and protection; 6. Through the cultivation of the perfections of great compassion, great loving-kindness, great equanimity, and great sympathetic joy; 7. [The realization of] the realm of sentient beings and the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).

1.118 Through the convergence into the suchness of the elements (*dhātutathatā*), through the thorough investigation of the omniscient gnosis that has two aspects, through not abandoning any sentient being, and through having no longing for the Lesser Vehicle—these seven factors lead to the fulfillment of the accomplishment of the *vidyā-mantra*. 1.117.

Eight qualities lead to the convergence upon the accomplishment of the purpose of the practice of knowledge-mantras. What are the eight? Faith in the visible and invisible fruits; freedom from doubt through curiosity and the desire to know; awakening—

The fruit of the clarity of one’s inner being (*sattvaprasāda*) through the miraculous transformations of supernatural power (*ṛddhivikurvaṇa*); through the unerring reception of mantras and reverence for the guru; through receiving the instructions of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the masters of one’s own mantra-tantras, and remaining free from deception; through the renunciation of all one’s possessions; through skillfully revealing the dreams that indicate whether a site is a place of accomplishment (*siddhakṣetra*) or not; through the removal of the stain of envy and the complete abandonment of sloth and torpor while initiating heroic effort (*vīryārambha*); through constantly offering oneself to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; in brief, through being armored with the great armor of insatiable roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*); through the desire to strike down all obstacles; through the embodiment of great renown by longing for the great enjoyments of approaching the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*); and through meeting with persons of great renown and never being separated from spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), such as the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī in his form as a youth—these eight qualities lead to the convergence of the goal and accomplishment of mantra practice. (1.118)

In brief, O noble ones, for one who is not separated from the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), who has faith in the Three Jewels, and who—even if they are of extremely poor conduct—is untiring in mind and constantly devoted, there is accomplishment arising from a mind produced by the outflow of the infinite and wondrous bodhisattva practices found in this section on my mantras. It should not be understood otherwise; having become free from conceptual construction, it should be practiced even for the sake of mere inquiry. Thus [ends the verse]. 1.119.
Then that entire assembly, empowered by the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas, uttered these words: || 1.120 ||

"Excellent, excellent, O Son of the Conqueror! This teaching of the Dharma, which follows the entry into the methods of the Dharma for the purposeful activity of the various mantra-practices, has been well-expounded for the benefit of all sentient beings. Oh, how well-spoken is this practice of mantra-conduct that accords with the diverse teachings of the Dharma, O Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta! For whoever, O Great King, shall recite, uphold, or attend to this chapter on the Assembly, or shall place it upon the back of an elephant at the head of an army, or shall worship it with various flowers, incense, perfumes, and ointments—we shall manifest our presence there. We shall bring their adversaries and enemies under control, and we shall cause the destruction of the enemy forces. Or, having had it written in a book, if one places it in their own home—whether it be a son of good family, a daughter of good family, a great king, a queen, a monk, a nun, a layman, or a laywoman—we shall provide them with great protection, great wealth, long life, health, and a constant increase in prosperity. || 1.121 ||
When this had been said, that entire assembly became silent.

Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, having surveyed the entire circle of the assembly, entered the samādhi called "The Surveying of the Entry into the Pledge of All Beings. As soon as Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, had entered that samādhi, a ray of light issued forth from the region of his navel. Accompanied by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rays, it illuminated the entire realm of all beings on every side, and then, having again illuminated that abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, it remained there.
Then Vajrapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Speak, speak, O Son of the Jina! Recite the detailed exposition of the mandala-chapter called 'The Entry into the Samaya of All Beings,' which is the accomplishment of conduct common to all beings, by entering which beings shall attain your collection of mantras and the mantra-attainments of both the mundane and the supramundane."

Thus addressed by Guhyakādhipati, the lord of yakṣas, Mañjuśrī, in his form as a youth, spoke the tantra of the Supreme Secret Maṇḍala. He manifested a display of supernatural power called "The Incitement of All Vidyās" and, raising his right hand, traced the circle of the assembly with the tip of his finger. From that fingertip, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of vidyādhara kings emerged. Having emerged, they illuminated the entire realm of Śuddhāvāsa with a great radiance and remained there. 2.3.

Then Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince, [taught] the heart-mantra of Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, which accomplishes all rites, is the sole hero, and is preeminent among all mantras for summoning, dismissal, pacifying, enriching, malevolent magic, invisibility, traveling through the sky, entering the subterranean realm (pātāla), walking on foot, attracting, causing enmity, and subjugation, as well as for all perfumes, garlands, ointments, lamps, and independent mantras. In brief, however it is employed, so it is accomplished. It is the three-syllabled one, of great power, the accomplisher of all aims, the Great King of Wrath. And what is that? 2.4.

Oṃ āḥ hrūṃ! This is the heart-mantra of the Great Wrathful One, effective for all rites, taught by the Great Being Mañjughoṣa for all maṇḍalas and all mantra practices, and it destroys all obstacles. (2.5)

Homage to you, [the essence] of all Buddhas! May the Blessed Buddhas, whoever they may be, residing in the world-systems of the ten directions, and the Bodhisattvas of infinite and boundless extent who possess great supernatural power, attend to me and empower this samaya.

Having spoken thus, he whirled that King of Wrath around and hurled him forth. As soon as the Great King of Wrath was hurled, he went throughout the entire world-system and, in a mere instant, having subdued those beings of evil intent who possessed great supernatural power, he brought them back. He caused them to enter that great maṇḍala of the assembly in the Śuddhāvāsa heaven; and having established them in their proper places, he became wreathed in flames on all sides and stood upon the heads of the wicked beings. 2.7.
Then Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince, again surveyed that circle of the assembly and said:

"Listen, all you beings! For this King of Wrath will bring about the subjugation of anyone who transgresses this, my own commitment (samaya). Since the paths of the secret mantras and the meaning of the words of the commitments of the Blessed Buddhas and of the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power are not to be transgressed, I shall speak of them by way of a concise exposition. Listen to it; attend to it well and thoroughly; I shall speak. 2.8.
Homage to all Buddhas! Oṃ ra ra, remember! O you whose teaching is unimpeded, who assume the form of a youth! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! 2.9
"O worthy ones, this is my root mantra named Noble Mañjuśrī. The mudrā known as the Great Mudrā of the Five Crests (pañcaśikhā-mahāmudrā) should be employed with this root mantra. (2.10)
The heart-mantra is effective for all rites. I shall proclaim the auspicious mantra that performs all actions:
Oṃ vākye da namaḥ. 2.11.
And here the mudrā is known as the Triśikhā, which increases all enjoyments. || 2.12 ||
And here there is a secondary heart-mantra: *hūṃ* at the end of the sentence. 2.13.
And here the mudrā is that known as the Triśikhā, which attracts all sentient beings. 2.14 And here is the supreme single-syllable heart mantra: Oṃ. 2.15
And here the mudrā is known as the Peacock Throne (mayūrāsana); it brings all beings under control and is the heart of all Buddhas. (2.16)
Furthermore, there is the eight-syllable mantra named Mahāvīra, which leads to the supreme good.

It is a great purifier, a severer of the path of the three realms of existence, a preventer of all miserable rebirths, a bringer of all peace, a performer of all rites, a secure refuge that leads to the attainment of nirvāṇa, and stands present before one’s very eyes like the Buddha himself. Mañjuśrī, this Bodhisattva has appeared in person for the sake of all beings in the form of a supreme secret mantra, which fulfills all hopes; by the mere recollection of it, one purifies even the five deeds of immediate retribution—how much more so through its recitation! And what is that? 2.17.
Oṃ āḥ dhīra hūṃ Khecara!

"O noble ones, this is that very thing: the eight-syllable Great Hero, the supreme secret heart, like Buddhahood itself, which has appeared for all purposes in brief. Its vast expansion of great qualities cannot be fully described—even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas—due to the limitlessness of its virtues. And here is the mudrā known as Mahāvīryā, which fulfills all hopes. (2.18)
And here is the invocation mantra:

Oṃ he he, O youth of universal form, who awakens all that is spoken by children! Come, Blessed One, come! You who hold the play-lotus of the youth, stand, stand in the center of the maṇḍala! Remember your pledge! O you of unimpeded command, hūṃ! Do not delay! Act! phaṭ svāhā! 2.19

This, O Blessed One, is the mantra for summoning Mañjuśrī, as well as for all sentient beings, all bodhisattvas, all pratyekabuddhas, noble śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, piśācas, rākṣasas, and all elemental spirits. || 2.20 ||

Having consecrated sandalwood water seven times with mantras, one should sprinkle it in the four directions—above, below, and across—in every direction. Then all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, Mañjuśrī himself along with his retinue, all mundane and supramundane mantras, all hosts of spirits, and all sentient beings shall arrive. 2.21.

Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! Oṃ dhura dhura dhura, you who dwell in incense, you who are the radiance of incense, hūṃ! Abide! Remember your pledge! Svāhā! This is the incense mantra. 2.22.

Having combined sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, one should offer incense to the Tathāgatas, all the Bodhisattvas, and all sentient beings. Those whose minds are refreshed by the incense become attracted. Regarding this, there is a mudrā known as the Lotus Garland (Padmamālā), which is auspicious and attracts all sentient beings. And these are the invocation mantras: this very same auspicious Lotus Garland mudrā [is used]. 2.23.

And for all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have arrived, as well as for all the sentient beings who have arrived, an offering of water (arghya) should be presented. Having stirred the water with camphor, sandalwood, and saffron, and having mixed it with jasmine, *navamālika*, *vārṣika*, *puṃnāga*, *nāgakesara*, *bakula*, *piṇḍī*, and *tagara*—or with any one of these flowers, or with fragrant flowers appropriate to the season—one should present the offering with this mantra. (2.24)

Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! It is as follows: He he, O Great Compassionate One, bearer of universal forms! Accept the offering, cause it to be accepted; remember the pledge! Stay, stay! Enter into the center of the maṇḍala, enter! O you who have compassion for all beings, seize, seize! Hūṃ! To the one who wanders through the sky, svāhā!
And here the mudrā is renowned as Pūrṇā, which is constant and follows all sentient beings. And here there is the mantra of fragrance: || 2.26 ||

Homage to all Buddhas! Homage to the Tathāgata Samantagandhāvabhāsaśrī! It is thus: *Gandhe gandhe gandhāḍhye gandhamanorame pratīccha pratīccheyaṃ gandhaṃ samatānucāriṇe svāhā!* (O fragrance, O fragrance, you who are rich in fragrance, you who are delightful with fragrance, accept, accept this fragrance for the one who dwells in equanimity, svāhā! 2.27.
And here there is a seal called Pallavā, which fulfills all hopes; and here there is also a flower-mantra. 2.28.
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! Homage to the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarāja! It is as follows: *Kusume kusume kusumāḍhye kusumapuravāsini kusumāvati svāhā!*
One should fumigate with that very incense mentioned previously, using that same incense-mantra.
(2.29) Having paid homage to all the Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous, I shall proclaim the bali-mantra spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One. (2.30)

Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas whose teachings are unimpeded! It is as follows: He he, Blessed One, Great Being, O Buddha-Avalokita, do not delay! Accept this offering! Grasp it, hūṃ hūṃ! O All-Pervading One, ra ra ṭa ṭa phaṭ svāhā!

With this [mantra], one should cause the food offering (nivedya) and the bali for all spirits (sarvabhautika) to be presented; and in this regard, there is the Śakti mudrā, which wards off all evil beings.

Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded and who destroy all darkness and gloom. Homage to the Tathāgata Samantajyotirgandhāvabhāsaśrī. It is as follows: He he, Blessed One, whose body is adorned with hundreds of thousands of light rays! Manifest, manifest! O you whose form is illuminated by the universal blaze of the great Bodhisattvas! Leap, leap! Behold, behold all sentient beings! Svāhā!
The mantra of the lamp: one should cause the lamp to be offered with this. The mudrā is named Vikāsinī, the beholder of all sentient beings. (2.34)
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! It is as follows: jvala jvala jvālaya jvālaya | hūṃ | vibodhaka harikṛṣṇapiṅgala svāhā! || 2.35 ||

These are the mantras for the fire-ritual. And in this regard, there is a mudrā known as the "Casket" (sampuṭā), renowned in the world, which illuminates all sentient beings; it was spoken of old by the supreme sages for the sake of the wise Bodhisattva. (2.36)
Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, addressed the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi:
"O Lord of the Guhyakas, these mantra-words are accompanied by secrets and are supremely secret."
Your son, renowned in his lineage, who is terrible and most cruel,
is indeed the one [to be invoked] among all mantras being accomplished by the wise.
This vidyā shall now be fully proclaimed for the purpose of destroying that which is known as the *mūrdhaṭaka*, belonging to both the Vajra and Lotus families. (2.39) {S29} ap2.40

Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas whose teachings are unimpeded! Oṃ kara kara! Accomplish, accomplish my purpose! Shatter, shatter all obstacles! Burn, burn all Vajra Vināyakas! O Mūrdhaṭaka, O bringer of the end of life, O you of great and hideous form! Cook, cook all the wicked! O Mahāgaṇapati, bringer of the end of life! Bind, bind all seizing spirits! O six-faced one, six-armed one, six-legged one! Bring Rudra here! Bring Viṣṇu here! Bring the gods beginning with Brahmā here! Do not delay, do not delay! Protect, protect! Cause [them] to enter the center of the maṇḍala! Remember the pledge! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!

O Lord of the Guhyakas, this is that most secret Mañjuśrī of great heroism, the great wrathful king named Ṣaṇmukha, the destroyer of all obstacles. Merely by reciting this, even bodhisattvas established on the ten stages flee; how much more so, then, malevolent obstacles? Merely by reciting this, a great protection is established. And here there is a mudrā known as the "Great Spear," which destroys all obstacles. This is the heart-mantra of this very wrathful king. 2.41.
Oṃ hrīṃḥ jñīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ! Destroy all enemies, paralyze them, phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!

By means of this mantra, one causes all enemies to be seized by a great piercing disease (*mahāśūlaroga*) or by a quartan fever (*cāturthaka*). Through constant recitation, this continues until they take pleasure [in their suffering] or do not attain a state of friendliness (*maitratā*). If, however, they attain a mind of compassion (*karuṇācitta*), there shall be no release at the end of the recitation; they will die. This is to be performed against those who harm the Three Jewels (*ratnatraya*) and not against others who possess a gentle mind. 2.42.
One should employ the mudrā of the great trident. And here is the upahṛdaya mantra:
Oṃ hrīṃḥ kālarūpa huṃ khaṃ svāhā. 2.43.

The mudrā of the great trident alone should be employed; it causes all wicked beings to do whatever one desires. This is the supreme heart-mantra, empowered by all the Buddhas, known as the "Single Syllable. 2.44.
Hūṃ.

This is the performer of all rites. Only the Great Trident mudrā should be employed; it wards off all misfortunes and brings all spirits under control. In brief, this King of Wrath (Krodharāja) is to be applied in all rites. Recitation performed in the center of the maṇḍala is especially distinguished at the time of attaining accomplishment. 2.45.

The dismissal mantras are as follows: *Namaḥ sarvabuddhānām apratihataśāsanānām* | *Tadyathā* | *Jaya jaya sujaya mahākāruṇika viśvarūpiṇe* | *Gaccha gaccha svabhavanam* | *Sarvabuddhāṃś ca visarjaya saparivārān svabhavanaṃ cānupraveśaya* | *Samayam anusmara* | *Sarvārthāś ca me siddhyantu mantrapadāḥ* | *Manorathaṃ ca me paripūraya svāhā* || 2.46 ||

This is the mantra for dismissal (visarjana), which should be employed in all rites. The mudrā is renowned as the Bhadrapīṭha; one should offer the seat with this [mantra]. Dismissal is performed by reciting it seven times mentally. 2.47.
Apastamba Dharmasūtra 2.54,

From all mundane and supramundane maṇḍalas and from all mantras, the accomplishment of mantras (*mantrasiddhi*) arises; it should be applied during the observances of the pledges (*samaya*), recitation, and the fixed times. Thus [ends section] 2.48.

{S30} Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, once again gazed upon that abode of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsabhavana*) and that great assembly circle (*parṣanmaṇḍala*), and spoke this extensive chapter on the mantras and the host of vidyās belonging to himself. 2.49.
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! Oṃ riṭi svāhā!
This is the follower of Mañjuśrī, the vidyā named Keśinī, effective for all rites; it should be employed with the five-crested great mudrā in all operations concerning poisons. 2.50
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded. Oṃ niṭi.
This knowledge-mantra named Upakeśinī accomplishes all rites; one should employ it with the Vikāsinī mudrā in all rituals concerning planetary spirits.
Homage to all Buddhas of unimpeded movement! Oṃ niḥ!
This auspicious vidyā named Nalinī accomplishes all rites;
when joined with the Bhadrapīṭha mudrā, it will certainly summon a yakṣiṇī.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous; joined with the power of the mudrā, she is the slayer of all ḍākinīs.
Oṃ jñaiḥ svāhā. || 2.53 ||
This knowledge-mantra named Kapālinī was spoken by Mañjughoṣa; it is praised by all the Buddhas everywhere and possesses a divine form.
Homage to all Buddhas who move with unimpeded gait. It is as follows: Oṃ varade svāhā!
One whose nature is auspicious should join the mudrā with the three-pronged [gesture]; the goddess, who assumes many forms, swiftly accomplishes the attainment of enjoyments. 2.55.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous!
Oṃ bhūri svāhā!
This mudrā, when joined with the trident, destroys all fevers. Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous! Oṃ ture svāhā!
The lore named Tārāvatī is praised for all ritual actions; when joined with the spear-staff mudrā, it is the destroyer of obstacles.
Ap 2.58: Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous!
Tadyathā: Oṃ vilokini svāhā!
The Vidyā named Lokavatī brings all the worlds under her control;
when employed with the facial mudrā, she bestows all happiness. (2.58)
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous!
It is as follows: Oṃ viśve viśvasambhave viśvarūpiṇi kaha kaha āviśāviśa | remember the pledge (samaya)! Ru ru tiṣṭha svāhā! || 2.59 ||

This knowledge, of great power, has been revealed by the leaders of the world; joined with the fang-seal (*daṃṣṭramudrā*), it is auspicious, capable of entering all beings as a weapon, a granter of boons to all spirits, and is proclaimed as "Viśvā" (the All). 2.60.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous. It is as follows: Oṃ śvete śrīvapuḥ svāhā.

When placed with the peacock-posture mudrā, she performs all rites; renowned as Mahāśvetā, she possesses an inconceivable and wondrous form. She bestows good fortune upon the world and brings men and women under her control. (2.62)
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous!
It is as follows: Oṃ khi khiri khi riri bhaṅguri, paralyze all enemies, crush them, delude them, bring them under control, svāhā!
This knowledge is proclaimed as the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) and the Yoginī; when joined with the mouth-seal (vaktramudrā), it pacifies even malevolent beings.
Ap 2.65: Homage to all Buddhas who move with unimpeded gait. It is as follows: Oṃ Śrīḥ. 2.65.
This knowledge, Mahālakṣmī, was taught by the Lords of the World;
when joined with the Sampuṭa mudrā, it bestows great sovereignty. (2.66)
Ap 2.67: Homage to all the Buddhas, who bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings!
It is as follows: Oṃ, O unconquered one, you who possess the form of a youth! Come! Approach! Accomplish my task! Svāhā! Ap 2.68:
She is renowned as Ajitā (the Unconquered), a maiden born from the nectar of immortality.
When joined with the full mudrā, she wards off all enemies. || 2.68 ||
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous!
It is as follows: Oṃ jaye svāhā! Vijaye svāhā! Ajite svāhā! Aparājite svāhā! 2.69
Known as the Four Sisters, they are attendants of the Bodhisattva; performing acts of grace for sentient beings, they wander throughout the entire earth.
Their brother, known as Tumburu, is their attendant. Mounted upon a boat, they dwell within the waters; when applied with the Fist-seal (muṣṭimudrā), they fulfill all desires.
Homage to all the Buddhas, the sovereign lords of the world.

Namely: Oṃ, Kumāra, Mahākumāra, play, play! Six-faced one, authorized by the Bodhisattva, peacock-throned, hand raised with a spear, red-limbed, fond of red perfumes and unguents, kha kha, eat, eat, eat, eat, hūṃ! Dance, dance! Your form is worshipped with red flowers; remember the pledge! Wander, wander, cause to wander, cause to wander, cause to wander! Move quickly, move quickly, do not delay! Accomplish all my tasks, accomplish them! To you who assume manifold forms, stay, stay, hūṃ! Authorized by all the Buddhas, svāhā!
When these words were spoken by the Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa, the Protector, the entire earth trembled in six ways on all sides.
For the benefit of all beings, to ward off wicked beings, the terrible son of Maheśvara has come here for the sake of those to be trained.
Having clearly identified Skanda and Aṅgāraka by their planetary signs, I then spoke with sweet words, my mind filled with compassion.
This great-souled Bodhisattva, acting for the benefit of the ignorant, wandered everywhere throughout the world, engaged in the conduct of a being.

When joined with the staff of the power of the mudrā of that Great-Souled One, he causes even those beginning with Brahmā to turn back; how much more so the fruit of human [attainment]? (2.77) In brief, his entire youthful armor is ready at dawn. This mantra of Kārttikeya and Mañjuśrī has been proclaimed. (2.78)
A Bodhisattva has come here for the sake of wishing to favor sentient beings; the three-syllable heart-essence of this mantra has been proclaimed. (2.79)
Intent on attracting enjoyments for the sake of the welfare of all beings,
when applied with the power-staff of the mudrā, it accomplishes all rites.
Oṃ hūṃ jaḥ.
This mantra, in brief, shall produce human results.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms illuminate everywhere.
Oṃ vikṛtagraha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! || 2.82 ||

And its subsidiary heart-mantra (upahṛdaya), when joined with the power of the mudrā, likewise causes the spirits, along with the grahas and the mātṛs, to turn back. When applied among all the sealed mudrās, it becomes effective; it terrifies the spirits and releases those possessed by evil ones.

This is the youth named Kārttikeyamañjuśrī, a follower of the youthful Mañjuśrī, who performs all rites. By mere recitation alone, he accomplishes all activities; he terrifies all spirits, draws them forth, brings them under control, withers them, and slays them. Whatever the vidyādhara desires, he brings all that to fulfillment. 2.85.
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! It is as follows: Oṃ, Brahmā, sublime Brahmā, in the splendor of Brahmā, bring peace, svāhā!
This mantra, Mahābrahmā, was uttered by the Bodhisattva;
at that very moment, all beings attained a cooling peace.
When joined with the five-crested mudrā, it quickly brings about well-being; it is recited in all rites of sorcery within the Atharvaveda.
Thus has his ritual procedure been briefly stated in summary. (2.88)
Homage to all Buddhas, whose teachings are unimpeded.
It is as follows: Oṃ! O you who have Garuḍa as your vehicle, O wielder of the discus, four-armed one, huṃ huṃ! Remember your pledge! The Bodhisattva commands: svāhā!
Commanded by Mañjughoṣa, he swiftly accomplishes the welfare [of beings] and brings auspiciousness. He terrifies the spirits of embodied beings in the form of Viṣṇu.
When joined with the three-crested mudrā, it is firm and swiftly accomplishes one's aims.
These extensive ritual manuals (kalpa) taught in the Vaiṣṇava tantras were spoken by Mañjughoṣa for the sake of those beings who are to be disciplined through skillful means.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose teachings are unimpeded.
Namely: Oṃ, Mahāmaheśvara, Lord of Beings, Bull-bannered One, wearer of a crown of long matted locks, whose form is grey with white ashes, hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! The Bodhisattva commands: svāhā! 2.92
This mantra has been proclaimed by me out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings; when joined with the trident mudrā, it is the destroyer of all malevolent spirits.

94. Regarding that ancient kalpa which was previously recounted by me, beings dwelling upon the surface of the earth shall call it "Śaiva. Various expansions of qualities have been declared by me in the Śaiva Tantra.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose teachings are unimpeded.
It is as follows: Oṃ śakuna mahāśakuna, you whose wings are spread like a lotus, destroyer of all serpents, kha kha khāhi khāhi! Remember your pledge! Hūṃ! Stay! The Bodhisattva commands: Svāhā!
This mantra is of great power and is renowned as that of Vainateya.
It is the supreme subduer of the difficult-to-tame and the destroyer of the venom of serpents.
Joined with Mahāmudrā, he destroys most terrible misfortunes; he destroys poisons, both stationary and mobile, without a doubt. (2.97)
By the command of the Bodhisattva, that king of birds of great splendor wandered about in the form of a garuḍa to discipline sentient beings through skillful means.
99. As many extensive ritual manuals as have been taught in the *Gāruḍa* tantra, all of them have been proclaimed by me alone for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings.
Garuḍa, who is indeed a bodhisattva, has come here for the purpose of Vainateya.
One hundred [beings] in the form of birds wandered about for the sake of destroying the poison of those possessed by it.
(2.100) As many worldly mantras as there are, they have all been proclaimed in this ritual manual (kalpa). Indeed, for the sake of training sentient beings, I wander in such and such ways. (2.101)
Furthermore, those mantras belonging to the Tathāgata family, as well as those of the Vajra and Lotus families, have already been taught previously within this extensive ritual manual.
Just as a nurse diligently caresses a child in many ways,
so do I move among those of childish intellect in the form of a mantra.
What was previously taught by those possessing the ten powers has now been spoken by me;
the youth of great splendor has also declared the entire meaning of the mantras and tantras. 104.104.
And those songs which were sung by the supreme Jinas, the sons of the Ten-Powered One— those were sung by Mañjusvara, whose form is inconceivable and wondrous.

Then, Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, having surveyed the entire abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods and that great circle of the assembly, entered the meditative absorption named "The Exhortation of All Samayas. Established in this absorption, with a mind intent on the conduct that brings about the liberation of all sentient beings without exception, he caused all sentient beings to become established therein.

Immediately upon Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta’s entry into meditative absorption, the entire abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods became a maṇḍala adorned with a variegated array of precious jewels and gems, a display of the inconceivable and marvelous miraculous transformations of a bodhisattva. Even for bodhisattvas who have entered the conduct of all pratyekabuddhas and noble śrāvakas, or even for those lords established on the ten stages (bhūmis), it is impossible to draw or have drawn that maṇḍala; what need is there to mention ordinary beings?

Then, having seen Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta abiding in that divine state of the accomplishment and maintenance of the Noble Maṇḍala Samaya—Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta being seen by all the Blessed Buddhas, all the Pratyekabuddhas, all the Noble Śrāvakas, all the Bodhisattvas established on the ten stages who have attained the consecration of the crown prince, those engaged in the conduct, and all beings, both with outflows and without outflows—of Mañjuśrī...

Through the empowerment of the Youthful (Kumārabhūta), they perceived themselves as having entered a maṇḍala that was inconceivable, produced from the flow of the conduct of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and arisen from the mind through a particular meditative concentration. It is not possible for ordinary beings to take even that as an object of their minds, let alone to draw it or have it drawn. 2.108. {V25}

Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, addressed those beings who had entered the assembly of the great maṇḍala circle: "Listen, sirs! This commitment (samaya) of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas is not to be transgressed;
how much less so for other beings, whether noble or ignoble? (2.109)

Then Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince, addressed Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of the Guhyakas: "O Son of the Conqueror, you have explained the supramundane ritual procedure arising from the mind. Now I shall speak of the mundane [procedure] for those Tathāgatas who have entered final nirvāṇa, by entering which all mantras—both worldly and transcendent—shall attain accomplishment."
Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Guhyakas, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Speak, speak, O Son of the Conqueror! Speak now, as you deem it the right time."
When the unsurpassed Lord of the World, the Lion of the Śākyas, has entered final nirvāṇa,
your maṇḍala shall exist upon the earth for the sake of sentient beings, just like Buddhahood itself.

For in this world, mantras attain success merely upon being seen; however, they fail when practiced by one who lacks knowledge, is devoid of the prescribed rite, or is unauthorized by the covenant. 2.113
Even for a high-souled Brahmin, mantras will not attain success if he is uninitiated in this tantra and has not perceived the rules proclaimed therein. 2.114
Mantras do not attain success even with repeated effort if they are devoid of the application of the *samaya* rules, even for Śakra himself despite his exertion. (2.115)

They do not fail to attain the accomplishment of mantras, how much less so on the earth among human beings? (116) For those who know the reality of the *samaya* and the scriptures, and who are engaged in the rites of conduct and the means of attainment (*sādhana*), the mantras—both noble and worldly—are accomplished as soon as they are recited. (2.116)
Having entered the second maṇḍala of Mañjughoṣa, which performs all rites, his accomplishment of mantra is certain, just as in the teaching of the Youthful One. 2.117
Aphorisms 2.118,
Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Guhyakas, entreated that Great Being: "O, O Great Bodhisattva, for the sake of sentient beings, please explain the ritual procedure for the maṇḍala in brief."
Thus addressed by the Lord of the Guhyakas, Mañjuśrī, in his youthful form, spoke the ritual procedure for the maṇḍala for the benefit of all sentient beings.

First of all, during the fortnight of the Pratihāraka, in the months of Caitra or Vaiśākha, on an auspicious day of the bright fortnight observed by pure planets and joined with a favorable lunar mansion—either on the first day of the bright fortnight or on the full moon, or at another time excluding the rainy months—one should occupy the ground in the forenoon. || 2.120 ||

Having resorted to a great city, or where he himself may dwell, the Maṇḍalācārya should resort to a river that flows into the ocean, or to a place near the shore of the ocean; in the northeastern direction of the great city, neither too far nor too near, the Maṇḍalācārya should construct a leaf-hut in a secluded spot and reside there for seven days or for a fortnight for the sake of sentient beings. 2.121.

In that place, one should prepare a very clean area of ground, square on all sides, measuring sixteen cubits or twelve cubits, free from stones, gravel, ash, charcoal, husks, potsherds, and bones— a very clean and well-prepared plot of earth.

Then, that area of ground should be square on all sides, measuring sixteen cubits, twelve cubits, or eight cubits. Among these, the sixteen-cubit [mandala] is the superior, the twelve-cubit is the middling, and the eight-cubit is the inferior. This threefold mandala has been proclaimed by the All-Seeing Ones. For one desiring sovereignty, the superior is used; the middling increases enjoyments; and the inferior, which is merely the pledge (*samaya*), performs all rites and is auspicious. (2.123)

Then one should draw a mandala that is desired by the mind. There, one should dig that spot of earth to a depth of two cubits. If stones, charcoal, ashes, bones, hair, or various kinds of living creatures are seen there, one should dig another spot of earth. It should be free from defects and free from disturbances. If not, then on a mountain peak, a riverbank, the shore of the ocean, or a great heap of sand on the bank of a large river, one should draw it after having prepared it with great effort—having thoroughly inspected it, made it very clean, and rendered it free of living beings. (2.124)
With water free of living organisms,
scented with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, and consecrated one thousand times.
One should sprinkle the area of ground in the four directions; thus one should cast [the water] everywhere—above, below, across, and in the intermediate directions. 2.122.
Or, with the wrathful king Yamāntaka mixed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), joined with the great mudrā of eight or five locks of hair,
that aforementioned spot of earth should again be sprinkled with water free from living organisms.

It should be filled with earth from a riverbank that has been mixed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), or with pure earth from an anthill, or with earth from a place where there are no living creatures. Having filled it, one should have it well-compacted, level, and made into a threefold mandala of the desired dimensions on all sides. In the four directions, one should drive in four stakes of *khadira* wood using the King of Wrath (*krodharāja*) mantra itself.
Apastamba Dharmasūtra 2.12.8,

Having consecrated it seven times, one should encircle that mandala on all sides in a square shape with a five-colored thread that has been consecrated seven times with the heart-mantra of the Wrathful One. || 2.125 ||

In this manner, one should cause it to be made square in shape both in the middle space and within. The Maṇḍala Master, stationed in the middle space, should recite the root mantra of the Vidyā eight thousand times. Having bound the Great Mudrā of the Five Crests (*pañcaśikhā*), protection for his companions and protection for himself must be performed with the root mantra. While reciting, he should go outside; having circumambulated that maṇḍala, facing east and seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, he should keep all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in mind. He should surround that maṇḍala on all sides with a square enclosure. And right there, having kept two men who have fasted for one night outside the gate, he should dismiss them. (2.126)

In that regard, the mandala master—who has completed the preliminary practices (*puraścaraṇa*), is skilled in the independent mantras, is devoted to the Mahāyāna for the sake of sentient beings through skillful means, has fasted for one night, and is accompanied by good companions—should, according to the ritual procedure seen in the treatises, place that powder in the center of the mandala. This powder should consist of five colors, be fine and radiant, well-prepared, and have been consecrated with the six-syllable mantra and further empowered with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). || 2.127 ||

Outside, one should prepare a section of ground adorned with four archways decorated with raised banners and flags, with clusters of fruit-laden bunches suspended from plantain pillars, and resounding with the sounds of beaten kettledrums, clay drums, conchs, and lutes; while reciting Mahāyāna sūtras suitable for the fourfold assembly to hear the Dharma, such as follows: 2.128.
With auspicious sounds in the four directions toward him.

One should have the Blessed Prajñāpāramitā recited in the southern direction; the Āryacandrapradīpasamādhi in the western direction; the Āryagaṇḍavyūha in the northern direction; and the Āryasuvarṇaprabhāsottamasūtra in the eastern direction. Thus, one should request persons who are Dharma-preachers and have studied these four sūtras to listen to the Dharma, as there may be a lack of physical books. Then, the Maṇḍala Master, having risen, should scatter that entire maṇḍala with white fragrant flowers mixed with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron while reciting the root mantra. Having scattered them, he should go outside. 2.129.

After seven days, one should admit two or three highly skilled painters who have subsisted on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), have generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and have observed the *upoṣadha* fast. Having bound their topknots with the root mantra itself, they should then receive gold, silver, and various jewels, as well as five kinds of diverse, brilliant, beautiful, and fine powders; and having been provided with great wealth by wealthy beings and righteous great kings, they should cause [the painting] to be drawn—[a work] directed toward awakening, leading to awakening, and certain [of success]. (2.130) {V27}

If even by the mere sight of the maṇḍala [such results are attained], how much more so when accomplishing the mantra! When the Bull of the Śākyas has passed into nirvāṇa, for beings of little merit, from where could such enjoyments come? Nevertheless, this ritual procedure is being described. (2.131)
Having seen the impoverished people, Mañjughoṣa, of great splendor,
[acted].
One should proclaim, in brief, the summary of the ritual procedure for the mandala.
One should color it with fine powders of śāli rice, brilliant with five colors: white, yellow, red, black, and green. (2.133)

The Maṇḍala Master himself should take the powder previously prepared, bind the five-crested Mahāmudrā, and consecrate that powder while reciting the root mantra. Meanwhile, another master—the practitioner—should construct a fire-pit outside the maṇḍala in the south-eastern direction according to the prescribed ritual; it should measure two cubits in height and one cubit in depth, and be shaped like the pericarp of a lotus on all sides. (2.134)

Outside, having kindled a fire with fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood shaped like lotus buds, one should summon [the deity] by forming the *mudrāmuṣṭi* while holding fresh fuel-sticks of *śrīphala* wood—one *vitasti* in length, smeared with curd, honey, and ghee—reciting either the root mantra or the six-syllable heart mantra. Having summoned [the deity], one should again offer oblations one hundred and eight times with the aforementioned single-syllable root mantra-heart.

Then, the Maṇḍala Master, having bound the uṣṇīṣa and prepared himself, should employ highly skilled painters. Then, the Maṇḍala Master, keeping the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in mind, burning incense with the previously mentioned incense-mantra, joining his palms in *añjali*, bowing to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and paying homage to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, should take the powder and draw the forms. Each form must be completed by the painters. By this procedure, first of all, one should paint the Blessed Buddha Śākyamuni, endowed with the excellence of all aspects, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne in the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, teaching the Dharma. Once it has been painted, the assistant of the Maṇḍala Master, having performed the self-protection rite with the root mantra, should offer a *bali* to all the elemental spirits. He should scatter it in the four directions, above, below, and outside the maṇḍala. (2.136)

Then, having bathed and gone near the fire-pit, being pure, clothed in clean garments, and having performed the rites of protection, one should offer eight thousand oblations of ghee mixed with saffron using the root mantra. Thereafter, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, one should remain right there while performing the recitation (*jāpa*).

Having consecrated eight hundred white mustard seeds with the mantra of Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, one should place them in a covered vessel made of two earthenware bowls (*śarāva*). Upon seeing any kind of obstacle—whether it be a storm of wind and rain accompanied by various distorted and terrifying forms and sounds, or any other hindrance—one should, while filled with wrath, offer seven oblations of the mustard seeds into the fire. Thereby, the obstacles will perish. Or, if there are human obstacles, five oblations should be offered; [the obstructors] will be paralyzed, rendered powerless, or the men will die. Or they will be seized by non-human beings at that very instant. Of this there is no doubt whatsoever. Even Śakra would quickly die, let alone humans with evil intent or other obstacles; terrified by the fear of the wrathful Yamāntaka, they flee in all directions, crying out, "This way! This way! (2.138).
Apastamba Dharmasūtra 2.13.7,
