Then the assistant (anusādhaka), seated upon a bundle of kuśa grass at that very spot, should remain performing the recitation (jāpa) of Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath. Then, on the right side of the image of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Maṇḍala Master should depict two Pratyekabuddhas seated upon lotus thrones in the full-lotus posture (paryaṅka). Below them, two Great Śrāvakas should be depicted listening to the Dharma. 2.139.

To their right also is the Blessed One Āryāvalokiteśvara, adorned with all ornaments, white as an autumn reed, seated upon a lotus throne, holding a lotus with his left hand and displaying the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) with his right hand. To his right is the Blessed Lady Pāṇḍaravāsinī, holding a lotus in her hand, bowing to the Blessed Śākyamuni with her right hand, seated upon a lotus throne, wearing a crown of matted hair, clothed in white silk garments, with a silken upper robe, and marked with three tufts of black ash. In this same manner, Tārā and Bhṛkuṭī are to be depicted, well-established in their respective seats and modes of deportment. Above them, the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā, Tathāgatalocanā, and the Uṣṇīṣarāja are to be depicted. 2.140.

In this manner, sixteen bodhisattvas are to be depicted. They are as follows: Samantabhadra, Kṣitigarbha, Gaganagañja, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Apāyajaha, Maitreya with a yak-tail whisk in his hand, Vimalamati who gazes at the Blessed Buddha, Vimalaketu, Sudhana, Candraprabha, Vimalakīrti, Sarvavyādhicikitsaka, Sarvadharmīśvararāja, Lokagati, Mahāmati, and Patidhara. These sixteen great bodhisattvas are to be painted with serene forms, adorned with all ornaments. (2.141)

The principal Knowledge-King and Knowledge-Queen, as well as all others in the Lotus Family, should be drawn in their respective positions according to tradition, according to the manuals, and according to the ritual hand-gestures (mudrās). Finally, in that location, one should prepare a square-shaped area strewn with lotus flowers, [with the thought]: "May those deities of the knowledge-mantras who have been recollected abide in this place. (2.142)

Thus, on the right side of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, two Pratyekabuddhas, Gandhamādana and Upāriṣṭa, are to be depicted. In this manner, the mandala should be made facing east, with an entrance door on every side. On the left side of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, two other Pratyekabuddhas, Candana and Siddha, are to be painted. Below them, two great Śrāvakas, Mahākāśyapa and Mahākātyāyana, are to be depicted. 2.143.

To their left is the noble Vajrapāṇi, with the dark luster of a blue water-lily, of pleasing form, adorned with all ornaments; his right hand holds a yak-tail whisk (*cāmara*), and his left hand, in the form of a wrathful deity, forms the vajra-fist (*vajramuṣṭi*). Vajrāṅkuśī, Vajraśṛṅkhalā, Subāhu, and Vajrasenā—these should be depicted according to their recollection, with their respective attire, emblems, positions, seats, and the forms, seals (*mudrā*), and so forth of all the vidyārājas, vidyārājñīs, and their retinues. To their left as well, one should draw a square shape containing the double-vajra seal (*ubhayavajramudrā*). Having drawn it, one should say: "In whatever place the hosts of vidyās were not remembered, may they abide in this place. (2.144)
Apastamba Dharmasūtra 2.14.7,
Ap2.150: One should not eat food that has been brought by night from a house where a corpse is present.

Above them, the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) and the Blessed Lady Māmakī are to be depicted, adorned with all ornaments and possessing serene forms. Above them as well, the eight Uṣṇīṣa Kings are to be depicted, surrounded by garlands of flames on all sides. Having formed their respective mudrās, they are to be painted in the form of great wheel-turning kings (mahārājacakravartin), golden-colored, with very serene faculties, adorned with all ornaments, and gazing slightly toward the image of the Tathāgata. They are as follows: Cakravarty-uṣṇīṣa, Abhyudgatoṣṇīṣa, Sitātapatra, Jayoṣṇīṣa, Kamaloṣṇīṣa, Vijayoṣṇīṣa, Tejorāśi, and Unnatoṣṇīṣa. || 2.145 ||

These eight Uṣṇīṣa kings are to be painted to the left of the Pratyekabuddhas. At the door, two Bodhisattvas are to be depicted. To the right of the entrance is the one named Lokātikrāntagāmī, wearing a crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmakuṭa*), with a serene form; holding a rosary in his right hand and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his left, he faces the door with a slightly frowning face. To the left of the entrance, the Great Bodhisattva named Ajitañjaya is to be painted; with a gracious form, wearing a crown of matted hair, his left hands resting upon a staff and a water-pot, holding a rosary in his right hand, making the gesture of granting boons (*varadamudrā*), and facing the door with a slightly frowning face. || 2.146 ||

Beneath the lion throne is the Wheel of Dharma, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides. Beneath that as well is a jeweled celestial palace. Seated there is the Blessed One, the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, in the form of a youth; he has the appearance of a youth, his form is fair as saffron, his body is serene, and he is of beautiful countenance with a slightly smiling face. His left hand holds a blue lotus, and his right hand, holding a *śrīphala* fruit, is in the gesture of granting boons (*varada*).

Adorned with all the ornaments of a youth, beautified by five locks of hair, wearing a pearl necklace as a sacred thread, with a silken cloth as an upper garment and dressed in fine silk, he is radiant on all sides and surrounded by a garland of flames everywhere. Seated upon a lotus throne, with his gaze fixed upon the wrathful king Yamāntaka and facing the entrance for entry into the maṇḍala, he, who is beautiful to behold, should be painted everywhere. 2.148. {S42}

On its right side, beneath the lotus, the wrathful king Yamāntaka is to be depicted. Having a greatly distorted form and surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, he is to be painted everywhere as receiving the command and casting his gaze toward the Great Bodhisattva. On the left side, beneath the lotus, five bodhisattvas in the form of sons of gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm are to be depicted. They are as follows: Sunirmala, Sudānta, Suśuddha, Tamodghātana, and Samantāvaloka. All of them are to be depicted as seated upon the grounds of the Śuddhāvāsa abode, appearing like surfaces of rock blazing with many jewels, variegated with flames on all sides, strewn with flowers, and possessing beautiful forms. 2.149.

Outside, on all sides, an inner maṇḍala should be fashioned, square in shape with four archways in the four directions, blazing with various five-colored hues, and bound by lines possessing the quality of excellent radiance. In the eastern direction, above the Blessed One Śākyamuni, in the center among the lines, a small-sized image of the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarājendra should be fashioned, seated upon a lotus throne, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, with his hand in the gesture of granting boons, and seated in the cross-legged posture.
Aphorisms 2.151,
Apastamba Dharmasūtra 2.15.4,

To his right, the *uṣṇīṣacakravartin* mudrā should be drawn; to the left, the *tejorāśi* mudrā should be drawn. Above Tathāgatalocanā, the *prajñāpāramitā* mudrā should be drawn. Above the Blessed One, the noble Avalokiteśvara, and to the right of the *prajñāpāramitā* mudrā, the Blessed One Amitābha should be depicted in the form of a Tathāgata, with his hand in the gesture of granting boons (*varapradāna*), seated upon a lotus throne, and surrounded by a halo of flames on all sides. 2.151.

To the right of that as well, the mudrās of the bowl and the robe should be made. Likewise, in sequence, at the entrance, a lotus mudrā should be made. To the left of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarāja, the uṣṇīṣa-tejorāśi mudrā should be drawn, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides. To his left, the Tathāgata Ratnaketu should be depicted, seated upon a mountain of jewels, teaching the Dharma, with various flames of blue beryl, emerald, and ruby issuing forth from him, and he should be painted with light radiating everywhere in all directions. 2.152.

To its left, the Jayoṣṇīṣa mudrā, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, should be depicted. To its left, the Dharmacakra mudrā, possessing flames on all sides, should be depicted. To its left, the mudrās of the mendicant’s staff (*khakharaka*), water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), rosary (*akṣasūtra*), and the auspicious seat (*bhadrapīṭha*) should be depicted. In order, at the position of the door, the earth-vajra (*bhūvajra*) with three prongs on both sides, possessing flames on all sides, should be depicted. Below the Blessed Mañjuśrī, the great mudrā named Pañcaśikhā and the Utpala mudrā should be depicted; these two, possessing flames on all sides, are joined together. 2.153.

The drawing should have the form of a universal mandala. From the entrance, facing inward, the [central figure] should be made facing east. In all cases, the outer mandala is to be drawn outside the inner mandala; it is brilliant with five-colored pigments, variegated and beautiful to behold, divided into four corners, having the form of four archways (toraṇas), and measuring two cubits in each of the four directions. || 2.154 ||

In the eastern direction, Mahābrahmā should be depicted with four faces, dressed in white garments and wearing a white upper robe; he has a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), is golden-colored, wears a crown of matted hair, and holds a staff and water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his left hand. To his right, the divine son Ābhāsvara is to be portrayed: golden-colored, his form absorbed in meditation, dressed in silk garments with a silk upper robe, with a very serene countenance, wearing a crown of matted hair and a white sacred thread, seated in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*), and granting a boon with his right hand. 2.155.

To his right, the Akaniṣṭha son of the gods should be depicted, adorned with all ornaments, of serene form, his mind absorbed in meditation, dressed in silk garments, with a silken upper robe, seated in the paryañka posture, granting the boon of charity with his right hand, and wearing a white sacred thread (yajñopavīta). In this same sequence, the sons of the gods beginning with Santuṣita, Sunirmita, Paranirmita, Suyāma, and Śakra should be painted according to their respective order and positions. Below Śakra, the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods—namely the Sadāmattas, the Mālādhāris, the Karoṭapāṇis, and the Vīṇādvitīyakas—should be depicted. Furthermore, the terrestrial sons of the gods should be painted in their proper order and according to their respective attire.
Aphorism 2.157,
Aphorism 2.158,
Aphorism 2.159.

In this manner, in the southern direction, the sons of the gods such as Avṛha, Atapā, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, Parīttābha, and Puṇyaprasava are to be depicted according to their respective attire and positions. Likewise in the western direction, and likewise in the northern direction. Below them, they are to be depicted arranged in two rows. 2.157.

Outside the second circle is the third circle. In the four directions, the four Great Kings are to be painted in successive order. In the northern direction, starting from the entrance on the right, Dhanada is to be depicted standing near a treasure, adorned with all ornaments, his crown slightly tilted, in the form of a yakṣa. To his right, the two yakṣa generals Maṇibhadra and Pūrṇabhadra are to be painted. 2.158. {S44}

In this manner, Hārītī, the great Yakṣiṇī, should be depicted in due order. The youth Priyaṅkara, seated upon her lap, should be depicted gazing at the maṇḍala. Pañcika, Piṅgala, and Vibhīṣaṇa should also be depicted. And near them, the hand-seals (mudrās) of the Yakṣas should be depicted. 2.159.

In this manner, Varuṇa, holding a noose in his hand, is to be depicted in the western direction in due order; and the two nāgas, Nanda and Upananda, as well as the eight great nāga kings beginning with Takṣaka and Vāsuki, are to be depicted. 2.160.
In this way, those residing in two rows [are arranged] in successive order.

Yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and ṛṣis; siddhas, pretas, piśācas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, humans, non-humans, and so forth; medicinal herbs, various kinds of precious gems, mountains, rivers, and islands—all these, in their proper sequence, should be depicted as the foremost, those known as the most eminent. 2.161–163.

In the southern direction, Yama is to be depicted with his retinue and the seven Mothers. In the south-eastern direction, Agni is to be drawn, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, with a staff, water-pot, and rosary held busily in his hands,
dressed in white garments and wearing a silk upper robe.

Kanaka-varṇa, marked with the triple sectarian mark of ashes, and others distinguished by various ornaments, weapons, attire, postures, and complexions, are to be depicted arranged in two rows. (2.162)

Entering from all sides into the outer maṇḍala: Umāpati, mounted on a bull, holding a trident in his hand; and the goddess Umā, golden-hued and adorned with all ornaments. And Kārttikeya, seated upon a peacock, with a spear raised in his hand, in the form of a youth (*kumāra*), six-faced, his body radiant red, clothed in yellow garments, with a yellow upper garment; holding a bell and a red banner in his left hand. Following in succession: Bhṛṅgiriṭi, of extremely emaciated appearance; Mahāgaṇapati; Nandikeśvara and Mahākāla; and the seven Mothers, who are to be depicted according to their respective ornaments, weapons, attire, and postures. 2.163.

The eight Vasus, the seven Ṛṣis, and Viṣṇu with his discus in hand, four-armed, holding a mace, a conch, and a sword, seated upon Garuḍa and adorned with all ornaments; the eight planets and the twenty-seven constellations that move across the terrestrial mandala; the eight secondary planets (Upagrahas) and the gods should be depicted. In successive order: the fifteen lunar days (Tithis), both bright and dark; the twelve zodiac signs (Rāśis); the six seasons; the twelve months; and the year. The four sisters;
[and] one wearing a crown of matted hair and a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). Thus, ap2.165 ap2.166.
Apastamba Dharmasūtra 2.16.7,

"Those mounted on boats, with the brother as the fifth, and those dwelling in the waters"—in brief, the deities are to be established within the mudrās; they should be arranged in two rows according to their sequence. (2.164)
In brief, even in the three mandalas, that which rests upon the three circles should be depicted; furthermore, this arrangement of squares applies to all three mandalas as well. (2.165)

In brief, the Buddha, the Blessed One, must certainly be depicted as the foremost of all sentient beings. To the right, Āryāvalokiteśvara of the Lotus family must certainly be depicted; to the left, Āryavajrapāṇi of the Vajra family must certainly be depicted. Āryasamantabhadra, the foremost of the Bodhisattvas, must certainly be depicted; Mañjuśrī in the form of a youth must certainly be depicted. These [deities] are to be depicted according to their established positions within the hand gestures (*mudrās*). This is the inner maṇḍala. 2.166.

In the central mandala as well, Brahmā Sahāmpati must certainly be depicted in the eastern direction. Likewise, Ābhāsvara in the southern direction, and the Akaniṣṭha and other gods of the realm of form (rūpin); the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), who are unmanifest and circular in form; and in the northern direction, Śakra, king of the gods, Suyāma, Saṃtuṣita, Sunirmita, Paranirmita, and the sons of the gods beginning with Parīttābha—each of these kings of the gods must certainly be depicted. These [deities] are to be established within their respective mudrās. 2.167.

Likewise, in the third maṇḍala, in the northern direction, Īśāna, the lord of beings, must certainly be depicted together with Umā. Near the second gate, Kārttikeya and Mañjuśrī, seated upon a peacock, holding a spear in their hands, their forms radiant red, dressed in yellow lower garments and upper robes, with a bell and a red banner attached to their right hands, having the appearance of youths, should be shown looking toward the maṇḍala. In the eastern direction, Vainateya in the form of a bird [should be depicted], and the seer Mārkaṇḍeya must certainly be depicted. These [deities] are to be established within their respective mudrās. 2.168.

To the southeast, four maidens together with their princely brothers, situated upon a boat, are wandering about the great ocean; and Agni, the king of the gods, must certainly be depicted there. Likewise, in the southern direction, the city of Laṅkā and Vibhīṣaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, [are to be shown]. There, the Bodhisattva in the form of a yakṣa named Jambhalajalendra, resting under a *picumarda* tree, must certainly be painted. In this same sequence, King Yama, who possesses great supernatural power over the hungry ghosts (*preta*), must certainly be depicted; likewise, the king of the piśācas named Vikarāla must certainly be depicted. These [deities] are to be established within their respective seals (*mudrā*). 2.169.

In this way, in the south-western direction, the two chief nāgas, Nanda and Upananda, must certainly be depicted, as well as the chief of the planets, the Sun. In the western direction is the eminent sage named Kapila, the bull among the Nirgrantha teachers, appearing in the form of a Nirgrantha. These should be established in their respective positions according to the sequence of the seals (mudrās). 2.170.

And in the northwestern directions, the Yakṣa king Dhanada, the Gandharva king Pañcaśikha, and the Kiṃnara king Druma—these must certainly be depicted. They, along with their respective mudrās, should be drawn in successive order, established in their proper places. || 2.171 ||
Apastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.17.2,
Apastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.17.5,

The fourth mandala is outside, filled with five lines and adorned with garlands of mudrās; it is square, shaped like four archways, and embellished by the four Great Kings. They are situated in successive order, as follows: the mudrās. (2.172)

At the entrance, a blue lotus is to be depicted. To the right and left, there should be a lotus, a vajra, an axe, a sword, a trident, a mace, a wheel, a svastika, a vase, two fish, a conch, an earring, a banner, a flag, a noose, a bell, a dagger, a bow, and an iron arrow. With these various forms of weapons and mudrās, one should surround the square on all sides with a garland. Outside of this, in the four directions, the four great oceans are to be established. (2.173)

In the northern direction, having made a square-shaped mandala, one should place a double-vajra (ubhayavajra) in the form of three prongs, with flames blazing all around. In the eastern direction, having made a triangular-shaped mandala, one should place a lotus with flames blazing all around. In the southern direction, having made a bow-shaped mandala, one should place an alms-bowl with flames blazing all around. In the western direction, having made a mandala in the form of universal radiance, one should place a blue lotus, complete with its stalk and petals, with flames blazing all around. (2.174)

And in the intermediate directions there are four mudrās. In the northwestern direction, having made a circular mandala for the noose, it should be surrounded by flames. In the southwestern direction, having made an elongated mandala, one should place the staff, surrounded by flames. In the southeastern direction, having made a triangular mandala for the axe, it should be surrounded by flames. In the northeastern direction, one should place the sword, surrounded by flames. (2.175)

"Having drawn [them] on all sides"—meaning upwards, downwards, and across—three seals (mudrās) should be drawn with colored powders alone outside the mandala near the doors, namely: a garment, a fan, and a pair of sandals; for these are to be depicted as being surrounded by flames on all sides. 2.176.
This procedure for the mandala has been taught here in brief by the wise Mañjughoṣa, out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings. (2.177)

Then, the mandala master should first of all accept as disciples those who have their faculties unimpaired, whose limbs are beautiful in every way, and who belong to the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes; who have generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), who follow the Mahāyāna, and whose nature is free from longing for other vehicles; who are great beings (*mahāsattva*), full of faith, possessing virtuous qualities, and desiring great sovereignty; who loathe meager enjoyments and take delight in great wealth; who are auspicious, disciplined, and observant of moral conduct; who are monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen established in their vows and observing the *upoṣadha* fast and its restraints; who do not harbor malice toward great Bodhisattvas, who are born into noble lineages, and who by their very nature practice the Dharma. (2.178)

Having fasted for a day and night, clothed in clean garments, with fragrant hair, bathing three times a day, and observing silence; on that day, having perfumed their mouths with camphor, saffron, and cloves, constantly performing ritual sipping (ācamana), seated upon bundles of *kuśa* grass, having performed the rites of protection, practicing celibacy, and being truthful—they should be stationed outside the circle of the *brahmāñjali*, neither too far nor too near. They must be pure, very clean, numbering from eight down to one, and no others. Furthermore, they must not touch one another. This applies even to Kṣatriyas who have been consecrated as great kings (*mahārāja*).
Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.80,

And their sons, both boys and girls, were ignorant of the ways of the world. The Blessed One, the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, who assumes the form of a youth, the awakener of childish beings and one devoted to youthful play, was the cause [of their appearance].

Therefore, the prince should be admitted first of all. It increases the life, health, and sovereignty of the great king, and especially increases his desire for enjoyments; furthermore, the accomplishment of mantras for children is certainly established. Thus [ends verse 2.180].

Having placed these [implements] as previously established, accompanied by good friends and remaining vigilant, the mandala master, burning camphor incense, should then go out from behind the mandala. Having gone out, he should bathe and perform ritual sipping (upaspṛśya) with water that is pleasant for the season and has been consecrated one hundred and eight times with the root mantra, sealed with the great mudrā of the five-crested [hair-tuft]. Then, clad in clean garments and purified, he should proceed to the fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa). || 2.181 ||
Seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, facing northeast, one should offer eight thousand oblations mixed with camphor, saffron, and sandalwood.

Having invited [the deities] and dismissed them again according to the previously mentioned rite, one should re-enter the maṇḍala. Having entered, one should present eight full jars—adorned with clean cloths and decorated with mango sprouts, their interiors filled with gold, silver, jewels, grain, and rice—to the Blessed One Śākyamuni; the second to all the Buddhas; the third to the entire community of Pratyekabuddhas and Noble Śrāvakas; the fourth to all the Mahābodhisattvas; the fifth to the Mahābodhisattva Noble Mañjuśrī; the sixth to all the gods; and the seventh and eighth should be placed in the gateway chamber of the second maṇḍala. Adorned with clean cloths, one [of these two] is for all spirits (bhūtas), and the second should be placed as common property, dedicated for the sake of all sentient beings. 2.183.

Then, burning incense according to the very same procedure previously described and having formed the great mudrā with five crests (*mahāmudrā-pañcaśikhā*), one should again perform the invocation. One should invoke all the Buddhas, all the Pratyekabuddhas, the noble Śrāvakas and Mahābodhisattvas, all spirits (*bhūta*), and all sentient beings, as well as Mañjuśrī in his youthful form (*kumārabhūta*), according to the procedure previously described. (2.184)

In this manner, one should offer flowers, incense, perfumes, lamps, and food offerings by means of the very same ritual procedure previously described. One should perform this for all [deities] in every respect, following the proper sequence. By the mention of "lamps," one should offer a lamp of ghee. For all [deities], whether noble or non-noble, by the mention of "food offerings," one should offer boiled rice with *śāli* grain accompanied by curd. (2.185)

One should offer to all the Tathāgatas cakes prepared with honey, milk-rice, and various special ingredients, fried in ghee, as well as *aśokavartī*, sugar-candies, and other such delicacies. One should offer to all the Pratyekabuddhas, noble Śrāvakas, Great Bodhisattvas, and noble deities foods cooked in milk, honey, and clarified butter, along with *śrīveṣṭa* and other offerings filled with sacrificial oblations (*havir*). Likewise, one should offer to all the hosts of gods and spirits, and to all sentient beings who are empowered by mantras, according to the ritual rules, various types of sweetmeats (*laḍḍuka*) and other specific preparations made from flour. 2.186.
In the same way, [one should offer] fragrant flowers— such as *jāti*, *tagara*, *nāgapuṣpa*, *puṃnāga*, and so forth,
as previously specified— to all the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, noble Śrāvakas, and Great Bodhisattvas.
Apastamba Dharmasūtra 2.18.9;

One should offer [the flowers] to the noble and the non-noble; specifically, the *jātī* flower to those born in the Tathāgata family, the lotus (*padma*) likewise to the Lotus family, the blue water-lily (*kuvalaya*) to the Vajra-handed one, and other [flowers] to the other mantras. Thus [it is said]. (2.187)

Camphor incense is for the Tathāgata family; sandalwood is likewise for the Padma family. Guggulu is recommended for the Lord of the Guhyakas, the Vajrī himself. To all other mantras, one should offer different incense. One should cause butter lamps to be offered to all the noble (ārya) mantras; however, to the non-noble (anārya) mantras, one should cause fragrant oil to be offered.
By means of the gradual rite and according to the previously seen cause,
just as with the scent, so it has been taught for all mantras at all times.
"Whatever has been proclaimed by Avalokita and whatever has been proclaimed by Vajrapāṇi,
for the purpose of accomplishing the practice of mantra within their respective tantras— all those are to be seen here in this ritual manual and should always be followed. (2.190)

Then, the mandala master, having performed the rites of invocation, worship, incense offering, and the presentation of food offerings according to the previously observed procedure, the skilled assistant, acting with haste, prepared a non-meat *bali* offering for all spirits (*sārvabhautika*) on all sides, accompanied by the sounding of drums, conchs, and joyful cries, and adorned with garlands of incense, flowers, and lamps.

In the four cardinal directions and the intermediate directions— thus above, below, across, and everywhere outside— the Maṇḍala-ācārya, having circumambulated [the mandala] clockwise and scattered the *bali* offering for all spirits (*sarvabhautika*), bathes and [offers] oblations of *śāli* rice grains smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of those [substances] previously prepared and for which the protective rites have been performed.

For those who have generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), who have offered their very bodies to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who share [their merit] for the sake of the success and enjoyment of sentient beings, who are skilled in ascending to the seat of unsurpassed awakening (*anuttarabodhimaṇḍa*), and who desire to attain the Buddha-knowledge of omniscience—by the mere sight of the mandala, they are liberated from all sins. Even those people who have committed the crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) are liberated at that very moment. (2.192)

Then, the Maṇḍala Master, having covered the faces of those wishing to enter the maṇḍala with a cloth that is unwashed, drawn from the Tantra, free of hair, consecrated seven times with the root mantra, and anointed with fragrant sandalwood and saffron, should first cause a prince who has been consecrated (*mūrdhābhiṣikta*), or a son of a Kṣatriya, or another person of great energy desiring a great kingdom—ranging in age from sixteen years down to three years, and adorned with five locks of hair, or one lock of hair, or a topknot, or even with no head-covering at all—to enter. 2.193.

Having wrapped the face of one situated in the second mandala and formed the utpala mudrā, one should recite and cause the root mantra of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta to be recited once; then, having offered fragrant flowers mixed with sandalwood and saffron while performing oblations with the heart of the six-syllable root mantra, [one acts] for the sake of the great beings who have entered the mandala and have accepted discipleship under the mandala master.
[The rules] concerning those who observe the *upoṣadha* fast.
With very clean hands, flowers should be caused to be scattered; whichever flower settles upon him, that mantra should be given to him. 2.194.

It is called one's own mantra. That very mantra follows him through his succession of births; it alone acts as his spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for the sake of proceeding to the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and fulfilling the wisdom of the Great Bodhisattvas. It alone is what must be accomplished by him. It also brings about for him association with persons of great wealth, great sovereignty, and great renown. Even in this very life, without deliberation, that which is to be accomplished is achieved in all ritual actions. (2.195)

Thus, for those desiring accomplishment, [the initiation] should be given to one person at a time in this sequence, up to eight, and not to others. For others, it may be given as desired merely for the sake of purifying their sins; such would be the rule. When the Maṇḍala Master bestows the consecration, he should first prepare a plot of ground outside the maṇḍala, neither too far nor too near, in the northeastern direction. Having empowered it and purified it with mantras, he should do so with the root mantra. Then, regarding himself as being like one receiving the royal consecration, he should initiate one person at a time—beginning with one up to five—who possesses exclusive faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; who is devout, highly energetic, never separated from the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), a follower of the Mahāyāna, a benefactor of the Three Jewels, has unimpaired faculties, is blameless, and desires to accomplish the mantras in this very life. He should be of noble disposition, his mind intent on the practice of mantras, curious by nature, and even if seeking knowledge, his mind should be focused on the meaning of the mantras without conceptual distraction. Those remaining should be excluded. Only those who are wise and of unerring conduct should be initiated, and no others. (2.196)

Then, having gathered the requisites for a universal royal consecration—or whatever else might please the preceptor—the candidate should proceed with great honor. With a canopy spread above, with banners and flags raised high, and with a white parasol held over his head; being fanned with white yak-tail whisks; amidst the sounds of drums, conchs, kettledrums, and mṛdaṅgas, and the shouts of "Victory!"; and being praised with auspicious verses, with hymns of benediction, and with the Jina’s own words; he should circumambulate that maṇḍala, bow down to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, prostrate his head at the feet of the preceptor, and speak as follows: [2.197]

"O Master, [I wish] to enter into the accomplishment of the mantra-practice of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; to enter into the secret maṇḍala of liberation that transcends all worldly things; and to attain Buddhahood, which is the entry into the sovereignty over all dharmas. In brief, it should be said: 'May I become a Buddha. (2.198)

Then, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass and facing the east, having caused [the practitioner] to tie five topknots (*pañcaśikhā*), he should cause him to recite the mantra. Then, whichever mantra is pleasing to him should be written with yellow pigment (*gorocanā*) on a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*). Having written it, one should smear both hands with sandalwood and saffron, as well as the pair of earthenware bowls (*śarāvasampuṭa*). Then, that birch-bark leaf, placed inside the pair of earthenware bowls, should be deposited at the feet of the Bodhisattva. 2.199.

Then, having sat down there, one should recite the root mantra of the vidyā one hundred and eight times beforehand; thereafter, that person seated upon a bundle of kuśa grass is to be consecrated. [One should take] the full jar, which was previously placed outside the mandala and is common to all sentient beings.
Apastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.199,
Apastamba Dharmasūtra 2.20.5,

Having taken him near the door, he should be consecrated on the head by the preceptor while reciting the root mantra; the remaining [consecrations] are to be performed with water as desired. || 2.208 ||

Then that pair of earthen bowls should be given to him alone; he should be made to recite [the mantra] by means of a lamp. If it is that very same mantra, it will be accomplished through effort in due course. If it is another mantra, it is accomplished simply by recitation. If the mantra has been given with syllables deficient or in excess, it is accomplished even during the first stage of practice; thus, without hesitation, this is what was previously written by the Master. One who practices with the three stages of accomplishment succeeds without effort. In this manner, one should first bestow the initiation of knowledge (*vidyābhiṣeka*). 2.201.

The second maṇḍala consecration: In the second maṇḍala, one should consecrate [the disciple] on the head with the full flask (pūrṇakalaśa) that was offered to all the deities. Or else, by the very same procedure as before, one is liberated from all sins. One is authorized by all the Buddhas for all mundane and supramundane samaya-maṇḍalas and for the accomplishment of all mantras and mudrās. One is empowered by all the Bodhisattvas. Thus, one should bestow the master’s consecration (ācāryābhiṣeka). 2.202.

In the third mandala, one should consecrate [the disciple] on the head with a full flask that has been offered to all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, according to that very same rite. It should be said: "You are authorized by all the Buddhas and the bodhisattvas of great supernatural power to write, recite, and teach the mandalas, mantras, tantras, mudrās, and conduct of all mundane and supramundane mantras; or to practice them yourself or instruct others. In this very life and in successive births, until the final one, you shall certainly attain Buddhahood. Thus [it is said]. 2.203.

In the same way, during the consecration of Jaya and Vijaya, one should likewise perform the consecration with the full vase offered by the Blessed Buddha and the full vase offered by the Bodhisattvas, according to the previously prescribed ritual. And it should be said: "You are authorized by all the Blessed Buddhas, by the great Bodhisattvas, and by the Śrāvakas. (2.204)
Invincible to all beings, unconquered by all embodied ones, may you be victorious over all mantras; accomplish whatever you desire.

Then, by the mandala master, the five empowerments should be bestowed upon each individual according to their desire; however, for all [disciples], exactly five [empowerments] are to be given. (2.206) {V36}

Then, having led them into the maṇḍala in due order and having offered them to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should circumambulate the maṇḍala three times to the right and dismiss them. On the following day, they should be instructed in due order and enjoined to the practice of mantras. At that very moment, taking the full jar which was previously offered to the Blessed One, the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, one should have those who have entered the maṇḍala face the east and cause them to drink three handfuls of water. And they should be addressed as follows: [2.207]

"O noble ones, do not transgress this secret pledge (*samaya*) of the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, lest you produce much demerit. No mantras whatsoever should be rejected; no Buddhas or Bodhisattvas should be deceived; and the Guru must be propitiated. Otherwise, there would be a violation of the pledge, the mantras would not attain accomplishment, and there would be much demerit. Thus should they be dismissed. (2.208)

Then the Maṇḍala Master should again offer oblations of *śāli* rice grains smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, using the eight-syllable heart mantra. Then, having risen and entered the center of the maṇḍala, he should mentally offer the *arghya* to all [the deities] with the flowers previously specified and according to the previously mentioned rite. With the same incense as before, he should fumigate all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas and Noble Śrāvakas, and all the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, bhūtas, yogins, siddhas, and ṛṣis, as well as all sentient beings; having done so, he should scatter flowers and consecrate them with sandalwood and saffron water. He should dismiss them according to the very rite previously mentioned. "Liberation for all through the mind"—thus it is said. (2.209)

Then the mandala master should cause the offerings, the sacrificial cakes (*bali*), and the ritual powders to be washed away in a river, or they should be given to suffering living beings. Having made the area of the earth well-swept, well-scrubbed, and beautifully adorned, it should be smeared with cow dung, or washed with water, or smeared with very clean clay, or with sand. Once this task is completed, one may go wherever one desires. Those who have entered the mandala must subsist on a diet of milk-rice or on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*). Thus [ends the section]. 2.210.

Thus concludes the second chapter, the Instruction on the Ritual for the Maṇḍala, from the Extensive Section on the Bodhisattva Chapter, [entitled] "The Miraculous Manifestations of the Youthful Mañjuśrī," from the Great Sovereign King of Kalpas, which is an Ornament of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
{S53} {V37} Chapter A3:
Now begins the third chapter.

Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, having again gazed upon that abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods and having paid homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas assembled in the great circle of the assembly, spoke the single-syllable mantra—the supreme secret, the destroyer of all poisons, effective for all rites, the means for accomplishing his own mandala, and to be employed in all minor activities. And what is it? 3.1: OṂ VĀKYE.
Homage to all Buddhas! It is thus: *jaḥ*. O worthy ones and you hosts of all beings, this is the second mandala ritual for this very single-syllable mantra; it should be applied in brief. 3.2.

Having purified a plot of ground measuring eight cubits or four cubits, one should draw it oneself using powders of five colors, and not by others; there is no fault whether it be drawn here or elsewhere. It should be level, square, and adorned with three circles. First, one should draw the great seal (mahāmudrā) of the five crests. Then, one should draw the lotus seal, the fang seal, the face seal, and the staff seal of the Blessed Mañjuśrī. These seals are to be drawn in the eastern portion of the inner mandala. 3.3.
Apastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.210,

Then, at the base of the outer gate, one should depict the forms of a lotus, a vajra, a blue lotus, a banner, a flag, a parasol, an archway, a chariot, an elephant, a horse, an ox, a buffalo, a svastika, a peacock, a goat, a ram, and a young man. They should be drawn arranged in a row according to their sequence, situated within the three circles; thus they should be made. || 3.4 ||

Then, with the single-syllable mantra alone, the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) should be performed in the southeastern direction. One hundred and eight oblations of *apāmārga* wood, smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, should be offered. Then, an offering of water (*arghya*) should be given with flowers. With the same single-syllable mantra, the offering of food (*bali*), the presentation of the lamp, and the incense should be given as desired. One should perform the invocation and the dismissal. Thus [ends section] 3.5.

Then one should cause [the patient] to enter. One desiring sovereignty should be drawn into the middle of a city; one desiring enjoyments near a banyan tree (*vaṭa*); one desiring a son near a *putrañjīvaka* tree; one who is childless, or one desiring elephants and horses, in an elephant stable or a horse stable; one bitten by a snake in a great lake or a temple of Nāgas; for those with quartan fever, constant fever, or all types of fever, in a place with a single linga or in the southern direction of the village; one possessed by a *rākṣasa* in a cremation ground or an empty house; one possessed by a *piśāca* near a *vibhītaka* tree or an *eraṇḍa* tree; for those possessed by all the *mātṛs*, at crossroads or near a house where there has been a death or birth; one possessed by a *brahmarākṣasa* at a *tāla* tree or a *śleṣmāntaka* tree. For one who has administered poison, by means of the single-syllable mantra itself, water should be consecrated seven times and poured right there in the center of the maṇḍala. He is liberated. (3.6) {S54}
In this manner, for a woman or a man seeking fame, [the diagram] should be drawn at a crossroads or in a sacred precinct (*brahmasthala*); for one whose children have died,
it should be drawn in the middle of a field where rice has ripened.

Because it removes the corruption caused by the three types of diseases, one should draw this *rakṣoghna* [mantra-diagram] on a river sandbank, on a bank, or on a mountain peak for all diseases in every respect; even those caused by *ḍākinīs*, one should draw it in a Brahmin’s grove (*brahmavāṭikā*), in an empty house, in a secluded place, or in a low-lying area. (3.7)

In this manner, for all rites, it should be drawn at midnight or at midday, or at any time whatsoever. Having offered water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) with flowers using that very same one-syllable mantra, and having dismissed [the deities], the mandala should be flooded with water. Thus, great protection is established for all who are ill. 3.8.
One is liberated from all diseases and one's desired aims are accomplished; the childless obtains a son, and the unfortunate becomes fortunate. (3.9)
A poor person obtains wealth merely by seeing the mandala;
whether it be a woman or a man, even for one who is faithful and observant of the ritual rules, they shall always attain various kinds of prosperity according to their desire. (3.10)
Thus ends the third chapter, the Ritual for the Mandala, from the *Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta-mūla-kalpa*, an extensive section of the *Bodhisattvapaṭala*.
The Unconditioned and the Conditioned;
The Nature of the Path and its Fruit.
On a fruit-bearing tree, or on a milky sap tree such as the *pratara* and others, for one who is childless.
It should be written for those afflicted by major diseases.
Ap 4.2 Ap 4.3 Ap 4.4
Chapter A4.
Homage to the Buddha and to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Then Mañjuśrī, having surveyed the entire abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods and once again looking upon that great assembly gathered in the maṇḍala, prostrated at the feet of Śākyamuni; with a smiling countenance, he addressed the Blessed One as follows. 4.1.

Therefore, it would be well if the Blessed One, for the benefit of all sentient beings, would cause to rain down the Dharma-cloud that issues from the accomplishment of the ritual procedures for the practice of mantra, according to their desires.

From the extensive section on the accomplishment of the fruits, this is the ritual procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*), which brings forth the seed of perfect enlightenment and brings forth the entirety of the knowledge of the Omniscient One. 4.2.

In brief, it is that which is correctly joined with the fruits of all mantras; which brings them to fruition; which makes the practice of the seeker non-vain; which fulfills the conduct of sentient beings; which is donned with the great armor of the Bodhisattva; and which overcomes and turns back the forces of all Māras. Therefore, may the Blessed One speak of it out of compassion for us and for all sentient beings. 4.3
When Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had spoken thus, the Blessed One Śākyamuni then said this to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you have set out for the benefit of many people and out of compassion for the world, thinking thus to question the Tathāgata regarding this matter. Listen to it, and attend to it well and thoroughly; I shall speak to you. I shall explain to you the detailed procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*), the practice for accomplishing the welfare of all beings, and the method of entry, in due order, as previously taught by all the Tathāgatas. I too shall now speak."

First of all, on a clean area of ground free from dust, cotton wool should be taken and purified by beings who have entered the pledge (*samaya*). Having purified it, the mandala master should consecrate that cotton wool with this mantra one hundred and eight times. 4.5.

Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who move with unimpeded intelligence and gait! Homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha, the King of Kings, Saṃśodhana-duḥkhapraśamana-rājendra! It is as follows: Oṃ śodhaya śodhaya, O destroyer of all obstacles, O Great Compassionate One, you who assume the form of a youth! Manifest, manifest! Remember your vow! Stay, stay! Huṃ huṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! 4.6 {S56}

Then, [the practitioner] should select a maiden who has not yet known the ways of the world, born of a brahmin family, a kṣatriya family, or a vaiśya family; one who is not of an excessively dark complexion, free from defects in her lineage, with all limbs beautiful and unimpaired, approved by her parents, having observed the *upoṣadha* fast, having generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), compassionate, of pure complexion, and free from other colors; in short, one endowed with the most excellent marks of female characteristics. On an auspicious day during the bright fortnight, when observed by white and auspicious planets, when smoke and dust have cleared away, when clouds have departed, and when the wind has subsided, there arises the production of unsurpassed merit.
The fulfiller of all hopes, [the essence of] all awakening.
Aphorism 4.11,
Aphorism 4.12,
Aphorism 4.13.

In a clean place, having bathed the previously described maiden and having dressed her well in pure garments, one should perform protection for her using this very mantra together with the *mahāmudrā*. Then, having stirred white sandalwood and saffron with water free of living organisms, one should sprinkle the girl as she drinks it with that same purifying mantra. 4.7.

And one should scatter white sandalwood and saffron water in the four directions, as well as above, below, and in the intermediate directions. Having combined white sandalwood, saffron, and camphor, one should first cause them to be given, or give them oneself, or have the practitioner or the preceptor give them. This very thing should be spoken three times with words. 4.8.
May the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the great bodhisattvas established on the ten stages, preside over this cloth-thread. 4.9

Then those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the great Bodhisattvas take heed. At that time, while burning incense, various auspicious birds—peacocks, curlews, swans, cranes, ruddy geese, and cakravākas—whether moving on water or land, or traveling through the air, shall go forth or utter auspicious cries. Then the practitioner should know: "This rite of mine is fruitful; it has been blessed by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the great Bodhisattvas. My life in this birth is well-lived; my accomplishment of the mantra is not in vain. (4.10)
There may arise the sounds of kettledrums, war-drums, clay drums, conchs, lutes, flutes, small drums, and large drums; or at that very moment, they might suddenly say:
"Victory! Success! Accomplished! Given! Bestowed! Take! Prosperity! Fruitful! Śakra-abundant! (4.11)

They utter such and other auspicious sounds, or there may be the resonance of bells or the sound of joy. Then the vidyādhara should know: "This is the empowerment of the Blessed Buddhas and the great bodhisattvas; it is nothing else. Success is unfailing. Thus [ends verse 4.12].
Then at that time, they utter cruel words:
"Seize! Eat! Make him eat! He is lost! He is ruined! Woe! Far away! Very far away! He does not exist! (4.13)

Such sounds as these issue forth; the cries of monkeys, buffaloes, jackals, donkeys, cats, and other loathsome animals—whether two-legged or four-legged—may issue forth. Then the practitioner should know: "I have no success. In this life, he must cease [the practice]. Or, having performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) again, he should begin once more, and so on up to seven times. Even for one who has committed the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*), success is attained on the seventh application of the rite. (4.14)

Then the practitioner, having performed the protection-rite for that maiden, should have her sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass. Having established her facing either the east or the north, he himself should subsist on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) and feed that girl with sacrificial food as well. On that very same bundle of *kuśa* grass previously prepared, he should have her spin the cotton according to this procedure. (4.15)

Having gathered that well-spun white thread from a girl previously instructed, the knower of mantras should prepare these highly praised counts—starting from eight, five, three, or one, up to sixteen *mātrās*, *palas*, or *karṣas*. For the medium [rite], there are eight; for the others, five or one, in minor rites to be accomplished. According to his capacity, the knower of mantras should perform all rites. (4.16)
From that time forward, whatever evil karma was previously committed perishes at that very moment through the contemplation of the meaning of this Sūtra. (4.17)
One should place this collected Sūtra inside a clean vessel; having placed it there, one should fumigate it with camphor incense. 4.18.
Or [an image] produced from non-living materials, such as saffron, sandalwood, and the like; or one honored with fragrant flowers, such as jasmine, campaka, and so forth. || 4.19 ||

Having established [the image] in a clean place, secured with protective rites, the knower of mantras, skilled in all rituals, having performed his recitation and being well-composed, [should proceed]. 4.20.
Then, having gone to a weaver and given him the price as desired, [he obtained] one who was free from bodily defects, not emaciated, and always devoted to pure righteousness.
One who is not afflicted by disease, nor aged, and who is free from cough and asthma; one who is free from cough and asthma, not impotent, and born of a pure womb.
One who is blameless, not hunchbacked, and devoid of lameness or leprosy; endowed with all auspicious marks, praiseworthy, and of pleasing appearance.
One who desires success should request here that person—who possesses pure intellect and conduct and follows the worldly way of life—for the weaving of an excellent cloth.

Those who are praised for their auspicious appearance, who are intelligent and well-trained, are superior even to the most excellent and best among those skilled in weaving cloth. (4.25) One should employ the highest quality materials for the finest work, and middling means for middling work; with other inferior materials, one should perform only lowly tasks in every respect. (4.26)
Having paid the craftsman according to the price, that knower of mantras should act as the craftsman dictates at the first instance of his speech. AP 4.27.
One should then quickly give the merchandise; this is called "heroic purchase. And by the mere request of the reciter, it becomes the nature of the merchandise.
"For this supreme, unsurpassed cloth-painting brings swift success;
it performs all rites, is worthy of worship, and bestows divine and human happiness. It was spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One for the welfare of all beings. (4.29)

Then, having had the weaver observe the *poṣadha* fast, the Vidyādhara—during an auspicious lunar mansion, during the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), on a bright day under the aspect of favorable planets, or at another time in the bright fortnight; during the season of spring when the mango trees are in full bloom with clusters of blossoms and excellent flowers; at that most excellent of seasons, at that very time, when the sun has risen in the forenoon—should cause the aforementioned weaver to eat sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), to be dressed in clean garments, to have his head bound with a turban, to be well-bathed, well-anointed with white sandalwood and saffron (or either one of these), his limbs smeared, his face scented with camphor, his mind joyful, and free from hunger and thirst. Then, having washed all the vessels and the necessary implements such as ropes with clay and cow dung, he should wash them repeatedly with fresh five-fold cow products (*pañcagavya*). 4.30.

Then, having washed [the image] with water free of living organisms, one should consecrate it with white sandalwood and saffron. On a pure spot of earth, free from clamor, devoid of people, in a secluded seat that is serene, protected, and honored with flowers; then the practitioner, having empowered white mustard seeds eight hundred times with the purification mantra itself, should scatter them in the four directions, as well as above, below, and in the intermediate directions. Then, having struck the weaver with the mustard seeds and bound the five-crested great mudrā, one should perform the binding of the topknot (*śikhābandha*). Thus, great protection is established. 4.31.

Ap 4.32: If it is the superior cloth, it should be four cubits in width and eight cubits in length; this is the measurement for that which is woven by the weaver. The middling [cloth] is two cubits in width and five cubits in length. The inferior [cloth] is the measure of a Sugata’s span (*vitasti*) and one-and-a-half cubits in length. In this context, the Sugata’s span is proclaimed to be equal to one full cubit according to the standard measurement of a man from the Middle Country; by this measurement, the standard size is declared. 4.32.

4.33 Arise! For the foremost among men have declared that the highest success (*jyeṣṭhā-siddhi*) belongs to those who desire sovereignty, while the middling success belongs to the supreme sage [who desires] invisibility.
4.34 [The lowest success belongs] to men who seek great enjoyments, such as the gods and asuras who possess celestial pleasures.
Success is declared for the lowest [grade]; middling success for the middling. || 4.34 ||
Minor rites are always accomplished on a canvas of the lowest quality; indeed, all tasks and all substances are always successfully accomplished [on it]. (4.35)
The accomplishment taught in all three paintings is for men who seek the highest good; yet, if one deviates from the prescribed rule, it will not be achieved even by Śakra, the lord of Śacī.
Thus, all rites are accomplished quickly and without effort for even one who has lost their way, provided they are joined with the prescribed ritual procedure. (4.37)
This path has been fully proclaimed by the Victors and the sons of the supreme Victors, for the welfare of all beings who are poor, protectorless, and suffering. (4.38)
Indeed, the entire path to awakening has been shown by those who see reality; this path, which is the cause of awakening, has been revealed through the way of mantra. (4.39)
The mantras of all worldly maṇḍalas are accomplished without effort, and even those supramundane maṇḍalas that have been described are accomplished.
Success shall always belong to those whose minds are intent on the cause of awakening; success is never said to belong to others who are always harmful to the world. 4.41
Success is always proclaimed for those beings who have set out for awakening, especially here for the great-souled youth Mañjuśrī. (4.42)
In order to accomplish his task quickly, he should obtain everything from this complete [collection]; thereafter, the artisan should diligently weave the cloth in the proper sequence. (4.43)

In five, eight, or sixteen days, or in two or four [days], or indeed very quickly in a single day and night, is the completion of the weaving of the cloth. (4.44) Indeed, for those desiring the attainment of the highest excellence, it is accomplished in a day and night, provided the artisan is endowed with purity and proper conduct and is constantly supervised. (4.45)
Having gone a distance from his dwelling, he should void urine and excrement; then, having bathed with his clothes on and having put on other garments, he should enter again. 4.46.

Wearing white garments and adorned with a garland, having sipped water again and again, and having anointed his limbs with white sandalwood paste, he rubbed his hands together before the artisans. (4.47)
One should weave it further with effort, always [using] fine, well-washed [thread].
By means of these and other such applications spoken by the Jina,
{V42} one who is reflective by nature should, with effort, complete the weaving of the cloth without remainder.
But when the cloth has been completed, as described in the previously mentioned rites.

One should perform [the rite] equally on an auspicious day during the fortnight of the waxing moon, while remaining within the means of valid cognition and not deficient; then one should cause it to descend through the tantras on that most beautiful bright fortnight.
Having made the cloth clearly distinct and beautifully adorned with attached fringes, and having taken up the cloth bound to a bamboo pole, one should then proceed.
Having gratified the artisans with extensive gifts and portions for their benefit, the minister—being of excellent conduct and firm in his vows—should depart as he pleases. (4.52)
Having worshipped it with fragrant flowers, one should place it in a clean location; and by means of this very mantra, its protection and covering should be performed.
With that very same [mantra] by which that cotton cloth was previously purified many times, one should perform the protection of both oneself and the cloth.
The great hero Mañjuśrī has been spoken of in the form of a mantra by many past [buddhas], and by me as well, now and again. (4.55)
He alone is the one who moves through all mantras, appearing in the form of mantras; he is of great heroism and great splendor, the accomplisher of the purpose of all mantras.
The diverse beings dwelling in Jambudvīpa, whose thoughts and conduct are deluded, perform various and manifold acts for the sake of protection.
(4.57) But those who lack faith, who are perverse, and who are greedy for wrong conduct, do not succeed with mantras nor indeed with any ritual substances. (4.58)
For this very reason, they wander in the dark prison of saṃsāra;
whereas he whose mind is always pure, who is faithful, curious, and ever devoted to auspiciousness— (4.59)
Always eager in the grasping and retaining of all mantras, those great-souled ones, desiring accomplishment, possess great energy and great splendor.
For them, the mantras spoken by the Jina succeed without effort; however, for beings who lack faith, the pure Dharma does not take root.

"Just as a seed sown in saline soil produces no sprout, so too faith is said by those who see all truths to be the root of the Dharma. For those who practice the Dharma for its true purpose, the accomplishment of mantra is always proclaimed. (4.62) {V43}

Then, for the accomplishment [of the rite], an artisan who is a well-trained painter, or one who is himself skilled in drawing, should paint [the image] using non-adhesive pigments. Taking a color-paint that is brilliantly radiant and endowed with all colors, according to the very same procedure as before—just as in the case of the weaver’s loom—and by means of a painter endowed with the proper characteristics, the detailed description (*peyāla*) should be performed at length; just as in the previous procedure for the weaver, so too should that cloth (*paṭa*) be painted, either by another or by oneself. 4.63.

The cloth should be perfumed with camphor, saffron, sandalwood, and so forth. While burning incense, one should recite that same mantra eight hundred times; then, having scattered over that cloth flowers such as *nāgakesara*, *puṃnāga*, *bakula*, *campaka*, *vārṣikā*, *dhānuṣkārika*, and *mālatī*, one should paint that cloth while facing east, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, with a composed mind, with the thought directed toward all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, holding a fine brush in hand, and with a mind free from effort. 4.64.

First of all, one should depict the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, endowed with the excellence of all aspects, his body marked by the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics; seated upon a jewel-lotus, blazing all around, his form beautified on every side for the span of a fathom, teaching the Dharma, with a serene appearance and endowed with the excellence of all aspects. 4.65.

In the center, one should depict a lotus with a stem of beryl; below it, two nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda, who are white, adorned with all ornaments, and have human forms with the lower halves of their bodies as serpents. They should be shown supporting that lotus stalk, gazing at the Tathāgata, and paying homage with their right hands. And all around that...

Regarding the root-lotus stalk and the branch of the Blessed One, from that very place many lotus flowers have emerged, rising in successive tiers. On the left side are eight lotus flowers; upon those lotuses, the forms of the eight great Bodhisattvas are to be depicted seated. 4.67–68.

Apastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.4.71–73: 71. A student who has completed his studies shall not dwell for long in a village. 72. He should live with a teacher or with one’s son, or he may live at home during the rainy season.
He should always remain chaste, except during the period following the menstrual flow.
The lotus pond should be depicted with lotus leaves, flowers, buds, blossoming aquatic plants, and living beings such as birds and fish. 4.66.
First of all, the noble Mañjuśrī, slightly pale-yellow like the filaments of a lotus, pervades [the space], his form beautifully radiant and long-established as it is arrayed without exception.
Having the color of saffron or gold, in the form of a youth with the appearance of a young boy,

his head adorned with five locks of hair; bowing to the Tathāgata with his right hand, of beautiful form, his gaze fixed upon the Tathāgata, of gentle aspect, with a slightly smiling face, and surrounded by a circle of flames blazing on all sides.

In another lotus, the noble Candraprabha as a youth should be depicted in the same manner. In the third, Sudhana; in the fourth, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin; in the fifth, Gaganagañja; in the sixth, Kṣitigarbha; in the seventh, Anagha; and in the eighth, Sulocana. All of these should be depicted in the form of young boys, adorned with the ornaments of youths. (4.69)

On the right side of the Blessed One are eight great bodhisattvas, adorned with all ornaments, with the exception of Maitreya. Near the Blessed One is the noble Maitreya, wearing the garb of a celibate student (*brahmacārin*), his head bound with a crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmakuṭa*); he is golden-colored, wears saffron-red robes, has a red silk upper garment, and bears the mark of three sectarian lines (*tripuṇḍraka*). He has a physical form, holds a staff and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his left hand, and has a black antelope skin draped over his left shoulder. With his right hand he holds a rosary, pays homage to the Tathāgata, and gazes at him; his mental activity is directed toward the object of meditative concentration (*dhyānālambana*). 4.70.

On the second lotus, Samantabhadra is to be depicted in the same manner: dark green in color like the priyaṅgu plant, his body adorned with all ornaments, holding a cintāmaṇi jewel in his left hand and a śrīphala fruit in his right, with his hand in the gesture of granting boons (varada), and possessing a beautiful form. 4.71.

In the third [panel]: Noble Avalokiteśvara, white as an autumn reed, adorned with all ornaments, wearing a crown of matted hair and a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). He bears the noble Amitābha—the One Possessed of Ten Powers—upon his head, seated within the matted locks; he is of beautiful form, with his left hand resting upon a lotus and his right hand in the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), his mental activity directed toward the object of meditation, his body illuminated on all sides. 4.72. {V44}

In the fourth [panel], the noble Vajrapāṇi, golden-colored, adorned with all ornaments, holding a vajra in his left hand, and granting a boon with his right hand which holds a fruit; he is of beautiful form and gentle appearance, his body draped with necklaces and half-necklaces, wearing a sacred thread of pearl necklaces, a crown radiant and studded with jewels, lower garments of silk, and an upper robe of white silk cloth; likewise, the noble Avalokiteśvara and Samantabhadra, their bodies clad in lower garments and upper robes of bark-fiber, and in appearance as previously described. 4.73.
Adorned with the ornaments of a youth, he holds a blue lotus in his left hand.

A woman who has been married according to the *gāndharva* rite may, after three menstrual periods, go to another man if her husband is absent, impotent, diseased, or devoid of desire. 80. A woman who is excessively wicked, or who acts contrary to the interests of her husband, may be abandoned at any time. 81. A wife who drinks liquor, is a thief, is rebellious, or is afflicted with a foul disease, may be superseded by another wife. One who is barren may be superseded in the eighth year; one whose children have died, in the tenth; one who bears only daughters, in the eleventh; and one who is hostile toward her husband, immediately. However, a wife who is devoted to her husband's welfare must never be superseded.

Likewise, on the fifth lotus is the noble Mahāmati; on the sixth, Śāntamati; on the seventh, Vairocanagarbha; and on the eighth, Apāyajaha. These are the bodhisattvas who are to be depicted, with their hands holding fruit and books, beautifully adorned with all ornaments, wearing upper garments of fine silk cloth, decorated with every kind of ornament, and dressed in lower garments of silken fabric. 4.74.

And above them, eight Pratyekabuddhas are to be depicted. Wearing the robes of monks, their bodies endowed with the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), clad in saffron-colored garments, they sit cross-legged upon jeweled lotuses, characterized by peaceful composure and surrounded on all sides by a garland of blazing light. Fragrant flowers are strewn about; specifically, the cloth painting is shown being showered from all sides with flowers such as the *mālatī*, *vārṣikā*, *dhānuṣkārikā*, *puṃnāga*, and *nāgakesara*. 4.75.

To the left of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, above Ārya Mañjuśrī, one should depict a celestial palace-maṇḍala constructed of many jewels, elongated in shape, adorned with the king of mountains, and resembling a mountain covered with precious stones. Therein, one should draw eight Blessed Buddhas, as follows: || 4.76 ||

One should depict the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin, whose light extends for a fathom in all directions and is suffused with the radiance of beryl-jewels; who is brilliantly illuminated on all sides by various great and exquisite maṇi-jewels such as ruby, sapphire, emerald, beryl, and agate; whose body has the color of the sun slightly risen; who wears a yellow upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and a yellow lower garment (*nivāsita*); who sits cross-legged teaching the Dharma; whose body is armored with the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) and whose form is adorned with the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*); who is serene in appearance and endowed with the excellence of all attributes. Thus one should paint the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin. 4.77.

One should depict the second Tathāgata, Saṃkusumitarājendra, golden in color; one should depict him as being profusely strewn with flowers such as the nāgakeśara and bakula; gazing upon the Noble One, he is all-pervadingly radiant, his light shimmering and diffused with the splendor of jewels. 4.78.

One should depict the third Tathāgata, Śālendrarāja, with the luster of the filaments of a lotus, teaching the Dharma. Fourth, one should depict the Tathāgata Sunetra, just like this Duḥprasaha. Sixth, the Jina Vairocana. Seventh, Bhaiṣajyavaidūryarāja. Eighth, one should depict the Tathāgata Rājendra, the Pacifier of All Suffering. All these forms of the Tathāgatas should be made golden in color, with hands bestowing the gesture of fearlessness. 4.79.

And above the Tathāgatas, situated within the clouds at the corners of the cloth, two divine sons from the Śuddhāvāsa realm should be depicted, discharging a rain of flowers from both sides. Remaining in the atmosphere, they should be depicted paying homage to all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas. 4.80.

And above the Pratyekabuddhas, eight great Śrāvakas are to be depicted, seated in a position slightly lower than the heads of the Bodhisattvas. They are as follows: the Elder Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, Rāhula, Nanda, Bhadrika, and Kaphiṇa. 4.81 {V45} ap4.82 ap4.83
Aphorisms 4.84,

The Pratyekabuddhas were also there, such as Gandhamādana, Candana, Upariṣṭa, Śveta, Sita, Ketu, Nemi, and Sunemi; all of them were exceedingly beautiful, wearing peaceful attire and appearing perfectly self-controlled. The great Śrāvakas likewise stood with palms joined, gazing at the Blessed Buddha Śākyamuni. 4.82.

And above, near the Śuddhāvāsa gods, two other sons of gods should be depicted, holding a long, beautiful canopy of silk streamers on all sides above all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas; these two sons of gods are wearing divine garlands and garments. 4.83.
Aphorism 4.87; Aphorism 4.88;
Aphorism 4.89.
At the foot of that mountain,
one should depict the practitioner with his body bent at the knees, wearing his proper attire and assuming the prescribed posture, with his gaze fixed upon Mañjuśrī. 4.87.

Above the Blessed One Śākyamuni, one should depict a jeweled canopy well-arranged with silk cloths, strung with pearl necklaces and gems such as ruby, sapphire, and others, and adorned with hanging strings of pearls. 4.84.

At the summit is a cluster of jewel-threads, and extending all around and downward from the lotus seat of the Blessed Buddha as far as the vicinity of the feet of the noble Mañjuśrī, beside the Naga king Upananda, there is a great mountain of jewels rising up from a lotus lake— a jewel-tree encircled by jeweled sprouts, caves, grottoes, and coral creepers, frequented by great sages and perfected ones.

On the summit of that mountain, one should depict Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, of most terrible form, with a noose in his hand and a staff grasped in his left hand; with a frowning face, awaiting commands, his gaze fixed upon Noble Mañjuśrī; with a wolf-like belly, hair standing erect, resembling a black cloud of crushed collyrium, with a long, fierce, tawny beard, long nails, and blood-red eyes; his neck adorned with snakes, clad in a tiger skin, the destroyer of all obstacles, most exceedingly dreadful, the Great King of Wrath, Yamāntaka, blazing with flames on all sides. 4.86. {S65}

Near the king of the Nanda nāgas, below and to the right of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, one should depict the great sovereign king of jewel-mountains rising from a lotus lake, as described by the Tathāgata; one should depict it as being free from the wrathful king Yamāntaka and strewn with divine flowers. One should depict the noble Avalokiteśvara upon that mountain; one should depict that high and lofty mountain as a ruby stone, shaped like a single-sprouted peak made of lapis lazuli. 4.88.

Therein, one should visualize the Noble Lady Tārā, the compassion of the Noble Avalokiteśvara, who is adorned with all ornaments, wearing a red silk upper garment and a multicolored silk lower robe; her entire body is decorated with feminine ornaments, she is golden-hued and slender-waisted, her mind absorbed in meditation,
and she receives a command from her left hand which holds a blue lotus, appearing neither too thin, nor too young, nor too old, with her right hand [extended].

Seated upon the surface of the earth on a stone slab, his hand occupied with an incense burner, he is depicted according to his traditional conduct; while the noble Avalokiteśvara sits cross-legged with his body slightly bowed toward him, his gaze turned away slightly, and is surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides. 4.89.

On that very same peak of vaidūrya gem, one should depict the Blessed Lady, who completely covers [the tree] with her presence; she is surrounded on all sides by *puṃnāga* trees, whose branches are everywhere adorned with fully blossomed flowers, and whose branches—though devoid of foliage—are entwined with sprouts of coral, radiant with various colors and forms, as she gazes toward the face [of the practitioner]. 4.90.
The goddess who destroys all obstacles, the supreme destroyer of fear—one should draw that auspicious bestower of boons for the protection of the practitioner. (4.91)
The Goddess who assumes a female form, the compassionate daughter of the One Possessing Ten Powers, the bestower of boons, should be depicted for the welfare of all beings. 4.92.
4.93 Here, the mother of the youth Mañjughoṣa, the goddess of great splendor, [should be placed] on all sides for the sake of destroying all obstacles for the practitioner.
4.94 For the protection of the lords of men and for their welfare, one should place on the cloth that very Lord of Wrathful Kings who is stationed upon the mountain peak.
For the destruction of all obstacles, it has been taught by the sons of the Supreme Victors:
he who is most formidable, most venerable, most fierce, and most radiant.
(4.95) He is intended solely for the subjugation of those beings who are hostile to the Teaching; yet, for the protection of the practitioner, he is the destroyer of all obstacles. (4.96)
Terrible and wrathful by nature, the mantra-deity is invoked;
most fearsome and of horrific form, he is the restrainer of all who are merciless. (4.97)
And he shall bring under his control those who are unsubdued and who act with wickedness and cruelty—whether they move through the sky, upon the earth, or even throughout the netherworld.
It destroys all those who are wicked and hostile toward the teaching of the Sage; one should indeed paint a square cloth with four corners on all sides. 4.99.
Furthermore, at the bottom edge of the cloth, one should depict the abode of the vast ocean,
marked by the coils of the serpent, each one extending all around.
Born with bodies in human form, possessing bright and auspicious limbs,
they always stood with their heads turned toward the north and their hands joined in the gesture of reverence.
The seventh, named Ananta, was of great heroism and renowned as a great lord; adorned with precious jewels, he gazed upon the Tathāgata. (4.102)
One should draw Tārā, the goddess Tārā, who is most beautiful, of lovely form, adorned with jewel ornaments,
garlanded with flames, and renowned as the great king of nāgas.
103–105. This procedure for the cloth-painting is the supreme one spoken by the Jina; it was previously taught by the Tathāgatas as being described both in brief and in detail.
Indeed, for that wise person who should draw [this], the merit is infinite;
whatever extremely terrible sinful karma has been committed over ten million eons [is thereby purified]. 4.106
Upon seeing that cloth upon the ground, even one who has committed the five acts of immediate retribution, one who is immoral, or one who is loathsome, is destroyed at that very moment. (4.107)
For those engaged in all manner of evil, wandering in the darkness of saṃsāra,
and born into the lowest of destinies and wombs—
their viewing of this cloth taught by the Lord of Sages shall not be in vain.
Upon merely seeing it, they are instantly liberated from that evil.
How much more so, then, will human beings attain accomplishment, being ever-striving for the perfection of mantra, which consists of a perfectly pure conduct due to its pure nature? (4.110)
Whatever merit belongs to all sentient beings from worshipping [the Buddha] for ten million eons, a practitioner of mantra shall obtain that merit by painting a cloth-painting on the earth. (4.111)
As many as are the grains of sand in the Ganges that have been proclaimed, so many Buddhas shall there be, along with the supreme sons of the Pratyekajinas. (4.112)
Having repeatedly performed various sacrifices in the world, those disciples who possess the sword-like [wisdom] shall obtain that fruit as mortals simply by seeing the painting of this cloth. 4.113
For one who merely hears [this], or performs its worship, or even rejoices in it, the accomplishment of mantras is certain; all rites are ordained for such a person. 4.114
"Whatever worldly mantras have been spoken by the preeminent Jinas,
as well as those by their divine disciples— the sword-wielding Bodhisattvas of great soul—
all mantras indeed attain accomplishment upon the most excellent of cloth-paintings. (4.115)
From the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, a Mahāyāna sūtra, this is the fourth [chapter], 116.
The first section on the ritual procedure for the cloth painting (*prathamapaṭavidhānavisara*) is completed. {S68} {V48}
Chapter A5:
One who is devoted to the welfare of the entire world and has entered the teaching of the Sage should draw [the deity] as dwelling by a river, for the destruction of all obstacles. 4.104.
Ap 5.1 Ap 5.2 Ap 5.3
ApDhS 1.5.4; ApDhS 1.5.5; ApDhS 1.5.6
Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed that entire circle of the assembly, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
"Mañjuśrī, there is yet another method for your medium-sized cloth painting (*paṭa*). I shall speak of it; listen well, pay close attention, and take it to heart. (5.1)
