First of all, by means of the very same cord previously specified, according to the very same procedure previously described, and by artisans previously selected, one should have that central cloth made according to the previous measurements—extremely beautiful, white, well-woven, with even fringes, using non-staining pigments free from hair, refuse, and so forth; exactly as it was done for the first [image], so should one do for that cloth, except for the size and form, which must subsequently be painted upon the cloth. 5.2.

First of all, one should depict the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, beautiful in appearance on all sides and composed of radiant jewels, adorned with white pearl necklaces. In its center, the Blessed One Śākyamuni is to be painted, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, teaching the Dharma, endowed with the excellence of all marks. 5.3.

On the right side is the noble Mañjuśrī, with the luster of a lotus filament or the color of saffron and the sun; on the region of his left shoulder he holds a blue lotus, his hands joined in the gesture of reverence (*añjalipuṭa*), gazing at the Blessed One Śākyamuni with a slightly smiling face. He has the form of a youth, his head adorned with five locks of hair, decorated with the ornaments of a young child, and his head is bowed toward the circle of his right knee. 5.4.

And on the left side of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the noble Avalokiteśvara—white as an autumn reed—is to be depicted exactly as before; however, he should be shown waving a yak-tail whisk for the Blessed One. Beside him, the noble Maitreya, Samantabhadra, Vajrapāṇi, Mahāmati, Śāntamati, Gaganagañja, and Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin are to be depicted in succession. Just as with the first, all of them are to be painted adorned with every ornament. 5.5.

And above them, eight Buddha-Bhagavats should be depicted standing, with their right hands granting the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayapradāna*), their bodies clad in yellow upper robes (*uttarāsaṅga*), with the corners of their robes held by their left hands, wearing well-draped saffron lower garments with a slight reddish luster, possessing a universal radiance, and endowed with all excellent marks. They are as follows: the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarājendra, Ratnaśikhī, Śikhī, Viśvabhuk, Krakucchandaka, Bakagrīvī, Kāśyapa, and Sunetra. These are the Buddha-Bhagavats who should be depicted. 5.6. {S69}

On the right side, near the Blessed One Āryamañjuśrī, the great assembly maṇḍala should be depicted. The eight great śrāvakas and the eight pratyekabuddhas should be depicted exactly as they were before; however, Āryamahāmaudgalyāyana and Śāriputra should be painted standing, fanning the Blessed One Śākyamuni with whisks. 5.7.

In this manner, the sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm are to be depicted; as well as Śakra, the lord of the gods, Suyāma, Saṃtuṣita, Sunirmita, Śuddha, Vimala, Sudṛśa, Atapa, Ābhāsvara, Brahmā Sahāmpati, and Akaniṣṭha.
Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.11,
Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.14,
Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.17,

Devas such as these, belonging to the realms of form and desire, should be depicted in successive order, standing near the noble Mañjuśrī, arranged within the surrounding assembly circle, and painted wearing their own characteristic forms and attire. 5.8.

Beneath the lion throne of the Blessed One, a great mountain rising from the great ocean should be painted all around, extending as far as the edge of the cloth. In one corner of the cloth, the practitioner should be painted according to his actual dress, appearance, and form, with his knees, elbows, and head bowed down, and his hands occupied with an incense burner. And on that jewel mountain, beneath Ārya Mañjuśrī, the wrathful king Yamāntaka should be depicted exactly as previously described. 5.9.

On the left side, beneath the Blessed One’s lion throne and near the feet of Noble Avalokiteśvara, the goddess Tārā should be depicted as seated upon that mountain of jewels; she is to be painted exactly as previously described. And all around that cloth [painting], it should be strewn with loose flowers—scattered everywhere over the cloth with blossoms such as the campaka, blue lotus, saugandhika, mālatī, vārṣikā, dhānuṣkārī, puṃnāga, and nāgakesara.

And above, in the corner at the edge of the cloth, at both ends, two sons of gods (*devaputra*) are to be depicted, white in color, wearing various forms, emitting a great shower of flowers, stationed in the intermediate space, hidden within clouds of water, and appearing as if flying upward. Thus [ends section] 5.11.
This is declared to be the Madhyamaka, the emergence of the cloth for the sake of supreme welfare; for the middling accomplishment of men on this earth depends upon it. (5.12)
Whatever evil has been committed previously while wandering through saṃsāra, that perishes in this very instant by the sight of the cloth-painting here. (5.13)
Deluded beings, wandering through the five realms of existence, do not know [this],
except for those who behold the painting of Mañjughoṣa in the center.
Even one who is a wrongdoer, or even a perpetrator of the five deeds of immediate retribution, [shall attain liberation].
Even for one of immoral conduct, the mantras spoken in various ways may be successful. || 5.15 ||
Even one who has performed the recitation shall attain accomplishment even more swiftly;
the sick are freed from disease, the poor obtain wealth,
and the childless obtain a son upon the middle viewing of the cloth painting.

Merely by seeing it, one shall then obtain vast and great merit; that person will certainly become a partaker of the happiness of gods and humans, and at the end of his life, Buddhahood will surely be his. (5.17)
By writing, by reading, by worshiping and transcribing, as well as by seeing and touching it, one is liberated from all sins. 5.18
For such is the prayer and entreaty for this cloth of great splendor.
It is not possible to express it in words, even throughout tens of millions of eons.
Whatever merit a living being may obtain from beholding this cloth-painting, [may that be theirs]. Thus [ends verse 5.20].

From the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, this is the fifth detailed chapter. The second section on the ritual for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhānavisara*) is completed.
{S71} {V50} · Chapter A6 ·

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni again addressed Mañjuśrī, the Youthful: "Mañjuśrī, there is yet another secret procedure for the cloth-painting, the third one called 'the minor' (kanyasa), by which all sentient beings may attain accomplishment without even effort. 6.1

According to the very same procedure previously described, the cloth should be painted by artisans as before, measuring one span of the Sugata in width, and likewise even and square, using the pigments previously specified.

First of all, the noble Mañjuśrī should be depicted sitting upon a lion throne in the form of a young boy, teaching the Dharma as before, with beautiful features and emitting rays of light in all directions. On his left side, the noble Samantabhadra should be depicted as before, standing upon a jeweled stone, holding a yak-tail whisk in his right hand and resting a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) in his left hand, with a complexion dark like the *priyaṅgu* flower. On the right side of the noble Mañjuśrī, the noble Avalokiteśvara should be painted standing upon a jeweled stone, as before holding a yak-tail whisk in his right hand and resting a lotus in his left hand, his entire body radiant. 6.3.

Below the lion throne, a golden-colored mountain should be painted as far as the edge of the cloth. At the corner of the edge of the cloth, beneath the lion throne of the noble Mañjuśrī, on the right side, the wrathful king Yamāntaka should be painted as before; likewise, the practitioner should be depicted with an incense burner in his hand, just as previously described. 6.4.

Above the noble Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarājendra should be painted, measuring sixteen finger-breadths, nestled within a cave of a jewel mountain. Ten mountains resembling peaked pavilions should be painted; one should depict that cloth [painting] as being surrounded on all sides by the forms of mountains. And above, situated at the corners of the cloth and joined to the mountain slopes, two sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm—one named Śuddha and the other named Viśuddha—should be painted as before, emitting a flood of flowers from ascending celestial palaces. That cloth should be caused to be depicted strewn with various flowers. Thus ends section 6.5.
All this has been told regarding the threefold characteristics of the cloth;
indeed, this one called the "inferior" cloth is superior for minor rites.
Whatever extremely terrible evil karma has been committed or even caused to be committed, [it is all purified].
One obtains a fruitful birth, and rejoicing [in merit] brings swift results.

Indeed, upon merely seeing the cloth, one is liberated at that very moment. A wise person who would honor thousands of millions of Buddhas does not approach even a sixteenth part of the merit gained by seeing this inferior cloth. (6.8)

Whatever merit is gained by performing worship to all the Buddhas, the Protectors, that same merit the wise person shall obtain upon seeing the painting for the first time. Furthermore, one should perform auspicious deeds here for the sake of enjoyment. (6.9)
Whatever mantras there may be, spoken by Brahmā, Indra, and the ṛṣis, or proclaimed by Vainateya, Varuṇa, Āditya, and Kubera—

All the mantras spoken by the Rākṣasas, including Dhanada and others, by the lords of the Dānavas and the great serpents, by Soma, Vāyu, Yama, and others, and by Hari, Hara, and the rest—have all been brought here; they are perfected before this cloth-painting. (6.11)

"One should always perform rites of pacification (śāntika) and likewise rites of enrichment (pauṣṭika) here; one should avoid those that are cruel, for they are censured by the supreme Victors in this world. (6.12)

From the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, this is the sixth detailed chapter. The third [section], the ritual procedure for the small cloth-painting (*kanyasapaṭavidhāna*), is thus completed.

{S73} {V51} Chapter A7: Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One Śākyamuni three times, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:

Excellent, excellent! This Dharma discourse has been well-spoken by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of all who practice the vows of knowledge, and out of compassion for the world. The skillful means of the Bodhisattvas have been demonstrated; it is a path leading toward Nirvana, a distinguished entrance, a continuity that is certain to culminate in enlightenment. It is the means for accomplishing the purpose and practice of all mantras for Bodhisattvas. This will be the cause for spreading this secret of mantras among all people. 7.1

In the future time, when the Teacher of the World has passed into nirvāṇa, when the sun of the Tathāgata has set, when the lineage [of the Dharma] has been abandoned in all buddha-fields, when the vessel of the world has become shrouded in darkness—devoid of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas—and when the Noble Path has been severed; when the world is bereft of all sciences, mantras, medicinal herbs, jewels, and gems; when it is abandoned by virtuous people and the realm of sentient beings is without light—the beings there will become indolent due to the loss of aspiration, lacking faith, fragmented, taken hold of by non-virtuous friends, deceitful, fraudulent, and of rogue conduct. (7.2)

Having heard this Dharma-discourse, they will fall into terror; delighting in indolence and laziness, they will not have faith; seeking after sensual pleasures, they will not believe; and being devoted to false views, they will produce much demerit.
By the mere sight of the cloth, one is liberated for thousands of millions of eons.
Ap 7.6 Ap 7.7 Ap 7.8

They are destroyers of the true Dharma, destined for the Avīci hell, having gone from terrible to even more terrible states. For the sake of those suffering ones—who are powerless and yet must be brought under control—for those who are already subdued, grant them fearlessness; O Blessed One, please speak the ritual procedure for the mantra-painting through the gathering of skillful means, whenever you deem it to be the right time. (7.3)
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni gave his approval to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you have asked the Tathāgata about this matter."

"Do you think, Mañjuśrī, that there exists this most supreme and secret expansion of the chapters on the ritual procedures for the cloth-paintings (*paṭavidhāna*) concerning the practice of the vidyā-vow and the means of accomplishment—the meaning of the supreme heart-mantras, which is most secret, of great significance, and the very treasury of all mantras? (7.4)

These six, which are the supreme heart-mantras of six syllables, attain accomplishment at that time through non-conceptuality. For the sake of subduing those beings, for the sake of entering the mantras of the equipment of skillful means, and for the sake of certain attainment of perfect awakening, they were previously spoken by seventy-six billion Buddhas. I too shall now speak them at this very moment. Out of consideration for future generations, listen well and attend thoroughly; I shall speak them to you. And what are they? 7.5 {S74}
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke this mantra: Oṃ vākyārthe jaya.
Oṃ, [the word] *sva* [is used] as a supplement to the statement.
Oṃ, the method of the speech.
Oṃ, this is the culmination of speech.
Oṃ, homage to Vākyeyī.
Oṃ, obeisance to Vākyeda. 7.6.

Thus, Mañjuśrī, these six mantras of yours consist of six syllables; they possess great power, equal and uniform potency, and are supreme heart-mantras. They are supremely accomplished, arisen like Buddhas themselves. For the benefit of all sentient beings, they have been proclaimed by all the Buddhas; they are embraced by the *samaya*, thoroughly activated, and effective for all rites. They are instructors in the path to enlightenment, the most excellent mantras in the Tathāgata family, and are applied in three ways—superior, middling, and inferior. Bestowing beautiful results and maturation of karma, they will attain accomplishment at the time when the teaching is on the verge of disappearance. 7.7.

Those who will accomplish these [practices] for the sake of protecting the eye of the True Dharma at the *samavasaraṇa* will accomplish them by means of that very expenditure of wealth for the sake of great kingdoms, great enjoyments, and sovereign power. At that time, in that very moment, they will attain accomplishment most swiftly. Therefore, even for the sake of mere inquiry, these supreme heart-mantras (*paramahṛdaya*) should indeed be accomplished. In brief, however they are employed, in that same way they will attain accomplishment. In summary, this is the procedure for their cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*).

At that time, at that moment, during the Great Terrifying Age of the Five Corruptions, sentient beings will have little merit; they will be of little renown, short-lived, possessing few enjoyments, and weak in vigor, such that they will not be able to undertake rituals such as the extensive procedures for cloth-paintings (paṭavidhāna). For their sake, I shall speak [a ritual] that is much more concise. 7.9
Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.10;

Oṃ he he, Blessed One, wearer of many forms, possessor of divine vision! Behold me! Behold me! Remember your vow! O Great Bodhisattva who assumes the form of a youth, why do you delay? Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!

Having performed the recitation with this mantra, one should sleep right there. In a dream, it will declare success or failure. Then, having risen—if one has seen a dream that is a sign of unimpeded success—one should have that cloth-painting (paṭa) painted. If, however, dreams indicating failure are seen, then one should remove that cloth from that vessel and dry it in the sun. Having dried it, one should place it again in another new vessel. One should keep it well-concealed and protected by performing the ritual of protection (*rakṣā*). Then, once more, taking any one of those supreme heart-mantras (*paramahṛdaya*), one should recite it—preferably the six-syllable mantra—for a further hundred thousand times. Thereafter, that cloth-painting will quickly attain accomplishment. || 7.13 ||

First of all, having taken that cloth, on the fortnight of miracles (prātihārakapakṣa), or on another bright day joined with an auspicious constellation, on an auspicious lunar date, or on a day of the waxing moon, when there are very beautiful omens and during a night esteemed as auspicious—at the time of midnight—one who has observed the fast (upoṣadhika) should have that cloth painted by a painter in a clean place while burning camphor incense. || 7.14 ||

First of all, one should visualize the noble Mañjuśrī in the form of a young boy with five locks of hair on his head; then, having treated the cloth as one with him using water free of living organisms and colors that do not smear, [scented] with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron.

Having stirred sandalwood, saffron, and camphor with pure water in a new vessel, one should soak a cloth [with it] and place it for three days sealed with a tight lid. Having performed the protection rite in a clean place, and having become pure oneself, on the full moon day of the bright fortnight, one should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing east before the cloth and the vessel, and recite these mantra-words one hundred and eight times. They are as follows: [Mantra follows] (7.11)
Adorned with the ornaments of a youth,
wearing a blue silk upper garment,
and seated in the half-lotus posture.

One should have him depicted as seated upon a lion throne supported by a jeweled footstool, adorned with all ornaments, beautiful to behold, with a slightly smiling face and a gaze directed toward the practitioner.

One should have [the Buddha] painted golden-colored, clad in a blue silk lower garment, teaching the Dharma while seated upon a lion throne; on his right side, the noble Samantabhadra should be depicted standing upon a white lotus seat, wearing a blue silk lower garment and a pearl necklace as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), dark green like the *priyaṅgu* flower, with his left hand holding a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), fanning [the Buddha] with a white yak-tail whisk, beautiful in all his limbs, and adorned with all ornaments. || 7.16 ||

To the left side of Noble Mañjuśrī is Noble Avalokiteśvara, white as an autumn reed, dressed in a fluttering garment of blue silk, beautiful in all his limbs, adorned with every ornament, and wearing a sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) of pearl necklaces. In his left hand he holds a white lotus, and in his right hand he holds a golden-handled white fly-whisk (*cāmara*) being waved; he has a serene appearance and his gaze is directed toward Noble Mañjuśrī. Noble Samantabhadra is likewise [depicted]. Both of these should be painted as seated upon white lotus thrones. (7.17) {S76}

There are three lotuses arising from a single lotus grove. In the center, upon the pericarp of the root lotus, is the lion throne and jeweled footstool of noble Mañjuśrī. On the second lotus is noble Samantabhadra, seated upon a white lotus throne. On the third lotus is noble Avalokiteśvara. That beautiful lotus stalk has the appearance of emerald, is adorned with many budding lotus flowers and leaves, and rises from the great lake Anavatapta, which is filled with blossoming and half-blossoming lotuses. The stalk of that lotus is supported by two nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda, who grasp its stem. 7.18.
Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.19; Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.20;
Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.21.
And those two were white in color.

Their bodies should be depicted as adorned with all ornaments, their forms marked by the coils of snakes on half their bodies, half-submerged in water, and their hoods beautified with precious jewels. || 7.19 ||
In this way, the mantras indeed succeed for [the practitioner], but not for others who commit evil deeds.
There are two Naga kings, adorned with seven jewels, with human bodies from the waist up, gazing upon the noble Mañjuśrī.

And all around the great lake, beneath it, on the right side at the corner of the edge of the cloth, the practitioner should be depicted according to his dress and complexion, looking toward the face-mandala of the noble Mañjuśrī, with an incense burner held in his hand, his head bowed, and his body positioned with elbows and knees bent. 7.20.

Above the noble Mañjuśrī, in both upper corners of the cloth, two divine sons (*devaputra*) wearing garlands and holding flower-garlands should be painted, flying upward, hidden within the clouds, emitting a great shower of flowers, and exceedingly beautiful. Furthermore, one should paint that cloth strewn all over with flowers such as *nāgakesara* and others; and it may be painted as desired, presided over by three forms. 7.21.

The noble Mañjuśrī while teaching the Dharma, the noble Samantabhadra, and the noble Avalokiteśvara with fly-whisks held in their hands should be caused to be painted; or else, three forms according to the practitioner’s preference must certainly be caused to be painted. They may have whatever appearance is desired, or be arranged in whatever configuration suits the practitioner; they should be painted exactly as it pleases him. 7.22.

In the center is the noble Mañjuśrī, and at both ends are the noble Avalokiteśvara and Samantabhadra. Other [deities] should certainly be caused to be painted according to one’s desire. On whatever cloth fragment is available—whether measuring a span or a cubit—it should be caused to be painted either by oneself or by another artist, whether that artist observes the *poṣadha* vows or does not, whether they are faithful or faithless, pure or impure, or possessed of moral discipline or lacking it. The practitioner himself must necessarily have performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), be faithful, and have generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). 7.23.

Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.1–2: *apṛkta ekāl pratyayaḥ* (An uncombined suffix consisting of a single phoneme is called *apṛkta*). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.1–2*: [Rules concerning the doubling of consonants]. *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.2*: *nādinyākrośe putrasya* (In an abusive expression, the *t* of *putra* is doubled when followed by *nādini*). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.3*: *ye ca taddhite* (The *t* of *putra* is also doubled before a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *y*). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.4*: *na kapi* (The doubling does not occur before the suffix *kap*). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.5*: *pūrvapadāt sañjñāyām agaḥ* (The doubling occurs after a preceding word ending in *a*, provided it is part of a proper name). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.6*: *nityam samāse 'nuttarapadasthasya* (In a compound, the doubling is obligatory for a word ending in *a* that does not stand at the end of the final member). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.7*: *ahno 'dantāt* (The doubling of the *h* of *ahan* occurs when it follows a word ending in *a*). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.8*: *rātrer dīp-samāse* (The doubling of the *r* of *rātri* occurs in a *dvigu* compound). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.9*: *chandasi punarvasvor ekaśeṣe* (In Vedic usage, the doubling occurs in the *ekaśeṣa* formation of *punarvasū*). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.10*: *vibhāṣā phālgunī-śravaṇā-kārttikī-citrāsu* (The doubling is optional in compounds containing these lunar mansions). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.11*: *sarva-ekānyakiṃ-yat-tadaḥ kāle dā* (After *sarva*, *eka*, *anya*, *kiṃ*, *yat*, and *tad*, the suffix *dā* is added to *kāla* to denote time). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.12*: *saṅkhyā-viṣaye dhamuñ* (The suffix *dhamuñ* is added to *kāla* when a number is the limiting factor). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.13*: *vipsāyām dviḥ* (In the sense of distributive repetition, a word is reduplicated). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.14*: *parervarjane* (The prefix *pari* is reduplicated in the sense of exclusion). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.15*: *pratiḥ pratinidhi-pratidānayoḥ* (The prefix *prati* is reduplicated in the senses of representation and exchange). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.16*: *upary-adhy-adhasaḥ sāmīpye* (The words *upari*, *adhi*, and *adhas* are reduplicated to express proximity). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.17*: *vākyāder āmantritasyāsūyā-saṃmatikopakutsana-bhartsaneṣu* (The first word of a sentence, if it is a vocative, is reduplicated in cases of envy, approval, anger, censure, or threat).

*Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.18*: *śeṣe vibhāṣā* (In other cases, the reduplication is optional). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.19*: *eka-bahuṣu pāda-dhveṅ-kṣuḥ-prakṣu-dhvam-su* (The forms *pāda*, *dhve*, *iṅ*, *kṣuḥ*, *prakṣu*, and *dhvam* are optionally reduplicated when they refer to one or many). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.20*: *juṣṭārpite ca chandasi* (In Vedic usage, *juṣṭa* and *arpita* are optionally reduplicated). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.21*: *cchandasi vāprāṅ-pūrvāt* (In Vedic usage, the reduplication of *pra* is optional when it is preceded by another prefix). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.22*: *om-abhyādāne* (The particle *om* is reduplicated when used as an introductory formula). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.23*: *yatheti pūjāyām* (The word *yathā* is reduplicated in the sense of respect). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.24*: *sūtre 'ṣv-ādīnām* (In a technical rule, the reduplication of *asva*, etc., is optional). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.25*: *karmadhāraye 'niṣṭhā* (In a *karmadhāraya* compound, a non-participial (*aniṣṭhā*) word is reduplicated). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.26*: *īṣadarthe* (The reduplication of a word expressing slightness is optional). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.27*: *nañ* (The negative particle *nañ* is reduplicated in a *karmadhāraya*). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.28*: *kṣepe* (The reduplication of *nañ* occurs in the sense of reproach). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.29*: *naṭ-nindāyām* (The particle *naṭ* is reduplicated in the sense of censure). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.30*: *na-samāse 'vyayam pūrvam* (In a compound where an indeclinable stands first, the reduplication is optional). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.31*: *tatpuruṣe śālāyā napuṃsake* (In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the word *śālā* is reduplicated when it is neuter). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.32*: *giri-nadyādīnām ca* (And the words *giri*, *nadī*, etc., are reduplicated in a *tatpuruṣa*). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.33*: *upasargasya ghañy amanuṣye bahulam* (The initial vowel of a prefix is diversely lengthened before a word ending in *ghañ*, except when referring to a human being). *Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.2.34*: *īṣad-daḥ-ṣṇaḥ-khana-kaṣa
The king of mantras is accomplished for one who possesses faith in this very way and not otherwise; for faith is the supreme vehicle by which the Vināyakas travel.
In a person devoid of faith, the pure dharma does not sprout, just as a green sprout does not emerge from seeds scorched by fire. (7.26)

For a mortal established in faith (*śrāddha*), the undertaking of awakening is indeed accomplished through ritual action; the deities are attained by him, but for one lacking faith, they are not attained. {V54} Moreover, all mantras, especially [those of] the *viśeṣa* [class], [are attained]. 7.27.
Whether they be worldly deities or likewise those that are supramundane, all indeed are accomplished for one who has faith and is free from defilement. (7.28)
For those whose minds are fixed upon that, success is swift and their awakening is certain; for others, no success is spoken of, as it is barred within this teaching. (7.29)
A small cloth or a slight distinction is proclaimed as the middling [type];
now, however, I shall explain the means for all ritual actions. || 7.30 ||

Thus concludes the fourth detailed exposition on the ritual procedure for cloth-paintings, from the seventh chapter of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra belonging to the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
{S78} {V55} Chapter A8:
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni addressed Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince.

"Mañjuśrī, for the sake of those beings whom you have described, this detailed procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*) has been taught. They shall accomplish their goal by means of even a slight application. For their benefit, I shall fully explain the division of the ritual actions (*karmavibhāga*), categorized according to the distinctions and expansions of qualities suitable for accomplishment. Listen to that; attend to it well and thoroughly. I shall speak for the benefit of all sentient beings. (8.1)
Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"Excellent, excellent, Blessed One! Well-spoken by you are these words, which illuminate our own realization and bring about the manifestation of the perfection of the qualities of mantra practice. Therefore, may the Blessed One speak it, if you deem it the right time, for the sake of compassion toward us."

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed the entire circle of the assembly, smiled. Then, from the mouth of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, rays of light—blue, yellow, crystal-colored, and so forth—issued forth. As soon as they had issued forth, these rays illuminated the entire circle of the assembly and became the three-thousandfold great world-system, wherein the mantra-deities are to be accomplished.
Ap 8.4 Ap 8.5 Ap 8.6

Having eclipsed the entire thousandfold world-system and all the abodes of Māra, as well as the radiance of all the stars, luminaries, and mountain ranges—even those [luminaries] where the moon and sun, possessed of great supernatural power and majesty, are themselves eclipsed by that light so that they no longer shine, become lusterless, do not gleam, and appear dimmed; and having rendered lusterless the radiance of all jewels, mantras, herbs, and gems, it vanished once again into the opening of the Blessed One Śākyamuni’s mouth. 8.3.

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi was present, having assembled in that very circle of the assembly. Seated there, he rose from his seat with a sense of urgency, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not manifest a smile without cause or without condition. What, O Blessed One, is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of this smile? (8.4)
When this had been said, the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi:

"It is so, Vajrapāṇi, it is so! It is just as you say. There is no smiling on the part of the Tathāgatas that is without cause or condition. There is a cause, there is a condition, for those who will enter into, follow, uphold, recite, and have faith in this sovereign king of sūtras, the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, which has issued from the Cloud of Dharma—the convergence of the means for the accomplishment of rites and the practice of vidyās. 8.5

Having committed it to writing, they will worship it with sandalwood powder, ointments, incense, and garlands; or with parasols, banners, and flags; or in various ways with special musical instruments, diverse types of drums, and percussion instruments. At the very least, they will attain a mental continuum accompanied by sympathetic joy, or they will experience horripilation. Or, having heard the power and majesty of the spell (*vidyā*), they will rejoice and approve of it, or they will undertake its practice. I have prophesied that they shall all become Buddhas, Blessed Ones, in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. For this very reason, the Victors manifest a smile, and not otherwise. Thus [ends verse 8.6].

First of all, one who has seen the ritual conventions (*samaya*), completed the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), and received initiation in this King of Rituals (*kalparāja*), having taken up either the heart-mantra or the subsidiary heart-mantra of the Root Tantra, or another mantra, or even a single-syllable mantra—or whichever other [mantra] is desired—should go to a great forest and recite it three million times while subsisting on fruits and water or eating roots and leaves; thus he becomes one who has completed the preparatory rite. 8.7 {V56}

Then, having ascended a mountain peak and installed the principal cloth painting facing westward, one should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing eastward. One should offer one hundred thousand white lotuses, anointed with white saffron, beneath the painting to the Blessed Śākyamuni, all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Noble Śrāvakas. One should burn camphor incense according to one’s means, and perform worship to the sons of gods and *nāgas* with whatever flowers are available. (8.8)

Then, at the time of midnight on the full moon of the bright fortnight during a *prātihāraka*, having prepared a fire-pit in front of the cloth painting in the shape of a lotus and kindled a fire with white sandalwood logs, one should offer eight thousand oblations of saffron and camphor mixed together according to one's means, while maintaining the protective rite (*kṛtarakṣa*). 8.9.
Ap 8.7 Ap 8.8 Ap 8.9
Apastamba Śrauta Sūtra 8.10,
Aṣṭaka 8, Chapter 13;
Aṣṭaka 9, Chapter 1,
Verse 2.

Then, rays of light issue forth from the Blessed One Śākyamuni, and the cloth painting becomes a single mass of flame on all sides. Thereupon, the practitioner, assuming the form of Sattvaramaṇa, should circumambulate the cloth three times to the right, prostrate before all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Noble Śrāvakas, and take hold of the cloth. 8.10.

When the aforementioned practitioner takes it from the edge of the painted cloth, he rises up immediately upon grasping it. With a mere snap of the fingers, he transcends the world of Brahmā and arrives in the world-system Kusumāvatī, where the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarājendra, resides, stays, maintains himself, and teaches the Dharma. There he beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face-to-face and hears the Dharma. He also sees many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas and attends upon them. For a thousand great aeons, he dwells in a state free from old age and death. 8.11.

The cloth remains right there, empowered by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. One perceives their empowerment, traverses hundreds of thousands of fields, or manifests hundreds of thousands of bodies. One becomes endowed with manifold miraculous powers and has the noble Mañjuśrī as a spiritual friend. Thus, one becomes destined for enlightenment. 8.12

This concludes the first chapter from the *Aṣṭama*, the extensive Mahāyāna sūtra which is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, from the detailed section on the ritual procedures for the supreme means of accomplishment.
{S81} {V57} Chapter A9:
Then indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni addressed the hosts of gods seated within the entire circle of the assembly:

Listen, worthy sirs, to this most secret of secrets, the supreme heart-mantra spoken by all the Tathāgatas, which is the means for accomplishing the practice and mandala-mantra of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta for the protection of the practitioner; by the recitation of which, all mantras are considered recited. 9.1.

"O assembly of gods, this King of Vidyās is not to be transgressed. Even Mañjuśrī, while still a youth, was summoned by this King of Vidyās, brought under control, and made compliant. What need is there to mention others? It destroys all obstacles—both worldly and supramundane mantras of the Bodhisattvas. This one of great heroism possesses such power that he alone is declared the foremost of all mantras; he alone is declared the single syllable among all single syllables. And what is that? (9.2)

The single syllable that accomplishes all aims, performs all tasks, cuts through all mantras, destroys the evil deeds of those who act wickedly, annihilates all sins, fulfills all mantras, and brings about auspiciousness; it stands above and beyond all worldly and supramundane mantras. It is the unimpeded heart of all Tathāgatas, fulfilling every aspiration. And what is it? Namely: *kḷhīṁ*. 9.3.

O noble ones, this is that King of Vidyās named Ekākṣara, the most supreme secret, effective for all rites; it is not to be transgressed by any sentient beings, unassailable by any spirits, the auspiciousness of all Buddhas, the accomplisher of all mantras, and the sovereign lord.
Ap 9.7 Ap 9.8 Ap 9.9

He is the lord of all worlds; the master of all wealth; the embodiment of loving-kindness toward all who hate him; compassionate toward all living beings; and the destroyer of all obstacles. In brief, he acts in whatever manner he is invoked; even if not formally propitiated, he performs his deeds. 9.4

By reciting the mantra, whoever he touches becomes subject to his will. Having consecrated garments with the mantra, he should put them on; he becomes fortunate. Having consecrated a tooth-stick, he should chew it; it removes toothache. Having consecrated a tooth-stick of white *karavīra*, he should chew it; food appears without having been requested. 9.5.

For eye pain, having powdered rock salt (*saindhava*) and empowered it seven times with mantras, one should fill the eye; this removes the eye pain. For ear pain, one should cook a small ball (*chatrikā*) made from elephant dung that has not yet been trampled by a herd, wrapped in *keduka* leaves, over a gentle fire. Once it has become soft and pleasantly warm, and having purified it with rock salt powder, one should fill the ear with it after empowering it seven times with mantras; it brings relief instantly. 9.6.

At the time of childbirth, for a woman suffering from obstructed labor or overcome by pain, one should grind the root of *āṭaruṣaka* with water free of living organisms and smear it upon the region of the navel; she will give birth with ease. Or, for a man whose splinter has been lost, one should empower aged ghee eight hundred times with the mantra and have him drink it, or smear that region with it; at that very moment, he becomes free of the splinter. 9.7.

In cases of indigestion, cholera, or diarrhea, one should take either black salt (*sauvarcala*), rock salt (*saindhava*), or any other salt, and after consecrating it seven times with mantras, consume it; one is then freed from that disease and becomes healthy on that very day. In cases of both types of diarrhea or acute diarrhea, one should grind the fruit of the *mātuluṅga* and [drink it] with water free of living organisms; by this, one is freed from that affliction, whether the mantra has been recited once or more. 9.8.

For a woman who is barren or one whose nature is not to conceive, desiring offspring: having boiled the root of *aśvagandhā* with cow’s ghee and ground it with cow’s milk, one should administer it after mixing it with cow’s milk alone and reciting the mantra twenty-five times. At the time of her menses, and after she has bathed, the householder—avoiding the wives of others and abstaining from sexual misconduct—should approach his own wife or his husband; thus he shall procreate a son. 9.9.

Whether it be an excess of the gestation period beyond three or five years, or being obstructed for many years, or caused by the supreme mantras, tantras, and herbs of others, or by the malevolent acts of enemies, or by the retention of the fetus, or by the arising of disease, or any other ailment whatsoever—whether caused by the obstruction of others, or by artificial and natural poisons of both stationary and moving beings, or produced by the application of all roots, mantras, herbs, friends, or enemies—one should take twenty-seven times aged ghee and peacock feathers, combine them, and grind them together. Then, having made a fine paste and mixing it with sugar, one should consume a dose the size of a *harītakī* fruit for seven days. 9.10.

One should have [the patient] drink boiled milk mixed with sugar after consecrating it repeatedly. In the case of a headache, one should rub [the head] with a crow's wing feather that has been consecrated seven times; [the patient] becomes healthy. 9.11.

In cases of diseases such as menorrhagia and the like, one should grind the root of *ālambuṣā* with milk, combine it with the root of *nīlikā*, empower it by reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times, stir it with milk, and have the patient drink it. In this manner, [it cures] quartan, quotidian, tertian, quaternian, continuous, and chronic fevers, as well as irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*) and so forth.
One should have [the patient] eat milk-rice mixed with ghee that has been consecrated one hundred and eight times; he becomes healthy. 9.12.

Thus, for those seized by *ḍākinī* spirits, one should empower one's own face with one hundred and eight recitations and look upon them; they will become healthy. Likewise, for those seized by all non-human, wicked, and cruel entities such as *mātṛ*, *bālapūtanā*, *vetāla*, and *kumāra* spirits, one should empower one's own hand with one hundred and eight recitations and touch the head of the afflicted person; they will become healthy. 9.13.

By reciting it once, there is protection for oneself; by reciting it twice, protection for one's companions; by reciting it thrice, protection for the house; by reciting it four times, protection for the village; by reciting it five times, protection for those who have gone out into the vicinity of the village. In this manner, up to a thousand recitations, protection for the entire camp and its circle is accomplished. Furthermore, all these and other minor rites are performed even when [the mantra] has not been mastered.

Now, if one wishes to accomplish minor rites (*kṣudrakarma*), one should go to a solitary place in a secluded region—either at the source of a river flowing to the ocean, on the shore of the ocean, on the bank of the Gaṅgā River, or resorting to the bank of a great river—in a pure location. Having constructed a hut, bathing three times a day, changing clothes three times, observing silence, and subsisting on alms-food, barley gruel, milk, fruit, or *yāvaka*, one should recite [the mantra] three million times. Then, having perceived the signs of success (*siddhinimitta*), one should begin the formal practice (*sādhana*). || 9.15 ||

In that very region and at that place, having performed a great worship of the superior cloth-painting (*paṭa*), one should offer one hundred thousand lamps to the painting—lamps made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, filled with either *turuṣka* oil or cow’s ghee, with wicks fashioned from pieces of fresh cloth. One should present all of these. 9.16.

Simultaneously and on all sides, rays of light issue forth from the cloth by means of garlands of lamps that have been ignited immediately [before]. By those rays issuing forth simultaneously, the cloth becomes enveloped on all sides by a garland of flames. Furthermore, in the sky above, drums resound, and the sound of "Well done! is heard. 9.17

Then, by the Vidyādhara, appearing in a form of great haste, the previously painted cloth [deity] emerges from the corner of the practitioner’s cloth. Having offered the *argha* water, circumambulated [the deity], and bowed to all the Buddhas, it should be grasped. As soon as it is grasped, together with all the beings holding lamps, one flies up or proceeds toward a celestial mansion (*vimāna*) characterized by a single additional [unit]. That practitioner is consecrated into the sovereignty of a Vidyādhara Cakravartin, surrounded on all sides by Vidyādharīs accompanied by divine musical instruments, sweet-sounding songs, instrumental music, and dance. Together with those lamp-bearers, he becomes one who sports like one who is ageless and immortal; he remains for a great eon (*mahākalpa*), resembling the rising sun, his limbs adorned with divine beauty, and decorated with variegated garments. (9.18)

These very ones become his servants; together with them, he wanders about as the sovereign of all *vidyādharas*. They attend upon him in the capacity of slaves. He becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of the *vidyādharas*, long-lived, and invincible to all accomplished masters (*siddhas*). He becomes supremely handsome to the maidens of the *vidyādharas*. He gains mastery over all substances. He worships the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Then, in a mere instant, [he attains...]
He goes even to the world of Brahmā; he does not reckon even Śakra, much less other vidyādharas. In the end, he attains the state of Buddhahood, and Noble Mañjuśrī [protects] him. 9.19

The practice becomes most intense. Then, having gone to a solitary place, free from people and devoid of attachment or social ties, one should enter a great forest. At whatever spot there is a lotus pond provided with a river and situated by a single mountain, one should ascend the mountain peak. There, taking up either the Single-Syllable King of Vidyās spoken in the *Mañjuśrī-kalpa*, or one spoken by other Tathāgatas or Bodhisattvas, or whichever other mantra one prefers, one should recite it thirty-six hundred thousand times while subsisting on lotus roots and fruits or consuming only milk, according to one’s desire. At the conclusion of the recitation, having installed the supreme cloth-painting (*paṭa*) according to the previously described ritual, one should kindle a fire with *khadira* wood and offer thirty-six thousand previously prepared lotuses that have been anointed with white sandalwood and saffron. 9.20.

Then, at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, rays of light issue forth from the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) of the Blessed One Śākyamuni. Having illuminated the practitioner, they vanish into his crown. As soon as he is touched by them, the practitioner becomes possessed of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*). Having attained the stage of a Bodhisattva, possessing a divine form, he wanders at will. He lives for thirty-six eons (*kalpa*), traverses thirty-six Buddha-fields, and perceives their power. He retains the teachings (*pravacana*) of thirty-six Buddhas and delights in honoring and serving them. Finally, he is destined for enlightenment and is taken under the care of the noble Mañjuśrī as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). This continues until he reaches the ultimate goal of enlightenment, culminating in *nirvāṇa*. (9.21)

Thus ends the ninth chapter from the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka; specifically, the section on the ritual procedures for the supreme means of accomplishment.
{S85} {V60} Chapter A10:
Then indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke once more the supreme accomplishment of ritual action.

In this *Kalparāja*, having taken up any one of the mantras, one should descend into the great river Gaṅgā and, staying upon a boat in the middle of the Gaṅgā, subsisting on a diet of milk-rice, perform thirty hundred-thousand recitations (*lakṣa*) over as many days as desired. Then, at the conclusion of the recitation, one beholds all the *nāgas*. Thereafter, one should begin the ritual practice (*sādhana*). Right there in the middle of the boat, one should have a fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*) constructed in the shape of a lotus. Then, having performed a grand worship of the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) with *nāgakesara* flowers, one should install the superior painting facing west and sit oneself upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing east. Having consecrated each individual *nāgakesara* flower seven times with the mantra, one should offer them into a fire kindled with fuel of *khadira* wood—only these *nāgakesara* flowers purified with white sandalwood and saffron, and no others—for thirty thousand offerings. One must await the vision of the *nāgas*; they will attempt to entice one with perfected substances (*siddhadravya*), but these must not be accepted. 10.1.
The Noble Second [Chapter],

Then, at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, he flies up together with the boat. He becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of the *vidyādharas*. All the kings of the *nāga* lords become his attendants; they remain like servants. He lives for thirty intermediate eons (*antarakalpa*), moving according to his own will, his gait unimpeded. He beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face. He touches him on the head, and as soon as he is touched, he becomes possessed of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*). He certainly attains the state of Buddhahood. 10.2.

Furthermore, there is another means for accomplishing the supreme rite: having descended into the great river Gaṅgā, one should construct a boat from a single piece of wood made of the *bilva* tree, ensuring it is well-examined and well-crafted. Having boarded that vessel made of *bilva* wood, the practitioner himself—being clearly manifest, skillful, and most diligent—should steer that boat. He should navigate it along the great river Gaṅgā without leaving its course, moving either crosswise or lengthwise in all directions. Then, having taken up one of the mantras—whether the root mantra, the six-syllable, the eight-syllable, or the single-syllable; or one of the wrathful ones, a female messenger (*dūtī*), a male messenger (*dūta*), or any other mantra—he should install the supreme cloth-painting (*paṭa*) right there facing west, while he himself faces east. At first, he should follow the previously seen procedure as instructed, and subsequently do as he pleases. His diet should consist of milk, barley-gruel, or fruit; or water, tubers, roots, and fruit. He should observe silence, bathe three times a day, change his clothes three times, practice pure deeds, and maintain a very pure mind. First, in front of the cloth-painting, he should recite the *vidyā* six million times according to the previously taught method. Then, at the conclusion of the recitation, the boat will proceed toward the great ocean. 10.3. {S86}

Then the practitioner, having gathered the necessary implements, should place them right there on the boat as previously arranged. Thereafter, one traveling upon the great ocean should not be afraid, nor should one attempt to turn back; indeed, it is impossible to cause the journey to cease, except by the power of the practitioner himself. Then, in a mere moment, one enters the great ocean even if it is situated at a distance of a thousand *yojanas*, let alone a short distance. 10.4.

Having entered there into the abode of the serpent (the ocean), one should begin the rite of accomplishment. Having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood in a fire-pit prepared previously, or in an earthen vessel made by a potter, one should offer sixty million oblations of *nāgakeśara* filaments mixed with white sandalwood and camphor—either in very small quantities or in large amounts. 10.5.

And as [the practitioner] offers oblations, the Rākṣasas dwelling in the city of Laṅkā, assuming many forms, raise a cry of "Hā! Hā! and the Nāga kings dwelling in Bhogavatī, the city of the Nāgas, rise up, assuming various forms—both more cruel and more gentle. Those Nāgas and Rākṣasas speak thus: "Arise, Blessed One! Arise, Blessed One! Be our lord! In this way, the Asuras, Yakṣas, Devas, Mahoragas, Siddhas, and all humans entice him. [The practitioner should think: "I must neither rise nor be afraid. 10.6.

Then, while reciting the mantra, the practitioner should threaten them with the index finger of his left hand. Thereupon they flee; they run away hither and thither, and they perish. Then, at the conclusion of the fire offering (*homa*), that boat takes the practitioner and in an instant goes to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. He also goes to and returns from other world-systems. He becomes one who knows the minds of Bodhisattvas, possesses the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), and is endowed with great supernatural power and great majesty. He constantly beholds the noble Mañjuśrī, and all *nāgas*, all *rākṣasas*, all gods, all asuras, and all sentient beings become subject to him; they carry out his commands.

Setting aside all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas, as well as those here who have attained success through mantras, they become compassionate toward him, granting their approval, and he becomes invincible to all beings. 10.7.

Furthermore, there is another supreme means for the practice of ritual action (*karmopayika*). One should have a large boat constructed from *bilva* wood, or else from a collection of logs of a single type of timber. One should also construct a large platform on an island situated in the middle of the Ganges, and upon that, one should place the boat. In that boat, one should station one hundred and twenty persons dressed in white garments, who have performed the protective rites (*kṛtarakṣā*), who hold lamps in their hands, and who have embarked upon the vessel. They should be positioned in front of the image established according to the previously described procedure for the Great Cloth (*jyeṣṭhapaṭa*). Then, having performed a great worship of the cloth, one should offer thirty-six thousand oblations (*āhuti*) of *nāgakesara* powder mixed with saffron, white sandalwood, and camphor, into a fire of *khadira* wood. 10.8.

Then, at the conclusion of the fire offering, she goes with that person to the world of Brahmā in a mere moment. She returns as desired and wanders about. One beholds Noble Mañjuśrī face to face; and upon merely seeing him, one attains the [bodhisattva] stages, becomes endowed with the five superknowledges, lives for a long time, remains for a great eon, and becomes a universal monarch of the great vidyādharas. Those lamp-bearers become his accomplished vidyādharas and companions. Together with them, he wanders as he pleases; he moves according to his own will. He becomes devoted to making offerings to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and in the end, his attainment of Buddhahood is certain. 10.9.
Furthermore, it becomes the supreme means for accomplishing ritual actions (*karmopayika*).
On a riverbank, on the shore of the ocean, or likewise on the Himavat mountain, or on this Vindhya king of mountains—one should accomplish the highest rite. (10.10)
On Mount Sahya and Malaya, as well as on Arbuda and Gandhamādana,
and on this Trikūṭa, the king of mountains— one should accomplish the supreme rite.
In the great ocean, as well as on mountains rich with trees and abounding in flowers—in these regions, indeed, the mantras spoken by the Jina are accomplished.
In a secluded, pure, and remote place, free from the ways of village life,
or likewise in a mountain cave, all the kings of mantras are accomplished.
In a delightful place for dwelling and sitting at the edge of the forest, likewise praised by the Best of Jinas,
and free from malevolent beings, all the kings of mantras are accomplished.
When the king is righteous, when the people in the land are devoted to purity and proper conduct, when they are devoted to their mothers and fathers, and when the twice-born castes are not excluded,
then the deities attain success in that place, and not otherwise.
On the delightful bank of the Bhāgīrathī and the most beautiful Yamunā, [the deities attain success].
On the banks of the Sindhu and Narmada, and on the pure shore of the Candrabhāgā;
the Kāverī, the Sarasvatī, and the white Devamahānadī—these have been declared by the sons of the Ten-Powered One to be fields of supernatural power (siddhikṣetra). || 10.16–17 ||
The ten-powered ones have described the fields as the mountains of the northern region: in Kaśmīra, in the land of Cīna, in Nepāla, and likewise in Kāviśa. || 10.18 ||
Furthermore, in Mahācīna, there are indeed the fields of accomplishment and the sites of attainment without exception;
whatever mountains and rivers exist, they all rely upon the northern direction.
And those lands which are declared to be meritorious, where people eat barley and wheat, and where beings are compassionate— in those places, success will certainly be achieved.
On the great mountain Śrīparvata, known as Dakṣiṇāpatha,
at the shrine of Śrīdhānyakaṭaka on earth which contains the relics of the Jina.
There, indeed, mantras are quickly accomplished in all matters and rites—
at the Vajrāsana, at the Great Caitya, and at the beautiful Dharmacakra.
The supreme sage attained peace there as well, and perfection is seen even there—
at the great shrine of Devāvatāra and at Saṅkāśya, where the great miracle occurred.
In the great city named Kapila, in the excellent grove of Lumbinī, the preeminent place praised by the most eminent of Victors, the king of mantras is accomplished there. (10.24)
Likewise on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, always in the Śītavana grove on earth, in the excellent and delightful city named Kusumapura, and always in the city of Kāśī; 10.25.
In Madhura, Kanyakubja, and the city of Ujjayinī on earth;
likewise in Vaiśālī, at the Caitya, and always in Mithilā on earth.
But for those who are leaders of cities and towns, or others born among the common people, success is ordained for them in a highly praised and meritorious region.
These and other regions—villages, districts, and market towns; cities and excellent capitals, or sacred places situated along rivers. || 10.28 ||
There, following the practice of alms-gathering, one should be devoted to recitation and fire-offerings,
always in a dwelling, in the open air, or in an empty shrine.
One should perform the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) for all rites of the mantras.
In the Middle Country, the practitioner should always recite the mantra everywhere. || 10.30 ||

Always engaged in the recitation of mantras, disciplined, and devoted to the practice of renunciation, the knower of mantras (mantravid) should be virtuous in conduct and observance, truthful, and intent on the welfare of all beings.
(10.31) Having faith in the practice of mantras, the practitioner (vratī) should first perform the recitation in a pure place, a fertile field, free from barbarians and thieves. (10.32)
In all [places] such as those inhabited by crawling reptiles, it is prescribed that one should avoid [such spots]; however,
[it is recommended] in a place endowed with fruits and flowers, which is praiseworthy and possesses pure water.
All these mantra-knowers proclaim the mantra; it is not recited in other places.
[It is recited] in a temple or in a cremation ground, or in a place characterized by a single tree. 10.34.
Likewise, at a solitary linga in a remote place, the knower of mantras,
having performed self-protection for himself and his companions, should indeed perform the *puraścaraṇa*.
The mantra-practitioner, always joined with the mantra, should constantly practice the supreme mantra in a great forest, by a large tree, rich in flowers and yielding fruit.
On a mountain peak,
at a waterfall, in a pure and clean place of water, or on the excellent bank of a great river.
One who knows the mantra should practice it in these places here:
in the eastern region, at Lauhitya, and at the Mahānadī, the auspicious river. 10.38–39ab.
Likewise, in the region of Kāmarūpa, in that most excellent city called Vardhamāna,
where that most meritorious and foremost of rivers flows, closely joined by a stream.
In that place, the practitioner of recitation (jāpī), being pure, should always resort to a beautiful grove;
therefore, one should indeed perform the preliminary service (pūrvasevā) for all ritual acts.
Likewise, at Gaṅgādvāra and constantly at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean,
one who is pure and observant of vows should indeed recite the mantra during its practical application.
These are the great cremation grounds; there the reciter should always perform his recitation.
(42) There are rivers with pure water, free from worms.
(10.42) For this very reason, the reciter, being composed, should recite the mantra there.
Indeed, no merit whatsoever is seen there in the activities of the world.
But rather, under the pretext of [learning] mantras, he should indeed dwell there for some time;
or else, at the proper occasion during a lunar eclipse, he should go elsewhere from that place.
When the time has arrived, he may dwell there for a short while, but not otherwise;
or else, the mantra-knower who is capable should depart from there quickly.
One should always dwell upon the ground at the shrines where the Sugata has resided; [one should avoid] all worldly pilgrimage sites and those fallen into wrong views. 10.46
A knower of mantras should always avoid other sacred sites;

the one who knows the mantra should not dwell there, for such places give rise to the path of false causes. (10.47) That ground which has been traversed by the supreme Jinas and by the Pratyekabuddhas who possess the sword-like wisdom—
48. Together with the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, and the śrāvakas, the sons of the supreme Victors.
The knower of mantras, reciting the mantra, should frequent all those places;
first, with such diligence, he should always practice in that location.

One who knows the mantras should recite the mantra again and again according to the prescribed rule; for through recitation and burnt offerings, he destroys all the sins of embodied beings without exception.
Therefore, with every effort, one should recite the mantra with a well-composed mind. || 10.50 ||

These locations have been prescribed for all rites, as well as for the practices conducive to the supreme rite. In the absence of these, one should perform the preliminary service (*pūrvassevā*) in any pure place whatsoever.

One who is devoted with faith should carry out the supreme rite conducive to the practice. First, having installed the senior cloth-painting (*paṭa*) facing west, and having positioned oneself facing east, [one should take] earth from the top of an anthill, or...

Having taken clay from the bank of the Gaṅgā river, or having mixed uśīra, white sandalwood, saffron, camphor, and other substances, one should fashion the form of a peacock. Having placed it before the cloth painting (*paṭa*), and having fashioned a circular shape with uncut-tipped *kuśa* grass grown in a pure place, one should hold it with the right hand while holding the peacock with the left hand before the cloth painting. On the night of the full moon, having performed a great worship of the cloth painting and burning camphor incense, one should recite the mantra until dawn. 10.52. {S91}

Then, at the time of sunrise, that clay [image] becomes a peacock, the Great King of Peacocks. The discus also blazes. And he himself possesses a divine body, adorned with celestial garlands, garments, and ornaments; he resembles the rising sun, able to assume any form at will. Having prostrated before all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and circumambulated the cloth painting, he takes hold of the painting and sits upon that peacock throne. In an instant, he transcends the Brahma-world. Surrounded by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of millions of *vidyādhara*s, he becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of the *vidyādhara*s. He lives for sixty *manvantara*-kalpas. His movement proceeds according to his desire, his gait being unimpeded. He is endowed with divine prosperity and beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face-to-face. That very one becomes his spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), and in the end, he attains Buddhahood.
"He attains," [it is said]. 10.53.
In this manner, [he fashioned] various specific weapons made of clay, such as a staff, a water-pot, a sacred thread, red arsenic, yellow orpiment, a sword, iron arrows, slings, and axes.

Having washed or sprinkled with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) all two-legged and four-legged beings, specific mounts such as birds, lions, tigers, bears, and the like—whether made of anthill clay or riverbank clay—and those overflowing with fragrant scents; having consecrated them one hundred and eight times with the purification mantra, the single-syllable mantra, or any other mantra taught in this King of Rituals (*kalparāja*), excluding only those mantras used for the subsidiary practice (*anusādhana*); then, having performed protection for oneself and having provided refuge for one’s companions, one who is well-versed in the secrets of the mantras and tantras may, according to his own desire and preference, [use] all these specific jewels, all specific requisites of renunciants—such as rosaries, sandals, wooden clogs, bowls, robes, water-strainers, needles, and tools—whether made of flower-metal (*puṣpaloha*) or otherwise, including any collection of utensils and implements, whether made of flower-metal, anthill clay, or riverbank clay, in the previously specified locations.

Having established [the image] facing west and performed a great worship of the cloth-painting as before for oneself, while burning camphor incense for the eldest [deity], one should take up any one of those previously specified weapons, implements, or all the various special [objects], including the previously mentioned artificial ones, on the night of the full moon of the month of Jyeṣṭha; and during that night, one should recite the mantra until the time of sunrise. 10.54.

In this interval, a cloth [painting] encircled by a great radiance is seen. If a particular vehicle has been taken up by the practitioner, then having mounted it, he goes wherever he desires. If it is a particular ornament or a particular weapon, having taken that, he becomes a venerable universal monarch of the *vidyādharas*. He goes wherever he desires with a divine form, resembling the rising sun, encircled by a great radiance, his body flashing like lightning, the lord of all *vidyādharas*, long-lived, remaining for a great *kalpa*, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of millions of *vidyādharas*, and moving about with divine great jewels and gems. (10.55)

Whatever vehicle was previously envisioned by which he was seen and by which he attained accomplishment, that very thing becomes his source of great power. That alone becomes his vehicle; that alone becomes his companion. Having warded off the accomplishments of others' mantras, he remains constantly devoted to the accomplishment of his own mantra, characterized by a nature of loving-kindness and desiring the welfare [of others]. Whatever specific weapons, ornaments, jewels, seats, beds, vehicles, living beings, and so forth he possesses, those very things become his constant attendants for the sake of great protection, covering, and guarding. (10.56)

He becomes possessed of great majesty, great heroism, and a vast body. He beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face, who grants him his approval. By being touched upon the crown of his head, he obtains the status of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) until he reaches the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*). He will certainly attain the state of the Ten Powers (*daśabala*) and become worthy of worship by all sentient beings. He shall be invincible and unassailable by all spirits (*bhūta*), and he will not sever the lineage of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). He attains the [Bodhisattva] stages (*bhūmi*) and enters the certainty of the Bodhisattvas regarding the Ten Powers. In brief, one who abides in the supreme state, who delights in supreme worship before the supreme cloth painting (*paṭa*), should perform only supreme deeds. (10.57)

For the sake of attaining the state of a *vidyādhara*, the power of traveling through the sky, entry into the stage of a *bodhisattva*, the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), and the attainment of the [bodhisattva] stages; for the sake of traversing world-systems with this very body; for the sake of fulfilling the lineage of the Ten Powers; for the sake of the direct vision of the noble Mañjuśrī; for the sake of hearing the teaching of the Dharma from one whose vision is never fruitless; for the sake of ensuring the non-interruption of the lineage of the Buddhas; for the sake of gradually attaining the knowledge of the Omniscient One; for the sake of entering into the outpouring of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*); and for the sake of pacifying the afflictions by bearing a rain of nectar that dries them up—this is the activity of benefiting the world.
For the sake of practice,
and for the sake of making the words of the Tathāgata fruitful.

For the sake of manifestation, for the sake of proclaiming the Dharma of the greatness of the Buddhas and the noble Śrāvakas, this extensive collection of the King of Rituals (Kalparāja) is to be accomplished. 10.58.
For the sake of protecting the eye of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, [this is] the method for the practice and accomplishment of mantras, common to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Pratyekabuddhas.

In all worldly and transcendent mantra-calculation manuals (*mantrakalpa*) and all tantras, including those associated with the *apratibhāṣa* mantras and situated near the foremost of the elder scrolls, this King of Scrolls is to be accomplished through the ritual path in brief, even by means of rites spoken in other manuals. The accomplishment of those mantras will be swift; whatever has been taught by me shall certainly succeed. (10.59)

The tenth chapter, the detailed section on the ritual for the supreme cloth-painting, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, is completed.
{S93} {V66} Chapter A11:
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī, the Youthful:

"Mañjuśrī, there exists your medium-sized cloth-painting ritual (*paṭavidhāna*), the procedure for the practice (*sādhanavidhi*) suitable for middling rites. I shall speak of it in brief. Listen to it; attend well and thoroughly to it. I shall speak. (11.1)
Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, spoke thus to the Blessed One:

"May the Blessed One, the Teacher who has compassion for the world and delights in the welfare of all beings, speak now, if he deems it the right time; out of compassion for us and having regard for future generations. (11.2)

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī, the Youthful: “Listen, Mañjuśrī! First of all, there is the procedure for ethical discipline (*śīla*), vows (*vrata*), purity (*śauca*), conduct (*ācāra*), observances (*niyama*), recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), and meditation (*dhyāna*), in which all ritual actions for the practice and accomplishment of mantras become unfailing and fruitful. Quickly, all ritual actions for the practice and accomplishment of mantras become unfailing and fruitful; and quickly, all applications of mantra attain success. And what is that? I shall speak it; listen, O Youthful. (11.3)

First of all, one should initially undertake the undertaking of the vows of knowledge, conduct, and discipline. First, one should enter the time of instruction from a Maṇḍala Master, as clearly stated in your King of Rituals (*Kalparāja*). Having found an intelligent person who has received the initiation of a Master (*ācāryābhiṣeka*), who is knowledgeable in the teaching, skillful, clear-minded, righteous, truthful, highly energetic, grateful, firm in friendship, neither too old nor too young, free from desire for all gain and honor, celibate, and compassionate—one who does not speak falsely out of mere greed, for the sake of enjoyment, or for the sake of compliance, let alone [for other reasons].

One who possesses even a small measure of compassion toward all beings through various forms of greed and delusion, who is habituated to giving, who recites the secret mantras of yours, who has entered your mandala in the proper sequence, who knows the world, who knows the ritual rules, who is benevolent, who has business [with the Dharma], who is discerning, who is intent on the highest good, who is fearless, undaunted, not timid, firm in vigor, free from disease, and who—whatever that disease may be—is not habitually inactive, and who is born of a very high family: one endowed with these qualities becomes a master of the mandala. (11.4)
One who is firm in his vow, equanimous, has performed the preliminary rites, and has mastered the sciences through prior service.
The practitioner—whether equal to or slightly inferior to him—in having requested such a Maṇḍala Master with the appropriate preliminary rites, should entreat him as follows:

“O Master, I desire to enter the samaya of the Great Bodhisattva, the youthful Ārya Mañjuśrī. Therefore, may the Master, out of compassion for us, with a mind intent on our welfare and full of mercy, speak [to grant this]. (11.5)

Then, that mandala master, having examined the disciples according to the previously described procedure as before, should cause them to enter. Having conferred the empowerment as before, he should bestow the mantra. He should duly and sequentially reveal the commitments (samaya), as well as the secret tantras, mudrās, and ritual actions. Only after examining them thoroughly over a long period and knowing their disposition should he reveal the ritual actions pertaining to all tantras, mantras, and so forth, and not to others. This is the rule proclaimed. 11.6.
Then, the disciple should offer himself and his possessions to the mandala master according to his ability, or whatever else might please the master. (11.7)
Then, that mandala master should establish the notion of [the disciple] as a son; he should behave toward him like a son, and provide him with the mother’s enjoyments. || 11.8 ||

Then, having taken up a certain mantra, that practitioner should go to a secluded place and, in a location previously specified, perform—using those very same mantras—the extensive rites of summoning, dismissal, and the offering of lamps, perfumes, incense, and bali-oblations according to the procedure taught for the maṇḍala. Having summoned [the deity] and offered water for the feet (*argha*) and a seat, he should perform the recitation (*japa*) every day at the three junctions of the day, bathing three times and changing his clothes three times. In this context, "time of the junction" (*sandhyākāla*) refers to the period beginning from the end of night until the sun has risen to the height of a yoke; within this interval, it is called the first junction. At midday, when the solar disc is situated in the sky at a distance of one yoke’s length from both ends, it is called the middle junction. And at the time of sunset, when one yoke’s length remains [before the sun sets], it is called the third junction. || 11.9 ||
One who is endowed with moral conduct and vows, a teacher who is skillful and wise, born of a great and noble lineage, and possessed of firm vigor in every respect. || 11.10 ||
Devoted to mantra and tantra, with an intellect skilled in all undertakings,
he is subtle, proficient in knowing mantras, and always upholds the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Possessing great energy and brilliance, disregarding worldly dharmas, I am one who has faith in the dharma of the supreme sages, while worldly things have been abandoned by me. (11.12)
One who has performed the recitation, who understands discernment, and who practices the preliminary service;
one who knows the mantra of Mañjughoṣa and is intent upon having witnessed its efficacy;
{S95} one who knows the application of worldly mantras spoken by the Buddha, who has established protection, possesses firm strength, and is always devoted to pure conduct.
Following in every respect the path taught by the Buddha, I am devotedly engaged in this praiseworthy recitation of mantras, which has been extolled by the Conqueror.
Always perceiving the fruits of actions in this world and likewise in the next world,
one should be fearless regarding all evils, even those as small as an atom;
moreover, one should be pure, skillful, free from excessive laziness, wise, and pleasant to behold.

The mantras taught by those possessing the ten powers, as well as by the sons of the Victors, and whatever worldly mantras belong to the Vajra and Lotus families—for these he has constantly exerted effort, being a bearer of the meaning of the texts and treatises. (11.17)
Free from disease, not subject to incapacity, and devoid of both old age and childhood;
having perfected mantras, likewise protected, and swift in action in every respect.
Not procrastinating, likewise free from pride, and especially skilled in discerning gestures;
a celibate student of great wisdom, he took no pleasure in the company of others.

One who has received initiation, who is heroic, and who is skilled in this tantra spoken by Mañjuśrī; one who is engaged in the completion of recitation and likewise accomplished in the sciences (vidyā).
He was of great majesty, a knower of the world, a contemplator of the truth of the states of existence;
he was devoted solely to the highest good, a giver, and intent on the welfare of all beings.
Likewise, one must always indeed request a distinguished preceptor;
the mandala of mantras written by him attains accomplishment.
By bestowing the consecration in this manner, a great fruit is obtained.
Those disciples who desire spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) should always honor him as they would a sage.
His word must be diligently obeyed by the disciples; they should offer him enjoyments according to their available means.
Whether it be of very little measure or abundant, by whatever means he attains satisfaction— for the sake of his body and life— he should offer his mind and his person to his father;
in that same way, a student who knows the Dharma should give wealth to his teacher.
One shall obtain fame, success, long life, and indeed health.
The disciple who honors that guru attains an abundant state;
and his mantras become effective through the teacher's demonstration of the path of ritual procedure. 11.27
Through serving them, through honoring them, and even through worshiping them, all the Buddhas as well as the sons of the supreme Victors are likewise pleased. (11.28)
All the gods are indeed pleased when there is always proper honor shown toward the guru.
All this has been told regarding gurus who perceive the mantras.
First, at the very beginning, for the practitioner who has entered the samaya, whether it be a person equal to him, similar to him, or even superior—if such a one should exist—30.11.30.
A guru must never be disparaged, whether he is equal to oneself or even superior;
for in this tantra, instruction must always be given by him to one who has attained mastery in mantra, as it is observed for the sake of sentient beings. (11.31)
One should not be envious toward this disciple previously prepared;
for those whose bodies are well-established, the eye follows with affection. 11.32
One should indeed practice discipleship toward teachers who act for the sake of their disciples;
where there exists a mutual conformity characterized by a continuous flow of affection.
In that situation, the teacher should indeed impart the mantra to one whose mental continuum is affectionate; likewise, a disciple should do so upon seeing the guru. 11.34.
Both of you shall be ever eager for constant union with her;
indeed, you two shall always follow the path of their mantra-practice and contemplation.

Both were knowers of mantras who followed their practice with fruitfulness, each being like a father to the other; thus both the disciple and the teacher always attained steadfastness and contentment.
A son who is devoted to the Dharma must always be protected with great effort;
for such individuals, the nature of the Buddhas is indeed one of non-interruption.
