Indeed, in the absence of that [patron], one should give the mantra as prescribed to those who are destitute—especially to poor beings and to the weak—and to all beings whatsoever; the practice of mantra is superior for them all. One should perform it at all times: whether in inferior, superior, or middling circumstances.
39. One should always, in all matters, act for the sake of benefiting others. || 11.39 ||

One should give [the gift] even to those who are worthy of it, for such is the destiny and birth resulting from one's conduct; indeed, the disciple himself, having received the mantra from him according to his capacity, [should act accordingly]. 11.40.
One who desires success should strive in that [path] alone, which is taught by Him, and not otherwise; for all others are dependent on it.
Having bowed with his head as if to a father, he should indeed depart humbly as he pleases; then, having gone to a solitary place, he should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind.
But the mendicant monk, subsisting on alms-food, observing silence, and reciting prayers three times a day, should proceed according to the path as previously described. 11.43.
Then, following that [practice], he should be a practitioner of service in a secluded place,
a sanctuary, a great forest, on a mountain peak, or likewise on the pure bank of a river.
In a cow-pen, or even in a great city, in a secluded place devoid of people; in an empty temple, at a tree, at a solitary linga, or on a mountain peak.
On the delightful banks of a great river, or on a sandbank, or at a lamp-lighting site,
or in various other charming locations previously specified—

by these and other such places, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind, accompanied by friends who possess the proper characteristics and are experts in the logic and meaning of the mantra.
[He was served] by those who knew the truth of gestures and facial expressions, who were like himself and similar to him,
who were heroes who had conquered in battle, and who were virtuous and patient.

In this teaching proclaimed by the Victor, one should perform the ritual service of mantras with faith, accompanied by assistants who are praiseworthy, endowed with the [auspicious] marks, and patient. (11.49)

For him, indeed, all rites are accomplished without any effort. Having risen from bed in the morning and bathed in pure water— specifically in water free of living organisms that originates from a river or a great lake— {S98} [he attains success].
Having rubbed his body with powdered clay and cow dung, the knower of mantras [should proceed].
Then, having purified the clean and perfectly clear water with mantras, the practitioner of recitation, with a disciplined mind, should bathe; he must not let the proper time pass by.
Then, having risen and stood on the bank, he washed his hands with clay twenty-one times— seven, seven, and again seven.
Then, having sat down there, one should employ a tooth-stick;
having discarded the tooth-cleanser, one should then pay homage to the Protector (Tāyin).
Having paid homage to the Lord of the World, one should perform a delightful worship.
Having praised him again and again with various offerings of hymns of praise.
Then, having offered an *argha* with fragrant flowers to the Teacher,
the practitioner of recitation should bow his head to the Buddhas who have arisen as disciples.
57. One should confess one's sins in the presence of those Lords of the World, and having offered food there, in front of the central painting.
Seated there, composed and concentrated, having formed a bundle of kuśa grass, one should perform the recitation with effort using that rosary. 11.58.
One should indeed recite only the mantra as it was received, and not another mantra at that time; one should avoid what is excessively inferior or excessively superior.

The practitioner of the vow should always recite the mantra in a moderate tone during intermediate rites; he should carefully avoid speech that is excessively loud, as well as any other [inappropriate] speech.

The medium [speed] is praised for medium activities and extolled by the Victors. One should always recite with a medium speed—neither too high nor too low—for this was the word joined with excellence by all the Buddhas of the past. (Ap11.47, 11.61)
One should never mutter [the mantra] in the presence of others or within the range of another's hearing;
rather, one should mutter the middling mantra in a secluded place known only to oneself.
Likewise, if someone well-versed in the meaning of the mantra should apply himself to the recitation,
he should recite that mantra again if he desires middling accomplishment.
Therefore, when [the obstacle] has departed from the being who is well-versed in the true meaning of the mantra—
64. But the reciter of mantras should recite them in solitude, free from the bustle of others. || 11.64 ||
In the fourth part of the night, at exactly half of that [quarter], when the solar disc has risen just a yoke’s length high and is copper-red; || 11.65 ||
Thus has the first twilight been described by the foremost of sages; the middle [twilight] is proclaimed to be four cubits, measuring a yuga.
Then, when the sun had risen into the sky, he should cease the recitation of the mantra.
Having ceased the mantra-recitation and performed the ritual dismissal (visarjana), the observer of the vow offered the arghya water.
Then, for the remainder of the time, he is engaged in what is wholesome within this teaching of the Sage, such as the recitation of the true Dharma, the Perfection of Wisdom, and so forth.
The books known as the *Daśabhūmika* should always be honored and recited;
therefore, when the time has come, one should indeed bow down to the preeminent Jinas.

Then one should go to one’s own mantra and the Lord of Mantras, and not for the sake of a livelihood. (70) Thus engaged as a practitioner of Time (*kālacārī*), eating at the proper time, with senses subdued, (11.70) virtuous, diligent in practice, and with serene faith in the Buddha’s teaching, one should enter among the villages observing silence, always devoted to pure conduct. (11.71)
The practitioner of recitation should always enter the house of a righteous being for alms, [using] water that is free of living organisms, prepared, and considered pure. (11.72)
In such a family, where the Buddha’s teaching is serene and possesses the consort of right view, one who seeks alms should always receive his begging bowl.
Just as a well-armored warrior may enter the thick of battle, constantly crushing his enemies and never being slain by them; 11.74.
In this way, the practitioner, subsisting on alms, should always enter the village;
likewise, having seen a pleasing form or indeed auspicious sounds, [he should remain undisturbed].
For the sake of pacifying passion, one should contemplate both the impure and the pure.
Having seen a female body adorned with the conduct of youth,
one should contemplate it as impure, foul-smelling, and loathsome, consisting of putrid urine and other such things.
Drenched with worms, this impure body lying in the cemetery is impermanent and suffering.
Fools, indeed deluded by mantras, wander through the five states of existence;
bound by the threads of karma, they shine for a long time.
But those deluded ones, shrouded by ignorance, are like those blind from birth; they are the cause of suffering, for therein creatures with perverted intellects become attached and perish. (11.79)
Adorned with various ornaments and colored in many ways,
they were mounted upon long swings and busied themselves with coming and going.
But those beings who delight in impurity, though engaged in the movements and gestures of dancing, sink down for a long time upon that path. (11.81)

For those born from the waters of the ocean of existence, their births— which resemble the buckets of a waterwheel— never come to an end as they remain submerged in the flood of the waters of suffering.
For it has been said by the Buddhas, as well as by the Śrāvakas, Bodhisattvas, and Pratyekabuddhas, that woman alone is the root of suffering. (11.83)
This great ocean, difficult to dry up and unshakeable—the sea of existence—in which beings, their consciousness deceived, sink because of women. (11.84)
He always has access to hell, the world of animals, the world of hungry ghosts along with that of the asuras, the human world, and indeed the divine realms; such is his constant destiny.
Indeed, they wander about in every direction, powerless and deceived by women;
they sink into the great mire of the prison of the ocean of saṃsāra. Fools who are attached to women are like jackals attracted by a corpse.
Where beings are constantly attached, they indeed endure intense sufferings.
Those who have destroyed all pure dharmas and yet have entered the teaching of the Buddha ward off all sufferings within the ocean of existence.
Those who are devoted to the practice of mantra-recitation, who possess the vision of Maheśa, and are wise;
those who are radiant and have conquered their enemies—for them, no suffering exists.
(11.89) Those who are self-restrained, who know the truth of Brahman, and who worship their gurus and deities.
For those who are devoted to their mother and father, no suffering exists among women.
For those who pursue the ultimate truth, the female body is impermanent, suffering, and empty; for those who recite mantras, it is like a tumor or a thorn. (11.91)
One who is passionate, foolish, and of corrupt intellect, who has not fled from saṃsāra and is constantly addicted to women—for him, there is no accomplishment. 11.92
For one who recites [the mantra] here while being of immoral conduct, there is no superior destination, nor even a middling destination; there is not even the lowest accomplishment. 11.93
The Lord of Sages has not taught the accomplishment of mantras for one of immoral conduct;
nor has he taught the path or the direction leading to the city of Nirvana.
How indeed could mantras succeed for a fool in this contemptible state?
Moreover, there is no happy rebirth for that person of immoral conduct in this world.
Nor indeed will they reach the vault of heaven, nor will they be devoted to happiness;
how much less, then, could they attain the accomplishment of the mantras spoken by the Jina?
But when a palmyra tree has been cut down at its very top, it is incapable of becoming green again or of producing new sprouts. (11.97)

Thus, the accomplishment of mantras has been proclaimed here for the fool; but how can the king of mantras be accomplished by one who is of evil conduct, a doer of wicked deeds, always attached to women, and associated with unwholesome friends? 11.98.
Therefore, one who is self-controlled, always reciting mantras, and not reflecting upon the faults of women—let him avoid attachment to them; for accomplishment is ordained through them. 11.99
Success has not been declared for others—those who are foolish or infatuated with women. The wise man, delighting in composure, pure, skillful, and free from attachment, [attains it].
One who is of noble birth, firm and brave, friendly, and pleasing to behold;
one who knows how to discern between righteousness and unrighteousness—for such as these, success is not difficult to attain.
Thus engaged and knowing the mantras, he should enter a village for the sake of alms.
Having gone to this previously prepared place as desired,
one should eat there;
having gone to a pure location, one of pure intellect should set down the alms-bowl.
Having washed his feet and gone out from that dwelling,
he should first wash only his shank in water that is free of living organisms.
Then, with his second left hand, he should embrace and rub his shank;
having performed this again on the right side, he should wash his hands with clay.
Then, using seven vessels that have been previously consecrated, which are pure, clean, stainless,
and purified by mantras, one should place [the offering] in a clean and spotless bowl.
Having taken cow-dung and lime that has flowed from a tawny cow,
and having mixed it with water free of living organisms, one should prepare a circular mandala for the Teacher.
First, one should especially construct a [stūpa] one cubit in size for the Best of Sages;
second, for the Lord of the Good Mantra; and third, for the Family Deity.
Whatever the mantra-reciter may do at that time, he should always perform it again as the fourth [offering] for the enjoyment of all sentient beings.
Here, in the southern mandala of the Lord of the World, it is always [performed].
For the sake of the Three Jewels, one should construct that mandala as a square.
The second belongs to the Pratyekabuddhas, and the third to the sons of the Ten-Powered One. Thus, these seven mandalas are square on all sides.
The reciter of mantras should then perform this daily in a secret place, for one cubit or even half a cubit in size, day after day; it destroys all sins every single day.
Then, having risen, the mantra-practitioner should again wash his hands with care;
having sipped water in clean, pure water that is free from living organisms.
In a pure and clean vessel, carefully brought from a great lake, a spring, a well, or the flowing current of a river; (11.114)
Having sipped water again two or three times, the mantra-practitioner should always do so after [the water] has come from a pure place and been drawn up by a pure being with his hands. (11.115)
Then one should touch the face, the ears, and likewise the eyes,
the nostrils, and the arms;
one should also touch the head and the region of the navel with auspicious water.
One should perform all this according to the rules, either one hundred and seventeen times or fifty-seven times.
(11.117) Having become pure and perfected in the conduct of purification, the practitioner of recitation (*jāpin*), taking his alms-bowl, should go to a body of water. (11.118)
Wherever a river flows or originates, there he should always wash his alms-bowl from rivers, springs, and the like. (11.119)
Then, having risen from there, he should go again to the monastery or indeed to his dwelling;
he should go to that very place where he previously resided and remained.
Having gone to that place, the reciter should set down his bowl;
then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśya), he should quickly take up the bowl again.
One should offer the presentation to the Teacher in a vessel made of clay, a leaf, silver, or even gold; or likewise in one of copper or bark.
The King of Mantras, moreover, should present the food offering to the Teacher with his own mantra.
Having approached even a single guest among those who are suffering, he should give according to his ability. (11.123)
One should not offer an excessive amount of the oblation in any respect;
the knower of mantras should act with skill in every way, never failing himself.
He always gave her food only sufficient to fill her belly; thus,
neither afflicted by hunger nor thirst, she was able to accomplish the purpose of the mantra.
Neither eating excessively nor eating too little, one who is capable of following the mantras—precisely for this reason was it said by the Lord of Jinas for all embodied beings. (11.126)
Food is the sustenance of sentient beings, by which humans live,
as well as gods, asuras, gandharvas, nāgas, yakṣas, and kiṃnaras.
Neither Rākṣasas, nor Pretas, nor Piśācas, nor Bhūtas, nor those who drive away spirits, nor Grahas—none of these exist who can look upon him with hostile intent. (11.128)
The Tathāgata has declared that beings who consume food in gross forms are called those who take solid food, while those who consume subtle food are indeed the subtle-eating beings.
The divine beings who subsist on the food of meditative absorption (dhyāna) manifest activities belonging to the realm of form;

the gods of the formless realm (ārūpya), indeed, enjoy the fruit of meditative concentration (samādhi). Intermediate state beings are proclaimed to be sustained by the food of movement; likewise, the various beings in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) consume diverse kinds of food.
The Kāmikas [are the lords] of the asuras and mortals; they subsist on food consisting of morsels. || 11.131 ||
For this very reason, the Lords of Jinas have declared that the subsistence of all sentient beings through food has been proclaimed by means of the causes of karma.
But for one who recites [the mantra] constantly and with steady application, the very act of eating itself is the measure;
for established in this eating, he is indeed capable of practicing the mantras. (11.133)
But for one who is purified in conduct, skilled in the practice of celibacy, and possesses moderation in eating, success is not difficult to attain. (11.134)
Just as one anoints the axle of a cart with oil for the sake of its long-term endurance and as a means for bearing heavy loads, so too [is this practice].
In the same way, the mantra-practitioner who knows the mantras should provide food for the maintenance of the body;
the reciter of mantras should always nourish it for the sake of sustaining it.
For the sake of accomplishing mantras and for the cause of gathering the requisites for enlightenment,
one should likewise recite the mantra among mortals for the purpose of benefiting the worlds.
For this very reason, the sage of great splendor said, "I am the best of munis," and in former times on this earth, he was always known by the name Kāśyapa.
Indeed, for the sake of the welfare of all beings, he spoke this mantra for all the suffering people of the world who are wretched and distressed by poverty.
For the sake of those who have ceased their exertion and are afflicted, it was spoken for their benefit;
likewise, for the welfare of beings wandering in saṃsāra, one should recite this supreme mantra for the sake of the sustenance of beings. 11.140–141ab.
"May all the śrāvakas and those who rely upon awakening listen!
Receive this word of mine, this mantra that destroys disease."
But those beings who are afflicted by the disease of hunger, and those who are thirsty—listen, you who desire prosperity, for the sake of pacifying all suffering. (11.142)
Having spoken thus, that Kāśyapa, who was like a sage and possessed of great splendor, [spoke]; and the disciples, with contented minds, entreated that Lord:
"O Knower of Dharma, King of Dharma, Great Sage, please teach us the mantra."
Compassionate toward sentient beings, the supreme commitment has now arrived.
Having spoken thus, the foremost of sages should recite the mantra in detail—its sound like the warbling of a kalaviṅka bird, and its resonance like the drum or the thundercloud.
The Conqueror has the voice of Brahmā and possesses great heroism; for he is the leader of the Brahmās.
Let all the hosts of beings, whoever have come here, indeed listen! 11.146.
Whether they have no feet, many feet, two feet, or four feet— in brief, for the sake of all sentient beings, I shall proclaim this mantra that brings about happiness.
"Beings of the past and future have come here in the present;
I shall speak in brief—listen, you who desire prosperity! (11.148) {V76}

Homage to all the Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! It is as follows: Oṃ gagane gaganagañje! Bring [it] all, quickly, quickly! Remember your vow! O summoner, do not delay, do not delay! Accomplish for me whatever is desired, svāhā! Having spoken thus, the Blessed One Kāśyapa became silent. (11.149)

In the meantime, by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, through the extensive words of the spells and mantras, the entire sky was seen to be filled with clouds of most precious food. The whole of this triple-thousand great thousandfold world system was seen with the surface of the sky completely covered by clouds of food. To whichever being desired food according to their inclination, whatever nourishment they preferred, that very thing was provided for them. And with such nourishment as they desired, the function of eating was fulfilled for the sake of pacifying the suffering of hunger; and for those who were thirsty, there was drink and water endowed with the eight qualities.
There, a stream of water fell exactly as desired.

And at that time, at that very moment, all sentient beings had their every affliction of hunger pacified and their every thirst removed. That entire assembly, struck with wonder and filled with joy, having rejoiced and delighted in what the Blessed One had spoken, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and vanished right there. The Blessed One—

Apastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.15.153–155 1.153 When one's own father is alive, one should perform the Śrāddha for the ancestors on the day after the full moon; however, some teachers maintain that it should be performed on the very day of the full moon. 1.154 One should offer the Śrāddha to the ancestors on the new moon day, as well as on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada. 1.155 On the occasion of a birth, one should offer the Śrāddha to the paternal ancestors, while on the occasion of a marriage, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a son’s first cutting of hair (Cūḍākaraṇa), one should offer it to both sets of ancestors. On the occasion of a thread ceremony (Upanayana) or a marriage, one should offer the Śrāddha to the paternal ancestors alone. On the occasion of a house-warming, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a journey, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a sacrifice or a wedding, one should offer it to all the ancestors. On the occasion of a death-impurity (Aśauca), one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of land, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of gold, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a cow, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a horse, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a house, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a garment, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of grain, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of sesame seeds, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of iron, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of salt, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a bed, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a bull, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a goat, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a sheep, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a horse, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a chariot, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a slave, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a field, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a village, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a kingdom, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a daughter, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a bride, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a son, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a grandson, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a great-grandson, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a great-great-grandson, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a daughter-in-law, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a sister, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a brother, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a wife, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a husband, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a son-in-law, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a father-in-law, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a maternal uncle, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a nephew, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a teacher, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a pupil, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a friend, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a relative, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a kinsman, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a guest, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a servant, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a laborer, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a king, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a Brahmin, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a Vaiśya, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a Śūdra, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a woman, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a child, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from an old man, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a sick person, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a traveler, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a forest-dweller, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a hermit, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a sage, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a deity, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a spirit, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a ghost, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a demon, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a celestial being, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a human being, one should offer it to the ancestors of both lineages. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from an animal, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a bird, one should offer it to the maternal ancestors. On the occasion of a gift of a messenger from a fish, one should offer it to the paternal ancestors. And Kāśyapa shall dwell in the dwellings of the Tathāgatas; this has been spoken and approved by me, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, in this supreme King of Ritual Manuals (Kalparāja).

{S106} For the sake of all sentient beings, for the purpose of removing hunger and thirst, and especially for those who recite mantras, the practitioner must first accomplish this mantra. If one is unable to wander for alms, one should ascend a mountain peak and recite it six hundred thousand times, subsisting on the three white foods or consuming only milk. 11.152.

Then, on that very mountain peak, having installed the medium-sized cloth painting (*paṭa*) of the noble Mañjuśrī and having performed a great worship as before, one should present a most magnificent *bali* offering. Having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood fuel using this very mantra spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa, one should offer eight thousand oblations of fresh *audumbara* wood sticks—one cubit (*vitasti*) in length—smeared with curds, honey, and ghee, or else *śrīphala* wood sticks. || 11.153 ||

Then, at the time of midnight, a great circle of black clouds and wind will arrive. One must not be afraid, nor should one rise and depart. One should perform self-protection with the eight-syllable heart-mantra of Noble Mañjuśrī, as well as the binding of the mandala for one's companions, as previously described. Then that circle of black wind will vanish. And women, adorned with all ornaments, garlanded with light, illuminating the quarters of the sky, will appear before the practitioner and say:
"Arise, O Great Being! I have been accomplished."

Then the practitioner should offer an *argha* oblation with scented water mixed with *jātī* flowers. Thereupon, she vanishes right there. On that very day, she provides twenty-five portions of food for himself or for his companions as they desire, and she supplies whatever implements are required. Then the practitioner, having dismissed her and offered the *argha*, should circumambulate the cloth-painting three times, take up the painting, and bow down to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. He should then go to a desired location suitable for practice, as previously described—a great forest, a mountain peak, or a place devoid of humans. Having constructed a hut there with himself or his companions, he should dwell there. While dwelling in that place, he should perform such deeds as traveling through the air. || 11.155 ||

Then the practitioner, seated as before upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, having set up the central cloth painting and kindled a fire with *khadira* wood as before, should offer eight thousand oblations of white flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee at the three junctions of the day for twenty-one days. (11.156) {V77}

Then, at the time of midnight, at the conclusion of the fire offering (homa), one beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face. He grants the desired boon: whether it be the power of moving through the sky, invisibility, the state of a Bodhisattva-bhūmi, the state of a Pratyekabuddha, the state of a Śrāvaka, or the possession of the five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā); or long life, great sovereignty, great wealth, or being beloved by kings; or wandering together with the noble Mañjuśrī—briefly stated, he grants everything that is wished for. Whatever one asks for, he bestows that upon one; or [he grants] perfected substances (siddhadravya).

One obtains everything; one performs the summoning of great beings (*mahāsattvas*). In brief, whatever is spoken, all that one accomplishes. Furthermore, it purifies past karma or transgressions—thus spoke the Blessed One Śākyamuni. 11.157.

Furthermore, there is another intermediate means for the ritual application. First, in a distinguished place, a pure location, or on the sandy bank of a river, having performed everything as previously described, one should install the cloth painting facing west. Then, facing east oneself and seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, the procedure should be carried out in detail as before. One should recite the mantra three times a day for six hundred thousand times. Upon the completion of the recitation, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *karṇikāra* flowers mixed with white sandalwood or saffron.
Having kindled the fire in the same manner as before. || 11.158 ||

And at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (*homaparyavasāna*), if the cloth (*paṭa*) trembles, one attains the status of a mantra-master (*mantritva*); if it is illuminated by rays from the cloth, one attains kingship; if a ray issues forth, one attains sovereignty over the Four Great Kings (*caturmahārājakāyika*); if the cloth is enveloped in a garland of flames on all sides, one attains the lordship of the Thirty-three (*trayastridaśa*), the state of Śakra; if the cloth utters a teaching of the Dharma, one attains the lordship of the three stages of a Bodhisattva; and by touching the arms or the head of the cloth, one attains the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), the seven stages, and the certain attainment of the ten powers (*daśabala*) in due succession. || 11.159 ||

Now, when the practitioner has accomplished the mantra spoken by the Blessed One Kāśyapa (160), and has attained the means for warding off hunger and thirst, he should practice the dharma conducive to accomplishing the purpose of the mantra-conduct according to that very same procedure and with those very same requisites; otherwise, there is no success. Thus [ends section] 11.160.

Thus, the practice of the gradual mantra-conduct should be performed in brief. It will certainly succeed; even the substances, implements, and medicinal herbs, as well as all the remaining jewels and gems, will be effective just as previously described. || 11.161 ||
In that place, the mantra-knower, reciting the mantra with a mind focused on the prescribed ritual, should then eat white rice prepared by one born of a pure family.
But having eaten with a satisfied mind and always with well-nourished faculties,
he should take that remnant in his bowl and go to a river of pure water.
Having discarded it in a secluded place, the observer of the vow gave it to the animals.

Having given it to the animals, he diligently washed the vessel. He then carefully subjected the earthen vessel to firing again. As for the remaining vessel, he made it free of grease and free of meat.
Having completely abandoned even the scent [of food], the excellent sage should not eat his meal in that vessel in which he wanders for alms. (11.166)
One should never eat edible fruits there;
one should not eat from a lotus leaf, nor from those produced from the *kuvalaya* lily. One should avoid fragrant flowers (*saugandhika*); the mantra-practitioner does not eat from them.
168. And those leaves which come from the *kaumuda*, the *plakṣa*, and the *udumbara* trees.
Nor indeed should *karṇaśāka* be eaten by those suffering from abdominal tumors using *vaṭa* leaves,
nor likewise with mango leaves or those produced from the *pālāśa* tree.
With *śāla* leaves and *śirīṣa* flowers grown from the Bodhi tree,
where that Blessed One, the Buddha, the Lion of the Śākyas, sat.
One should avoid that tree with great effort, nor should one even dig up its wood. One should not strip off the leaves from *nāgakesara* trees.
Nor should one ever eat at any time or place that which is forbidden by the wise;
nor, out of delusion, should one ever step over the leaf-huts of the sages.
The mantra-practitioner falls from his commitment by eating on those leaves;
the practitioner should not eat his meal there using any other leaves. 11.173.
He always took his meals from vessels made of clay, those specified as being of copper, as well as those of silver produced from the *śāta* mountain, and likewise from those of crystal and stone.
Nor did he eat from the backs of leaves, nor likewise from the palms of his hands—
those leaves that had been offered by the sons of the Ten-Powered One to the Enemy of Māra.
The reciter should avoid those who are Pratyekabuddhas and those who are Śrāvaka individuals; he should not step upon their leaves with his feet.
The mantra-practitioner should not, even with effort, take for himself various kinds of edible cakes, nor likewise drinks and food, nor indeed anything at all that has been offered to the Jinas,
those who follow the conduct of the Jinas, and the individuals who are Śrāvakas.
The practitioner of recitation should always avoid that which has been offered even to the Three Jewels.
Even for embodied beings, his mantras do not succeed in the slightest degree;
how much less so [the mantra] that is divine, esteemed as all-auspicious, and conducive to the highest good?
The rites for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*) and pacification (*śāntika*), which fulfill all hopes—these do not succeed for one who eats the offerings and sacrificial cakes (*naivedya-bali*). 180.11.180.
The mantras of one who is pure, skillful in character, compassionate, and likewise righteous, and who is devoted to the practice of cleanliness and proper conduct, succeed everywhere. (11.181)
Having first given food to all, the reciter does not eat there;
he should not eat any other food that has been offered to others. (11.182)

One who knows the mantras, acting in this manner, should take only a small measure of food, even if it is self-offered; for him, success rests in the palm of his hand. Following this rule, the practitioner observing the vow should take that food while reciting the mantra.
It is highly praised by the sages for the accomplishment of all mantras.
ApDhS 1.18.5–7 185. He shall not eat food that has been brought by night from a Śūdra; nor shall he eat it if it has been brought by day from such a person who lives outside the village. 186.

He shall not eat food that has been brought by a woman during her courses, nor food that has been brought by a man while his hands are wet; nor shall he eat food that has been brought by a woman who is pregnant. 187.

He shall not eat food that has been brought by a woman who has recently given birth, nor food that has been brought by a woman whose breasts are flowing with milk; nor shall he eat food that has been brought by a woman who is carrying a child on her hip.
I have briefly explained the rules prescribed for all acts of eating;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the mantra for the purification of everything.

Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśya), the reciter should always recite this mantra; then, having recited it seven times for the purification of the body, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) [should proceed]. (11.186)
Listen to the detailed explanation of its meaning, O goddess who dwells among the hosts of beings:
having touched the entire body, the Sage spoke this mantra. (11.187)
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! It is as follows: Oṃ, O destroyer of all sins, destroy, destroy all those employed by the wicked; remember the pledge! Hūṃ Jaḥ Svāhā! 11.188

With this mantra, whatever monk’s rice-meat (*bhikṣaudana*) or other food one consumes should be eaten after having consecrated it with the mantra. Having eaten and performed the ritual sipping of water (*upaspṛśya*), one should, as before, stroke the entire body starting from the head; then one should rest. Having rested for a moment, or for half a watch, or even a full watch, one should then pay homage to the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) and recite the books of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) of all the Buddhas. || 11.189 ||

The Noble *Prajñāpāramitā*, the Noble *Candrapradīpa-samādhi*, the Noble *Daśabhūmika*, the Noble *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, and the Noble *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī*. One should recite any one of these while standing at the height of a yoke, as high as the sun. Then, having dedicated [the merit] and recited according to one's ability, one should set aside the book, or cover it with clean cloth, and bow to the True Dharma. Thereafter, going to the bank of a river or a great lake to bathe, one should take earth free of living organisms, consecrate it seven times with mantras, and sprinkle water with this mantra. Which one? 11.190. [The mantra follows.]

Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! It is as follows: Oṃ, paralyze all evil ones, hūṃ! O you who hold the blue lotus, you who assume the form of a sporting youth, bind, bind! Remember the pledge! phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! 11.191

Having performed protection by means of this [mantra], as well as the binding of the directions (*diśābandha*), the binding of the mandala for one's companions, the binding of the mouth (*tuṇḍabandha*), the summoning of all the wicked and malicious ones, and the binding of semen (*śukrabandha*) with a thread over which the mantra has been recited seven times tied around the waist, one may wander everywhere. At all times during the period of recitation and at the time of bathing, one should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*) for the purpose of pacifying and destroying wicked obstacles. Thereafter, it accomplishes all rites. One should employ it in all activities accompanied by the great mudrā of the five crests (*pañcaśikha-mahāmudrā*). It performs everything; it does not fail to do so. (11.192)

Then the practitioner, having taken earth, cow-dung powder, and so forth, should bathe as he pleases. He should bathe with water free of living organisms. In all cases and in all ritual actions, he should act only with [water] free of living organisms. Having bathed, he should not discharge phlegm, urine, excrement, or the like into the water, nor should he discharge a stream of saliva or urine, nor should he play. Feeling compassion for all sentient beings and reflecting upon himself—[seeing him] as one whose sensations are obstructed by selflessness, emptiness, and suffering, like one who is crushed and scorched, or like a being distressed by separation from a mother—the knower of mantras, though lacking the [external] means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), should proceed thus.

In such a manner, one should perceive oneself situated within the depths of the ocean of saṃsāra, obstructed by the foundations of suffering—such as being cut, pierced, mangled, and destroyed. Having beheld oneself as homeless, unprotected, without refuge, and dejected in mind, one should meditate, standing in water reaching up to the neck or standing in water reaching up to the navel, establishing one-pointedness of mind right there in the midst of the water. (11.193–194)

First of all, one should meditate upon a great lotus stalk, endowed with great lotus flowers and adorned with great lotus petals, beautiful to behold, made of jewels, with its stem fashioned of lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*), its leaves of emerald (*marakata*), its filaments of crystal, and its thousand petals of crystal and ruby (*padmarāga*), fully blossomed. Therein stands a lion throne made of jewels, adorned with many gems and covered with a pair of fine cotton cloths. Seated upon it is the Blessed Buddha, teaching the Dharma, white as gold, garlanded with flames on all sides, adorned with a halo of light extending a fathom, of immense proportions, appearing as if scraping the very sky, seated in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*). 11.194.

And to the right is the noble Mañjuśrī, endowed with all excellent ornaments, seated upon a lotus throne, holding a chowrie for the Blessed One; he stands and does not sit, his limbs being reddish-white or the color of ground saffron. And to the left is the noble Avalokiteśvara, white as an autumn reed, with a chowrie held busy in his hand. Thus there are eight bodhisattvas: the noble Maitreya, Samantabhadra, Kṣitigarbha, Gaganagañja, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Apāyajaha, the noble Vajrapāṇi, and Sudhana—these are the ten bodhisattvas. 11.195.

To the south, one should meditate upon eight Pratyekabuddhas: Candana, Gandhamādana, Ketu, Suketu, Sitaketu, Ṛṣṭa, Upāriṣṭa, and Nemi. In that very place are also the eight great Śrāvakas, namely: the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, Gavāmpati, Piṇḍola, Bharadvāja, Pilindavatsa, the noble Rāhula, Mahākāśyapa, and the noble Ānanda. 11.196.

Thus, one should meditate upon an infinite saṅgha of monks in the presence of these great śrāvakas; one should meditate upon infinite pratyekabuddhas in the presence of the pratyekabuddhas; and one should meditate upon an infinite saṅgha of bodhisattvas in the eight places of the great bodhisattvas. In this way, one should meditate upon the surface of space as being praised and endowed with the great maṇḍala of the assembly. 11.197

Standing in water reaching up to one's navel, one should perform worship of the Blessed One with various kinds of divine and human flowers—*māndārava*, *mahāmāndārava*, *padma*, *mahāpadma*, *dhātuka*, *kārikā*, and *indīvara* blossoms—as well as with various large-sized flower-baskets heaped in great quantities. One should also perform a delightful worship of all the *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, and *bodhisattvas* with abundant divine and human powders, parasols, banners, and flags, and with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lamps. In this manner, all offerings and services such as oblations, incense, and food, whether divine or human, should be presented. 11.198.

One should meditate on a ray of light issuing from the *ūrṇakośa* (the circle of hair between the eyebrows) of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, illuminating oneself. For one who has just entered this meditation and performs the recitation (*jāpa*), there is the attainment of the fruit of Brahma-merit; one will certainly be destined for enlightenment. || 11.199 ||
These and other such meditations have been described by the preeminent ones of the world.
For the sake of the welfare of all beings and for the benefit of the ministers,
the supreme sage, the seventh, then spoke to the beings concerning the primary meditation for the welfare of all ministers.
In the first [chapter] spoken by the Sage concerning that aversion in the form of a mandala (202), there is also a second mandala, and after that, a third mantra. 11.202.
The highest accomplishment (*siddhi*) is in the first [grade], while the next is in the middling;
the inferior accomplishment (*kṣudrasiddhi*) is in the lowest—thus spoke the bull among sages.
Likewise, the banner-like meditation has superior, middling, and inferior forms;
in brief, that meditation is the destroyer of all sins.
Beyond this, the wise should not resort to any other form of meditation.
His mantras will indeed be accomplished when they are well-established in this meditation. || 11.205 ||
Having meditated upon the visualization as described according to the ritual procedure as desired,
the reciter should then dismiss the mantra there and offer an oblation (argha) at his ease.
Having emerged from that flood of water, one should then proceed at ease to the previously designated place,
which is prescribed by rule and well-restrained.
Then the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra as previously prescribed;
having performed the rite, he should dismiss the mantra and the deities who were summoned there.
Then, having likewise performed the protection of his companions, he—being skilled, knowing the true nature of the ritual, and devoted to the performance of the rites—is considered [fit]. (11.209)
Having praised the Foremost Person (Agrapudgala) with various offerings of hymns,
[one should praise] one's own mantra, the Lord of Mantras, as well as the Śrāvakas and the Pratyekabuddhas who possess the rhinoceros-like horn.
Then, rising again from that seat, those practitioners of mantra [beheld] the bodhisattvas, the great beings, who are capable of bestowing grace upon the three worlds. (11.211)
Having gone far from his dwelling, outside and to a place sheltered from the wind, he should void feces, snot, urine, and excrement. (11.212)
During the day one should face north, and at night one should face south.
One who recites mantras should never contemplate worldly matters there.
One should certainly not recite a mantra there that has been spoken according to the traditions of one's own specific ritual lineage.
Then he sat upon the ground, auspicious with the marks of his gait and other signs.
Having sipped water in pure water that has been strained through the hem of a clean garment,
he should wash his feet up to the knees with exactly seven applications of clay.
One who has urinated should perform seven *grahaṇīs*. In the case of discharging feces, there are thirty [clay balls] at both ends of the hand.
Likewise, for the discarding of phlegm and for nasal mucus, there are two each.
Then, having touched water with effort, he [should remain] at a distance from the dwelling on the ground;
likewise, having gone [a certain distance], there is the casting away of things such as road-dust and the like.
Then, beyond that, one may go at will toward that southern direction outside [the village],
even to a ravine, a field of parched grain, or likewise to a place strewn with sand.
One should avoid crossing over rivers and should abandon places that are refuse heaps or impure. In a concealed, secret, secluded, and remote place devoid of people,
one who is confident should then act as a wise counselor and perform the discarding of foul matter.
One who recites mantras and knows the proper time should not suppress the natural urges.
Then, having gone to a pure region as he desired, in a secluded borderland according to the rules,
he should construct a hut and a water-shed in that place at his ease.
At dawn, or in a secluded, covered, and protected spot upon the ground,
one should always urinate while remaining silent and free from attachment.
Once he has voided urine and feces, the observer of the vow should always perform purification using clay that is soft, pleasant to the touch, well-ground, and free of living organisms.
Having always taken three [fingers] at the anus and likewise one, as well as both hands at the two ends; having first taken them as previously specified by the mantra-practitioner on the ground.
Having carefully washed both feet, and specifically the right one first,
the practitioner of recitation should always keep the two feet from touching one another.
The detailed purification for those who recite mantras was explained previously;
however, the purification consisting of being free from odor and stains was taught by the pure ones of old.
Thus, this purification for the practitioners of mantras has been stated in brief.
"Purity comes from being free from both odor and stain; one should always remain pure.
This is seen throughout this entire tantra," so said the Lord of Sages. 11.227
Then, having touched water for purification, the practitioner who mutters the mantra, being devoted to the performance of successful rites,
should act according to the previously stated rule with a mind that is inwardly pure.
Purity is declared to be fivefold for practitioners in all tantras: bodily purity, as well as [purity of] speech, mental purity, and meditative absorption are proclaimed;

the fourth is the purity of truth, and water is said to be the fifth. (11.229) Those who possess the dharma of truth, who have conquered anger, who know the tantras, who perceive the scriptures, who are skilled in the meaning of the subtle reality, who know the mantras, and who are proficient in ritual action—(11.230) [they are the ones for whom this is intended].
For those who are skilled in the internal cause, accomplishment is not difficult to attain;
one should not speak of false worship that is devoid of the true Dharma. (11.231)
Cruel and even more cruel, entirely devoid of truth,
causing hatred, full of wrath, harsh, and piercing the vital spots.
But one who is devoid of truth and righteousness, who oppresses other beings, who is malicious, possessed of a defiled mind, and abandoned by all wholesome qualities— [233] 11.233.
One who constantly practices violence, one of evil conduct, or even one who follows the dharma [only nominally],
must always be avoided by a practitioner of mantra-recitation; likewise, one who engages in vulgar conduct,
as well as one who speaks falsely or is prone to anger, must be avoided by one who is deeply afraid of the next world.
It is censured by all the Buddhas and by the wise Bodhisattvas. (11.235)
Furthermore, in this world, both the Pratyekabuddhas who possess the rhinoceros-like horn and the Śrāvakas always,
as well as those on earth who desire the attainment of supernatural powers, must avoid false speech.
The speaker of falsehood goes to the most terrible hells;
furthermore, he is always reborn among animals, as well as among the hungry ghosts (preta) and in the world of Yama.
There they dwell eternally, subsisting on falsehood:
in Tapana, in the terrible Durmati, in Kālasūtra, and in Pratāpana;
likewise in Sañjīva, in Asipattra, and in the Śālmalī forest.
A living being who speaks falsehood shall dwell there for many eons.
How indeed could the mantras be accomplished for one who speaks falsely? One who deludes others with false speech causes living beings to tremble;
therefore, that person of deluded action will certainly not see the accomplishment of the mantra.
And thus it is said: "There is no accomplishment for practitioners of mantra through mere speech;
how could there be accomplishment for such a person even after many millions of kalpas? (11.241)
He by whom the teaching of the Buddhas has been rejected upon this earth shall then fall into a terrible state of great fear, [the realm] of ignorance.
In the Sañjīva, Kālasūtra, and Pratāpana hells,
he shall dwell for a great kalpa because of his destruction of my True Dharma.
Foolish people, having despised the true Dharma, are cooked in the most terrifying hell, enveloped by blinding darkness. 11.244
Those who, out of ignorance or childishness, are deluded and possess false pride,
fall into a terrible hell if they indeed despise the King of Vidyās.
Therefore, one should not commit evil, nor engage in contemptible and false actions; indeed,
one should not despise the true Dharma, for wrong views are censurable.

Therefore, always being faithful, one should constantly practice the ritual procedure of the mantra. Truthful, a knower of mantras, and always intent on the welfare of sentient beings—the knower of mantras should devote himself to the mantra; for him, success is indeed certain.
One performs various actions—superior, inferior, and middling. For action indeed produces karma, whereas non-action is never beneficial.
For one joined with action and karma, success shall always arise.

Since all that has action as its purpose is for the sake of the goal, action is always for the sake of karma. Both non-action and action, as well as action and karma, are appropriately joined together.
The action of one whose action is thus fruitful is always successful. (11.249) In this way, an unperformed act becomes an act with fruit, and an act with fruit is always [realized];
that which is without fruit comes to bear fruit, and fruit itself is always fruit. (11.250)
Whether fruitless or fruitful, all that arises from fruit is accomplished through conjunction;
conjunction accomplishes the mantra, while disjunction from conjunction and conjunction from disjunction each accomplish their respective counterparts.
But the relationship of probandum and probans is not established among those [entities];
for substances that are established are everywhere contradictory causes of establishment. (11.252)

The mantras of those who have mastered the spells, which are the causes for accomplishment, are not [previously] established. That which is most desired by the agent is the object (*karman*), arising from the action of one desiring to perform the act. (11.253)
One should not perform any action among all actions that lack the cause of ritual action;
rather, one should undertake every rite while being joined with the meaning of the mantra and the tantra.
One should undertake an action that ought to be undertaken, and one should certainly not undertake what is not an action.
For all embodied beings, mantras do not succeed if there is no performance of the undertaking.
In the past, this was sung by the most excellent sages who proclaim all the true Dharma; it reveals the convention of the sons of the Conquerors regarding the practice of mantra.
The practitioner here, who knows all mantras, [finds] in this King of Rituals (Kalparāja) another path taught in the form of mantras as the cause for awakening.
All mantras succeed wherever there is always the proper application; such a person shall attain their desired accomplishment in no long time.
For the sake of the welfare of all beings, the Fully Awakened Ones have indeed proclaimed [this] in the form of those who go to the city of Nirvāṇa. 11.259
Likewise, the path to enlightenment is eternal and fulfills all actions and purposes;
Buddhahood is the first station, its ultimate consummation and final resort.
In this way, one shall attain fruitful accomplishment here in effortless spontaneity;
for those who know the phenomena of diverse actions, there shall be the application of mantras.
This attainment of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and liberation has been briefly explained by the foremost of Victors as the means for accomplishing all goals. Through it,
one shall obtain abundant aims and rely upon the supreme state.
Likewise, O Lord of Yakṣas, those who are base for the sake of sovereignty shall always [attain] the status of ministers over all the worlds of men, gods, and asuras;
thus, he exercises lordship over them and makes their actions fruitful.
Endowed with purity and proper conduct, always delighting in ethical discipline and meditation,
the practitioner of mantra should then recite the mantra spoken in all the tantras.
He performs various deeds, both superior and middling, and he should also perform inferior ones,
desiring the prosperity of his ministers.

For the practitioners of recitation (jāpin), there is an increase in enjoyments in the lowest [level], and for those with bodies in the intermediate [state], in the middle; however, the most excellent [attainment] is obtained only by the highest.
At the end of the recitation, the practitioner should rest for as long as he awaits [the sign];
when the time has arrived, the reciter should perform the sādhana there.

Thus all rites are accomplished; nevertheless, in that regard, the practitioner of mantras who constantly performs recitation effects the destruction of the sins of men through the performance of rituals according to the prescribed rules, which has been established throughout the succession of ritual actions.
Success remains unattained for that person until it reaches completeness;
therefore, the reciter of the mantra should recite the mantra again for the sake of destroying evil, whereby his karma is eliminated. (11.270)
May the mantras be efficacious—those that are supreme, those that are middling, and those that are inferior, yet honored by the world.
By their recitation, they destroy without exception all evil committed throughout the succession of one's births. (11.271)

Thus, the sins of all embodied beings perish; he creates a charming woman adorned with various limbs and diverse ornaments, endowed with all excellent qualities, who eternally bestows the sovereignty of the Yakṣas. By reciting the mantra of the Tathāgatas, they attain the accomplishment of all aims. || 11.272 ||
{S118} {V86} Chapter A12:
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again surveyed the entire abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince:

Listen, Mañjuśrī! To you who follow the vidyā-mantras, and for those beings engaged in the welfare of all sentient beings—listen to the procedure for the rosary (akṣasūtra) by which mantras are recited or by which they are caused to be recited; it is the common means of accomplishment for all mantras in all tantras. Listen to that well and properly, and take it to heart; I shall speak. 12.1
When this had been said, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"Excellent, Blessed One! Please speak for our sake, out of compassion for us, for the benefit of those beings who have entered the samaya of all mantra practices, and for the sake of all sentient beings."
When Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince, had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to him:

Listen, Mañjuśrī! I shall explain in detail and with full analysis that by which beings engaged in all mantra practices accomplish all their aims. And what is that? First of all, there is the mantra: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānām acintyādbhutarūpiṇām*. It is as follows:
*Oṃ kuru kuru sarvārthān sādhaya sādhaya sarvaduṣṭavimohani gaganāvalambe viśodhaya svāhā*. 12.3.
With this mantra, one should perform all rites regarding rosaries; one should perform such rites as purifying, piercing, grasping, and purging. || 12.4 ||
First, one who has performed the protection rite and observes the vow should consecrate the rosary beads and the tree thirty-seven times. (12.5)

He shall sleep there for one night, and in his dream he will see a non-human being, either endowed with beauty or deformed and hideous; O son of Sumitrā, they will speak to him of the matter concerning his home exactly as it is.
Then that practitioner, having risen in the morning, should go to that tree;
nor shall he see any dream that is deformed or extremely terrifying.
The mantra-practitioner should avoid that tree, or else go elsewhere.
First is the *rudrākṣa*, and after that, the *indrākṣa*. (12.8) {S119} ap12.2
One should climb a *putrañjīvaka* tree, or a desired one, or any other fruit-bearing tree, with companions who are well-equipped for climbing trees. (12.9)
In the absence of companions, or even alone, the practitioner of recitation (japin) should ascend;
the observer of the vow (vratin) should stand upon the high branches where the fruit is located, [not] in a thicket. 12.10.
Always vigilant in that regard, having emerged upon the upper branches,
he should grasp the fruit of the upper branches and apply himself to higher action.
In the upper [level], the supreme accomplishment has been taught by the foremost of persons;
in the middle, the middling accomplishment; and in the lower, indeed the inferior one.
Having taken up their fruit therein, they are always free from revulsion toward living beings.
Having reached the western branches, the causes for [attaining] substances are perfected.
In the north, one should always summon deities such as those born of the yakṣa womb.
The ritual known as Ākarṣaṇa is for the sake of bringing peace and accomplishing the welfare of all beings.
The gods, asuras, gandharvas, kinnaras,
and rākṣasas perform their respective duties for the nourishment and welfare of all living beings.
It renders all actions performed on earth fruitful;
that branch which stands in the eastern direction is the source of fruit.
One should always apply effort toward them for the sake of attaining long life and prosperity;
through their fruits, one always accomplishes various forms of mantra-siddhi.
But that branch which goes toward the south, adorned with leaves and shoots—
a reciter of mantras should diligently avoid it, for it is a destroyer of the life-force of sentient beings.

Whatever fruits are raised high upon branches growing toward the south, one should recite [the mantra] an equal number of times with those seeds; this brings about the destruction of the lives of enemies.
The reciter should avoid those with great effort, for they are causes of much demerit;
specifically, those fruits which are said to be hanging from branches pointing downwards.

One should go to Rasātala; by means of those [fruits] belonging to the women of the Dānavas, having taken a rosary of those fruits, it is proclaimed. Having descended to their dwellings in Pātāla, one should go there by that [means].
Having entered there, the practitioner indeed attains divine happiness.
If he remains attached to the *āsurī* [mantras], he shall stay there for an eon;
having grasped all the *akṣaphala* [seeds], the reciter should then descend.
Having performed the protective rites together with his companions, he should then proceed at his ease.
Having gone to a distant place, he should always remain in a pure location.
The practitioner of mantra should stand there and purify those produced from the beads;
having taken the seed-beads, being disciplined, he should thoroughly cleanse them in every respect.
Having thoroughly purified them on all sides, those who possess the mantras should pierce the dice. They [should do so] for three, seven, eight, or one time, or twenty-one times. 12.26.
One who knows the reality of mantras should always purify [the site] with the preceding mantra; when it has been recited seven or eight times, purification is then considered accomplished.
The practitioner, observing the vow, should prepare a wick using thread spun by a maiden, consisting of five strands of triple-twisted fibers made from lotus stalks.
One who knows the true nature of mantras should string together fruits that are subtle, perfectly round, always free of holes caused by insects, unimpaired, and not contemptible; indeed,
they should be beautiful, of lovely color, without holes, and likewise uncracked.
Or thirty rudrākṣas, or a *sutajīva*, or indeed an *indrākṣa* fruit.
Then the practitioner, being disciplined, should carefully string together a rosary that is unbroken, beautiful, always free of defects, and esteemed for its fruits. (12.31)
Now, [the vessel] is prescribed as being made of gold, or silver, or of ruby, or originating from crystal; or it may be made of conch-shell, musāragalva, or even pearl.
One should fashion various garlands for the rosary out of coral;
one may also fashion an auspicious, divine rosary from other precious gems.
With a concentrated mind, one should string together round pellets made of earth upon a thread;
or alternatively, other pellets made of various fruits or derived from minerals.
Furthermore, the practitioner who performs the recitation with diligence should also fashion knots at the tips of *kuśa* grass.
Or thirty-five, twenty-five, or fifty cubits for the middle [size].
The mantra-practitioner, being composed, should string together this garland of beads;
he should make the "eldest" (jyeṣṭhikā) garland consist of one thousand and eight beads.
This fourfold garland should be strung daily by practitioners;
having then made the knots, they should be three or two *mātrās* in length.
Then, one should string together a garland in its entirety using bracelets made of flower-metal (puṣpaloha), or of gold, silver, or even copper.
Then, at the end, having made a loop, one should place [the cord] there in successive order;
one should wrap it very carefully so that, once bound, it remains fixed.
Then, having made the appearance of a mandala-form clearly manifest, it is encircled and adorned with the form of a serpent’s coil.
Having the appearance of a pearl necklace, fashioned in the form of a neck-ornament;
then, having bathed in auspicious water, or in a pure river or pond.
Having bathed, he should emerge from the water as before;
having sipped water according to the rule, he should perform the domestic rite prescribed by the syllables of the *akṣasūtra*.
Having washed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) as well as with powdered earth,
and having washed it again in auspicious water, one should anoint it with fragrant unguents.
Having washed it with effort using excellent pigments, as well as white sandalwood and saffron, one should then proceed from there to the *uḍaya*.
Having gone to their respective places where that central cloth-painting is located—
wherein is the best of Jinas, the preeminent Sage, the Lion of the Śākyas, the supreme among men— there,
one should always [offer] to the image of the Teacher, as well as to the Jina who bears the relics upon the earth.
46. One should place that garland before him, nearby.
Having installed [the deity] upon that cloth which was present before him,
he recited [the mantra] one thousand eight hundred times, and one hundred and eight times in a single session.
Having fasted for a day and night, he offered the garland to the best of sages.
Having previously performed the recitation according to the prescribed measure, he becomes equal to that.
Having recited [the mantra] over the rosary one hundred and eight times, he should then place it right there at night;
the knower of mantras should sleep right there on the ground upon a bed of *kuśa* grass.
If, in a dream, he should see auspicious dream-visions, then success is ordained for him according to those dreams indicated. || 12.50 ||
If [the practitioner] sees the Buddha, his disciples, or the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas] in a dream,
the mantra-practitioner’s ritual performance will certainly succeed and bear fruit.
"If, having seen in a dream a child with the form of a youth, variegated and beautiful to behold, one likewise offers him a garland,
then his mantras— accomplishers of all aims— will succeed without fail. (12.52)

Thus concludes the twelfth chapter, the detailed section on the ritual for the rosary (*akṣasūtra-vidhi-paṭala-visara*), from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the *Bodhisattvapiṭakāvaṃsaka*. {S123} {V90}

Chapter A13 Then indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Mañjuśrī, there exists for the practitioner of vidyā who is engaged in the rite of *homa* according to the specific procedure laid out in the entirety of your chapter on mantras, a particular rule for the service of the fire, wherein all beings devoted to the practice of vidyā are established. And what is that? It consists of the secret words of the vidyā-mantra. They are as follows: [13.1]"
Oṃ! Arise, O tawny-yellow one with reddish-brown eyes! Give, cause to give! Hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! Destroy all obstacles! Svāhā!
This, O Mañjuśrī, is that supreme heart-mantra of fire, which performs all rites and grants all desires. 13.2

First of all, the practitioner, having recited this Heart of Fire once, should offer three oblations of clarified butter into the fire. Thus the fire becomes summoned. For one who applies it in this manner, there are three kinds of fuel-wood for the rites of pacification, enrichment, and subjugation. 13.3.
For the purpose of pacification, a piece of *aśoka* wood that is still moist is especially recommended; it should be one *vitasti*, one *hasta*, or even three finger-breadths (*tryaṅgula*) in height.
A glossy appearance is indeed praised; this is the prescribed method that is ordained: it should be without hollows, without cavities, and likewise resembling a parrot’s wing.
One should avoid wood that is green, white, or black in color;
one should also reject wood eaten by worms, but may employ wood that is free of hollows.

Those of a different caste, those that are not excellent, and those that are inferior or discarded should be avoided. One should not begin with wood that is too dry, nor too moist, nor that which is burnt. (13.7)
One should avoid that which is putrid, crooked, and also excessively high. Then, one should construct a fire-pit that is square on all sides.
Then one should carefully dig downwards with a measurement of four cubits, or three cubits, or two cubits, or likewise even one cubit.
It should always be free from living beings and prepared with sand;
then, one should fashion an altar in the shape of a lotus, circular on all sides,
and likewise, with effort, one should make it square or even in the shape of a bow.
It resembles the form of a vajra, with two tips and three prongs.
One should construct this fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa) measuring two cubits across, in a pure and well-swept place, or likewise on an excellent riverbank.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) with great fervor in a solitary place, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, and likewise on a mountain peak;
as well as always in an empty temple and in a great forest.
Those places for practice which have been described by the foremost of persons.
14–16. There, one who knows the mantras should especially perform the rite of homa.
By means of these [mantras], accomplishment (siddhi) established in those very places will quickly be attained; of this there is no doubt. 13.16.
Facing either east or north, the mantra-practitioner should perform rites for pacification and nourishment; however, he should avoid performing those rites pertaining to Rudra while facing south.

Success in rites of pacification (*śāntika*) is attained when facing east, and success in rites of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*) when facing north. With these [directions], the practitioner of mantras should always begin the recitation of mantras.
One should perform rites for prosperity using wood from the bilva, āmra, plakṣa, and nyagrodha trees; for malevolent rites, one should use wood that is dry, bitter, sour, or pungent.
One should always avoid all those [prohibited items] which have been forbidden by the sages.
For rites of pacification (śāntika) and for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika), wood that is still moist is recommended.
Likewise, dry wood from trees used for fierce rituals is always avoided by sages;
in the absence of such sacrificial fuel, one should prepare wood from those [other] trees.
One should prepare a seat strewn with kuśa grass on all sides, with the tips pointing in both directions,
using blades that are green, glossy in appearance, and resembling the neck of a peacock.
With such *kuśa* grasses, one should always perform rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*). Likewise, with dry blades of grass resembling the color of emeralds,
one should always perform sinful deeds— those which have been forbidden here by the best of Jinas.
And in water that is stainless, pure, and always free from worms. || 13.24 ||
Then, having sprinkled [the site] all around, he should also perform a circumambulation; with a composed mind, having touched water according to the rule, he should kindle the fire.
With clean grass or wood, one should fashion a torch according to the prescribed measure;
having made it about the size of a fist, one should then carefully ignite it with fire.
Nor should one ever [fan him] with the breath of the mouth or with the edge of a garment; he must be avoided by both undergarment and upper robe, and not by any other clothing.
Nor should one fan [the fire] with the wind from the hands, nor with a broom, nor likewise with a cloth or even with leaves, out of a desire for amusement. 13.28.
When the fire has been kindled and fanned by these means, one who knows the mantras of fire, desiring to perform the *homa*, should ignite the fire with a well-composed mind.
(13.29) These locations have been described for the ritual of *homa* in all respects. Having sat upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass at a distance of one cubit from there, (13.15)
Then, having performed the rite with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), one should sprinkle water three times;
thereafter, one should indeed offer three oblations of cow's clarified butter there.
Then one should indeed perform prostration to all the Buddhas, the Protectors;
thereafter, one should worship one's own mantra and the Lord of Mantras according to one's desire.
Then, having recited the mantra from the *Agnihṛdaya* constantly with a concentrated mind,
he should invoke the Fire-god with fragrant flowers alone.
One who knows the mantras should always summon [the deity] and provide a place;
having offered a seat and a location, one should do so with that specific mantra and no other.
One should offer three fuel-sticks soaked in curd, mixed with clarified butter, and smeared with honey, for the purpose of worshipping the fire, using the mantra-rite in every respect.
Then one should perform that which pertains to both [the fire and the self], consisting of kindling wood mixed with ritual substances;
likewise, it should be joined with clarified butter and honey, as well as mixed with curd.
The practitioner of secret mantras should likewise recite the mantra one thousand times, or a mere hundred thousand, or even one hundred and eight, and then cast it into the fire;
that is, into a fire with many flames, or likewise into one with a single flame.
One should perform the fire-oblation for pacification (śāntika) when there is smoke, and for nourishment (pauṣṭika) when there is no smoke.
When smoke arises during the performance of fierce rites—which are censured by some yet praised by the Conquerors—if the color of the fire becomes such while one is engaged in the homa ritual: 13.38.
In rites for pacification, white in color is always praised by the supreme Victors;
indeed, mantras are accomplished there for one who offers oblations into a white fire.
Likewise, a red color is always desired for the accomplishment of nourishing rites (pauṣṭika);
however, a black, smoky, or tawny color indicates an evil result.
Thus, this threefold accomplishment has been set forth in three ways:
it is described as having various forms and colors, such as the color of other [elements] or the color of the clouds.
Furthermore, there is no accomplishment of mantras upon this earth for those who possess such a complexion or are described as having various forms and colors. 13.42–43ab.
But having seen the fire blazing again, one should commence the ritual once more;
if the mantra has been recited yet again, the accomplishment of the mantra will surely come to pass.
One should again perform the oblation according to the rite prescribed by rule;
having performed the dismissal and the invocation, one should utter the mantra to the fire.

In this very mandala, according to the prescribed ritual, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the rites of dismissal and invocation by that same [method] previously established. One should perform all rituals therein by that same method during that very rite.
46. One should likewise undertake the fire-ritual (agnicaryā) in front of the cloth-painting (paṭa). 13.46.
There indeed mantras succeed, as was previously declared by the Tathāgatas; one should perform the rites praised by the Victors there, and not [seek success] elsewhere in every respect. 13.47
One should not perform other actions, especially those that are evil, which are censured by the supreme Jinas and are contrary to the world’s standards of decency. (13.48)
One shall arise as a universal monarch, or a bodhisattva, or a lord of the earth;
likewise, one shall obtain the five superknowledges, or attain the state of a deity, or achieve success.
One who is constantly disciplined in this painting and skilled in the rite of fire-oblation [shall attain these].
Or sovereignty over the fifty netherworlds, or even the power of moving through the intermediate space.
The state of being a terrestrial deity or a yakṣa is always [attained] through the summoning of a yakṣī;
likewise, sovereignty, lordship, or [authority] over this realm or even this village [is attained]. (13.51)
One gains mastery over the Vidyādharas and the state of an Asura, bringing all sentient beings under one's control;
and one has the power to summon spirits, great beings, and high-souled ones.
By means of the rite of homa, one can summon even the bodhisattvas, the great beings who abide on the ten stages; how much more so a human being on this earth?

Likewise, in this world, the command of an army, as well as sovereignty in particular, and even the state of being a king who has brought all beings under his control—these too [are attained through this]. (13.54)
