For the sake of subduing all beings, or likewise for the king on earth, one should always perform all rites everywhere by means of the fire-oblation (homa). 13.55.
One whose self is fully disciplined in every respect may undertake all actions;
for him, his action performed with constancy leads to the highest welfare. 13.56
The middling and even the lowest rites are accomplished;
all substances therein are said to yield success in three ways. 13.57
When the rite of *homa* has been undertaken, success is seen to be fruitful,
provided one has bound the five-crested *mudrā* and recited the *Keśinī* mantra.
One who possesses self-protection and is wise should perform all rites.
When engaged in the rite of fire-oblation (homa), one should then recite this mantra; in this rite, it should always be recited seven or eight times. 13.59.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas whose teachings are unimpeded. It is as follows: Oṃ jvala tiṣṭha hūṃ ru ru viśvasambhava sambhave svāhā.
By means of this application of the mantra, one should recite it over the wood again and again;
having recited it twelve times or seven times, the knower of the mantra should offer it into the fire.
(61) Or likewise, flowers, incense, and perfumes—indeed, everything from all sides—[should be offered].
One should sprinkle [the area] with water over which this mantra has been recited. Then, for the sake of the ritual procedure, one should commence all rites;
indeed, in all rites, they must be performed according to the previously established practice.
Having bound the glorious Mahāmudrā, known as the *apara-pañcaśikhā*, and having performed the ritual protection (*rakṣā*), one should then always be a reciter of the mantra of Keśinī.
Those who are confident should undertake all actions for the sake of success,
provided that auspicious omens are seen and sounds are always favorable.
His mantras are indeed fruitful in granting boons as desired;
when applied in the initial rites, they proceed by means of the power of the mantra.
In them, every kind of accomplishment is ordained, both fruitful and complete;
there is the sound of the word "Victory!", the beating of drums, and the resonance of kettledrums.
For success is declared to be everywhere for one who relies upon the rite of fire-oblation (homa), or else when there are other excellent omens or auspicious cries of birds. || 13.68 ||
The meanings of sounds described by the Victors consist of various types of resonances;
they are praiseworthy, divine, auspicious, celestial, charming, and manifold in their tones.
Parasols, banners, and flags, as well as women adorned with ornaments,
a full water-jar, and likewise the sight of the *argha* offering— these are the causes of success.
"Or those who possess various forms and colors, who are praiseworthy and honored by the world—for them, upon seeing [the deity], mantras of diverse domains are accomplished. (13.71)
Thus concludes the thirteenth chapter of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
{S129} {V95} Chapter A14.
14.1 Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī, the Youthful:

Mañjuśrī, there exists one who is authorized in all the mantras that serve as the means for accomplishing the secret vidyās of your [teaching], who has entered the clouds of Dharma issued from the Tathāgata’s treasury of Dharma, whose nature is like the sky, and who is the lord and most senior of all mantras—both mundane and supramundane—just as a prince is the eldest among all beings. In this regard, the Tathāgata is declared to be the most senior and the most excellent; he is the Buddha, the Blessed One, the bull among men for gods and humans. Thus indeed, O Prince...

Among all mantras, this King of Vidyās is declared to be the foremost and most excellent. It was previously taught by the Tathāgatas—those Blessed Buddhas whose merit is as ineffable as the sands of the river Gaṅgā—as the supreme heart-essence (*paramahṛdaya*) and supreme secret (*paramaguhyam*) of the Tathāgata Ratnaketu. It is esteemed as the most auspicious of all, praised and extolled by all the Buddhas; it provides consolation to all Buddha-beings, destroys all evil, grants all desires, and fulfills all hopes. And what is that? [14.1]

In that interval, from the *ūrṇā* hair-treasure of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, there issued forth a ray of light named "Exhorter of All Buddhas. Having illuminated all the Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, above and below, and having gladdened the minds of all sentient beings, it vanished into the *uṣṇīṣa* of the Blessed One Śākyamuni. And from the *uṣṇīṣa* of the Blessed One, there issued forth the King of Vidyās named Ekākṣara—a single-syllable [mantra] whose form was adorned with flames on all sides, unobservable by any sentient beings, invincible, arisen with great majestic power, its body adorned with a halo of light, possessing various forms and shapes, and appearing in the form of a great universal monarch (*mahācakravartin*). 14.2.

Having emerged, he illuminated the entire expanse of the sky; surrounded by all the kings of vidyās and preceded by many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of vidyās, he was honored by all the supramundane vidyā-cakravartin kings and praised by all mantras. Being empowered by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—great-souled ones who have attained the ten stages—he filled the entire vault of the sky. His body was adorned with great maṇi-jewels beautified by divine gems, and his form was lovely and exceedingly radiant. Emitting hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of emanations of various forms, uttering the sound of the single syllable, and releasing a great web of light rays, he stood in the atmosphere above the Blessed One Śākyamuni, gazing directly at him while illuminating the entire realm of the Śuddhāvāsa gods and the great circle of the assembly.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni [taught] the single-syllable sovereign of knowledge (*vidyācakravartin*), the heart of all Tathāgatas, named Ratnaketu—the supreme heart and most profound secret of the Tathāgata Ratnaketu—which was established by the Blessed One Ratnaketu and spoken and rejoiced in by the Tathāgatas Sālendrarāja, Amitābha, Duḥprasaha, Sunetra, Suketu, Puṣpendra, Supināntalokamuni, Kanaka, and others, and which was uttered and approved by all the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the past. And what is that? 14.4. [Oṃ. [End of Chapter 14]
It is as follows: Bhrūṃ.

This, Mañjuśrī, is that supreme heart of all the Tathāgatas, the single-syllable great purifier named the Vidyā-Cakravartin possessing all virtues. When this is accomplished, all mantras are perfected. O Youth, that which is your own supreme secret, conforming to all mantras in this best of ritual kings (*kalparāja*), is authorized as the foremost; it is the purifier of all karmic obscurations. One must certainly accomplish it. Furthermore, O Youth, in this ritual king of yours, all mundane and supramundane mantra-tantras and rites are to be accomplished. Having performed protection with this, one becomes unassailable by all spirits (*bhūta*) and is not overcome by any obstacles, whether mundane or supramundane. (14.5)

As soon as the Blessed One Śākyamuni had spoken these words, the entire trichiliocosm shook in six ways. All the Buddha-fields were illuminated, and all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, assembled in that circle of the assembly seated within the palace of the Pure Abodes. All the Bodhisattvas who had attained the ten stages and were irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; all the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; and all beings of great supernatural power, impelled by the rays of the King of Vidyās, arrived, having become subject to his will. Furthermore, many other beings dwelling in infinite and boundless world-systems, who were situated in the miserable destinies of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, were touched and illuminated by that great radiance of light. Their experiences of suffering, which had been fully awakened within them, subsided; their minds became gladdened with happiness, and they became destined for reliance upon the three vehicles. (14.6)
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having gazed upon that great circle of the assembly, addressed Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince.

Listen, Mañjuśrī, to this King of Knowledge (vidyārāja) of great supernatural power, the solitary hero, the performer of all rites, the universal sovereign of all kings of knowledge, the fulfiller of the hopes of all sentient beings. He has entered into the detailed ritual manuals of your own mantra-tantras throughout the entirety of all kalpas; he is the common ground for the practitioners of all mantras, a being of great majesty and great energy. He is the accumulation of merit and wisdom that purifies the entire path to awakening for practitioners through their specific skill in means, and which is adept at the stages of establishing others in nirvāṇa, ascending to the seat of awakening, and sitting upon the terrace of enlightenment. 14.7.

Thus, in brief, this detailed ritual manual for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*) and the maṇḍala, which serves as the means for accomplishment and follows the former course of mantra-practice—established therein, sentient beings shall accomplish the Great Wheel-Turning King, the King of Vidyās, the Great Being, the Supreme Lord of all mantras, the Radiant One, the Fulfilled of All Hopes, the Guide, the Benefactor of the Entire World, the Self-Existent One who stands manifest like a Buddha himself, and the performer of all rites in their highest, middling, and lowest forms. 14.8.
He who leads to security, who is auspicious and peaceful, the destroyer of all evils—the God even of the gods, the preeminent sage among sages.
The Buddha is bound to the sun, pure, renowned throughout the world, knowing the intrinsic nature of all actions, and untainted by the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
I shall proclaim the excellent ritual manual for those desiring prosperity; listen! First, on a divine cloth that is free of hair and devoid of adhesions, [one should proceed].
One should likewise paint upon a new, white, and especially well-woven cloth,
measuring two cubits in length and one cubit in width.
Likewise, [it should be] auspicious, stainless, beautiful to behold,
white, made of flax, bright, well-prepared, and free from bark-fiber.
On a cloth that removes impurities, which is white, made of fine silk (dukūlaka), or of flax (ātasya), or even of bark-fiber (vālkalai), pure and devoid of woven threads; || 14.14 ||
On such an excellent cloth, one should create a painted temple;
having depicted the image of the Teacher, adorned with a garland of light-halos.
Then, having painted him golden-colored, garlanded with flames,
solitary, hidden in secret, dwelling upon the mountain, and of great renown—
one should indeed fashion a canopy of cloth adorned with a garland of jewels.
Above, one should indeed paint both deities being supported. 14.18.
One should indeed construct a jeweled garland above the mountain,
and it should be adorned all around with pearl necklaces and half-necklaces beneath a canopy.
Having carefully depicted everything above the king of mountains,
one should likewise depict below the mountain the great ocean flooding [the earth].
And at the edge of the cloth, one should likewise paint flowers all around:
the *nāgakesara*, the *puṃnāga*, the *bakula*, and the *yūthikā*.
The *mālatī* flower, as well as *priyaṅgu*, *kurabaka*, the blue lotus (*indīvara*), the fragrant lotus (*saugandhī*), and thereafter the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*).
Various kinds of flowers as well as other fragrant substances—these very flowers [are offered]. || 14.23 ||
And they should also offer something pleasing to the Teacher for the sake of worship,
according to the previously prescribed rule, upon the superior cloth painting as well as on the [other] cloth painting.
The scribe, the weaver, and likewise the painter should be considered [qualified];
on the most pure day during the fortnight of miracles, one should have [the image] painted.
When the time has thus arrived and the recitation (jāpa) is being performed, one should perform everything exactly as previously prescribed for him. 14.26.
One should paint the entire universe of the Teacher, resplendent with colors, richly adorned, endowed with manifold forms, and possessing a luster like that of the *karṇikāra* flower. 14.27–28ab.
One should draw a radiance resembling a campaka flower, depicted in the color of gold;
having thus drawn the Sage, born from jewels, endowed with these physical characteristics.

One should paint that most fortunate Ratnaketu, the supreme bull among sages, who has attained mastery over all dharmas—that jewel of a Buddha. (14.29) [This painting should be done] on silk produced from worms and not from wind[-blown fibers], nor on anything else that is not of *akauśeya* origin, provided it is described as being suitable. (14.15)
Seated upon a mountain of jewels, adorned with precious caves,
he sat cross-legged, imparting instructions on the Dharma.
Having depicted the hero with a slightly smiling face outside the cave, with his mind fixed in meditation, one should likewise draw [him] below and all around.
The practitioner is seated at the corner of the edge of the cloth, with his knees and elbows [resting upon it], his hands occupied with incense, and his body slightly bent forward. (14.32)

One should depict [the Buddha] wearing the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), according to his dress and characteristics; below the Blessed One on the right, even down to the surface of the great ocean, one who is self-disciplined and seeks the highest good should paint the mantra-practitioner. This procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*) has been taught by those honored by the world.
Now, however, the maṇḍala of that deity shall be explained.
At that time, the minister, skilled in counsel and knowing well the sacred formulas, was devoted to the mantra;
he had always served it and practiced it for the perfection of recitation.
Then, he is consecrated by means of the mantra in this ritual manual spoken by Mañjughoṣa;
he is perfected in the conduct of the maṇḍala and is constantly consecrated.

One who has been consecrated is confident in this mandala of all mantras; being possessed of skill in means, he is always considered fit for the tantra, for self-protection, and for what is beneficial. 14.37
And the teacher of great splendor, having thoroughly examined his companions with protective charms that ward off evil, began the rites with great zeal for those who were observant of their vows.
Furthermore, one who possesses great wisdom, is very affectionate, illustrious, and always compassionate—one should prescribe such characteristics for all his companions as well. (14.39)
One, two, three, or likewise eight;
one should make disciples well-perfected, and one should avoid having too many.

One should always perform the previously described ritual procedure in this maṇḍala. Those maṇḍalas first taught by the One Possessing the Ten Powers belong to Mañjughoṣa; one should not draw another, nor perform any other rite.
(14.41) I shall now declare the dimensions of the maṇḍala of great splendor.
Four cubits, two cubits, or likewise eight; beyond that [is the maximum].
In a pure place, especially on a riverbank or a mountain peak,
one should [draw the mandala] with five-colored powders according to the ritual procedure previously observed.
It was square, with four gates adorned by four archways;
it had four corners, was level, divine, and possessed a splendor equal to that of a celestial abode.
One with good companions should undertake [the work] that is brilliant in color, variegated, of beautiful hue, very lovely, fragrant, and well-formed.
Silent, observing the practice of vows, and devoted to the eightfold path; with an unafflicted mind, knowing the proper measure, righteous, and always engaged in recitation.
Having undertaken actions free from evil for the sake of pacification and nourishment, one should enter there as a neutral person and draw [the figures] with the colors of the Teacher. 14.47.
First, one should draw that entire [mandala], adorned with various jewels:
the Tathāgata Ratnaketu, of great splendor, seated within a cave;
seated in the paryaṅka posture, he turns the wheel of Dharma.
Just as all that is worshipped by the Teacher should be painted upon the cloth. 14.49.
One should likewise decorate it with triple lines, [other] lines, and seals,
making all the rows completely covered on every side.
One should place them, both individually and collectively, without confusion regarding their respective positions;
in their midst, one should establish the Great Lord Cakravartin.
Exerting effort, one should draw the radiant youth who resembles the rising sun and follows the great wheel.
Having the appearance of a great king, adorned with the ornament of a crown;
the Great Being wearing a diadem, adorned with every kind of ornament.
Clad in a beautiful half-robe of fine silk and wearing a variegated silken garment, he wears a garland and possesses a gentle complexion; adorned with flower wreaths and fine raiment,
he smells a *bakula* blossom with his very right hand.
The god with a slightly smiling face, possessed of great heroism and sovereign power.
He was indeed of beautiful form and lovely appearance, devoid of both children and the elderly;
his left hand always held a wheel, and he was touching a radiant garland of nectar.

One should paint that form, possessing a divine complexion and beautiful appearance, seated comfortably in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka), with one half of his body resting upon his arm. 14.57–58ab.
Seated upon this fragment of jewels, the one of great splendor who is the source of all lineages,
the bestower of boons, has always set forth for the welfare of all mantras.
Blazing with the form of fire, adorned with a radiant mandala,
it blazes with a garland of flames on all sides, fanned by the wind.
Thus, by the application of mantras, human beings on earth are ignited;
such is that one of great heroism, the accomplisher of all mantras.
For whoever beholds him is a righteous soul and is liberated from all sins;
even one who has committed the five acts of immediate retribution, is of immoral conduct, or is dull-witted—[is liberated]. (14.61)

Indeed, one whose every sin has been pacified is liberated by the sight of the All-pervading Lord. Merely by seeing the mandala of the Wheel-bearer, the God of gods, one is liberated at that very moment from those other sins which have been enumerated.

Then, having purified the eastern gate with the mantra of the Lord himself, one should construct the entire mandala, clearly defined and beautiful in form, surrounded by arches and adorned with plantain trees. (63) One should then diligently offer the bali, incense, lamp, and auspicious perfumes and garlands according to the very same ritual procedure as before. (64)
One should place a full water-pot in the center in front of the practitioner of the wheel;
the knower of mantras should call that pot "Victory" and must not move it.
First, one should prepare the fire-pit according to the rite prescribed by rule;
the commencement of the fire-offering (*homa*) must be done with the *vibhu-mantra* and not otherwise.
One should perform eight thousand oblations with a fire fueled by *khadira* wood.
Also [the wood] of the *pālāśa*, the *śrīkaṇḍa*, the *bilva*, the *udumbara*, and the *akṣaka*.
Likewise, one should diligently offer apāmārga in all rites;
or else sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter and saturated with the fragrance of burnt incense.
One should always offer oblations one thousand and eight times in all rites;
at the three junctions of the day, one should perform the previously prescribed bathing and the wearing of a garment.
The wise have declared that the *triśukla* constellation is auspicious;
it is suitable for the previously specified rites, as well as for recitation (*jāpa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), and other such practices.
One should perform [the rites] with a mantra-endowed family of universal monarchs (cakravartin), or indeed,
one may perform all [rites] among all activities using the single-syllable [mantra] alone.
Endowed with great power and purpose, this solitary hero, ever supreme,
should always perform the ritual manual of all mantras while constantly engaged in recitation.
All rituals, both worldly and those esteemed by the world, are accomplished;
as well as those supramundane ones, the kings of vidyā-mantras of great heroism and great ascetic power. (14.73)

Indeed, all mantras are accomplished through this ritual manual (kalpa); for those mantras which were spoken by the sages as well as by the sons of the One Possessing the Ten Powers (the Buddhas), [they are all effective here]. 14.74
By Śakra and the other world-protectors, by Viṣṇu, Īśāna, and Brahmā,
as well as by the Moon and the Sun, or by others such as the lords of the Yakṣas and the Rākṣasas.
Likewise by the great serpents and the kinnaras, as well as by the best of sages on earth; by the garuḍas, the mātṛs, the worlds, and others who are designated as sentient beings.
Those mantras which have been spoken indeed attain accomplishment here;
he is the attractor of all mantras and the leader of all rites. (14.77)
He possesses mastery over all mantras, is the leader of all ritual actions,
and has mastery over all spirits through the extensive tantras and mantras.

This single-syllable mantra makes all practitioners successful merely by being recited; it attracts all the deities. It is the mastery over all ritual manuals, the great Lord of the single syllable; it produces various forms of diverse kinds as they have been well described.
One who is properly engaged shall accomplish the worldly mantras of the world;
having made the cloth-painting perfectly clear and beautiful to behold in its entirety. (14.81)
One should place it in a pure location, on a riverbank or a mountain peak;
by means of the previously described ritual application, one should always orient it facing westward.
The practitioner, facing the east, seated upon a bundle of *darbha* grass, should perform the recitation (*japa*) without distraction, according to the ritual procedure prescribed by rule.
Neither too loud nor too soft, and not with a mind intent on another, yet without harming any living beings—one will attain success quickly in this world. (14.84)
Always possessing a mind of loving-kindness toward those in the world who are suffering, wretched, constantly without a protector, dejected in spirit, afflicted by calamity, and extremely weak.
Then, filled with compassion for those fallen into this terrible saṃsāra, one attains accomplishment.
One should always diligently perform the great worship before the cloth painting. 14.86.
One should contemplate or even perform the mental, human, divine, and heart-born [forms] of the Universal Cloth of the Lord of Jinas. 14.87.
Right there, one who knows the principles should construct a fire-pit according to the prescribed ritual;
indeed, the practitioner should offer oblations into the well-prosperous fire there.
Having honored with a mixture of white sandalwood, camphor, and saffron,
the knower of mantras should offer one hundred and eight oblations into the blazing fire during the sixth lunar mansion.
One should always kindle a powerful fire using wood produced from the *khadira*, *plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, or even the *pālāśa* tree. 14.90
In the absence of these woods, one should gather another kind of wood—
neither the picumarda, nor the kadvam, nor the sour wood, nor likewise that which originates from the madana tree.
Those with thorns all over [the body] are declared to be excluded from evil rites.
(92) One should perform rites for pacification and nourishment using a single-syllable mantra alone;
success will come quickly for him, even if he should perform an evil deed. (14.92)

For here, the holder of all mantras, together with the ritual actions and the detailed procedures (*kalpavistara*), should be applied with non-conceptualization; they will always attain accomplishment. Then the mantras are drawn forth, and they indeed become bestowers of boons.
Of fuel-sticks made of *palāśa*, *udumbara*, or indeed *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha* wood—
smeared with ghee, mixed with curd, and combined with honey— he offered them with a concentrated mind.
{V102} A mantra practitioner on this earth who desires sovereignty should offer oblations from all sides;
one who longs for a kingdom should offer saffron and sandalwood to the Goddess. 14.95.
Desiring sovereignty over the gods of the vidyādharas, one should offer thirty-six hundred thousand oblations of lotuses together with their filaments.
At the conclusion of the oblation, one should indeed perform there the offering of water (arghya) and the presentation to the Teacher.
There, the most excellent cloth-painting, marked with the Conqueror (Jina), blazes forth on all sides. 14.97.
And as soon as it is touched, one shall fly up to the abode of Brahmā—up to the Akaniṣṭha gods and as far as the collection of the netherworlds (pātāla). 14.98
In this interval, he always becomes the king of all the Siddhas;
possessed of great heroism and firm in his vows, he puts all malevolent beings to flight.
He shall always be the king of the Vidyādharas in the accomplishment of his deeds;
furthermore, he shall live for the duration of an entire kalpa, traversing the long path of existence.
Having passed away from that great aeon, he is destined for enlightenment.
Thus has this other karma been described both in brief and in detail. (14.101)
Having gathered white lotuses combined with white sandalwood, one should perform one hundred thousand oblations; he shall behold Ratnaketu.
Having seen that supreme Jina, one shall then possess the five superknowledges;
one shall live for a long time, a great kalpa, and become an attendant of the Buddha.
And then he beholds the Buddhas residing in the infinite directions;
he should constantly worship them and dwell together with them.
There is a single realm named Ratnāvatī where that Blessed One resides.
The most excellent sage, the best, the foremost, the Tathāgata Ratnaketu.
There he dwells eternally, purified by mantra; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, another desired rite has been taught by the Foremost Persons:
having combined equal parts of *nāgakeśara*, camphor, sandalwood, and saffron, the practitioner of mantra should then perform seventy-eight hundred thousand oblations.
Then, at the conclusion of the oblation, the God arrives here with his chariot;
pleased and ever-granting boons, he touches the practitioner upon the head.
Then, merely by touching [it], the mantra-practitioner shall become the lord of the seven stages;
he is called a Bodhisattva, the legitimate son of the Victors.
But he who is destined for enlightenment will receive his prophecy;
from that time forth, whatever knowledge of the knowable belongs to the Son of the Victor,
he knows it all— the course and the exalted majesty of all mantras.
Upon merely seeing him, the King of Mantras becomes one endowed with the five superknowledges.
Whenever he always manifests his physical form in various ways,
he is constantly devoted to the practice of worship endowed with every excellent aspect.
At that very moment, he becomes intent upon the work of awakening;
in a single instant, he then travels to the worlds and Buddha-fields.
Then, thousands of world-systems, like cosmic eggs, wander everywhere; they behold the conduct of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
He hears the Dharma and is intent upon performing acts of worship for them; furthermore, there is another activity here concerning the arising of the Cakravartin and the Jina.
One should offer a lamp characterized by purity, with a clean wick and ghee, in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay. 14.116–117.
When those lamps had been ignited by men numbering in the hundreds of thousands,
placed there by groups of hundreds of thousands of sailors,
and surrounded on all sides by men— excluding women— who held lamps in their hands; || 14.117 ||
118. One should offer a cloth [painting] known as the image of the Teacher (Śāstṛbimba) in the ritual of worship.
But when all have proceeded equally and the mantra has been consecrated with the *eka-samantrita*, one should offer it to the Teacher with mantras; at that very moment, one should declare success.
On all sides there was the sound of thundering roars and the resonance of drums; indeed, many hosts of gods let out cries of "Excellent! (sādhukāra).
Then the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, stationed in the sky, said:
"Excellent, excellent! O wise one, you have performed a well-done deed."
Do you not see, moreover, the suffering submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra? You have taken refuge in Buddhahood— secure, auspicious, and fearless in nirvāṇa.
On the auspicious and pure path of the eightfold noble conduct, practiced by the virtuous,
you have taken refuge in the form of the mantra, O Goddess watched over by the single-syllable Cakrī.
Furthermore, there is action alone which is based upon the supreme destination;
it is understood as having great power and meaning, and has been fully revealed by all the Buddhas. (14.124)
Having taken a piece of wood made of *nimb*, one should fashion a three-pronged vajra;
both its tips and its middle side should be fashioned from the essence of the thunderbolt.
Then, having purified it with mantras, one should place it before the cloth-painting (paṭa).
Having touched it, the practitioner of mantras, being composed, should recite the mantras.
When sixteen hundred thousand [recitations] are completed, success is desired.
127. Then that vajra becomes a single flame, blazing forth on all sides. || 14.127 ||
Then he drew out that inconceivable [power], for he ascends upwards;
from there he goes to the world of Brahmā or to another realm equal to the gods.
Then, one shall travel through the sky as the foremost among all the Siddhas;
indeed, one exercises sovereignty over the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others.
Then that king becomes a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) in the presence of the gods;
he performs various kinds of physical movements and postures.
Remaining for ten intermediate eons (antarakalpa), he does not waver.
He shall always partake in happiness, be worthy of worship, and always possess a beautiful and handsome form.
One who possesses the conduct of the awakened mind is freed from the suffering of birth; such a person becomes a celestial being or a siddha, entirely devoid of all evil.
Having passed away from there, that mortal shall be devoted to manifold happiness;
wandering through all states of existence, he becomes one who is intent upon awakening.
In this king of mantras, infinite and diverse rites, honored for the sake of the welfare of many worlds, are recited according to their ritual procedures and extensive manuals.

Furthermore, it brings about sovereignty over the earth, the state of Śakra, or the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin); likewise, it effects the superior mastery of the Vidyādharas and the gods.
Or whatever form with many aspects is spoken of here, the practitioner who applies it well indeed attains all accomplishments. (14.136)
Having ascended a couch at night and recited [the mantra] while observing the vow, one attains perfection at dawn; the reciter shall become possessed of the five superknowledges. 137.137.
Having stepped upon a corpse in a cremation ground, the observer of the vow should recite that single-syllable mantra of great significance while remaining motionless; success is sought at dawn.
If one staying in a cremation ground should recite this King of Knowledge, possessed of great supernatural power,
he attains accomplishment within six months and produces whatever result he desires.
Whether in this place or that, when recited with great power,
it brings about accomplishment for those practitioners who apply it correctly while remaining in that very spot.
A white parasol, as well as a sword, a jewel, sandals, and earrings; a necklace, armlets, a garment, and likewise a finger-ring.
A waist-belt, as well as a garment, a wooden staff, and a water-pot;
a sacred thread, a turban, armor, and even a leathern shield;
a deerskin, a pitcher, a rosary, and a pair of sandals.
All those ornaments are supreme; in this world, both are equal.
(14.143) Together with gods, mortals, and others, all these ornaments here bring about success for the reciter in front of the cloth painting. (14.144)
All kinds of objects, as well as minerals, ornaments, and even jewels—all these various weapons were arranged before the cloth painting.
Then, having been purified by reciting it once, and empowered eight hundred thousand times, [the mantra] blazes when joined with all [the ritual elements]; the reciter shall rise up upon touching it.
Furthermore, the various types of beings, possessing diverse forms and appearances,
as well as their ornaments and weapons, may be either made of clay or natural.
Even from among flocks of various birds, those beings renowned as all-living creatures—whether artificial or natural—are of a nature that acts with beautiful form. (14.148)

Furthermore, those who possess the perception of a sentient being or are devoid of perception succeed when the mantra is worshipped; they are arranged with various substances and fashioned from various elements. 14.149
Or else, she who is highly honored as the source of all destinies (gati-yoni), having been placed before this cloth-painting according to the previously seen ritual procedure. (14.150)
Having endured that, the practitioner of mantra should recite it six hundred thousand and seven hundred thousand times;
at the conclusion of the recitation, when those [fires] blaze forth, he attains abundant success.
As soon as they are touched by it, that [light] shall rise up from them in the four directions;
he shall live long and obtain the long-lasting happiness of the inhabitants of heaven in this world.
In whatever manner this King of Vidyās of great supernatural power is employed,
in that very manner he shall be pleased and shall always become a granter of boons.
But those engaged in other activities, through their own ritual acts performed over the course of many eons,
will swiftly attain success as a Vidyārāja of great supernatural power.
Pure, with a pure mind, and always delighting in pure deeds, the knower of mantras attains pure accomplishment in a pure place. (14.155)
One should know that whatever action is performed, its fruit will correspond; from a superior [action], a superior result arises.

From a middling action, a middling result arises, and from an inferior one, an inferior result follows. One who performs an action after having bestowed abundant wealth acts with the conduct of a being.
But if not accomplished, the success of the rite will yield only a very small result.
By merely reciting this constantly, one becomes possessed of great enjoyment and great power;
it always brings about for the practitioner the favor of kings and the status of a minister. When this king of mantras is recited even once, his evil is utterly destroyed.
Recited twice or seven times, it becomes a great protection for oneself.
Chanted eight times, it provides protection for one's companions from all sides;
then the mantra-practitioner should likewise consecrate both garments with the mantra. 14.160.
Both garments, when consecrated with these mantras, liberate one from all diseases;
by touching them while those mantras are recited, the fever of embodied beings is destroyed.
And having consecrated either the face or even the eyes with effort, an angry person is destroyed by the mere sight [of them] by the practitioners when they are enraged. (14.162)
And as for those hosts of spirits who are wicked, harmful, and performers of evil deeds—
one should look upon their faces with this king of mantras recited thirty times.
One should consecrate one's own hand again and again;
by warding off their blows, one is released from all embodied beings.
One should always perform the bathing, drinking, and feeding of children with the most excellent mantra, which has been recited sixty times and is worshipped by the gods. (14.165)
All the wicked ones—the flesh-eaters, the mothers, and the seizing spirits—flee when terrified by the mantra; they perish and always abandon those who are foolish.
In this manner, he likewise performed many such deeds upon the surface of the earth for human beings; thus he always acted with great swiftness.
Whatever beings there are that move about, both various stationary and moving things, whether they be venomous or non-venomous, they perish when struck by the power of the mantra.
Whatever various sufferings there may be, whatever sensations experienced by sentient beings— when applied by the King of Mantras, they quickly bestow peace.
Whatever various miseries exist, such as the afflictions of great pestilence;
Thus, by the recitation of the mantra six hundred times, they are destroyed very quickly indeed.
One should perform the fire-offering rites with [substances] mixed with honey, liquor, and clarified butter;
indeed, one thousand and eight fragrant blue lotuses should be offered with worship.
Through the sesame seeds, the spirits attained peace and the people regained their well-being;
such were the many kinds of [miracles] that arose throughout many kalpas.
When well-employed by the practitioners of mantra, it indeed swiftly accomplishes everything;
by mere recitation, one should effect the destruction of the anger of enemies. (14.173)

For those who possess extensive ritual manuals (*kalpa*) containing the meanings of many mantras, their accomplishment (*siddhi*) is said here to occur through the methods prescribed therein. Furthermore,
one certainly performs minor rites by means of the recitation of mantras.
But when all [these mantras] are recited, they always swiftly accomplish one's purpose.
For the purpose of subjugating all beings, the recitation of the mantra at the three junctions of the day is prescribed;
one should also always perform the rite of fire-offering with *mālatī* flowers.
The mantra is prescribed to be prepared from white sandalwood, camphor, and saffron;
for one who has mastered the recitation, it always makes the mantra fruitful. (14.177)
The reciter shall accomplish his desired aims through constant fire-offerings (nityahoma).
Indeed, the constant fire-offering is prescribed as being prepared with camphor and other such substances.
One should accomplish various rites as they are conceived according to one's desire;
even from a very small rite, there arises abundant prosperity.
"In the middle [of the day], the accomplishment of middling rites is always proclaimed;
therefore, one should especially perform the fire-oblation (homa) in all rites. (14.180)

Thus concludes the fourteenth chapter, the detailed exposition on the ritual procedures for the mandala and the means of accomplishment for the cloth-painting of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*), from the *Ārya-mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Chapter 15. A15.
Ap 15.2: [The rules concerning] the *śrāddha* for those who have died abroad.

"Excellent, excellent, Blessed One! Well-taught, well-proclaimed, and most excellently spoken is this Great Dharma-cloud issued from the application of vidyā-mantras; it is the heart of all Tathāgatas, the sovereign wheel-turner among great vidyā-kings, the extensive great kalpa that fulfills all aims, fruitful, and the unsurpassed path to enlightenment for its practitioners. It is the path for those who follow the conduct of vidyā, including the various rituals, twilight recitations, burnt offerings, and the practice of vidyā, which produces causes and signs born of the conditions of immediate karmic results—a great marvel leading inevitably to the ascent of the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) through the mastery of the ten powers. Therefore, may the Blessed One, the Teacher, kindly explain the signs of dreams and the timing thereof, which are conducive to the accomplishment of mantras, so that beings following the practice of vidyā may undertake the rites for the signs of success, and so that all vidyās may become fruitful through their karmic signs. (15.2)

When this had been said, the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi: "Excellent, excellent, O Lord of Yakṣas! You have set out for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great mass of beings, and for the sake of those who accomplish all vidyās. Listen to it, and attend to it well and thoroughly; I shall speak to you. 15.3

First of all, having gone to a place free from attachment for all activities—whether at the foot of a mountain, on a riverbank, or in a cave or open clearing—and having prepared a dwelling in a pure location, one should install the cloth-painting (paṭa) there. Having performed a great worship according to the same procedure as before for all rites, during the bright fortnight or the fortnight of miracles, necessarily on an auspicious day, one should, in the first watch of the night, mix white sandalwood, camphor, and saffron together. Having kindled a fire with khadira wood in front of the cloth-painting, one should offer eight thousand oblations of ghee in a space measuring four cubits, when the smoke has ceased and the flames have subsided into embers. Then, at the conclusion of the homa, one should offer eight thousand lotus flowers smeared with white sandalwood. And at the end of the homa, having formed the mudrā of the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha), one should offer a seat for one’s own mantra using that very mantra. One should perform the homa with this mantra. (15.4)

Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! It is as follows: Oṃ, you who possess the form of a youth, show, show yourself! For the manifestation of my own prosperity, reveal to me a dream according to reality! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! (15.5) {S146}

Having performed the protection ritual with this mantra, one should perform all the rites for the fire-oblation (*homakarman*) in this practice. Then, having spread out *kuśa* grass with both ends pointing toward the practitioner, one should sleep not too far from and not too close to the front of the painting, using a bundle of *kuśa* grass as a pillow with the head directed toward the east. During the first watch of the night, intent upon the yoga of wakefulness, one should bow to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, confess one's misdeeds, and offer oneself to all the Buddhas. Thereafter, one may fall asleep at ease. (15.6)
Those dreams which occur during the first watch of the night, they know to be born of phlegm; those occurring in the second watch, arising from bile, are censured by the world. (15.7)
In the third [dream], one should recognize it as being caused by wind (vātika); in the fourth, arising from truth;
and in the case of one dominated by phlegm (śleṣmika), one should always see such dreams as these at the beginning of sleep. (15.8) {V109} ap15.3
He sees heaps of jewels and abundant pearl necklaces on all sides,
and he sees himself submerged in a mass of water.
It is strewn on all sides with rivers and submerged by the great ocean;
wherever one may stand, one shall indeed behold it within one's own body.
There, that region was crowded on all sides with lotus ponds,
pleasure groves, taverns, and mansions.
Furthermore, one may see the Himalaya mountain or another mountain, or a great river situated within crystal, being swept away on all sides by floods of water.
He sees a mountain of silver and a mountain of crystal, both inlaid with pearls; he also sees a heap of pearls covered by nets of pearls.
That Kahāvaha beholds a great rain and a flood of water;
he also sees a white, bright umbrella, or even a pale-colored ornament.
An elephant of white form is said to be a dream for one with a predominance of phlegm;
likewise, the sight of a man with a white chowrie or even a white garment [is such]. 15.15
The touching of rock salt and other salts on all sides [is forbidden],
as well as cotton, linen cloth, iron, silver, and likewise aloe-wood.
In the case of touching or swallowing phlegmatic substances, sleep is desired;
likewise, one should dream of beans, bloated bellies, sesame paste, and rice with molasses.
(15.17) Various kinds of bean-based foods are desired in a phlegmatic person’s dream; others include *svastika* cakes, *apūpika* cakes, *kṛsara*, and *pāyasa*. (15.18)
The consumption of these is prescribed for one with a phlegmatic constitution (śleṣmika) in dreams:
19. *śaṅkulī*, *parpaṭa*, various kinds of eatables, and diverse varieties of soups. 15.19.

From touching and from eating [impure things], as well as from [eating] phlegm and filth in a dream, there is an increase of impurity; for various kinds of food and drink have been previously approved. 15.20.
From eating and touching those [substances], there occurs in one with phlegm (kaphin) the behavior seen in dreams:
sitting, lying down, traveling, or riding vehicles produced by living beings.
If dreams such as touching or ascending [a mountain] are seen during the first watch of the night, all of this is said to occur for one with a predominance of phlegm (kapha). 15.22.
Dreams of this kind that involve activities arising from water,
or various visions of diverse kinds of food and drink, belong to those dominated by phlegm (śleṣman).
Having seen the activities of those with phlegmatic constitutions in their dreams,
[one should know that] indeed, many inconceivable dreams have been taught by the Leaders of the World.
Furthermore, the dreams of embodied beings belonging to the bilious constitution occur during the second watch of the night.
Or [one may see her] as a blazing form of fire, or as arising from various jewels.
If a person sees in a dream a firebrand, a great meteor, or a blazing conflagration in every direction, it is because that being is indeed overwhelmed by bile (pitta).
One should recognize the sight of a ruby, or another gem born of precious stones,
in a dream as belonging to a person of bilious temperament (paittika).
From attending the fire, from smelling, touching, or even eating [it], one sees various yellow-colored things in dreams when overwhelmed by bile. 15.28.
One who, overwhelmed by the body's heat due to pitta, constantly sees the sun scorching and always emitting a bitter glare in his dreams— 15.29.

If one sees that sky as golden-colored and the surface of the earth as yellow in a dream, it arises from a depletion of bile (pitta). [One may also see] fire blazing on all sides and the vault of the sky shining brightly.
For at this time of dreaming, the embodied being indeed sees [objects] when overcome by bile.
At that time, the earth, the mountains, or the peaks of stone will be golden in color;
likewise, great elephants and vehicles will all be made entirely of gold.
Constantly remaining in sleep, deluded by the activity of bile,
he sees everything as consisting of golden vessels, vehicles, ornaments, and mounts.
Furthermore, sitting upon or lying down on a seat or bed made of gold, as well as touching or climbing upon them, results in dreams characterized by the bile humor (paittika). 15.34.
Clad in yellow garlands and garments, adorned with yellow cloth,
rich with yellow-splendid perfumes, and wearing a yellow sacred thread.
And he who perceives himself as yellow in form in a dream,
due to the arising of a bilious faint, sees this in the second watch of the night.
Various dreams of such kinds as have been described, as well as those that appear yellowish and arise from bile, are of this nature. (15.37)
In the middle stage of the path, they are not specifically designated for embodied beings; rather, appearing in many forms, they arise with a yellowish luster. 15.38.
The dreams arising from bile have been described by the foremost ones in the world;
now those dreams which are wind-born are told in the third watch.
Indeed, all directions are seen as radiant on every side;
there is also movement through the sky, both horizontally and across the vault of heaven.
He constantly wanders everywhere in the atmosphere and across the firmament.
Such a dream is declared to be of the wind (vātika) type; this is what is prescribed.
Jumping, leaping, and climbing trees;
the study of all the scriptures, and especially of the mantras.

Excessive speaking and chatter, as well as climbing thorny trees and eating extremely bitter foods, [are causes] in the case of wind (vātika). (43) Furthermore, pungent and sour tastes, as well as the consumption of all kinds of hard foods, [are causes] in the case of wind (vātika). (15.43) {S149}
[He gave] fruits of the *vātaskandha* and other principal species to those whose wind-humors (*vāta*) had been provoked.
Furthermore, in dreams involving the eating of these, a condition arising from wind (vāta) is indicated;
likewise, among specific types of food and substances, those that increase wind are [to be understood as such]. 15.45
Likewise, a living being whose mind is deranged [is restored] by touch or even by eating;
and one becomes a servant to all beings merely by the sight of oneself.
Indeed, that which one sees in a dream is known as being caused by wind (vātika);
it consists of various forms, gestures, and the utterance of various signs. 15.47
Various terrible utterances [occur] in a dream-vision of one with a wind-constitution (vātika);
such dreams as these have been described by the preeminent ones in the world. 15.48.

Three types of applications have been taught for those possessed by passion, hatred, and delusion: one should know that for the passionate it arises from phlegm (śleṣman), and for the hateful it arises from bile (pitta). 15.49
That born of delusion is of the wind-nature, while that which is mixed is of the combined nature;
the impairment of sleep is called passion, which is the vision of vulgar conduct.
In a dream arising from phlegm (śleṣman), there may be an enumeration of women;
in a dream arising from bile (pitta), there is that which is called quarreling with those who are hostile. 15.51.
That which arises from delusion has a form of stupor when memory is lost;
indeed, dreams are always seen as joined with these mixed states.
Therefore, in every respect, that which is called a dream is devoid of substantiality;
it is described by the seers of reality as being equal to the time of ritual action. 15.53
Those beings characterized by phlegm (śleṣman) are said to be handsome, pleasant-spoken,
long-lived, dull-witted, of glossy complexion, and self-confident.
Fair-complexioned, tall, and well-proportioned, they are always devoted to the company of women;
they are most righteous, eternally heroic, and ever delight in great honor.
In the constellation [of birth], one may be designated by caste yet remain unmarked by its signs;
likewise, there are rulers of the earth and others established in the office of general.
They are born into the state of Bhogavatī and subsist according to their karma. This is determined by the fruit of one's own actions; there is no mantra devoid of action.
The leaders of the world have declared that ritual action is not the primary mantra. || 15.57 ||
Therefore, success is said on this earth for a being of phlegmatic temperament (śleṣmika).
May he attain mastery over the earth, great enjoyments, and success. 15.58
The practitioner of recitation should not excessively indulge in any foods that increase phlegm;
for when these are consumed in excess, they give rise to dreams whose objects are empty. 15.59

At that time, the mantra-practitioner should not indulge in those [sensual pleasures], for they are not described as being for the sake of accomplishment; nor should the wise and discerning one sleep at that hour.
Now, the conduct of a person of bilious temperament (paittika) is always described as follows:
he is angry with a look of hatred, dark-complexioned, and weak; he is cruel, performs cruel deeds, and is always crooked in his ways. (15.61)
He is always a hero, daring, and endowed with strength and intelligence;
he speaks much, possesses many friends, and has attained mastery over many scriptures.
One who is righteous, steadfast in his undertakings, yet described as having arisen from hatred, becomes a high-minded person of great power, characterized by aversion. (15.63)

He was a hater of the brave, possessed of great wealth, knowledgeable of the world, and pleasant to behold; yet he was liberated from worldly ties, free from desire, steadfast, and always difficult to withstand.
He will always be proud, envious, and angry toward women,
yet he becomes one who possesses great energy, firm counsel, and great enjoyment.
Having stepped upon beings according to their attainment of karma,
his mantras that obstruct the vital breaths are always successfully accomplished.
For the sage quickly accomplishes even fierce and powerful purposes;
whatever actions involve injury to living beings, they are accomplished for that embodied one. 15.67

However, those various ritual applications (prayoga) which have been employed by all mantra-practitioners— those succeed only when performed with reverence, not through rites involving other beings. Indeed, those mantras that are hateful and cause affliction to other sentient beings do not succeed.
Likewise, one should sever the supreme mantras; thus the Krodhasattva is accomplished.
Krodha-mantras succeed for the purpose of seizing the property of others and for those who obstruct the lives of others; however, one should not employ them in other types of mantras.
Furthermore, this being born from hatred exercises sovereignty;
he is black in color, or dark, or fair, or of mixed complexion. Such a mortal is born wrathful and devoid of a golden hue.
Then a man is born with a coarse complexion, or smoky, or tawny.
One born in the zodiac sign of Scorpio is brave, cruel, and likewise greedy;
situated in the domain of the planet Mars, such a person is dominated by phlegm (kapha) due to Jupiter.
For one who eats little and partakes of pungent and sour tastes, long life indeed arises; moreover, he becomes possessed of memory and mantras. (15.74)
I shall now describe the conduct and the behavior of a person with a vātika temperament:
he is discolored and has a rough complexion, yet his physical stature is not excessively weak.
One whose intellect is lost is always unwise; indeed, his heart is unstable and unsettled. There is trembling of the limbs, dizziness, vomiting, and excessive discharge. (15.76)
One who eats excessively and constantly indulges in food will indeed become a speaker of much talk;
he becomes an adversary to all people and is born with many enemies. (15.77)
Born upon the surface of the earth with both immoral conduct and suffering, the success of his secret mantras for invisibility is proclaimed. 15.78.
Those foods which provoke wind follow its nature;
a practitioner of recitation who desires the accomplishment of his rites should never consume them. 15.79
But for these beings who provoke the wind-humor, [the afflictions] arise from delusion;
indeed, these are said to be born of delusion, accomplished through deluded mantras. 15.80.
In those [circumstances], the success of delusions is always desired for the deluded;
when a water-born [planet] is in a lunar mansion or a zodiac sign, and is aspected by a planet for the sake of truth,
one should not perform auspicious rites while the wind is agitating the mind.
The subjugation and attraction of spirits, as well as their delusion and paralyzing, [are accomplished]. (15.82)
Even among beings afflicted by wind, these characteristics of dreams—which arise from delusion and the emergence of evil—are declared to be the vision of truth. 15.83
Indeed, these were described by the sages of old as the achievers of the welfare of sentient beings: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, and Leo. 15.84.
Libra, Virgo, and likewise Scorpio, Sagittarius, and Capricorn;
Aquarius and Pisces, the elephant, the divine monkey, and the asura.

The perfected ones (siddhas), gandharvas, yakṣas, and others who have been proclaimed among human beings—these are the zodiac signs (rāśis) of many sentient beings as taught by the foremost of teachers. 15.86.
Many kinds of diverse actions have been described in various ways;
in all those actions, the full range of qualities bears fruit.
Indeed, no action devoid of qualities is ever taught for embodied beings.
And when endowed with the qualities and joined with karma, he brings about rebirth once again.

Success arises in the mantras for one who possesses the qualities connected with dharma and artha; the reciter, knowing the reality of the qualities, [perceives] the merit and demerit of the bonds of karma. 15.89
One does not perform beneficial action if there is no proper application even toward the qualities;
for it is the action that accomplishes the task, not an action devoid of its constituent qualities.
Joined with the qualities of action and its object, he will accomplish it;
for the ritual action preceded by the prescribed method was taught of old by those possessed of the ten powers.
For these are indeed the functions, objects, and qualities, seen as the activities of a sentient being;
various forms like those in a dream are perceived, arising from karma. 15.92
Therefore, by means of dreams as their instrument, extensive ritual actions—varied in form, beautiful, pleasing, and lovely to behold—should be performed. 15.93
Forms of obstacles appear both with form and without form as causes for dreams.
(94) Men of great zeal and great heroism who desire accomplishment—(15.94)—for them, accomplishment is ordained among the highest, lowest, and middling [dreams]. {S153}
95. But fierce dreams involving cruel deeds always bear fruit immediately. 15.95.
The highest [mantras] are for the accomplishment of stable rites over long periods of time;
they are worldly [in nature], capable of producing qualities in those who are leaders of the world.
Various dreams are seen by those who recite mantras for the sake of attaining mantra-siddhi;
however, for the sake of non-attainment of mantras, sleep and lethargy are produced.
At that time, the mantra for the destruction of obstacles is prescribed; one who recites it should employ those mantras, which are of the nature of skillful means. 15.98.
Then the great wrathful one, six-armed and six-faced, was manifested; the four-syllable great mantra was issued forth from the form of Kumāra.
That king of gods, assuming a form as formidable as a boar, became Mahāghora of terrible aspect for the purpose of destroying all obstacles. 15.100.
Clad in a tiger skin, with a serpent’s coils hanging down,
sword in hand, that being of great power and immense energy assumed the form of Death itself.
Compassionless toward all obstacles, he is the slayer of the life-force of the Vināyakas.
Let all beings indeed hear this most formidable mantra in the Tantra.
The destroyer of those beings who have been seen [by him], the remover of all obstacles, the accomplisher of all mantras—O hosts of gods, listen to me!
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! It is as follows:

104. He he! O Great Wrathful One, six-faced, six-legged, destroyer of all obstacles, hūṃ hūṃ! Why do you delay, O ender of the life of Vināyaka? Destroy my bad dreams! Laṅgha laṅgha! Remember your pledge! Phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!

As soon as this Great Wrathful King was spoken, all the obstructors and leaders of obstacles—afflicted, terrified, with broken hearts and trembling minds—paid homage to the Blessed One Śākyamuni and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, and they remained established in their pledge. 15.105. {S154}
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed that entire abode of the Pure Abodes and that great mandala of the assembly, spoke thus:

"O hosts of gods! This is the King of Wrath. For any wicked being who should harass a practitioner while the mantras—both mundane and supramundane—are being accomplished, this King of Wrath shall subdue his entire family and wither them; yet he shall not take their lives. Having scorched and withered them, he shall establish them in the state of discipline. He shall remain for the protection, preservation, and guarding of the practitioner, and he shall provide him with strength. For whoever should transgress this pledge and harass the practitioner protected by the King of Wrath..."
"His head shall split into seven pieces like the cluster of blossoms on an Arjaka tree.
Having spoken thus, the best of sages then addressed Mañjughoṣa.
O Kumāra, [I shall explain] the extensive exposition of all the meanings of your mantras,
especially for practitioners who are engaged with the meaning of the mantra-tantras.
This King of Wrath, which destroys all obstacles, was taught in the Tantra;
indeed, it was likewise employed by the Lords of the World in the past.
For the destruction of wicked obstacles and the subduing of the wrath of enemies, this [mantra] should always be recited at night by those who practice its recitation. 15.110.
This [mantra] was taught by the leaders of the world for the protection of sentient beings and for the destruction of bad dreams, as a means for accomplishing the purpose of all mantras. 111.111
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the auspicious characteristics of persons,
among whom mantras— whether superior, inferior, or middling— are brought to accomplishment.
He was radiant and high-minded, with a golden complexion and a large belly;
he had wide eyes, was very gentle, free from passion, and devoid of anger.
One with eyes whose corners are reddish and who speaks kindly to loved ones attains the highest success.
Furthermore, one with thin skin, a dark complexion, slender limbs, and a body that is not too tall [is also successful].
Possessing great energy and great splendor, contented and auspicious in every way; excellent by birth and pure, yet having few desires and being weak.
For such a person, success in all undertakings is seen to be certain and supreme; moreover,
he is complete in his limbs, dark-complexioned like dūrvā grass, and possesses great majesty.
With an unafflicted mind, wise and always pure in his holy life,
he is constantly delighted in his dwelling, knows the world, and is virtuous in the Dharma.
He always has many friends, is ever-generous, and always acts with moderation;
he is pure, skillful in character, and constantly devoted to cleanliness and proper conduct.
One who speaks the truth and is compassionate attains the highest success;
such a person is always of noble birth, righteous, and possessed of the full expansion of all excellent qualities. 15.119
One who is devoted to his mother and father, who honors Brahmins and guests, who is exceedingly compassionate and steadfast—for him too, supreme accomplishment is attained. (15.120)
He is dark-complexioned yet fair, affectionate, speaks little, and is always pure;
he desires delicious food and approaches his wife only when she is clean.
A person who knows the world and is highly esteemed by beings also attains supreme success;
he is neither too short nor too tall, and his hair is like crushed collyrium.
With affectionate eyes and a pleasing complexion, always pure and devoted to bathing, he was full of faith in the Three Jewels; for him too, the supreme accomplishment was attained.
Engaged in supreme activity and knowing the intentions of sentient beings, the son of the Conqueror is patient, speaks kindly, and is serene;
then his supramundane accomplishment is held to be fruitful. (15.124)
The great being of great heroism, of great majesty, and of great vows;
possessing great wealth, he is a knower of mantras and one who understands the reality of all tantras.
By caste he was indeed a preeminent Kṣatriya, or perhaps a wise Brāhmaṇa;
he was always devoted to women and passionate, and by complexion he was like gold.
He is seen to be tall, fair-complexioned, with a prominent nose and mighty arms;
he has long-reaching shoulders, is heroic, and desires great sovereignty.
Devoted to the sons of the Conquerors, he is known as Strī, a worshiper of goddesses; he is faithful to the Three Jewels and adorned with the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
He is exceedingly compassionate and steadfast, though he may occasionally exhibit anger born of delusion.
He possesses great wealth, is a great renouncer, is of great splendor, and is difficult to overcome.
He is beloved by women and brave; for him also, there is supreme accomplishment.
He is fond of excessive drinking, yet brave; he is always attached to women.
He has a golden complexion, eats little, and has broad hips; he is pure, compassionate, merciful, skillful, knowledgeable of the world, and highly esteemed for his virtues.
Constantly reciting mantras and devoted to the Lords of Jinas, he will be a powerful illuminator.
Furthermore, among those sons of the Śrāvakas and the Pratyekabuddhas (Khaḍgins), he will always be preeminent;
as a leader of the world, he will be of auspicious complexion in his second birth.
He was free from physical defects in all his limbs, yet always fierce and impetuous;
he was generous by nature, had conquered his enemies, and was a judge of both righteousness and unrighteousness.
Neither too stout nor too lean, neither too tall nor too short—the person of medium build is the best; for him, too, there is the highest accomplishment.
With copper-colored nails, very glossy, and palms red, he is pure;
from the tips of his feet they are red and glossy, adorned with wheels and svastikas.
On his hands and feet, the marks of a great man are seen as banners, arches, fish, pennants, lotuses, and blue water-lilies. (136) 15.136.
Such a person is the most excellent; indeed, he is conceived as having attained the supreme accomplishment.
His teeth are white, without gaps, prominent, and even like mountain peaks. 15.137.
He has a prominent nose and large eyes; his eyebrows and chin are well-knit and auspicious.
His eyelashes are like those of a cow, his gaze is dark, and he is graced by beautiful pupils.
He whose forehead is broad and whose head is auspiciously shaped like a parasol, and whose head is likewise shaped like a turban (uṣṇīṣa), and whose ears are beautiful and auspicious; 15.139.
His jaw is always shaped like a lion's; his two lower lips have a luster like that of a ripe *bimba* fruit.
His tongue appears with the reddish glow of a lotus petal, and his palate is likewise beautifully red.
His neck is like a conch shell, his shoulders are full and well-developed;
his armpits and chest are auspicious and excellent, and likewise his breast is broad.
His navel region is slightly deep, broad, and firm, and is auspicious.
142. His navel is deep and clockwise-turning, and his network of veins is unobtrusive. 15.142.
His arms hang down long and his forearms are great; his hips are marked with the signs of a lion.
His thighs are rounded, and his elbows are free from any blemish.
His shanks are like those of the eneya antelope, and they are celebrated for being well-proportioned and rounded;
his feet are fleshy and elevated with well-formed toes.
His two hands were red, with red nails, glossy, elevated, and graced by flesh;
moreover, his head was beautiful, lovely to behold, and possessed the color of the earth's surface.
Not joined together, pure in color, praiseworthy, and marked by the signs of the world;
moreover, above them, the network of veins is not protruding.
The two channels for the flow of excrement have deep whirlpools and turn to the right;
they are praised as being always very small. The two testicles are round, auspicious, and frequently described as being unbroken and numerous.
When one relies upon the purity of the sexual organ at the conclusion of passion, || 15.148 ||
Furthermore, during the time of sleep or through the consumption of aphrodisiac foods and edibles, if the [semen] is seen to flow out, being blue or red in color, [it is a sign of disease]. (15.149)
One who has abundant secretions and is unctuous, marked with auspicious characteristics—such a being is called a *sattva*, and for him, the highest accomplishment (*uttamā siddhi*) is desired. 15.150

One who voids excrement three times and urinates six times, who is devoted to pure conduct and is himself pure; that person who indeed lies down at the end of the watch and rises in the morning—for such a one, the most excellent success is always seen in all undertakings.
He shall be an enjoyer of various kinds of fruits and great abundance; he will be distinguished by middling marks and likewise born under the constellations Puṣya, Revatī, or Phalgunī.
In Maghā, Anurādhā, Citrā, Rohiṇī, and Kṛttikā—
when one is born at dawn while the Sun is visible in these [asterisms] and is marked by an auspicious planet, success is seen for them. (15.153)

At midday, at dawn, and at the end of the day, the pure planets—the white ones, Soma, Śukra, Pītaka, Budha, and Bṛhaspati—survey all living beings for the sake of accomplishing their capacities and purposes. (15.154)
Furthermore, those humans who are born during this interval and perform auspicious deeds—
for them, mantras succeed without effort in accomplishing all aims.
At midday and thereafter, and always at the setting of the sun—
at this interval, cruel planets always behold embodied beings.
The Sun, Mars, and the cruel planets Ketu, Rāhu, and Saturn;
and those who are the foremost among the grahas, such as those causing earthquakes, thunderclaps, and meteors.
The star Apahāraka, as well as Ghoratama, and likewise Kṛṣṇa and Ariṣṭasama;
Kālamārakuru and Raudra are seen at that time according to the [course of] time. 15.158
At the time of sunrise, Budha beholds the earth;
at a height of one *yuga* (four cubits), Bṛhaspati beholds it from his chariot.
When the sun is in the conjunction [of the asterism] Śukra, that lord of wealth beholds it from beyond his riches;
at midday the moon becomes full, and there is the sight of the moon for those who possess lunar bodies.
During the time of Mercury, there shall be sovereignty; during that of Jupiter, it brings wealth and enjoyment.
During Venus, there is the attainment of riches, great kingship, and an abundance of enjoyments.
Likewise, during the Moon, there is long life as well as lordship that is fruitful. Similarly, at midday, the Sun is said to produce a neutral (mediocre) aspect.
When midday has passed, the sun always gazes toward the direction.
When the comet is lowered by the measure of a yoke (*yugamātra*) and not elevated, it is thus described; Rāhu, Śanaiścara, and Tamakālayugāntaka are likewise.
Beyond that, when it is lowered further, it causes misfortune, portents, meteors, and earthquakes.
When the sun had set, appearing like a mass of vermilion,
that chief of planets, possessing a form like a young child,
was seen with a spear in his hand, most cruel, resembling a glowing ember.
Then, when the sun has reached the end of the age, the sources of the auspicious planets [arise].
One born under Āditya-darśana will be cruel and impulsive;
one born under Satya-kāṅgāraka will be angry, greedy, and conceited.
When Ketu is present, there arise diseases caused by smoke-colored [planets];
people are always impoverished, afflicted by illness, greedy, and deluded. (15.167)
At that time, there were earthquakes, meteors, and the ominous portents of planetary conjunctions;
there were also celestial tremors, thunderclaps, falling stars, and blazing lightning bolts.
Likewise, the *Vajroriṣṭa* and other [mantras] are prescribed for those afflicted by bears and similar creatures;
however, the terrible sight of Rāhu is seen by all living beings.
Human beings are always born as poor, helpless, and immoral people, as wicked thieves, and as those afflicted by suffering, diseases, and calamities; they are lepers,
plagued by many ailments, one-eyed, lame, and suffering from scabies.

Eunuchs and impotent men, those childless and unfortunate among women, as well as those who are contemptible, and other men and women who are likewise despised for their adherence to false views—[these are the ones who do not see it]. 15.171.
In the world, various types of birth-omens arise within the very categories of birth;
among these, the white and yellow planets are the most excellent, as they bring about the auspicious arising of one's birth.
In terms of color, those that have a white or yellow luster are praised and extolled by the Victors.
The four foremost among the planets are Venus, the Moon, Jupiter, and Mercury.
For the sake of accomplishing the vision of those [deities] in all rites by the reciter, as well as for simple-minded beings, birth itself is always auspicious.
All forms of prosperity are always desired, so it has been taught by the Bulls of the World; even for a mere moment, or the blink of an eye, or a finger-snap.
This brief account of their birth has been told by the leaders of the world;
this alone is the measure of the planets as conceived by those who contemplate the world. Thus they always rise at this very time according to reality.
177. For these evildoers, though [seeking] what is better, wander perpetually like a wheel.
{S160} 178. Those who perform both auspicious and inauspicious deeds here always [chant] a mantra as one;
they have resorted to the world of the gods... [and so forth]. 15.178.
Among these, in some cases, a certain evil intention arises;
furthermore, from sentient beings, results both auspicious and inauspicious arise in many ways. (15.179)
They say that this is the vision of these planets who consume the fruits of karma;
they come swiftly toward beings, being themselves eager for rapid motion.
The visible and the invisible [occur] in moments; the movement of a finger-snap is swift. From that, time is calculated...
this measure of time has been shown by those of foremost intelligence.
Henceforth, I shall explain that which always pertains to a determined birth.
There are twelve muhūrtas, as well as the considerations of the right and wrong time; and the unworthy recipient shall also be described, whether they are a cause for success or not. (15.182)
Furthermore, he perceived the omens of the worlds through repeated sightings and non-sightings,
as well as the ruin of kingdoms, famine, and the prosperity of kings.
At that time, O noble one, the people always experienced both the timely and the untimely;
there were tremors of comets, as well as thunderclaps and smoke-shrouded meteors.
The movements of the lunar mansions, the days of the week, and the stars, both auspicious and inauspicious; the conduct of all living beings, and their deeds that are either propitious or calamitous.
I shall likewise describe the conduct of the flesh-eating *kravyāda* mothers who possess fierce natures and cause harm, as well as those wicked beings who subsist on meat. 15.186

Where the deities are pleased with those whose minds are fixed upon the supreme jewels of the Dharma—those who are ever engaged in auspicious deeds, possessing hearts of loving-kindness and compassion.
188. [He saw] those whose virtuous conduct, wealth, and intellects were dependent on the fulfillment of others, drawn away by mantras, liberations, medicines, and the means of sustenance.
I shall describe in detail their conduct, upon which their characteristics depend;
relying upon the bodies of others, they abide taking recourse in human beings.
There too, they go in two ways: again, as the cruel and the common;
there too, they go in two ways: into the fivefold destinies of the auspicious and the inauspicious.

Remaining there, they proceed through three types [of rebirths]: twenty, thirty, and incalculable [lifetimes], up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, the lords of the gods, the Yāma heaven, and the incalculable Abhūpa heavens.
As far as the infinite realms and worlds, including their auspicious and inauspicious states; as many as there are worldly beings and as many as there are noble Śrāvakas. (15.193)
[He sees] the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as their legitimate sons;
the Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, who are established on the ten stages.
In that same way, all sentient beings are always dependent upon the womb of sentient beings; all foolish creatures are dependent upon the destinies and wombs [of rebirth];
while for those who have been liberated from the ocean of saṃsāra, there is the womb of all the Noble Ones.
The constant characteristics and conduct of all [beings] are always present; however, I shall explain in detail their true nature as revealed through speech and gestures.
All beings are indeed drawn forth by means of mantras, tantras, and proper applications;
one who knows the mantras for summoning and drawing forth perceives those who have entered and taken refuge in another body.

Drawn down to the surface of the earth in the world of humans by mantra-reciters who are skilled in knowing wholesome and unwholesome karma, who are heedful, who possess the power of recitation, whose conduct is free from delusion, and all of whom are capable of both restraint and favor. (15.198)
I shall, however, explain in accordance with reality everything regarding the signs of their accomplishment,
for the sake of conforming to the bodies of those humans who are always afflicted by disease.
This is always intended for the sake of supreme Dharma and for the sake of liberation; therein lies the restraint of the wicked and the honoring of the pure.
In this way, the mantra and tantra are prescribed for both restraint and favor;
here, there is a threefold action for the three [humors]: wind, phlegm, and bile.
For these, one should prescribe pacification; indeed, a threefold sequence is intended.
In that regard, one should always perform the medical treatment of human beings with mantras.

The conceptualization of the great elements (mahābhūta-vikalpa), however, is traditionally held to be "the element" (bhūta) and "that which exceeds the elements" (bhūtādhika). Likewise, that which is overcome by the elements is called "the over-element" (adhibhūta).
"The gods [attain] merit," they say; "the asuras [do so] because of pride. Thus, those two classes of attendants there, the gods and the asuras, are of two kinds. (15.190)

When a living being produces a state of ill-health, then that which is not an element (abhūta) is conceptualized as a type of element (bhūtaprakāra), and it is indeed conceived as being twofold: 15.204–205. It is conceived as a sentient element (sattvabhūta) and likewise as a non-sentient one; [these include] bile, phlegm, wind, and whatever others there may be.
The four great elements and the fifth, space, are held to be mine:
water joined with fire, and earth joined with wind.
Furthermore, the wise always say that these are reckoned as non-sentient.
"For he is indeed the supreme lord of the pinnacle of the world," so spoke the one of great splendor. (15.207)
"For that which is not reckoned as a sentient being is indeed non-human," so said the one of supreme wisdom, the best among speakers, "is called a human being. (15.208)
Whether it be non-human or human, including all beings counted among sentient creatures as well as the gods—
for the sake of the welfare of all beings, there is once again the word of the Omniscient One.
