In this very way, karma— which brings about the arising of both auspicious and inauspicious fruits— has been taught by the Buddhas of the past, the future, and likewise those of the present.
The mere word of the Buddhas necessarily brings about the result;
because of that cause and due to the commonality of the spiritual lineage (gotra), accomplishment is indeed clearly perceived. || 15.211 ||
They say that omniscient knowledge is security, peace, and eternally pure;
it is held to be liberation, the ultimate reality, which is grounded in pure selflessness.
That very path among sentient beings is what this sutra has proclaimed;
therein, through the mantra, the seat, and the medicinal herbs, he spoke every word in its entirety.
The reality that has been and will be, absolutely honored by all scriptures,
the foremost in the world, the selflessness of phenomena, the state that is eternally peaceful and auspicious—
this is the speech of the Omniscient One; it is his ultimate, supreme state.
However, these two are conceived solely as arising from the knowledge of the Omniscient One.
The power of all the Buddhas and the wise Bodhisattvas, as well as the accomplishment of mantras in all rites everywhere, has been demonstrated;
for this very reason, the Lord of Sages has proclaimed this King of Ritual Manuals (Kalparāja).
Traveling by this path in the form of mantra for embodied beings, one reaches the city of Nirvāṇa, which possesses the wealth of peace and freedom from decay—
free from sorrow, stainless, secure, culminating in awakening, and eternally auspicious.
This tantra, which is the teaching of all the Buddhas for those who recite mantras,
has been taught on the surface of the earth in its entirety for those who recite mantras.
The object of knowledge for the wisdom of the Omniscient One is bound by the cause of karma;
all this, however, is the meaning of mantra, which flows toward the threefold awakening.
The complete knowledge of the Buddhas has been revealed here in this eon, and for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, it has been set in motion throughout all worlds.
Whatever is found in this *Kalparāja* is not seen in other *kalpas*.
That which was taught in other *kalpas* by the sons of the Sage, those best of sages—
all that exists here in this extensive ritual manual (*kalpa*) of all mantras.
For this very reason, it was said by the Lord of Jinas for all embodied beings: || 15.222 ||
And upon the surface of the earth, throughout these three worlds,
there is no one who has not been brought under control or subdued by this sovereign king of rituals.
When the moon-like Sage has set and the circle of the earth is empty,
he will act for the sake of the teaching while this world remains in this eon.
The youth Mañjughoṣa, ever auspicious among all beings,
shall likewise perform the work of a Buddha in this world and in this teaching.
Having heard the power of this King of Ritual Manuals (kalparāja), those who have long desired it will gain faith upon hearing it even once; for them, success shall always be attained.

(15.226) This speech is always auspicious and never in vain for all beings, [addressed] to practitioners who are constantly devoted to recitation and fire-offerings among all living creatures. (15.227)
Whatever knowledge functions among the knowledges pertaining to the three times,
that very same [knowledge] functions in this supreme king of manuals.
The establishment of mantras is here declared to be the teaching of the Buddhas;
yet that mantra is free from conceptual construction, though it is spoken here within this realm of conceptualization.
He brings about the welfare and misfortune, the auspicious and inauspicious, for all sentient beings;
likewise, he determines the destinies, the intellects, the nature of beings, and the prosperity and adversity of the worlds.
This is elaborated upon in the Kalpa: "The Tathāgatas are beyond conceptual proliferation; though they transcend the world and are self-awakened, they speak here for the sake of the world. (15.231)
Exceeding all phenomena, for he transcends the worldly dharmas; the practitioner performs various and manifold deeds that are honored by the world.
The King of Mantras, engaged in ritual activities for the benefit of the multitude of beings,
he is the youth Mañjughoṣa, who performs the work of a Buddha.
Its purpose is the accomplishment of qualities, the foundation of the world, and [the distinction between] the auspicious and the inauspicious.
I am indeed the requester and the speaker; it is not said that there is no dharma for one who requests.
This exclusive [teaching] spoken by the Buddha for the benefit of all sentient beings was spoken by all the Buddhas of the past and shall now be proclaimed.
One who has faith will cause the lineage of the Buddhas to remain unbroken;
for them, this [mantra] shall give rise to the knowledge of the Omniscient One in all the rites of practitioners.
But action that proceeds toward the wisdom of the omniscient one is alone praised.
One’s own former action in the world is now being experienced.
Therefore, one should perform action here in these births, even if it is difficult to do.
The mantras are accomplished without effort; even here in this world, that bondage of karma [is severed].
Success may arise even in this life through action;
therefore, all the Buddhas have praised action alone. When that action is joined with the prescribed ritual, success is achieved here in this very world.
Foolish beings, devoid of the proper method and utterly deluded, wander about.
Therefore, action is praised in every respect: one who is disciplined will accomplish that rite joined with action when it is conjoined with the prescribed method;
likewise, an action devoid of the method does not succeed even after a very long time.
"For there is no liberation without meditations, nor is there liberation devoid of meditation.
Therefore, the union of meditation and liberation is called awakening. (15.242)

Thus concludes the fifteenth chapter, the detailed exposition on the purpose of all ritual actions, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Chapter 16.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsabhavana), addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Listen, Mañjuśrī! I shall explain in detail, in the midst of this assembly, the extensive section on the ritual manual for the performance of all purposes belonging to you, which was previously indicated. This has been requested by the wise Vajrahasta, the king of the yakṣas."
Thus, in this context, all this has been told concerning the auspicious and inauspicious dreams of those who recite mantras, as they are connected with the meaning of all mantras.
Then the king of the yakṣas, with a joyful mind and having placed his joined palms upon his head, bowed his head to the Teacher and spoke these words: 16.3.
Indeed, for the sake of favoring the worlds, this has been told by the one of supreme intelligence; thus, out of compassion for me and for the arising of happiness for all beings.

16.5 For those who recite all mantras, [he knows] the auspicious and inauspicious dreams, their conduct, and the expansion of their qualities; [he knows] the lowly state of beings through his empowerment, and the activity of causal knowledge regarding the highest destinies and births.
Knowledge of the past and the future, knowledge of the present, and knowledge of the auspicious and inauspicious—
all-pervading knowledge of all things is the activity of the knowledge of the Omniscient One.

That which is without appearance and without an object of apprehension, free from conceptual proliferation yet manifested through proliferation, endowed with the excellence of all aspects—this auspicious peace has been proclaimed. (16.7)
The power of all the Buddhas has indeed been described by the one of supreme intelligence, especially for those who recite mantras and are engaged in the meaning of all mantras.
In the context of dreams, he was questioned concerning all actions and their fruits, as well as the time of the performance, the recipient, the location, and the attire. (16.9)
The Yakṣas [honored] the best of sages, the seventh Tathāgata;
for among those Buddhas who appear in the Bhadrakalpa, this seventh one is the Bull of the Śākyas.
This seventh one is designated as the Lion of the Śākyas, the Conqueror of Enemies;
in this degenerate age, he has attained perfect awakening as the Lord of the World, the Maker of Light.
The sage Mahāvīrya, possessed of great wisdom and exalted by great majesty—
the Bodhisattva Yakṣa Vajrapāṇi— paid homage to him. Then the wise one stood upon his own seat, having become silent.
Then Mañjuśrī, possessed of great wisdom, was questioned by the Sage at that time.
He entreats that Buddha, the youngest of the best of sages:
"It would be well, O Blessed One, Perfectly Awakened One, if you were to explain in full detail the karma and knowledge [of this being],
as well as his ever-auspicious Jātaka."
The conduct of many beings, together with their karma and knowledge, has its cause.
For those who have entered into settled conduct, who are intent on the means for attaining the highest good,
and who recite mantras— [for them] there are signs of success regarding what is to be accomplished or not accomplished.
Likewise, for those in the world desiring prosperity, for those longing for the enjoyment of power,
for those seeking excellence for the sake of sovereignty, and for those desiring the attainment of *siddhis* and *dhāraṇīs*.
"May all-encompassing knowledge be revealed in brief!
Thus spoke the supreme sage, having been entreated by the Son of the Jina.
The wise one, possessing the voice of the kalaviṅka bird and sounding like a divine drum; with a voice like that of Brahmā, a great hero whose resonance is like the roar of thunder;
impelled by the speech of the Buddha, pure in his utterance, the seventh Sage uttered this verse.

O Prince, this success has arisen for those who have attained the supreme goal and who act for the welfare of the world; may it lead the world toward the highest good and universal benefit, and may it abide for the sake of the liberation of the lords of beings.

For those who possess inexhaustible vigor and truth, whose minds are always delighted by non-arrogance and loving-kindness, and who delight in giving—in such people success will always prevail; no one else shall ever attain success in any way.

Those who always delight in contentment within this excellent mantra, or likewise in the teaching of Cakradhara or Mañjuvara—having subdued Māra and set the wheel in motion, they too are indeed joined here with Cakradhara.
His speech is eternally divine and enchanting, devoid of anything childish;
it is divine, delightful to the ear, pleasant, sweet, and agreeable.
"O Buddhas, proclaim that he is Mañju, who bestows the joy and bliss that gladden the mind—
[Mañju] whose non-existence cannot even be known by those [others], even through the specific wisdoms of the Tathāgatas. (16.24)
Furthermore, among them were ten sons who had entered the earth, possessed of divine and preeminent qualities;
even they, O Lord of Gods, being distinguished from the world, were unable to understand his divine power.
Formless, likewise formless, not of the earth, nor of the desire realm, nor divine, nor human, nor born of men;
having attained the perfection of yoga, they are thus the most distinguished in the world, the foremost among men. (16.26)
There is no being whatsoever to be found who can truly claim his splendors;
the Buddhas claim him as Mañjuśrī, which is equivalent to a name fashioned by mere glory.
"Mañjuśrī, this name 'Equal to the Imagined' was likewise given to you by former Victors;
it was established for you in the Saṃjñita eon by divine Buddhas of the past and those yet to come. (16.28)

Upon hearing this name, his mind shall not become perverted or impure, nor shall it be distracted; with a single-pointed mind, for him there shall be this auspicious peace, and supreme, distinguished enlightenment shall arise.
May all attain complete accomplishment and reach the state of the highest birth;
may they always rely upon the supreme Dharma and achieve success free from all obstacles. 16.30.
Having accomplished all desired mantras, he quickly proceeds to beautiful awakening;
having reached awakening, that foremost of sages sits down for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings.
He awakened to enlightenment and set in motion the wheel; this is the virtue proclaimed by the foremost of Jinas.
Remembering your name, "Mañju," which means "beautiful," inconceivable virtues have been proclaimed by the foremost of Jinas.
May your eternal power be revealed, which was previously described by all the foremost Jinas;
even if one were to speak for incalculable eons, O pure youth, it would not be possible to exhaust the hundreds of your mantras.
O Mañjuśrī, this practice of your mantra has been taught in its entirety by all the Buddhas without exception.
O Youth, these heroes, who have reached everywhere, hold your supreme teaching as their highest delight.
Those beings dwelling in the Pure Abodes are indeed all sentient beings by virtue of this very existence;
yet, your mantra never at any time, nor in any way whatsoever, steps over those who have not [received] your mantra. Thus [it is said].
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the detailed exposition of the section on verses, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra.
{S169} {V128} Chapter A17: The Seventeenth Chapter on Water.

Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni entered the samādhi called "The Miraculous Manifestation of All Tathāgatas. Immediately upon his entering it, rays of light issued forth from the circle of hair between the eyebrows of the Blessed One Śākyamuni—rays of blue, yellow, white, madder-red, and crystal color. Having illuminated this entire Buddha-field and lit up the intervals between all world-systems, they eclipsed all the planets and constellations in a mere moment and drew them forth. Having drawn them forth and stationed each in its own place, and having drawn that assembly-circle toward [himself] through the Buddha’s empowerment, they vanished right there into the circle of hair between the eyebrows of the Blessed One Śākyamuni. And all the planets, constellations, and stars, their luminosity being obstructed, distressed and terrified, approached the Blessed One Śākyamuni. With palms joined, they stood trembling, falling repeatedly to the surface of the earth. 17.1.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, for the sake of favoring all the planets, lunar mansions, stars, and luminaries, as well as embodied beings whose intellects are born of ignorance, uttered these words: || 17.2 ||

Listen, worthy sirs, you hosts of gods and humans! It is karma alone that differentiates the manifold variety of the world for sentient beings. Whether it be the accomplishment of the adamantine body (*vajrakāya*) of the Blessed Buddhas, or the accomplishment of the diverse bodies of the world—including gods and asuras—when that world has entered the wilderness and desolate forest of wandering saṃsāra, all this is born of karma; it is bound by what is auspicious and inauspicious. In this regard, no agent, no doer, no Lord (*īśvara*), no Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*), nor any Person (*puruṣa*) projected by the Sāṅkhya school, operates at all, with the sole exception of that which is born of karma. Produced by the conditions of all karma, it depends upon a cause.

And that [process] depends upon causes and conditions; thus, through the mutual conjunction of the conditions of dependent origination, the production of the humors (śleṣman) brings about the manifestation of the primary elements (mahābhūta). || 17.3 ||

And those great elements (mahābhūta) enter into another aggregate (skandha) from beginningless course-of-existence; having entered, they are reborn in various locations of existence with extensive distinctions. The latencies (vāsanā) constructed by karma—fanned by the fire of ignorance regarding the obstruction of time—are completely incinerated. They bring about the transcendence of the non-conceptual state (niḥprapañcatā), which is the equality of the three vehicles. The karma accumulated over a long period in the Mahāyāna proceeds as the self-arisen knowledge (svayambhujñāna) of the Pratyekabuddhas of the middle period, who are like rhinoceroses. For the Śrāvakas, who proceed by following the voice of another, there is sovereignty for only a short time. Therefore, for the deluded and ignorant, it is only the intellect that proceeds toward another dharma of extreme activity. 17.4 {S170}

Moreover, this world-arrangement, produced by diverse karma and characterized by various regions and costumes, looks toward the world-perfection that is auspicious, free from decay, devoid of sorrow and passion, stainless, liberated from the path [of rebirth], and perfectly cooled by being endowed with the eightfold [path]. Karma alone performs karma; it does not depend on anything else. (17.5)
Freed from both action and non-action, he remains free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). Yet, as long as one proceeds by means of the three vehicles, one does not attain any other peace.
The mantra is indeed threefold; action is proclaimed to be threefold; the accomplishment of the fruit is threefold; and the investigation is likewise threefold. (17.7)
The opposite of that, the threefold action, is likewise seen to be of three kinds;
that wholesome [action] is also declared to be of three kinds, as is further observed in the Tantra.
Furthermore, such a lineage as this is the peaceful locus of mantras;
it is the peaceful lineage of nirvāṇa for the Buddhas of pure mind.
That very same [lineage] is proclaimed as the specific portion of the limbs of mantra; likewise, the limb of astrology is devised in the world for the sake of accomplishment.
That very portion of karma indeed proceeds toward the portion of conditions.
For just as rice and other grains are distinguished by their sprout,
so too are perfected substances distinguished by their characteristic marks.

For just as the color white is conceptually constructed through conventional usage, so too is the application of astronomical principles constructed for the sake of worldly practice. Among all applications, action alone is praised in every respect.
That deed does not exist anywhere without signs;
nor can it be established by means of signs, conduct, birth-constellations, or the lineage one has relied upon.
That action is constantly perceived through various birds;
nowhere is action seen as something separate, for it is observed only when latent within another.
Just as a living being afflicted with fever is perceived by various symptoms on all sides,
so too is the karma of embodied beings seen when it has taken hold within the body.
The prognostications based on bodily marks (*cihnajātaka*) are proclaimed to yield both auspicious and inauspicious results;
likewise, there are various omens (*śakuna*), diverse sentient beings arising from various karmas,
the times of strength, journeys, and the various cries of living creatures.
[The mind] always [yields] the fruits of the auspicious and the inauspicious. ||17.17||
However, one observes the sign for the purpose of conviction regarding success or failure;
the sign, the conduct, and the mark are thus designated as "conviction. (17.18)
Therefore, with every effort, one who is a reciter of mantras should rely upon the conditions for the sake of attaining success in the mantra. (17.19)
One should observe those individual karmas as being without deficiency;
for indeed, everything that is unobserved is subject to most terrible obstructive karmas.
Therefore, "all these are limbs"—such is the word of the Sage.
The omniscient Sālendrarāja entered the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) and uttered a mantra that destroys all obstacles, as well as evil dreams, ill omens, and all that is unbearable. (17.21)
When the mind of that Great-Souled One, the Omniscient, was directed toward enlightenment, Māra, with his malevolent intent, created a great and terrifying obstacle.
By him, at the foot of the tree, a great omen was indeed seen; from that omen there arose for him many forms of terrifying portents.

Through the empowerment of his merit, by him who had long desired it, the power of that [demon] was then broken; thus was Namuci defeated by him. Possessing supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), great heroism, and great splendor, he remained concealed.
By the power of his mantra, may I seek supreme enlightenment.
That very mantra shall be declared as the destroyer of ill omens, the remover of bad dreams and unbearable [calamities], and the warder-off of evil beings. (17.26)
May the hosts of gods indeed listen to the kings of mantras among the planets, constellations, and luminaries,
which were previously spoken by the Jina Śālendrarāja.
For the purpose of subduing the wicked, [I shall speak] of the planets, constellations, and stars;
and likewise of all spirits, so that they may awaken with gentle minds.
(17.28) Let all the hosts of spirits hear me—whatever beings there are who roam the earth: those without feet, those with many feet, those with two feet, or those with four feet. (17.29)
In brief, all beings whatsoever who are stationary in the three realms. || 17.29 ||
Homage to all Buddhas, whose teachings are unimpeded.
30 Oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi hūṃ hūṃ | jvala jvala prajvala prajvala | tiṣṭha tiṣṭha | ṣṇīḥ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā ||
This mantra, received from the Buddha, is proclaimed as the Jvāloṣṇīṣa. || 17.30 ||
Whatever eighty-five thousand various rites he performs,
he who is honored as the source of all auspiciousness shall,
by a single recitation, destroy evil dreams and ill omens.
He performs other deeds as the master of all mantras;
he has mastery over all sentient beings—this Buddha is the powerful teacher.
By the recollection of this mantra, all obstacles are destroyed;
having spoken thus, "O Buddha, the God beyond gods," the best of sages [said]. (17.33)
They stood silently for a muhūrta, awaiting the time;
and then the hosts of gods stood above the Śuddhāvāsa realm.
All the chief gods, along with the lunar mansions, planets, and stars,
having been addressed by the mantra of Uṣṇīṣa, became afraid and entered into a covenant.
Equal in power, of great heroism, known as Uṣṇīṣa, and possessing great radiance;
[the mantras consist of] four hundred and fifty, or four hundred, or likewise seventy, eighty, or ninety [syllables].
Sixty-two and another seventy-five are proclaimed as the Uṣṇīṣendras;
these kings of the hair-tufts (*mūrdhaja*) are auspicious and their number is incalculable.
This mantra is equal to them, for it is born from the hair-tufts of the Victorious One. 17.37.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, the detailed exposition on the conditions of one's own karma, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the *Bodhisattvapiṭakāvatamsaka*.
A24. Chapter 24.

Now, the Blessed One Śākyamuni addressed all the planets of great supernatural power and excellence, which are situated in all directions and included within all world-systems, among all the lunar mansions, planets, stars, and luminaries. 24.1.

"Listen, worthy sirs, to the words concerning the power and influence of all the planets and constellations. May you demonstrate your power; may you accomplish all the purposes of mantra-practice; may you abide by the pledge. In this King of Ritual Manuals (*kalparāja*) within the teaching of Mañjughoṣa, and in other King of Ritual Manuals hereafter, may you remain diligent. (24.2)

24.3 Now the Blessed One Śākyamuni shall speak of the movements of the planets for the sake of all sentient beings. For the benefit of all reciters and for the purpose of the mantras, he who knows all shall explain everything that has been established.
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and Kṛttikā—
these three constellations are indeed marked by the planet Aṅgāraka (Mars).
In the case of Aries (Meṣa), these two [periods] are proclaimed; in them, success does not arise.
Whether superior, middling, or inferior, success is seen [to vary].
One who is obstructed by malefic planets should not set out on any path whatsoever. 24.5.
Rohiṇī and Mṛgaśiras are called the moist (sārdra) lunar mansions; Punarvasu, Puṣya, and Aśleṣā are likewise proclaimed [as such].
Maghā and Phalgunī; both Hasta and Citrā likewise; as well as Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūla. (24.7)
The two Āṣāḍhas are auspicious and highly praised, beneficial for those who recite mantras; the constellations Śravaṇa and Dhaniṣṭhā are praised for cruel rites.
Śatabhiṣaj and Bhadrapadā—both are causes for success.
Under Revatī, one is born illustrious, skilled in battle, and wise.

But the remaining principal lunar mansions do not arise in this lowest age. Abhijit and Sucarita are proclaimed as the auspicious ones for success; Tiṣya is the secondary one, while Kaniṣṭha is indeed the final.
He is proclaimed as Bhūta, Satya, and likewise Lokāloka; he is Bhogada, Śubhada, Aniruddha, and indeed Ruddha;
he is Yaśoda, Tejarāj, Rāja, and likewise Loka. (24.11)
Twenty-four thousand constellations have been described in many ways;
yet their power does not exist in this time of the lowest age.
They are mentioned only for the sake of knowledge in this *Kalparāja*, which brings about the arising of happiness.
But at that time, during the Kṛtayuga, beings indeed possessed the power of self-existence; they were all able to travel through the sky and were free from old age and death.

At that time, in the first age, the supreme yuga, there were no lunar mansions, nor sun or moon, nor stars; there were no gods, nor asuras in the world. There was neither name nor clan, nor lunar day, nor birth horoscope.
There is indeed no fasting, no mantras, and no action, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
These wander according to their own will; there is neither food to be eaten nor an eater. Indeed, these beings are always pure, free from affliction, and manifold.
Indeed, the perception of the world as a vessel arises within that [state];
then, drawn by their former karma, they go to the surface of the earth.
On the earth, they were established in divine palaces, born from both gods and asuras;
then, when the middle age arrived, they took on human bodies.
For those greedy for food and drink, that radiance was destroyed;
indeed, there was a harshness in their limbs, a sign of both auspicious and inauspicious activity.
Then the days and months were indeed obscured by the light of the planets;
from that time onwards, whatever knowledge there was of the luminaries arose.
"For everything has been told by me, which is capable of benefiting all beings. Indeed, in former times, there was the guise of sages, and then the wise one assumed the guise of Brahmā."
Having assumed the body of Maheśvara, or again the form of Viṣṇu,
or having taken on the body of Garuḍa for those who move among Yakṣas and Rākṣasas,
he may even possess the body of a Piśāca; I declare this of him in every birth.
But the virtuous bodhisattvas, in those various births, [attain these qualities].
By the power of rebirth and for the sake of accomplishing the practice of awakening,
I myself was a bodhisattva in that former age.
For previously, I was a fool, shrouded in the darkness of ignorance;
whatever skills, crafts, and activities exist in this world, [I lacked them all].
In the scripture, there are the treatises on ethics and the Purāṇas, as well as the Vedas and grammar; likewise, prosody, astronomy, mathematics, and the ritual manuals (Kalpa).
False knowledge, as well as such-like knowledge, and likewise false conduct—
such was all the teaching sung by me in the world long ago.
Yet, I did not attain that knowledge by which this sage is indeed so tranquil.
For the sake of liberation through the causes of awakening, and likewise for the cause of release.
I am confined in the prison of saṃsāra and not yet liberated from my karmas;
[yet I seek] Buddhahood, which is stainless and peaceful, the immortal state of nirvāṇa.
Perfect enlightenment, which I have long desired, has been attained by me;
I have now myself reached it through the proper method and through meritorious deeds.
The primordial wisdom of the Self-Existent (Svāyambhuva) was attained by the Jinas as previously revealed;
I do not see such a state as being obtainable through the external path.
Deluded in the wilderness of saṃsāra, I did not obtain the knowledge such as this which belongs to the Self-Existent One, for the causes of awakening are difficult to find.
Now I have attained Nirvana, devoted to what is auspicious and joined with right action;
yet this compendium of the scriptures is being spoken by me solely for the sake of others.
And no causes for accomplishment are found apart from karma;
this long thread of saṃsāra is bound and constrained by karma.

This greatness of destiny belongs to him alone; it is he who experiences the ripening of both the auspicious and the inauspicious. These stars, planets, and celestial luminaries merely indicate [the results].
No such sign is seen for other men who are most unrighteous. For this very reason, the planets and others are said to be capable of bestowing grace regarding both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
The four world-protectors—water, earth, wind, and fire—are proclaimed to have become fireflies;
these are the great elements that cause the gathering of beings.
Indeed, when impelled by action for the sake of gathering sentient beings, the accomplishment of mantra arises from the regulation of time for them. (24.38)

Among those births, one must indeed strive to protect [the mind] from both the auspicious and the inauspicious. Even the preeminent leaders of the world, such as Śakra and the other lords of the gods, were themselves destined for that very time at the end of the eon.
In this lowest of ages, mantras are accomplished with great effort;
for this very reason, the Lord of Jinas has designated [this] as the Youthful Age (Kumāra-yuga). 24.40
Mañjughoṣa, possessed of great wisdom, takes the form of a young child;
capable of bestowing grace upon sentient beings, he wanders throughout this entire world.
At that time, the accomplishment of Mañjughoṣa will be seen;
at that time, there will be the knowledge of the stars and astrology.
Twenty-seven constellations and the muhūrtas have been proclaimed.
In that time of the lowest age (yugādhama), there will be thirteen zodiac signs (rāśi).
The planets, having been distributed, will indeed take refuge in the constellations (nakṣatra) and their respective signs;
all things, having become widespread, will resort to them individually.
Beings are established within the [three] heaps; they are born of delusion and are perverted, giving rise to the fruits of the auspicious and the inauspicious. 24.45
For this very reason, those aggregates, which speak of karma, repeatedly fashion the auspicious and inauspicious journey toward accomplishment for sentient beings. (24.46)
In the *Apadāna-jātaka*, he is described as being born under the constellation Rohiṇī;
he was illustrious, endowed with patience, possessed many sons, and lived a long life.
Likewise, he who possesses a share of wealth always acts as a commander of armies. He may be born in the sign of Taurus, or he may exert himself in the sign of Taurus;
or, being born in Mṛgaśiras, he is a knower of the world, righteous, and pleasing to behold.
Likewise, when the birth-constellation is clearly situated in the portion of Kṛttikā, the king will always behold the earth as the sovereign of the three oceans. 24.49
Furthermore, if one is endowed with the qualities of birth and Jupiter marks the [relevant] planet, the king shall rule over a limited territory or a difficult fortress in a single region. (24.50)
He shall be the enjoyer of the entire earth on all sides;
his reign is ordained for fifteen years.
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and a portion of Kṛttikā are prescribed as the Aries zodiac sign;

Likewise, the Himavat mountains were placed within his belly, along with those dwelling in inaccessible caves;
and kings were stationed as fortress-guards on all sides.
Then, on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, that lord of Tīrabhukti,
the king, will die from various torments of grief;
that lord of men will perish together with his sons and wife.

In whichever constellations there is an earthquake, one should predict smoke in those very ones. All directions will be filled with smoke and terrible, though devoid of rain-clouds; this shall persist for five days, always accompanied by many celestial portents.
Mortals born of human stock do not see one another there, for they are within the range [of their own senses] alone;
no mutual vision of humans occurs there.
One should know that a great danger exists there, which would destroy the king along with his kingdom.
In those very places where such a trembling occurs, there will be the falling of meteors on all sides.
Furthermore, a search is undertaken and a formidable array is deployed twice or thrice;
and at night, if there is a rainbow or a crow with white wings.
Now, a white-colored bird appears as black, and a black one appears as white;
the colors of the birds are reversed, and the cries of the seasons are inverted.
Wherever the birds appear thus inverted, there is great danger.
Those with two feet, those with four feet, those without feet, and those with many feet.

If birds fly sideways, it portends great danger; likewise, if dogs howl repeatedly with their muzzles pointed upward, whether by day or by night, there will be great peril wherever that occurs. When many such omens of various kinds manifest in manifold ways, there shall be drought, and the king’s dominion will perish.
No sign whatsoever is seen otherwise than through a prior cause;
obstacles and the occurrence of portents do not arise without a cause.

Thus concludes the twenty-fourth chapter, the detailed exposition on the light of the knowledge of omens, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Chapter A25.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni again addressed the hosts of planets, lunar mansions, stars, and celestial luminaries.
25.2 Listen, all of you! This King of Rituals (kalparāja) of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta—consisting of the procedures for mantras, tantras, consecrations, and mandalas—is not to be transgressed.

And for those engaged in the practice of recitation, fire-offerings, observances, and the accomplishment of vidyās according to this supreme ritual manual (*kalpa*), you must not create obstacles for the Vidyādharas who possess the higher knowledges (*abhijñā*) regarding the calculations of lunar days, constellations, and conduct, nor for those born under the constellations. All the hosts of gods must provide protection there for those engaged in this teaching. All malevolent beings must be restrained, obstructed, and disciplined; however, none at all must be killed. They should instead be established in their proper stations within this teaching of the Ten-Powered Ones. 25.2.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni entered the samādhi called "The Exalted Uṣṇīṣa of All Tathāgatas" for the purpose of warding off all malevolent beings among all sentient beings. As soon as the Blessed One Śākyamuni had entered this state, all those Tathāgatas residing in the world-systems of the ten directions beheld the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, staying in the palace of the Pure Abodes, and approached him. Having approached, through the inconceivable empowerment of their own buddha-nature, they addressed the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata.
Speak, speak, O Great Hero, for the arising of the welfare of the worlds,
as all mantras proceed according to the rules of their respective mantras and tantras!
This King of Vidyās of great supernatural power, the single-syllable, supreme, and foremost, has been proclaimed by all the Buddhas for the time when the Kali Yuga has arrived.
This supreme king of the Uṣṇīṣas, of great heroism and the warder-off of all malevolent beings, is the foremost of all mantras, as proclaimed by all the Buddhas. (25.6)

He is the restrainer of the planets and constellations, and of mothers with evil intent; likewise, he is the restrainer of all obstacles in the world and whatever others there may be who possess wicked minds.
Just as the Jātaka tales describe the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of living beings, so too do portents arise from those actions to produce good and evil fortune in this world.

For the sake of favoring sentient beings and for the arising of happiness for those who recite [the mantra], he is indeed the foremost in this entire teaching, a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*). (25.8) The King of the Uṣṇīṣas, of great heroism, is the supreme lord over all. (25.9)
Speak now, O Tathāgata, regarding the time for this.
When they had been addressed in this way, those Buddhas remained silent.

Then, through the gathering of those Buddhas, the entire great trichiliocosm and the world-receptacles of all sentient beings became a single mass of flame. Yet, not a single sentient being experienced any suffering; rather, by the empowerment of the Buddhas, great radiances were seen.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed that entire abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, the sons of the gods residing there, and all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas gathered in the great assembly of the Blessed One:

"May the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and all the pratyekabuddhas and noble śrāvakas attend to this: [the teaching] of the single-syllable sovereign of vidyās, belonging to the uṣṇīṣas of all the Tathāgatas."

Of the Blessed One, the Universal Monarch of the Uṣṇīṣa, who dwells ever on high, whose command is unimpeded, and whose strength and prowess are immeasurable—once again, I shall speak of the ritual manual in this time, in this degenerate age (kaliyuga). Now, I shall further declare the mantra of the Blessed One, whose teaching is difficult to transgress, the Teacher of the Three Worlds, who is honored by all gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, and who accomplishes the purpose of all rites, once again in the time of the kaliyuga.

At the time when the teaching is about to disappear, the Blessed One Uṣṇīṣacakravartin will become the protector of the teaching and shall attain accomplishment. At all times, and specifically at the moment when the teachings of all the Buddhas are vanishing, this Blessed Buddha will act for the benefit of sentient beings. This Blessed One is the protector, united with the Dharma-treasury of all the Tathāgatas. Listen, O hosts of gods and all sentient beings! 25.14
*Bhrūṃ*. 15.
This Blessed One, the omniscient, has been established by the Buddhas in the form of mantra; as the Great Compassionate Teacher, he wanders among all embodied beings. 25.15.
The glorious lord of mantras, renowned and honored as Uṣṇīṣa,
having descended from the foundation of compassion, stands here as this imperishable syllable.
Having emerged from the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), he stands here in manifold forms.
For just as the relics of the Buddhas, having issued from their bodies,
are honored by the world when they are accompanied by worldly offerings, yet they are especially so when free from such offerings.
The elements of the True Dharma are said to be non-material causes for the world;
those of the Lords of Jinas, possessing great supernatural power, are said to be material within the physical body. 25.18
The Moon-like Sages have proclaimed various elements (dhātu), both with outflows and without outflows; they have spread forth for the sake of the world, both worldly and world-transcending.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he remains in the form of mantra, blending with the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), as the Lord of the World, the Light-maker.
He who possesses all forms and is omniscient is indeed seen upon the surface of the earth;
this mantra, which accomplishes all aims, has been spoken by all the Buddhas.
This is the mantra in brief: when this is recited by oneself according to the ritual procedure, it indeed accomplishes every rite, always making one's desires fruitful.

Furthermore, at that time, the ritual procedure for this [mantra] will be proclaimed in brief: when the Tathāgata has passed away and the best of sages has departed from the world at the end of the age, the accomplishment of the ritual procedure (*kalpasiddhi*) is then declared to be the accomplishment of the mantra (*mantrasiddhi*).

25. Now, the ritual manual (*kalpa*) for the single-syllable [mantra] of the Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin—formerly set forth in detail, which belongs to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata-Uṣṇīṣa, the destroyer of the applications of others' rites, the Unconquered Victor (*Ajitañjaya*), the sovereign of all mantras, who is honored by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—is here presented in brief.

25.24 First of all, in whatever place this is recited, within a radius of one *yojana* along that path, all malevolent grahas flee, as do all mantras, even those that have attained accomplishment (*siddha*).

All the gods are unable [to resist him]; they abandon their presence except by the will of the practitioner. He takes away the accomplishments of other practitioners, both mundane and supramundane; he renders the mantras of others' applications severed, shattered, and uprooted, and liberates them. || 25.25 ||

25. One who wishes to sever a *vidyā* [spell] oneself should take a handful of green *kuśa* grass, empower it one hundred and eight times with mantras, and cut it with a weapon while aiming at that *vidyā*; thus, the *vidyā* becomes severed. Having fashioned an image [of the opponent] with this [grass], one should strike it in the heart with a pin; it becomes pinned. With a thread dyed with safflower and empowered seven times with mantras, one should tie a knot; it becomes bound. With a shallow bowl empowered one hundred and eight times, one should cover [the image]; it becomes obstructed. One should split the heart [of the image] in two with a weapon; it becomes pierced. One should dye [the image] with black mustard seeds colored with poison and blood; it becomes tormented. One should strike it with a *karavīra* creeper; it becomes oppressed.
He performs all magical rites at will everywhere. 25.26.

Excepting the karma performed twenty-five times previously, one should bathe [the image] with milk and perform a fire offering (*homa*). [This is] Peace 27. Through a fire offering of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), the pacification and nourishment of all is accomplished.

By clenching the fist, one paralyzes all mantras; by [unclenching] it in the mind, one releases them. One who wishes to accomplish a mantra should accomplish it after first restraining that person with this very [mudrā]. If one wishes to accomplish another ritual procedure (*kalpa*), one should accomplish it with this very [mantra]; it succeeds. With this very mantra, there is the invocation (*āvāhana*); again, with this very [mantra], there is the dismissal (*visarjana*). For whomever protection is performed with this very [mantra], he too becomes invulnerable. || 25.27 ||

If a mantra does not succeed or does not grant its response, one should recite it together with this very [mantra]. It will then quickly succeed or grant its response. If it still does not succeed and gives no response, that [practitioner] shall die.

One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee at the three junctions of the day for seven days. Whatever mantra one has in mind, its possessor becomes subject to one's will; he performs whatever task is commanded or provides a response. || 25.29 ||

Desiring to bring the gods under one's control, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *devadāru* wood; within seven nights, they become submissive. Desiring to bring the *nāgas* under one's control, one should offer the "three sweets" (*trimadhura*); they become submissive. Desiring to bring the *yakṣas* under one's control, one should offer curd-rice; they become submissive. One who desires to bring a *yakṣiṇī* under one's control should offer curd-rice. One brings a *gandharva* under control with all types of perfumes, or with the wood of *aśoka* and *priyaṅgu*, or with their flowers. (25.30)

One brings under control Yakṣiṇīs with *rājikā* seeds; a king with white mustard seeds (*siddhārthaka*); a Brāhmaṇa with an offering of flowers; a Vaiśya with curd, milk, and ghee; a Śūdra with chaff and dust; a woman with an offering of salt; a widow with an offering of black gram and *jambūlikā*; a maiden with an offering of parched grain; and all [others] with an offering of ghee and oil. In every case, one effects subjugation by performing this at the three junctions of the day for seven nights.
Having spoken thus, the Supreme Victor became silent.
Then, having addressed the hosts of gods, that seventh bull among sages, who knew the ways of the world, smiled; he was liberated, his mind then being disciplined.

Then the supreme sage addressed the eldest son of the Buddha; he then chose Mañjughoṣa, the bodhisattva of great supernatural power. This ritual has been proclaimed by me as but a single portion for the wielder of the wheel, whose [ritual] is vast, O wise Lord, God of Gods.
The measure of which cannot be expressed by the Jinas even in eons—I shall describe it to you in brief for the sake of bringing about the welfare of human beings.
When this had been said, the glorious Mañjughoṣa, possessed of great supernatural power, then made a request to that Buddha who was stationed above the Pure Abodes.
Speak, speak, O Great Hero, Perfectly Awakened One, Supreme among bipeds!
[Speak] for the arising of happiness for humanity at this lost time, at the end of the age.

"How is it that for this one of great splendor and great heroism, the king of mantras and the accomplishment of the cloth are seen? And how is the ritual procedure for the cloth performed quickly? (25.38)

Thus concludes the twenty-fifth chapter, the detailed exposition on the arising of the One-Syllable Universal Monarch, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
{S289} {V226} Chapter A26:

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Listen, Mañjuśrī, to the brief ritual procedure for the cloth-painting of the One-Syllable Wheel-Turning King of Great Power."
It occurs. What was previously explained in detail is now [stated] in brief. (26.1) In this debased age, sentient beings possess little vigor, little wisdom, and dull minds;
they are unable to accomplish the practice regarding the dimensions of the cloth in detail. (26.2)
Out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings, I shall speak in brief so that those practitioners of recitation may attain the supreme goal and its accomplishment. (26.3)

One who desires to perform the supreme sādhana should have the Blessed One painted on an unbleached cloth that has its fringes intact, is free of hair, and is colored with non-sticky pigments. He is the King of Dharma, the Turner of the Wheel of Dharma, the Lord of all worlds, the Supreme Person among bipeds, the Tathāgata-Ratna named Ratnaketu, the Best of Jinas, teaching the Dharma, surrounded by a halo of blazing light on all sides. 26.4.

Below are Brahmā and Ārya Vajrapāṇi; above are two divine sons bearing garlands; and below is the practitioner. In front of him, burning agalloch incense at the three junctions of the day, he should recite [the mantra] one million times. Thereafter, the ritual actions will succeed. 26.5.

One who desires to perform the first wheel-sādhana should fashion a twelve-spoked wheel made of *puṣpaloha* (flower-metal). During the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), one should recite [the mantra] one million times before the Blessed One at the three junctions of the day while burning *agaru* incense. At the conclusion, on the full moon day, having performed a grand worship and grasping it with the hand, one should recite until it blazes forth. Having taken hold of it, one becomes a universal monarch of the *vidyādharas*. Together with those by whom he is seen and those whom he sees, he flies up into the air. 26.6.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the parasol should have a new, variegated white parasol made, marked with a golden wheel and draped with silk cloth. Having placed it upon his head according to this very procedure, he should recite the mantra. The Vidyā will manifest of its own accord. Furthermore, before the Blessed One at the three junctions of the day, he should recite the mantra one million times while burning agallochum incense. At the end, on the full moon day, having performed a grand worship, he should grasp it with his hand and recite until it blazes forth. Taking hold of it, he becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) of the Vidyādharas. This is accomplished within five fortnights, during the fortnight of miracles, on each full moon day. As soon as it is accomplished, all dharmas become manifest before him. He attains all the superknowledges (abhijñā). Delighted by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he becomes one who enters into the company of all beings. Even in other world-systems, he becomes a universal monarch with a retinue of a thousand. 26.7.

Then, desiring to accomplish the uṣṇīṣa, one should fashion a staff one cubit in length made of gold, silver, copper, or jewels; one should recite the mantra until it blazes. Having grasped it, one wanders at will and teaches the Dharma to sentient beings; one lives for a great eon. || 26.8 ||

Now, one desiring to accomplish the auspicious jar (*bhadraghaṭa*) should fashion a golden auspicious jar, fill it with all kinds of seeds, jewels, and medicinal herbs, and wrap it in white cloth; one should accomplish it by means of this [mantra]. One should begin the rite during one fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*); it is accomplished during the other. Having placed it in one’s hand, whatever one desires, that one obtains. It becomes inexhaustible. 26.9.

Now, one who desires to accomplish the *cintāmaṇi* jewel should fashion a golden staff with a genuine gem and a crystal gem, or a golden [staff] from which a cloth hangs down, and accomplish it according to this very procedure. Whatever one thinks of, all that is accomplished. By holding this, among gods and humans, one possesses unimpeded strength and prowess. Then, if one recites [the mantra] ten million times for the Blessed One, one flies up in one's own body and lives for many great divine eons.

Or others, such as Asitātapatra and the rest—by this [mantra] recited one million times, the rites of the Blessed One are accomplished. Thus, this unimpeded Tathāgatoṣṇīṣa succeeds in whatever way it is employed, even according to the ritual procedures of other tantras; indeed, it succeeds before long. Recited one million times, the Blessed One Uṣṇīṣacakravartin accomplishes everything; he is the universal sovereign (cakravartin) and lord of all vidyā-mantras. 26.11

Now, one desiring to accomplish the vajra should fashion a single-pronged vajra made of red sandalwood, or else one made of "flower-metal" (puṣpaloha). Having washed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, having performed a grand worship before the cloth-painting (paṭa) and lit lamps of ghee, and having washed [the vajra] with scented water, the yakṣas become submissive. 26.12.

Having offered oneself to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and having performed protection by means of this King of Uṣṇīṣas together with his retinue—specifically the Tejorāśi and the Sitātapatra—and having performed the binding of the maṇḍala and the protection of one’s companions, one should take a vajra in the right hand and, after the first watch has passed, sit down during the second watch. With a one-pointed mind, one should recite [the mantra] until it blazes forth. In the meantime, all the Vidyādharas, all the gods, nāgas, and yakṣas assemble; and all the kings of the Vidyādharas arrive. Being praised by them, he goes to the city of the Vidyādharas and becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) of the Vidyādharas. His body becomes like that of Vajrapāṇi, and his strength is equal to that of Vajrapāṇi. In a mere instant, a moment, or a brief flash, he goes to the Akaniṣṭha celestial realm. Abiding for a great eon (mahākalpa), he beholds the Blessed One, the noble Maitreya, and hears the Dharma. When he dies, he is reborn wherever he desires. Whatever he wishes, he arises from the presence of Vajrapāṇi. 26.13

Now, one desiring to accomplish the sword rite should take a flawless sword, fast for a day and night, and perform a grand worship of the Blessed One. He should recite the mantra until, once it has blazed and been perfected, he flies up together with his retinue. With his hair curled in locks, having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, and never yielding the path to others, he becomes unassailable by all vidyādharas and lives for an intermediate eon. 26.14.
26.14 Now, one who desires to prepare realgar (manaḥśilā) should purchase it by means of a "hero's price" (vīrakraya).

Having fasted for three nights during the conjunction with the Puṣya asterism, one should feed the *saṅghoddiṣṭaka* alms-food and cause the formal authorization (*ājñā*) to be granted. Once authorized, one should enter the place of practice (*sādhana*). Having performed a magnificent worship, one should light a thousand lamps of ghee. Having fasted for three nights and generated a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*) toward all sentient beings, one should offer oneself and, taking realgar (*manaḥśilā*), recite the mantra until the threefold accomplishment is attained. One should first visualize [the signs] of heat, smoke, and flame. 26.15.

Having performed the *ūṣmāyamāna-tilaka* (the "smoldering tilaka") which grants unfailing accomplishment (*amuktasiddhi*), all gods, nāgas, yakṣas, bhūtas, piśācas, and so forth, as well as the beings dwelling in Jambudvīpa, become his servants; they become his attendants (*kiṅkara*). He lives for a thousand years. 26.16.

Having made a *tilaka* while [the mantra] is smoking, one becomes invisible. If one so desires, one becomes invisible even to the gods. In a moment, a brief instant, or a muhūrta, one is seen again and then becomes invisible once more. One becomes the king of all those who possess the power of invisibility. One lives for three thousand years. || 26.17 ||

By means of the blazing [mantra], one becomes a vidyādhara; together with one’s retinue, one flies up into the air. One becomes a king of the vidyādharas, possessing a body like that of a divine youth (devakumāra), invincible even to all the gods, let alone to the vidyādharas. One remains for an eon (kalpa). When one’s time has come, one is reborn in the Tuṣita realm of the gods. || 26.18 || {S292}

Now, one who desires to accomplish the trident should fashion a trident made of *puṣpaloha* (flower-metal) and recite the mantra for one year. Then, having fashioned a stūpa out of sand measuring one cubit in height and having performed a great worship of it, and having offered a magnificent *bali* sacrifice, he should take hold of the trident with his right hand and recite until—having assumed the cross-legged posture—it quivers, blazes, and emits thousands of rays of light. In the meantime, the gods headed by Maheśvara arrive; all the *vidyādharas* rain down a shower of flowers. Then, surrounded by them, he flies up together with as many as he beholds and as many as behold him. With three eyes like a second Maheśvara, honored by all the *vidyādharas*, remaining for a great eon (*mahākalpa*), he brings those of evil intent to ruin merely by his glance. He becomes unassailable by anyone in the world including the gods, much less by the *vidyādharas*. When he passes away, he is reborn in Sukhāvatī. 26.19

Now, as for the accomplishment of the Vetāḍa: having taken a man with uninjured limbs and seated oneself upon his chest, which has been secured with four stakes of khadira wood, one should offer oblations of powdered jewels. At the tip of his tongue, the Cintāmaṇi jewel will appear. Having seized it, one becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) of the Vidyādharas. Whatever weapons one thinks of, they appear by mere thought. One illuminates a hundred yojanas with one's radiance. One passes away at will. One goes wherever one desires; even in other world-systems, one becomes a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas. Upon passing away, one is reborn in the Vimalā world-system. || 26.20 ||

The second is the accomplishment of the *vetāla*. Having seized a *vetāḍa* with its limbs intact, one should pin it down with stakes of *badara* wood and offer iron filings into its mouth. Its tongue will emerge; having cut it off, one flies up with a retinue of a hundred. One lives for an intermediate eon (*antarakalpa*), playing and sporting upon the summit of Mount Sumeru. When one dies, one becomes a regional king (*ekadeśika-rāja*). 26.21.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the hook (*aṅkuśa*) should fashion a hook made of *kuśa* grass. Having washed it with either black or yellow *pañcagavya*, one should remain for one night. The handle of the hook should be made to the measure of a cubit (*hasta*). Having performed a grand worship, one should light a hundred ghee lamps for Vajrapāṇi and fashion a vajra. Likewise, one should perform protection for oneself with the Sitātapatrā [dhāraṇī] and the binding of the mandala with the Tejorāśi [dhāraṇī]. Having consecrated seven stakes (*kīlaka*), they should be driven into the ground in the four directions. Thus, the binding, the site, and the enclosure are accomplished. (26.22)

Then, during the second watch, with a one-pointed mind, having assumed the cross-legged posture and worshipped the hook (aṅkuśa) with perfumes, flowers, and incense, and having performed the protection rite, he should pay homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Taking the hook in his hand, he should recite [the mantra] until, in the meantime, the sufferings of the gods belonging to the hell realms are pacified. Having paid homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he flies up and becomes a king of the Vidyādharas.

With unimpeded movement and a hand grasping a goad, all the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and others, upon seeing him, offer salutation even from afar. Abiding for an eon, when he dies, he goes to the Vajra-abode and beholds Vajrapāṇi. 26.23–26.29/30.

If one accomplishes the cloth, by means of that blazing [cloth], one becomes a *vidyādhara*. If one wishes to accomplish a particular *kalpa*, one should recite the mantra of that [deity] one hundred thousand times while grasping its name. At the conclusion, having fasted for one night and performed a magnificent worship, one should kindle a fire with *arka* wood and offer eight thousand oblations of sesame seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. At the end of the *homa*, [the deity] arrives; he gives whatever wealth one desires and remains under one's control, as submissive as a servant. || 26.24 ||

Now, one who desires to make Maheśvara [subservient] should perform a great worship of Maheśvara; having kindled a fire with *arka* wood at the southern image, he should offer oblations eight thousand times. A sound of "hā hā" arises. One must not be afraid. Then he arrives and asks, "What is to be done? [One should say: "May all the mantras of Maheśvara be mastered by me. He grants whatever boon is desired. Having said, "So be it," he vanishes. || 26.25 ||

In this way, one attracts Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others. This same procedure should also be performed for whomever one desires; the rite must be carried out by one who has established protection. 26.26.

Now, if one desires to summon a yakṣiṇī, one should take her name and offer oblations of *aśoka* flowers for seven days. She comes and grants a boon; on the seventh week, she will certainly arrive. Whether she becomes a mother, a sister, or a wife, she does whatever one requests. If she does not come, her head shall burst asunder. This same ritual applies to one who wishes to summon a *nāgī*, using *nāga* flowers. 26.27.

One who desires to summon a yakṣa should offer curd-rice as an oblation for three months. At the conclusion, having fasted for one night and performed worship of the Blessed One, and having presented the yakṣa-offering and incitements to the yakṣas, he should resolve in his mind, "I shall perform the summoning of the yakṣas," and offer eight thousand fuel-sticks of the *vaṭa* tree smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. During this interval, Kubera and the other yakṣas will arrive. 26.28.

An offering (*argha*) is given to them with red flowers. They will ask, "What should be done? One should say to them: "On each day, send a yakṣa who carries out your command. Then they provide one yakṣa at a time. His command must be given; he brings a woman even from a hundred *yojanas* away, and returns her to that very place at dawn. He provides food for a retinue of a hundred. Mounting his back, one goes wherever one desires; he leads one there. He gives an elixir (*rasāyana*). When commanded, he performs everything. 26.29.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the practice of Vajrapāṇi should perform the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) fourfold or sevenfold. During the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), having performed an entirely magnificent worship until the full moon, and having performed worship on the full-moon day itself, he should feed the monks designated for the Saṅgha. He should then express his appreciation specifically to the Noble Vajradhara. Then, having performed a magnificent worship, when the first watch of the night has passed, he should sit in the second watch with legs crossed, and with a one-pointed mind, form the resolve: "I shall behold Vajradhara. He should offer oblations at night for one watch of *guggulu* resin pills the size of jujube seeds. Thereupon, the garland of the Blessed One will move; the earth will tremble; the clouds will rumble; and all the *vidyādharas* will rain down a shower of flowers. At that moment, the Blessed One—

Vajrapāṇi approaches, surrounded by all the vidyās; he approaches surrounded by the vidyārājas headed by Vidyottama, and surrounded by all the devas, all the nāgas, all the yakṣas, all the gandharvas, the kinnaras, and the bodhisattvas. 26.30–31.

At that very moment, the intense sufferings of the beings in the hells cease. One should offer water with fragrance as an *arghya* offering and remain prostrate. Then Vajradhara will say, "What boon shall I grant you? Whether it be the status of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) of the Vidyādharas, entry into a subterranean cavern (*bilapraveśa*), sovereignty over a kingdom, or invisibility—whatever one desires is obtained from the presence of that very Blessed One. Or, if one desires the status of a Universal Monarch of the Vidyādharas, one becomes a sovereign of all Vidyādharas, possessing a vajra-body like that of Vajrapāṇi. By mere thought, all weapons appear. One remains for a great eon (*mahākalpa*). When one dies, one goes to the Vajra-abode. (26.31)

This same procedure applies briefly to other Vidyādharas as well. Whatever rituals (*kalpa*) have been taught by Vajrapāṇi, whatever by Avalokiteśvara, and whatever rituals were spoken by the Blessed One—whether those in the *Brahmakalpa* or the *Maheśvarakalpa*—in short, whatever are to be accomplished in worldly or supramundane rituals, they are all accomplished through this very means of practice (*sādhana*). Great mantras that are not accomplished [by this] will not be accomplished. They should be recited together with this for seven nights; he will certainly grant a vision. If he does not grant it, he perishes. If one recites it in the presence of the gods headed by Maheśvara, he grants a vision within seven nights. If he does not grant it, his head shall split into twenty-one pieces.

During a lunar eclipse or a solar eclipse, one should prepare clarified butter, *vacā*, collyrium, purifying staffs, wooden rods, sacrificial threads (*yajñopavīta*), yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), red arsenic (*manaḥśilā*), and so forth. Now, for one desiring to accomplish a substance: having taken red arsenic and ground it with human milk, one should fashion five pills. Placing them in a casket of *agaru* wood, one should perform the accomplishment during a lunar or solar eclipse, together with white mustard seeds. Having performed the offering of oblations (*bali*), when the mustard seeds crackle (*ciṭiciṭīyanti*), then the first [pill] is accomplished; by means of that which subjugates all people, everyone belonging to the mundane world becomes obedient. Whatever is commanded, it performs all of that. Then, if it emits smoke, one becomes the king of all those who possess the power of invisibility and lives for an intermediate eon (*antarakalpa*). When it blazes, then, possessing the body of a divine youth (*devakumāra*) and the brilliance of the rising sun, one becomes a king of the *vidyādharas* and lives for a great eon (*mahākalpa*). In this same manner, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), yellow orpiment, and other such substances are to be accomplished. 26.33.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the eye-salve (*añjana*) should take *srotāñjana*, blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), *kuṣṭha*, and sandalwood (*candana*), place them together in a copper vessel, and recite the mantra during a lunar eclipse until it emits smoke. With eyes anointed by that [salve], one becomes invisible; able to assume any form at will, one becomes the king of all those who possess the power of invisibility. || 26.34 ||

Now, one desiring to accomplish the sword [sādhana] should take a flawless sword and, on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having performed an extensive worship of the cloth painting (paṭa) and the offering of oblations (bali), and having established protection, should grasp the sword with the right hand and recite [the mantra] until it quivers. When it blazes and quivers, one becomes a solitary Vidyādhara. By means of that which has blazed, one becomes the king of all Vidyādharas, possessing unimpeded strength and prowess. One flies up together with those by whom one is seen and those whom one sees. 26.35.

Now, one who desires to accomplish the vajra should fashion a vajra out of *puṣpaloha* (flower-metal), sixteen finger-breadths in length, with three points on each side. Having anointed it with red sandalwood, beginning from the first day of the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), he should perform a grand worship of the cloth-painting and recite [the mantra] every day. He should feed an increasing number of monks. At the conclusion, having fasted for three nights, he should install the painting in a shrine containing relics, perform a grand worship, light a hundred lamps of ghee, and sitting upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, grasp the vajra with both hands and recite until it blazes. Grasping it, he flies up accompanied by a retinue of seven; he becomes a universal monarch of the *vidyādharas*, with prowess equal to Vajrapāṇi. He lives for a great eon (*mahākalpa*). When his body is broken, he goes to the abode of Vajrapāṇi. || 26.36 ||
In this way, all weapons, such as the trident, the discus, the arrow, the spear, and so forth, [are likewise]. 37–38.

Cloth, sandals, wooden staffs, sacrificial threads, and so forth are to be accomplished according to the rules of other ritual systems. For all of these, there are three kinds of accomplishment. 26.37–43.

Desiring to perform a rite for pacification (*śāntika*), one should prepare an altar in the shape of a lotus, kindle a fire with sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*), and offer eight thousand oblations of the finest food mixed with curd, honey, and ghee using a *sruva* ladle. Within three nights, peace will come to oneself or another; within seven nights, it will come to a village or a city. During a great epidemic, one should offer oblations of *śamī* wood sticks mixed with curd, honey, and ghee. To remedy drought, one should offer oblations of *udumbara* wood sticks mixed with curd, honey, and ghee. One should offer the "three sweets" (*trimadhura*) in all cases, and supreme peace will prevail. One who subsists on alms should recite [the mantra] thirty million times. 26.38.

On the full moon day of the bright fortnight during the period of miracles, having fasted for three nights, one should drink black cow’s milk that has been consecrated eight hundred times during a lunar eclipse; it becomes a rejuvenative (rasāyana) endowed with excellent qualities. One should offer eight thousand oblations of young durvā shoots smeared with curd, honey, and ghee for ten nights; untimely death is pacified, and one becomes long-lived. || 26.39 ||

One should consecrate banners, conchs, and so forth with mantras. By seeing or hearing them, one paralyzes the enemy army. Having prepared a new jar filled with all kinds of grains and scented water, one should touch and bathe a person afflicted by Vināyakas with that jar over which the mantra has been recited one hundred and eight times. Once consecrated, the person becomes endowed with prosperity (*lakṣmī*). By means of this consecration, one is liberated from all sins. One performs the rites of the maṇḍala and the rites for the planetary spirits (*graha*). 26.40.

With a peacock feather over which the mantra has been recited one hundred thousand times, one destroys all poisons; with that same [feather], one destroys fever, eye-pain, diseases, and so forth. With a thread [over which it has been recited], one destroys all fevers. When employed together with the mudrā, the mantra destroys the magical mechanisms of the asuras. || 26.41 ||

Having descended into a river that flows to the ocean, one should cause a hundred thousand lotuses smeared with red sandalwood to float away. One obtains a treasure equal to a heap of lotuses; when it is given away, it becomes inexhaustible. One should offer eight thousand oblations of *bilva* fruits smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. One attains enjoyments. 26.42. {S297}

One who desires to bring the gods under one's control should offer eight thousand oblations of *agaru* wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee at the three junctions of the day for twenty-one nights. Having combined rice grains smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, one should offer them as oblations; then food becomes inexhaustible. 26.43.

For the subjugation of yakṣas, one should offer oblations of guggulu pills smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. For yakṣiṇīs, [one should offer] fuel-sticks of aśoka. For nāgas, [fuel-sticks of] nāgapuṣpa. For the noble Vajrapāṇi, [fuel-sticks of] agaru. For vidyādharas, [fuel-sticks of] damanaka. For gandharvas, [fuel-sticks of] agaru smeared with turuṣka oil. For pretas, by means of a homa of kunduru. For kinnaras, by means of a homa of śrīvāsaka. For vināyakas, by means of a homa of sarjarasa. For all [these], the homa consists of eight hundred [offerings] for seven nights. For a king, one should offer eight hundred [oblations] of royal mustard seeds smeared with oil at the three junctions of the day for seven nights. Facing the sun, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; one will be liberated from all sins. 26.44.

Desiring to perform the nourishment (*āpyāyana*) of all sciences (*vidyā*), one should subsist on cow’s urine and barley gruel (*yāvaka*). Having fashioned an image out of *uśīra* root and having worshipped it with white flowers, one should offer eight hundred oblations of milk. One should also bathe the image with milk. One should offer incense of *agaru* wood consecrated by eight hundred recitations. Thus it becomes nourished. By reciting [the mantra] once, protection for oneself is accomplished; by reciting it twice, for another; by reciting it thrice, protection for one's property is accomplished. (26.45)

Desiring to restore those [mantras] that are severed, split, lost, or pinned down, one should fashion an image out of *uśīra* root, worship it with white flowers, and before a cloth painting (*paṭa*), offer eight thousand oblations of royal mustard seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee while reciting this *Uṣṇīṣarāja*. Directed toward the *vidyā*, it becomes unpinned. 26.46.

Having ascertained that the knowledge [of the dream] is beyond the reach of wicked people, one should write it on birch bark with *gorocanā* pigment. Then, having consecrated it eight hundred times with one’s own mantra and having performed a magnificent worship of the Blessed One, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times together with this Blessed One and sleep right there upon a bed of *kuśa* grass. Whether deficient or excessive, [the deity] comes and speaks [the truth] in a dream. (26.47)

Now, one desiring to accomplish the lotus should fashion a lotus out of red sandalwood and, having performed a grand worship, remain for three nights fasting. Grasping that lotus with the right hand, he should recite the mantra until it blazes. He then flies up with a retinue of twenty and becomes a universal monarch of the *vidyādharas*. His movement is unimpeded, and when he dies, he is reborn in Sukhāvatī. || 26.48 ||

Now, one who desires to accomplish the single-pointed vajra (*ekasūcika-vajra*) should fashion a vajra from clay mixed with anthill earth and sand. Subsisting on alms, observing silence, and not looking back, he should take hold of the vajra and recite the mantra three hundred thousand times. A single-pointed vajra must be made. At the end of the recitation, that vajra should be placed in the midst of white mustard seeds (*siddhārthaka*) and kept there during a lunar eclipse. He should continue to recite until the mustard seeds crackle and pop. Then the vajra is accomplished. By holding that vajra, one performs all rites: it pulverizes mountain peaks, dries up the lakes of *nāgas*, makes rivers flow upstream, puts *nāgas* to flight, neutralizes poisons, paralyzes all living beings, bewilders them, causes them to fall, pulverizes mechanical devices, and paralyzes or crushes carts and the like. In this manner, one performs all such rites. This is the accomplishment of the single-pointed vajra. 26.49.

For one who accomplishes the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, no one at all is able to create an obstacle—not even Mūrdhaṭaka himself—provided it is done according to the ritual procedure and not otherwise. During the time of recitation for this [deity], Buddhalocanā should be recited constantly both before and after; in this way, gentleness arises and accomplishment becomes manifest. || 26.50 ||
[The rules concerning the performance of the *śrāddha* ceremony.]

Then, having descended into a river flowing to the ocean, one should offer one hundred thousand lotuses. Śrī, having arrived, grants a boon; she bestows a kingdom. Then, if one should offer three hundred thousand, one becomes a universal monarch (sārvabhauma) and becomes the sovereign of Jambūdvīpa. Having installed the cloth-painting (paṭa) before the opening, one should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times. All the mechanical devices fall down. One should enter without hesitation. Having entered, one extracts elixirs and alchemical potions (rasarasāyana). Or else, one remains right there. A fear of the Vaiṣṇava discus arises. Then, as soon as one enters, it is reduced to ashes by the mere thought [of it]. One raises it up by means of the mind alone. It never again enters that [opening]. 26.51.

Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should strike the big toe of the Blessed One three times a day with *jāti* flowers over which the mantra has been recited once, until a ray of light issues forth from the big toe and dissolves into the body of the practitioner. At that very moment, his hair becomes curled and ringed; he flies up together with his retinue and becomes a king of the *vidyādharas*, remaining for an eon.

Then, having installed the cloth painting facing west on the seashore and kindled a fire with *nāga* wood, one should offer a hundred thousand *nāga*-flowers into the fire, dedicating it to the ocean. Waves will arise in the ocean; one must not be afraid as a sign of success. When the ocean approaches in the guise of a brahmin, he will ask, "What should I do? One should say, "Become subject to my will. Thereupon, he performs everything that is commanded. (26.53) {S299}

Having drawn a thousand-petaled lotus on the ground and sat upon it, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times. Piercing the earth, [the practitioner] rises; accompanied by a retinue of a thousand, he flies up. He becomes a king of the *vidyādharas*, remaining for a great eon (*mahākalpa*). Bestowing what is not easily obtained, he illuminates five *yojanas* with his splendor. 26.54.

During the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), one should offer one hundred thousand *jātī* flowers above the crown-protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*) of the Blessed One, the King of Uṣṇīṣas. Each [flower] should be consecrated with a mantra-recitation (*japta*). This should be done until a ray of light issues forth from the crown-protrusion and dissolves into the body of the practitioner. At that very moment, he becomes possessed of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijña*). When recited one million times, in whatever way it is employed, if a *vidyā* is recited together with this Blessed One, she will certainly come; while being recited by him, she appears visibly before him. If she does not come, his head will split open and wither. (26.55) {V233}

And this Ekākṣara Uṣṇīṣacakravartin is indeed the Tathāgata himself in person. Who else in the world, including the gods, is the king of all mantras and vidyās? It is the Tathāgata alone. His retinue consists of Sitātapatra, Tejorāśi, and others. All the ritual procedures for the accomplishment (*sādhana*) of all the Uṣṇīṣa kings are to be applied right here. And all the Uṣṇīṣa kings are to be accomplished by means of this. One who desires the supreme accomplishment must not apply it in an improper place; if one does so, the supreme *siddhi* will not be attained. In brief, all the gods are summoned by this. 26.56.

Then one opens the treasure. Having gone to where the treasure lies, one should take the Akāla-jar, smear it with all kinds of perfumes, pour white sandalwood water into the jar, consecrate it eight thousand times with mantras, and place it over the treasure. If the treasure is present, then that ground will crack open. If the treasure lies at the height of a man, it should be touched with water; having dug down a cubit’s depth, it should be taken up. 26.57.
