Now, one desiring to accomplish the lion [rite] should fashion one from the clay of an anthill, smear it with *gorocanā*, and install it upon a pedestal. Having performed a magnificent worship, one should recite the mantra until it moves. When it has moved, success is attained. Mounting its back, with hair curled like earrings, one flies up together with four others, including oneself. One lives for nine thousand years with the lifespan of Brahmā, and becomes inaccessible to all *vidyādharas*. In this same manner, the elephant, horse, and buffalo are to be accomplished. When the lion lets out a roar, even the gods tremble on their thrones.

Having gone to a lotus pond, one should offer a hundred thousand lotuses; one obtains the sovereignty of a vassal king. One should perform a fire-oblation of a hundred thousand buds of red karavīra; one obtains a princess. One should cause a hundred thousand jasmine flowers to be carried away by a river flowing toward the ocean; one obtains whatever maiden one desires. All these supreme accomplishments (*sādhana*) are perfected. 26.59.

Wherever that Uṣṇīṣacakravartin goes, even Indra offers him his own seat. And all the kings of the gods, upon seeing him from afar, become afraid and terrified. He eclipses the radiance of all the kings of the gods within a range of a hundred yojanas.

This Tathāgata Cakravartin is here in the world of the gods; and all the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) of the Blessed One, the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, the Single Syllable, remain under his control. All mantra-tantras, together with their ritual manuals and in full detail, are inclined toward him. (26.61)
Thus spoke the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, the Lion, the Supreme among Men.

Thus concludes the twenty-sixth chapter, the detailed exposition of the ritual procedures for the Single-Syllable Universal Monarch (*ekākṣaracakravartin*), from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsabhavana) and all the hosts of gods dwelling there, as well as all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas, once more addressed Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince: 27.1.

Mañjuśrī, this Dharma-treasury, which is the very essence of all the Tathāgatas and resembles a wish-fulfilling gem, has been taught for the sake of fulfilling the aspirations of the world. At that time, during the age of degeneration when the Buddha-fields are empty and the guidance of the True Dharma of the Tathāgatas who have entered parinirvāṇa is disappearing, at that time and at that moment, for the purpose of protecting the treasury of mantras of all the Tathāgatas, it shall serve as a storehouse within this *Kalparāja* of your own boy-mantra-tantras. When recited according to the ritual, Mañjuśrī, it will be the very core; it will be the foremost among all the mantra-tantras of the Tathāgatas and within your own *Kalparāja* of the Boy. By the recitation of this single-syllable Universal Monarch (*ekākṣaracakravartin*), all the Vidyārājas of the Tathāgatas are considered recited. (27.2)

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, in your own King of Ritual Manuals (*kalparāja*), there was formerly a single-syllable [mantra] that was a treasure-trove, the very essence, the foremost, and the most excellent. In the past, in a time long gone, sixty-two eons ago—equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā—there appeared a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One named Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra. Merely by remembering him or by uttering his name, the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) are exhausted. Many beings who merely hear his name are destined for enlightenment; what need is there to mention those who seek the accomplishment of the mantra? (27.3)

Furthermore, those who recite all mantras must necessarily first bring to mind this Blessed One, the Tathāgata Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarāja; and they should speak with their voice: "Homage to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra. Then [they should pay homage] to Amitābha and Ratnaketu, and thereafter, having prostrated to all the Buddhas, the mantras should be recited as desired. They grant swift accomplishment. 27.4.

For this reason, the proclamation of the names and the homage to the Tathāgatas, as well as the prostration to all the Tathāgatas, for the sake of the great increase of merit, ensures that one becomes destined for enlightenment and is perfected in the accumulation of wholesome qualities. One enters the ranks of the Bodhisattvas, and the mantras grant him swift accomplishment. 27.5 {S302}

By the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, this single-syllable mantra—the heart of all Tathāgatas, esteemed by all mantra-tantras, and the accomplisher of all ritual purposes—has been taught. Mañjughoṣa, this supreme secret, most profound mystery, should be employed for the benefit of oneself within your own King of Rituals (kalparāja) by those in the world. 27.6.
And also toward one who is not a disciple, one who is unrighteous... [and] likewise toward one who has no faith in this teaching of the Teacher proclaimed by the Victor. 27.7
It should never be employed toward one who is wicked, arrogant, a violator of the Teacher’s instruction, or one who lacks faith in the sons of the Jina. (27.8)

To those who are incapable of honoring and supporting even the Śrāvakas and the Pratyekabuddhas, one must certainly not give the mantra; for such a person, no accomplishment (siddhi) is seen. [27.9] But one who is faithful, gentle-minded, and serene toward the teaching of the Jina, and who is likewise always a Bodhisattva intent upon honoring and supporting [the Sangha], [to him it may be given]. [27.10]
Success in this mantra shall be attained in this ritual manual proclaimed by me, in the great one-syllable mantra dedicated to Mañjughoṣa. (27.11)
Therefore, that Lord of the World bestowed the mantra that brings happiness, the heart-essence of all Buddhas and the source of all mantras. (27.12)
In the past, seventy-six crores of mantras were sung by the Self-Existent One for the sake of the welfare of embodied beings who are deluded by sin.
This [reality] is established as the limit of phenomena (dharmakoṭi) of the Buddhas who act for the welfare of the world.
Relying upon the guidance of the Dharma (dharmanetrī), this single syllable remains established. 27.15.
This mantra accomplishes all aims and wards off wicked kings;
it performs a variety of activities and brings all rites to fulfillment.
Likewise, it certainly performs eight thousand rites;
through the ritual procedure as prescribed, it bestows manifold prosperity.
This syllable *ma*, conjoined with the mantra, is the heart of Mañjuśrī. The syllable *u* is the knower of the eternal state; thus was it set forth in the world.
The King of Infinite Life and Wisdom has revealed the determined meaning;
this was set in motion by the Buddha for Mañjughoṣa through the cause of his mastery.
Then, at the end of this age, when the Teacher has passed into parinirvāṇa in this world,
he will swiftly attain accomplishment through ritual action as prescribed by the rules.
There was a buddha-field named Amitāyus;
there, that Blessed One, the Buddha who sets the wheel of Dharma in motion, resided. (27.21)
He remained for immeasurable eons, having empowered his lifespan;
for this very reason, his name became Amitāyurjñānaviniścaya (The Determination of Infinite Life and Wisdom).
This Tathāgata, the great king of kings of all worlds and possessed of great supernatural power,
bestowed upon the wise son of the Buddha this foremost and supreme mantra.
The eldest son of the preeminent [prince], in that great abode of vast supernatural power, then joined this [work] with his son Samantabhadra.
Then that son of the Buddha indeed bestowed it upon Mañjughoṣa;
now I, the Tathāgata, shall proclaim this foremost kalpa for him. This is that supreme mantra spoken by the King of Dharma.
For the sake of the welfare of all beings, he spoke this mantra:

"Homage to Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha. Homage to all the Buddhas, beginning with Śālendrarāja, Amitāyus, Amitāyus, Ratnaketu, and the rest. Having paid homage to these, the single-syllable mantra should be recited three times. And what is that? *Muṃ*.

All mantras have set, having taken refuge in the Teacher’s image; among them, this King of Vidyās, possessed of great supernatural power, is the very essence. Arranged as a single syllable, he proceeds eternally.

Friends, this was spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, while residing in the world-system Amitavyūhavatī. For the sake, welfare, and happiness of all beings; out of compassion for the world and for the benefit of the great multitude; having regard for future generations and knowing that the time for the disappearance of the teaching had arrived; and for the purpose of restraining wicked kings who harm the Three Jewels in the final, degenerate age—he bestowed it upon Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the eldest legitimate son of all the Tathāgatas. (27.28)

Through the empowerment of the Buddha, he gave it to Samantabhadra; the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra gave it to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta. Then, for the sake of favoring all sentient beings and by the power of great compassion, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta established it within his own body, residing in his heart. 27.29.

Foreseeing the future time, at the end of the degenerate age during the period when the teaching is disappearing, I am the final Tathāgata; in this wicked time, the Kali Yuga, this supreme mantra will act for the sake of protecting my teaching. (27.30)

I shall speak its ritual manual (kalpa) in brief; listen, O Kumāra Mañjusvara of beautiful voice, to this majesty and the detailed expansion of its ritual manual. I shall speak of this sovereign king of manuals in even greater detail.

First, having ascended a mountain peak, one should recite [the mantra] two million times; thus the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished. One should recite while subsisting on milk, observing silence, with the mind focused nowhere else but on the mantra, having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, having generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and having undertaken the vows of the *poṣadha* discipline and the bodhisattva vow. Thereafter, the ritual activities (*karmāṇi*) may be performed. || 27.32 ||

First of all, the cloth-painting (paṭa) must be caused to be painted by a painter who has observed the *upoṣadha* fast, using non-adhesive pigments on either a clean piece of cloth or a canvas that has been infused with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, in a pure location. By a pure painter who eats the three white foods and is dressed in clean garments, it should be caused to be painted from sunrise until midday on the fifteenth day of the month when the moon is full and the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) is pure; one should avoid painting beyond that time. In this manner, it should be done day after day until it is completed. || 27.33 ||

First of all, one should paint the world-system of Amitāyusvatī upon a cloth. On a cloth measuring one cubit, or on a rectangular panel of one Sugata-span, one should depict the world-system of Amitāyusvatī on all sides, adorned below by mountains of ruby, sapphire, crystal, and emerald, and above by the appearance of great jeweled celestial palaces, with the forms of raised banners and flags adorning it on all sides. || 27.34 ||
There, in the center, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, was the Tathāgata Amitāyurviniścayarājendra, teaching the Dharma, garlanded with a blaze of universal radiance, slightly reddish-white in hue.

On the left side, seated upon a jeweled stone, is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, holding a fly-whisk in his hand and gazing at the Tathāgata; with a citron fruit placed in his left hand, he is dark-complexioned like the *priyaṅgu* flower, his body adorned with all ornaments and surrounded by a universal blaze of light.

On the right side is the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, standing upon a jeweled stone, holding a fly-whisk in his hand, with his white hand raised and gracefully positioned; his left hand holds a jewel; he is adorned with all ornaments and a crest-jewel of gems, and is dark yellow like the priyaṅgu plant; he is clothed in a lower garment of blue silk, wears a pearl necklace and a sacred thread of jewels, and is encircled by a garland of flames on all sides.

On his right side, one should have depicted the noble Mañjuśrī, standing upon a jewel-stone, in the form of a youth, his head adorned with five locks of hair, decorated with the ornaments of a young boy, golden in color, dressed in a lower garment of blue silk, wearing a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) interspersed with strings of pearls and jewels, gazing toward the Tathāgata, with a slightly smiling face, gentle in appearance, beautiful in form, with palms joined in reverence, and endowed with all the most excellent characteristics. || 27.38 ||

Beneath that, the practitioner, wearing his characteristic marks and attire, holding a garland of lotuses, with knees and elbows resting on the ground and head bowed, should be depicted at the corner edge of the cloth. || 27.39 ||

Above the Blessed One, four Blessed Buddhas should be caused to be painted. On the right side, two [should be depicted]: Amitābha and Puṇyābha. On the left side, above, two Tathāgatas should be caused to be drawn: Sālendrarāja and Ratnaketu. They are all radiant, with flames on all sides, golden-colored, endowed with the excellence of all marks, strewn with all kinds of flowers, seated upon lotus-thrones and no other seats, teaching the Dharma, sitting cross-legged, and possessing a serene appearance. || 27.40 ||

Above the Blessed One, one should have depicted the Tathāgata-form named Sunetra, emerging from within a cloud while raining down a shower of flowers; he is endowed with all excellent marks, garlanded with a halo of light radiating in every direction, granting a boon with his right hand, and holding the corner of his robe with his left hand. 27.41.

This is the ritual procedure for the cloth painting (*paṭavidhāna*) of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra. This is the single-syllable mantra of this very Blessed One. He is the King of Uṣṇīṣas, the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, who rivals [the Buddha], possessing equal vigor and equal power. His expansion of qualities and power is inconceivable; he is of great supernatural might and great majesty. (27.42)

In brief, it performs all those extensive ritual manuals (*kalpa*) that have been taught for the King of the Uṣṇīṣas of all Tathāgatas, the Great Wheel-Turner, and for the Single Syllable [Mantra]. Even if not yet accomplished, it performs its activities through mere recitation; how much more so when it has been accomplished! It bestows the perfection of fruits according to one’s desire. Merely by seeing this cloth-painting, whatever is wished for and desired by the mind becomes attained. One will certainly become destined for enlightenment. {S306} ap27.44 ap27.45

By the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of that very Blessed One, Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, this is called the Heart of all Tathāgatas; it is called the King of the Uṣṇīṣas of all Tathāgatas; it is called the Wheel-Turner (*cakravartin*); it is called the Great Wheel-Turning King; it is called the Heart of Mañjuśrī in his youthful form (*kumārabhūta*); it is called the Single Syllable (*ekākṣara*). In brief, its power is inconceivable. For the empowerment of the Buddhas is indeed inconceivable; the miraculous manifestation (*vikurvita*) of the Buddhas is inconceivable. (27.44)

Even for one who has not performed the ritual, who has not completed the preliminary practices (*puraścaraṇa*), who is established in all kinds of household undertakings, and even for one who indulges in all types of food, liquor, meat, and sexual intercourse—provided they exclude those who lack faith and those who have not generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*)—there is no accomplishment (*siddhi*). This applies also to those who harm the Three Jewels and those who intentionally injure them; for these, even minor rites do not succeed, let alone middling or supreme accomplishments. For one who engages in the practice of all desires and follows the conduct of eating whatever is desired, eight thousand and eight hundred minor rites will succeed when applied. And what are they? || 27.45 ||

First of all, when recited once, it is self-protection; when recited twice, it is protection of others; when recited thrice, it becomes great protection. Even by a Great Bodhisattva established on the ten stages, it cannot be disturbed—how much less so by other beings? (27.46)

One should wrap [the waist] with a five-colored thread over which the mantra has been recited four times; thus the retention of semen (*śukrabandha*) is accomplished. Furthermore, he shall not suffer from disturbances in sleep, except by his own will. On that very night, if one so desires, it may be performed alone; if it is to be done day after day, it should be performed daily. Alternatively, if one does not desire it, one should take ashes consecrated seven times and touch the region of the navel; the retention of semen is accomplished for three weeks. Having meditated upon the Buddha, the Blessed One, if one touches someone while the mantra has been recited five times, that person becomes submissive. (27.47)

During a lunar eclipse—that is, during the seizure of the moon—within the lunar orb, one should kindle a fire with *arka* wood and, even without a cloth, offer ten thousand oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) while facing east. The rite of homa should be performed near a royal palace, separated by a river, or in a temple; it should be performed in the vicinity of that place where the king resides. At dawn, the king becomes submissive; he does everything that is commanded. When [the practitioner] no longer sees [the king], the king’s mind becomes fixed [on him], or he becomes sluggish, or he falls into a state of mental distraction. || 27.48 ||

One must perform the restoration again. One should offer eight thousand oblations of milk at whatever time or place. From that point on, the person becomes healthy. This ritual must not be performed for those who are faithful, who have confidence in the Three Jewels, and who have generated the mind of awakening (bodhicitta); if one performs it for them, they would incur a very great mass of demerit. It should be performed for others who are harmful, and for those with malicious or cruel minds, so that they may be seen day after day; thus they become gentle-minded. If they do not become so, they will be deprived of their great wealth and will be reduced to mere breaths remaining. 27.49.

Furthermore, there is another ritual: during a lunar eclipse, having kindled a fire with *palāśa* wood fuel, one should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter. At dawn, one becomes the king and lord of the country; he issues commands and what is to be deliberated upon is counseled. He reveals his true nature (*sadbhāva*). Within six months, he grants a village consisting of a thousand households. If one offers the oblation at midnight, [the result is obtained] in three months. If one offers it throughout the entire night, one obtains it within a single month.

If one offers oblations every night for a month, one obtains a territory, or a village equal to a territory, or some other kind of wealth. Enemies do not prevail. If they should prevail, the rite must be performed again. 27.50.

During a lunar eclipse, having kindled a fire with *apāmārga* wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *palāśa* fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee belonging to the enemy of the Brahmins. At the end, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *picumanda* leaves smeared with pungent oil. At dawn, the gentle Brahmins [will prevail], and the king becomes hostile. 27.51.

There is another rite as well: during a lunar eclipse, having kindled a fire with whatever wood is available, one should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter. At the conclusion of the homa, one should cast that ash in whichever direction the lord stands; he becomes submissive. Whatever [wealth] one desires, at whatever time it pleases, he provides extensive enjoyments and assistance. He bestows a small or large village, or even a province. And the accomplishment is unfailing; it is certain within six months. 27.52.

Now, if one of the four castes, with a mind full of anger, approaches another person at a place of deformity, or with a distorted and prominent appearance, [and that person] is a devotee of another deity among worldly ones—in whichever direction they stand, that very house he enters for him; he becomes agitated, or flees at night, or his family is divided. For the restoration [of peace], eight thousand oblations of milk should be offered. He becomes well again. 27.53.

There is another rite as well. During a lunar eclipse, according to that same procedure, one who is pure, dressed in clean garments, and has fasted for a day and night, should perform the rite before an image or cloth-painting of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, or a book of the True Dharma, or a stūpa containing relics, using water free from living organisms. He should prepare that place with dry flowers and fragrant substances, filling it with sandalwood and saffron, and perfuming it with camphor incense. 27.54.

{V239} Wherever this rite is employed—against a Brāhmaṇa with *palāśa* wood, against a Kṣatriya with *aśvattha* wood, against a Vaiśya with *khadira* wood, or against a Śūdra with other woods—one should kindle the fire and perform that very rite. For a Brāhmaṇa, one should use *palāśa* fuel-sticks; for a Kṣatriya, *aśvattha* fuel-sticks; for a Vaiśya, *khadira* fuel-sticks; and for a Śūdra, *apāmārga* fuel-sticks, or others as may be available. At the conclusion of the oblation of clarified butter (*ājyahoma*), one should perform the rite. 27.55.

In the same way, O Great King, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *aparājita* root fuel-sticks and eight thousand oblations of clarified butter. At the conclusion, one should cast that very ash in whichever direction the Great King resides or from which he approaches with a malicious mind. Having bound the *Uṣṇīṣacakravartin* single-syllable mudrā, or the *utpala* mudrā, one should cast [the ash]. He will turn back in terror, his wheel broken; or some other great portent occurs, such as a great calamity or mental distress by which his speech is brought to a halt. (27.56)

These and other such rites may be performed as desired. Having consecrated a garment with mantras, one should wear it; one becomes fortunate. Having consecrated one's eyes, one should apply collyrium; one becomes beloved by all people. One should perform the consecration seven times over one's eyes and face in its entirety, and then gaze upon the face of an angry person; he becomes submissive and gentle. Having consecrated a flower, fruit, or anything else that has fragrance seven times, [one should present it] to the king...

One should offer it. By merely smelling it, he becomes submissive. Or whatever other being there may be, that one becomes submissive by the mere sight of it. In cases of pain in all the limbs, having consecrated [the water] eight hundred times, one should bathe with warm water; one becomes healthy. 27.57.
One should not perform these rites for sentient beings who are suffering, nor for those who are destitute, fallen, impotent, or even for those who have taken vows within this teaching.
One who has faith in the Three Jewels should not perform such an act;
indeed, one should not perform this rite toward women, nor toward children, the elderly, or the sick.
One should not perform [this] rite for one who is poor, suffering, of little strength, or born of an improper womb; however, one should employ it for a being of great strength.
One should perform such an act against one who is brave, reckless, greedy, possessed of a great following, wealthy, excessively arrogant, and fierce;
likewise against one who hates the teaching, is wrathful, and is a thief of another's property.
62. [This applies] to all mantras, medicinal herbs, and yogins who lack faith. || 27.62 ||
One should employ these rites against a man who is arrogant, evil-minded, a king despised by the world;
one must avoid employing them against those who are righteous.
Furthermore, they call it "the other rite," which has been abandoned by the Buddhas.
Indeed, the reciter, when enraged, hurls that very ash toward whichever direction he desires. (64) 27.64.
Those enemies stationed there will become enraged, and the king as well shall perish;
those people too will certainly fall into a state of long-lasting exhaustion.
Furthermore, if a great plague or calamity is seen in that region,
one should not perform the ritual even if one has fallen into dire straits.
Within three weeks, all those rulers of men there will perish;
when that karma is fully exhausted, they shall be destroyed within two weeks.
In the first [week], there is distraction of mind; in the second week, however, there is exhaustion.
Likewise, death occurs at the seventy-third day; therefore, one should avoid that [time].
In the first [week] they flee; in the second, there is confusion regarding the location.
In the third week, there is destruction. One should not perform such a rite.
The leaders of the world have taught that those to be disciplined by pure goodness alone do not possess abundant prosperity; for those Buddhas are of pure mind.
All Buddhas have condemned any action that obstructs the vital breath;
therefore, a practitioner of recitation who desires supreme accomplishment should not perform such an act. 71.71.
Rebirth in hell is seen only among these very realms of desire;
however, this alone has been declared as the arising of the fruit of black karma.
Such is the majesty of the diversity of karma as it has been perceived by the best of bipeds.
It is powerful, always bringing about auspiciousness, and its dark form bestows welfare.
Likewise, mixed karma is taught as being indeed mixed.
Thus has this variety of karma been demonstrated by those who see reality.
The reciter of mantras should avoid that black karma, or indeed the mixed karma.
One should cultivate the pure, auspicious [state], which arises as the fruit of virtuous action.
But by obstructing the breaths, the reciter goes again and again to hell;
therefore, for the sake of desisting from that, the duty of non-violence is the supreme action.

Thus, heaven, as well as spiritual accomplishment and the auspicious course of mantras, are attained through meritorious deeds; conversely, that which is contrary is said to result from contrary actions.
I have declared dharma and adharma, and the practice for attaining omniscience. One who recites [mantras] constantly should always undertake auspicious actions with the desire for accomplishment.
The mantras of that practitioner who recites them succeed when he abides in auspiciousness;
for one devoted to pure deeds, liberation is indeed irreversible.
The Tathāgatas declare that for a counselor, success comes through spiritual excellence;
however, for the sake of disciplining sentient beings, the diversity of karma is taught.
One thousand rites, or even eight hundred and more, may be accomplished as desired; however, one should perform only minor rites, for the supreme one is not obtained.
The middling [mantra] is accomplished with some effort through recitation and fire-offerings;
the inferior [mantra] is accomplished quickly by means of ritual action performed according to the prescribed rules.
Threefold action has been taught: superior, inferior, and middling.
83. Thus, one who performs the highest recitation and practices austerity attains the superior [result].
27.83. Likewise, one who performs middling recitation shall obtain middling success in their action.
Likewise, one who constantly mutters very few mantras and is occupied with very few ritual acts.
One obtains only a minor accomplishment (kṣudrasiddhi), but does not attain any other accomplishment.
Furthermore, the measurement of time for recitation (japa) in the fire-oblation (homa) is seen to be threefold.
From a superior [mantra], a superior accomplishment is achieved; among those that are middling, a middling one is seen.
From a lesser [mantra], a lesser rite is obtained; this is called a minor accomplishment.

Thus concludes the twenty-seventh chapter, the extensive ritual procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*) of the Heart Mantra of Noble Mañjuśrī, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra. (Chapter 87) The Root Mantra of the Single Syllable. Noble Mañjuśrī. The Ritual Procedure for the Cloth-Painting is finished.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī, the Youthful:

Mañjuśrī, there is yet another procedure for your cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*), which serves as a means for accomplishment and achieves the purpose of all rites. By means of this very single-syllable heart-mantra, or the six-syllable one ending with *makara*, or by your root-mantra, or the six-syllable heart-mantra beginning with the syllable *oṃ*, or the single-syllable one—this very ritual manual (*kalpa*) is to be performed before the painting. In the future time, in the final age, when I, the Tathāgata, have passed into parinirvāṇa, when the Buddha-field has become empty, when the lowest of ages has arrived, in a world without protection, without refuge, and without resort—this very king of manuals shall become a protection, a refuge, a shelter, and a final resort. And what is that? 28.1.

First of all, one should first have the Blessed Buddha Śākyamuni painted on a previously unwashed cloth that is free of hair, seven cubits long and three cubits wide, with its fringes intact, and treated with a solution of saffron and sandalwood paste. He should be depicted seated upon a lotus throne, teaching the Dharma and looking toward Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta. On the right side, one should have Sudhana, Subhūmi, the noble Akṣayamati, and Mañjuśrī painted, all in the form of youths, their limbs adorned with every ornament, performing obeisance to the Blessed One. On the left side, one should have Samantabhadra, the noble Avalokiteśvara, Bhadrapāla, and Suśobhana painted. 28.2.

The image of the Blessed One should be depicted as somewhat shorter [in stature]. Noble Avalokiteśvara and Sudhana should be made with fly-whisks held in their hands; and below them, the Earth Goddess (Vasudhā) should be depicted with her upper body emerging [from the ground], holding a jewel casket in her hand. Above, two young Vidyādharas bearing garlands and clouds raining down along with lightning should be depicted. All the Bodhisattvas should be made looking toward the face of the Blessed One, adorned with ornaments and with serene gazes, depicted as if seated upon the upper part of their bodies in a slightly bent posture. 28.3.

Having placed such a painting in a shrine containing relics, one should recite one hundred thousand syllables of this Mañjuśrī facing westward. Remaining silent like wood, bathing three times a day, changing his clothes three times, and constantly observing the *poṣadha* vows, he should subsist on a diet of vegetables, barley-gruel, or whatever alms-food he receives. Having divided his food into four parts—one for the Three Jewels, another for Mañjuśrī, another for all sentient beings, and the remainder for himself—he should perform the recitation while maintaining an undiminished body, keeping the Blessed One in mind and regarding all sentient beings with a focused mind, reflecting: "I do nothing, nor will I do anything, for my own sake, but solely for the benefit of all sentient beings. (28.4)

One should offer bathing water, incense, flowers, incense smoke, sacrificial offerings (*bali*), and lamps. For the shadow of the cloth [painting], one should constantly offer bathing water below it, as well as incense, flowers, and sacrificial offerings. In that very place, one should first offer these to the Three Jewels; thereafter to Maitreya; immediately after that, to Avalokiteśvara, and to the noble Samantabhadra.

Having first offered incense, flowers, incense smoke, and an oblation to the noble Ākāśagarbha, the noble Akṣayamati Kumārabhūta, Candraprabha, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, the noble Vajradhara, the noble Tārā, the noble Mahāmāyūrī, the noble Aparājitā, and the Blessed Prajñāpāramitā— all these— he should afterwards offer them to the cloth painting.

Afterwards, in a certain spot outside, one should fashion figures of all the Vināyakas—camels, donkeys, horses, and elephants—out of the earth from an anthill, and offer them everything [without exception]. Furthermore, one must not forget to avoid oil-cakes, flour, sesame preparations, horse-gram, fish, meat, radishes, eggplant, lotus leaves, and bronze vessels. 28.6.

Seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, weary yet remaining in that very place, one should cultivate the recollection of all Buddhas (*sarvabuddhānusmṛti*). One should perform the recitation (*jāpa*) mentally. Elsewhere, in a secluded spot, one should prepare a bed on a layer of *kuśa* grass. One should avoid excessive drinking, excessive eating, excessive wandering, excessive sightseeing, and excessive sleeping. One should cultivate the recollection of the Buddha three times a day. One should practice the retention of seminal essence (*śukrabandha*). And one should not disclose auspicious dreams to anyone else; one should report them to the Blessed One. 28.7 {V243}

Thus, proceeding in due order with haste, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. At the conclusion, one should recite the *Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā*. During the time of recitation, one should perform the *japa* while looking at the face of the Blessed One or Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, ensuring that the syllables and words are not confused. At the end of the rosary, having performed a prostration, one should offer a dedication. Having performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) according to this rule, one should place the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) in some secure location and perform the ritual wherever there is satisfaction of the mind.
The ritual for the cloth painting is completed. || 28.8 ||

Thereafter, one should have an image of the Blessed Mañjuśrī made of white sandalwood, seated upon a lotus throne, holding the Blessed Prajñāpāramitā in one hand and a fruit in his right hand. Having placed that [image] facing west in a clean location, one should construct a fire-pit before it. For all rites, it should be square, measuring two spans, and one should cast perfumes and all kinds of grains beneath it. One should build [the pit] above them. Having generated a new fire according to this procedure with fuel-sticks of *aśvattha* or *aśoka*, and having brought together clarified butter, rice, cooked food, milk, curd, and honey, placing them in a copper vessel, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times and offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). 28.9.

Thereafter, on another day, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight (śukla-pratipad), one should perform the rite. Having kindled the fire with *aśvattha* wood and seeing that it is free of smoke, one should invoke the fire: "Come, O tawny-hued one, with flaming tongue, red-eyed one, tawny-hued one! Grant, cause to be granted—svāhā! (28.10)

With this mantra, one should offer three oblations. Afterwards, one should invoke the Blessed One: "Come, come, O Kumārabhūta! I am intent upon the welfare of all sentient beings; provide me with assistance. Accept this incense, flowers, and perfume. Svāhā! (28.11)

Whatever he gives, that should be given by him. To one who has arrived, the guest-offering (*argha*) should be presented with fragrant flowers and water; thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*). Having recited [the mantra] seven times, one should cast a single oblation. In this manner, for seven days, [one should offer] ghee, rice, sesame, and barley-gruel.
One should perform the nourishment rite (*pyāyana*). Within this interval, one will certainly behold the noble Mañjuśrī in the form of a youth. 28.12–13.

One should offer eight thousand oblations of sandalwood fuel-sticks measuring two finger-breadths in length; day by day, one brings a hundred lords of the earth under one’s control. One should offer one hundred thousand *jātī* flowers; the king becomes submissive. One should offer a thousand lotuses smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one obtains wealth. Having kindled the fire with *śamī* fuel-sticks, one should offer sesame seeds; one becomes a lord of riches. Rising early in the morning, one should constantly offer water into the water; one becomes beloved by all people. One should offer one hundred thousand *arka* fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one obtains a village of a thousand households. One should offer the *bahuputrikā* plant; one obtains whatever maiden one desires. One should offer *apāmārga*; it pacifies disease. (28.13)

Having kindled a fire with wood from milk-exuding trees (*kṣīravṛkṣa*), one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of sesame seeds. Whatever one has in mind when performing this, that one obtains. One who desires a kingdom should offer a hundred thousand lotuses; he obtains a kingdom. By offering a hundred thousand barley grains, inexhaustible food arises. One should offer guggulu and priyaṅgu together with clarified butter; one obtains a son. In the juice of *arka* and *kaulīna*, one should offer jasmine flowers (*jātīkusuma*) into water. Within seven days, one obtains a village. Taking each jasmine flower one by one, one should offer them into water. Whoever is given the remaining fragments to smell becomes submissive merely by the act of smelling them. Having placed saffron, musk, cloves, and jasmine flowers in one's mouth, one should recite the mantra. With whomever one converses, that person becomes submissive. 28.14.

Having consecrated eight thousand recitations over black pepper (*marīca*) and placed it in one's mouth, even if one is angry, one becomes beloved by word alone. One should bind one's topknot with this very [substance]; one becomes invisible. Upon seeing an enemy, one should call him to mind; he becomes free from anger. (28.15)

By constant recitation, one becomes beloved by all people. Having risen at the great dawn, one should offer water together with *jāti* flowers upon the ground in a clean place; [the practitioner] becomes a master of mantras, his word not to be transgressed. When fear arises, one should bring [the deity] to mind; then no fear will occur. Even toward another who is angry, having cultivated loving-kindness and recollected [the deity], one should look upon their face; they become free from anger. 28.16.

One should perform a fire offering (*homa*) with all kinds of fragrant flowers; whoever one performs it for becomes submissive. At dawn, one should drink water consecrated seven times; this exhausts karma that was destined to be experienced. One should wash one's face with water over which the mantra has been recited seven times; one will become beloved by all people. Having consecrated flowers, whoever one gives them to becomes submissive. (28.17)

By a single hundred-thousand oblations of rice grains, one attains the status of an *ācārya*. By [a hundred-thousand] oblations of sesame seeds, one attains the status of a provincial ruler (*viṣayapati*). One should offer a thousand lotuses; one obtains a thousand *dīnāras*. Having combined together *guggulu*, resin (*sarjarasa*), fragrant resin (*gandharasa*), and *śrīvāsaka*—which have been purchased from a hero—one should offer them on every fifth day for six months. When it is complete, one obtains a thousandfold [the reward]. (28.18)

Having fashioned an image with all types of perfumes, one should cut it repeatedly with a sharp, single-edged blade and offer it as an oblation; for a man, using his right foot, and for a woman, her left foot. Whomever one desires becomes subject to one's will. 28.19.

For seven days, at the three junctions of the day, one should offer oblations of *dhuttūraka* flowers; one obtains cattle. With *arka* wood, one obtains grain; with *śirīṣa* flowers, horses; with *aśoka* flowers, gold; and with *vyādhighātaka* flowers, one obtains garments. Whatever one desires, all that one accomplishes by means of an oblation of *jātī* flowers. If one offers flowers of whatever color into water at sunrise, one obtains garments of that same color. Having consecrated a vessel with seven recitations, one goes for alms; one receives inexhaustible alms. Rising at night and reciting over oneself, one personally sees auspicious dreams. (28.20)

Now, desiring to bring a king under one's control, one should take the dust from his feet, mix it with mustard seeds and oils, and offer it as an oblation for seven days at the three junctions of the day; he becomes submissive. Desiring to bring a queen under one's control, one should combine *sauvarcala* salt, *śatapuṣpā*, and *vārāhī* together and offer them as an oblation for seven nights at the three junctions of the day; she becomes submissive. Desiring to bring a royal minister under one's control, one should fashion an image out of *bhallātaka* nuts, sesame seeds, and *vacā* root and offer it as an oblation for seven days and seven nights; he becomes submissive. Desiring to bring a domestic priest under one's control, one should combine *brahmadaṇḍī* and *śatapuṣpā* together and offer them as an oblation for seven nights at the three junctions of the day; he becomes submissive. (28.21)

One desiring to bring Brahmins under control should offer milk-rice mixed with ghee; all will become submissive. Now, one desiring to bring a Kṣatriya under control should offer boiled rice with *śāli* grains mixed with ghee for seven days. For the subjugation of Vaiśyas, one should offer barley-gruel mixed with molasses; he becomes submissive. One should offer oil-cake; Śūdras will become submissive. If one offers these all together at once, everyone becomes submissive. || 28.22 ||

At a crossroads, or in a solitary empty house, having offered an oblation (*bali*), whoever is afflicted by illness becomes freed from it. Touching the mouth while reciting [the mantra], the fever departs. By tying a lock of hair (*śikhābandha*) over which the mantra has been recited one hundred and eight times, one is liberated from all diseases. Having bound a *mūśraka* against all maladies and performed the tying of the lock of hair, one should go to sleep; all diseases depart. One seized by disease is liberated merely by the recitation. In the case of throat obstruction (*galagraha*), one should apply an ointment after reciting over clay from an anthill; the disease departs. In the case of eye disease, one should offer oblations of indigo buds; it is pacified. This is the ritual for the sick person according to the procedure of the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*). 28.23.

According to the previously described procedure, on an unblemished cloth free of hair, the noble Mañjuśrī in his youthful form (kumārabhūta) should be depicted, adorned with all ornaments, red in color, and having the appearance of a youth, seated upon a lotus throne. On his right side is the noble Avalokiteśvara, and on his left side is Samantabhadra; these two should be slightly smaller than the noble Mañjuśrī. Having set up that cloth-painting, one should recite the mantra ten million times, and one becomes a king. One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of sandalwood fuel-sticks smeared with saffron, and one becomes a king. One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of agalloch wood fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, and one becomes a king. One should offer ten million oblations of jasmine flowers smeared with ghee, and one becomes a king. (28.24) {S316} {V245}

One obtains a heap of dīnāras equal in number to the heap of lotuses that one offers as an oblation. As long as he does not accept the [lotuses] while they are being recited, he becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of the *vidyādharas*. One should offer a hundred thousand *bhallātaka* fruits; it bestows a thousand *dīnāras*. One should offer a hundred thousand fruits of the *vyādhighātaka* tree.

One becomes a lord of great wealth. By performing eight thousand homas with *guggulu* wood, one obtains grain. By performing continuous homas with sesame seeds, one obtains an uninterrupted supply of grain. || 28.25 ||

One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of *gotaṇḍula* rice together with curd; one obtains a thousand cows. Having placed the fruits of the *bahuputrikā* and the fruits of the *śamī* tree together, one should offer them as oblations; whatever maiden one desires, that one obtains. One should offer *śamī* leaves as oblations; this grants all desires. One should offer *agasti* flowers smeared with milk as oblations; this is for the subjugation of Brahmins. One should offer white *karavīra* flowers for the subjugation of Kṣatriyas. One should offer *karṇikāra* flowers for the subjugation of kings. One should offer *dhuttūraka* flowers for the subjugation of Śūdras. One should offer a hundred thousand *arka* flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one is liberated from all diseases. (28.26)

By this very method, one should offer one hundred thousand fragrant flowers at the base of the feet; one will become eternally happy. Having kindled a fire with *aśvattha* wood, one should offer a thousand *śamī* flowers; the affliction caused by the stars (*nakṣatra*) is pacified. Having written the mantra with bovine gallstone (*gorocanā*) and bound it upon the head, one may enter into battle; one will not be touched by weapons. Placing Mañjuśrī at the front of the army upon the shoulder of an elephant, the enemy force is broken merely by the sight of him. Having fashioned the form of the Youth (*kumāra*) seated upon a golden peacock-throne at the top of the banner, one may enter into battle; by the mere sight of it, the enemy force is broken. (28.27)

One should offer one hundred thousand jasmine flowers at the base of the feet [of the image]. One should prepare a bed right there upon a layer of *kuśa* grass. [The deity] will speak in a dream according to one's desire. Having offered a thousand lamps, one should make a single lamp with a wick made from lotus fibers, wrap it with licorice (*madhuyaṣṭi*), light it, and look; one will see Mañjuśrī in his youthful form exactly as he truly is. The second procedure for the cloth painting is completed. 28.28.

Having fashioned an image of the Youth (Kumāra), either of gold or silver, who with his right hand grants boons and with his left holds the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā—one should place such an image before oneself together with its reliquary casket and recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. One should perform worship with fragrant flowers. Furthermore, young boys and girls should be fed in front of it. One should perform singing, instrumental music, and the recitation of the book. Upon the completion of the recitation, having offered an *argha* oblation with three flowers, one should dismiss [the deity]. The rites of invocation and dismissal are performed according to the previously stated procedure. 28.29.

Having formed the lotus mudrā, one should perform the recitation (*japa*). With the banner mudrā, [one performs] the circumambulation; with the svastika mudrā, the seat; with the full (*pūrṇa*) mudrā, the water offering (*argha*); with the single-liṅga mudrā, the flowers; with the wish-fulfilling (*manoratha*) mudrā, the lamp; with the twin (*yamala*) mudrā, the incense; with the peacock-throne mudrā, the perfume; and with the staff (*yaṣṭi*) mudrā, the food offering (*bali*). According to this procedure, one should perform these day after day at night until the completion of the recitation. Afterwards, one should perform the ritual activities (*karma*). 28.30.

One should float a hundred thousand *jātī* flowers in a river flowing toward the ocean; one obtains a kingdom. Having made a heap of *jātī* flowers at night, one should sleep before the Blessed One; one sees the Blessed One teaching the Dharma, surrounded by bodhisattvas. Whatever purpose one undertakes, one should perform that very rite; one should not perform it for anyone else. (28.31)

Having observed the *upoṣadha* fast, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should offer oblations of *śrīvāsaka* incense mixed with honey. One obtains a kingdom. If one recites the mantra ten million times (*koṭi*), one sees Mañjuśrī himself, who then delivers a teaching of the Dharma. If one converses with him, he appears directly before one’s face. One becomes an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva. This is the third procedure. 28.32. {V246}

One should have an image of the Youth (Kumāra) made of red sandalwood, with Priyaṅkara on one side and Vīramatī, leaning against an Aśoka tree, on the other. Having placed it on one side, one should fashion an effigy out of red sandalwood mixed with salt, mustard seeds, and *rājikā* (black mustard), and having cut it up again and again, one should offer it as an oblation in the name of whomever—that person becomes submissive. If one offers *udumbara* fruits in the name of someone, that person becomes submissive. One should offer *kākodumbarikā* fruits in the name of whomever—that person becomes submissive. || 28.33 ||

One should offer *śṛṅgāṭaka* for the subjugation of a Brāhmaṇa; for the subjugation of a Kṣatriya, one should offer lotus roots (*padmamūla*); for the subjugation of a Vaiśya, one should offer *kaśeruka*; for the subjugation of a Śūdra, [one should offer] salt and sugar. One should offer eight thousand oblations three times a day for seven days; he in whose name one offers becomes subjugated. One should offer eight thousand oblations of neem leaves (*nimba-patra*) smeared with pungent oil three times a day for seven days in the name of someone; he becomes subjugated. By every such fire-offering (*homa*), there is subjugation. 28.34.

One should offer a hundred thousand *bṛhatī* flowers; one obtains gold. One should offer eight thousand *kālāñjanikā* flowers; one obtains a large village. One should offer *pāṭala* flowers; one obtains inexhaustible grain. One should offer *śrīparṇī* flowers; one obtains gold. One should offer *vacā* root smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one becomes a superior debater in all disputations. Having placed the juice of *brāhmī* together with ghee in a copper vessel, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times; thereafter, one should drink it. One conquers all debaters. If one takes a clod of earth, consecrates it eight thousand times while angry, and hurls it before someone who is enraged, that person relinquishes their anger. This is the fourth procedure. 28.35.

On an unbleached cloth, free of hair, a painter who has observed the *upoṣadha* fast should paint the noble Mañjuśrī using non-adhesive pigments. He is seated upon a lotus throne, teaching the Dharma. On his right side is the noble Mahāmekhalā, and on his left side is the noble Prajñāpāramitā, engaged in recitation, adorned with all ornaments, and dressed in white garments. Below him is a lotus pond strewn with various kinds of flowers, from which two Nāga kings emerge, holding lotus stalks in their hands. 28.36.

On one side, the noble Aparājitā should be depicted destroying obstacles and impediments; she has a face like a flame of fire and eyes knit in a frown. On the other side, the noble Parṇaśavarī, her hands busy with a noose and an axe, her eyes black and red, mounted upon the back of a peacock, should be shown protecting the practitioner. The practitioner, his hand busy with a lotus garland, gazes toward the face of the Blessed Mañjuśrī. Above them, two sons of gods should be drawn, holding chowries, flower garlands, and drums. 28.37.

Having placed that cloth painting facing west in a shrine containing relics, one should recite the mantra ten million times. At the conclusion of the recitation, having performed a great worship and having caused the Blessed Prajñāpāramitā to be recited, one should recite it ten thousand times while gazing upon the face of Mañjuśrī. Thereafter, the cloth painting trembles; one obtains a kingdom, one obtains sight, and becomes a vidyādhara.
He laughs; he becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin); he speaks; he becomes a bodhisattva who has attained the first stage (bhūmi); and he hears his teaching of the Dharma. || 28.38 ||

In front of that very painting, one should take cow’s ghee from a tawny cow with a calf of the same color, place it in a copper vessel, and recite [the mantra] until it steams, fumes, and blazes. By drinking it while it is steaming, one becomes supremely intelligent and possesses a retentive memory (*śrutidhara*). When it fumes, one gains invisibility (*antardhāna*); when it blazes, one gains the power of traveling through the sky (*ākāśagamana*). Having placed *vacā* root in a hollowed-out earthen bowl and wrapped it with *jātī* flowers, one should recite [the mantra] until it sprouts. By eating it, one becomes a possessor of a retentive memory (*śrutidhara*). If one recites another ten million times (*koṭi*), one sees Mañjuśrī face to face and hears his teaching of the Dharma; one also gains deep faith (*adhimukti*) in it. 28.39. {V247}

Having had a golden lotus with a hundred petals fashioned, and having placed one’s right knee upon the ground, one should recite [the mantra] until it blazes. As soon as it is grasped, one becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of the *vidyādharas*, invincible by others. Having placed realgar, yellow orpiment, or collyrium inside a casket made of *śrīparṇī* wood, one should recite [the mantra] until it makes a *khuṭ-khuṭ* sound. As soon as it is grasped, one becomes an unassailable sovereign over the *rākṣasas* and *piśācas* who roam the earth. || 28.40 ||

Taking a sword that is free of blemishes and endowed with auspicious marks, one should recite [the mantra] until it stands up like a snake spreading its hood. Taking hold of it, one becomes a universal monarch of the *vidyādharas*, with a lifespan of an eon and invincible. Having encased realgar (*manaḥśilā*) in the three metals and placed it in the mouth, one should recite [the mantra] until it makes a *culuculu* sound. One becomes invisible; as the wielder of the sword, while invisible, one performs all actions associated with merit, excluding those associated with sensual desire. Taking the heartwood of an *aśvattha* tree growing on a *śamī* tree, having encased it in the three metals and placed it in the mouth, one should recite [the mantra] until it makes a *culuculu* sound. One becomes invincible and lives for a thousand years. 28.41

Having fashioned a silver wheel, one should recite the mantra before the entrance of the asura cave until the wheel pierces the asura-machines and enters. At that very moment, asura maidens emerge; having entered with them, one becomes a dweller for an eon (*kalpasthāyin*). Having fashioned an iron trident, one performs the recitation at the mouth of that cave; there, all the machines burst apart. One enters together with as many [companions] as one desires, and becomes a dweller for an eon. One also beholds the Blessed Maitreya. This is the fifth procedure for the cloth-painting (*pañcamaṃ paṭavidhānam*).

Having fashioned an image of the Blessed Mañjuśrī out of white *arka* wood, the size of a thumb, one should offer a hundred thousand *arka* flowers; one obtains a neighboring kingdom. Having fashioned [an image] out of the root of white *karavīra*, likewise the size of a thumb, one should offer ten million of those flowers; one becomes a minister (*mantrin*). Having fashioned [an image] out of *karahāṭa* wood, the measure of a span (*vitasti*), one should offer a hundred thousand of those flowers; one obtains the position of a general (*senāpati*). Having fashioned an image of the Blessed Mañjuśrī out of white sandalwood, the measure of a span, one should offer a hundred thousand *jātī* flowers; one obtains the office of a domestic priest (*purohita*). || 28.43 ||

Having had an image of the Blessed Mañjuśrī made from aśvattha wood, measuring exactly one finger-breadth in size, one should offer a water-pot at a place where no crows gather. One will become esteemed by many people. Having fashioned [the image] out of all kinds of perfumes, [one should worship it] with flowers of all kinds of perfumes.

Whatever he desires through these offerings, that he obtains. If the practitioner of mantra constantly and continuously offers oblations of *agaru* (aloe) fuel sticks, he becomes esteemed by many people. By constant recitation, he dispels the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*). At the time of death, he beholds Mañjuśrī, who delivers a teaching of the Dharma for him. 28.44.

Rising up again and again, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. One becomes invincible to all beings. Having recited over one's eyes, one should look at one's master; he becomes well-disposed. For whomever one performs this rite, if that person is located in the same place, it takes seven days; if in another village, twenty-one days; if in another district, four months; if separated by a river, six months. By means of the ritual procedure of one’s own family, and not by the procedure of another mantra, one accomplishes every rite, with the exception of those connected with sensual desire and malevolent magic (*ābhicāruka*). This is the sixth ritual procedure.
Thus it was spoken at the end of the eon for the benefit [of beings],
as well as for the sake of the welfare of those beings with little merit by the Sage in the past.
When the teaching of the Teacher, the ascetic Śākyasiṃha, has disappeared,
in that fierce and most terrifying time, he will attain accomplishment.
Indeed, the seventh [chapter] will be spoken here in this Kalparāja that brings happiness. This ritual manual (kalpa) of mine was taught for that most terrible time;
it is a path indeed set forth for beings of little merit.
It serves as the cause for the equipment of enlightenment and flows toward the paths of the three vehicles.
At that time, in that age, I display skillful means to sentient beings;
for indeed, sentient beings are deluded by craving and agitated by passion and hatred.
To them I show this path that follows the influence of craving;
yet those bound by the fetters of craving may, through the cause of their karma, attain what is wholesome.

Likewise, substances to be accomplished through siddhi, as well as mantras and tantras, have been fully proclaimed by the Leaders of the World for the sake of disciplining sentient beings. This is the majesty of the ritual action for practitioners who recite [mantras]. 28.52.
Having spoken thus, the supreme sage, the Lion of the Śākyas, the best of men, having explained in detail the power and efficacy of the mantras and tantras,
shall manifest unfailing accomplishment at that time, in this degenerate age.

Then the supreme Victor chose the Śuddhāvāsa heaven for the assembly of gods: "O worthy ones, this which has been proclaimed as the extensive King of Rituals (Kalparāja) is the teaching of Mañjughoṣa for the sake of the welfare of all the world. (28.54)

Thus concludes the twenty-eighth chapter, the detailed section on the ritual procedures for Noble Mañjuśrī, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the Bodhisattvapiṭaka-avatamsaka.
ap29.7 ap29.8 · CHAPTER A29 ·
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Abodes, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: 29.1.

"Mañjuśrī, in your chapter on the ritual procedures for the rite of the cloth-painting, there is a seventh procedure for the rite of the cloth-painting which one will accomplish at that time, in that moment, at the end of the age. For such a person, their accomplishment shall be unfailing; it shall be fruitful, bringing about happiness and resulting in happiness, to be experienced in this very life, warding off all miserable rebirths, and their accomplishment shall certainly lead to enlightenment. (29.2)
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke the heart-mantra of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

the six-syllabled mantra, which consists of the liberation from the six realms of existence; it is inconceivable, incomparable, peerless, and possessed of great supernatural power; it is the deliverer from the ocean of all existences and from the bonds of the fetters of existence consisting of the three types of suffering. (29.3)
Unbearable to all beings, it is anointed by the entire world; unassailable by all beings, it purifies the path of existence.

It brings about the attainment of the qualities of a Buddha, wards off all that is evil, is rejoiced in by all the Buddhas, and produces all forms of prosperity; it is the most excellent among all mantras in the teaching of Mañjughoṣa. (29.5)
And what is that? Oṃ vākyeda namaḥ.

The ritual procedure for this is as follows: subsisting on a diet of vegetables, barley gruel, or alms-food, bathing three times a day and changing one's garments three times, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. Thus the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished. Then, on a cloth with uncut fringes, a painter who observes the *poṣadha* vows should paint the noble Mañjuśrī using pigments that have not been mixed together. He should be depicted seated upon a lotus throne, teaching the Dharma, adorned with all ornaments, in the form of a youth, and wearing a loose upper garment (*uttarāsaṅga*) of pearls. 29.6.

To his left is Āryāvalokiteśvara, holding a lotus in one hand and a fly-whisk (*cāmara*) in the other. To his right is Āryasamantabhadra. Above them, two *vidyādhara*s emerging from the interior of clouds, bearing garlands, should be caused to be painted. Below, the practitioner, with a censer held in his hand, should be caused to be painted on all sides. At the bottom is a lotus pond. 29.7. {S323}
Mountain peak

Having installed the cloth painting facing west at a shrine containing relics, having performed a grand worship, and having lit lamps of ghee, one should strike the face of Mañjuśrī with eight thousand *jātī* flowers, consecrating each one individually with mantras. Then, a deep and resonant sound of "Hūṃ" will be heard, or the cloth painting will tremble. By the sound of "Hūṃ," one becomes a universal monarch (*sārvabhaumika-rāja*). When the cloth painting trembles, one becomes a superior debater among all disputants and a knower of all worldly treatises. Even if [the primary] success does not occur, one becomes capable of performing all rites. This is the first ritual procedure. 29.8.

One should offer as fuel sticks of agarwood measuring one and a half finger-breadths, soaked in *turuṣka* oil, into smokeless embers of *khadira* wood for the entire night. At dawn, one beholds the noble Mañjuśrī; he grants whatever boon is desired by that person, with the exception of those connected to sensual pleasures. 29.9.

Having offered an uninterrupted stream of sandalwood incense before that very painting, one should recite the mantra throughout the entire night. Then, the Noble Mañjuśrī appears in person and teaches profound dharmas. One gains faith in them; having gained faith, one becomes liberated from all diseases and attains mastery. 29.10.

Having fashioned a lotus made of red sandalwood with a circumference of six finger-breadths and complete with a stalk, having smeared it with red sandalwood paste, and having performed a thousand oblations of *sampāta* while consecrating it a thousand times with mantras, one should place it upon a lotus leaf in front of the cloth painting on the full moon day. Grasping it with the hand, one should recite the mantra until it bursts into flames. By grasping it, one becomes a divine youth (*devakumāra*) sixteen years of age, with the luster of molten gold and a brilliance exceeding that of the sun; honored by all the *vidyādharas*, one lives for a great eon (*mahākalpa*). When the body is cast off, one is reborn in the realm of Abhirati.

During a lunar eclipse, one should take white *vacā* root, wash it with the five products of a cow (*pañcagavya*), and support it with *aśvattha* leaves; one should recite the mantra until it steams, smokes, and blazes. By [its] steaming, there is the subjugation of all people and victory over all disputants. When it smokes, one attains invisibility and lives for thirty thousand years. When it blazes, one attains flight through the sky and lives for a great eon (*mahākalpa*). || 29.12 ||

Taking the ghee from a tawny cow that has a calf of the same color, one should place it in a copper vessel and, having covered it with seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, recite [the mantra] until the threefold accomplishment is attained. Having drunk that, one becomes a possessor of the Vedas (*śrutidhara*), gains invisibility (*antardhāna*), and the power of traveling through the sky (*ākāśagamana*).

{S324} Having placed a lotus seed in the mouth during a lunar eclipse, one should recite [the mantra] until it makes a "culu-culu" sound. Having encased it in the three metals and placed it in the mouth, one becomes invisible. When it is spat out, one is seen again. {A13r}

Having placed the scent of cloves in one's mouth, one should recite [the mantra] six hundred thousand times; whoever one addresses becomes submissive. Subsisting on milk and barley-gruel, one should recite it twelve hundred thousand times; one becomes a *vidyādhara*. Subsisting on alms and observing silence regarding wood, one should recite it one hundred thousand times; one becomes invisible. One should recite it ten million times; Noble Mañjuśrī teaches the Dharma in such a way that one becomes a bodhisattva in his final existence. Through constant recitation, the accomplishment of all aims occurs. 29.15.

Having made an image of someone with all kinds of perfumes, if one cuts it up and offers it as an oblation, that person becomes submissive within seven nights. One should offer one hundred thousand pills of *guggulu* resin, the size of jujube seeds and anointed with clarified butter; one obtains one hundred thousand *dīnāras*.

Having descended into a river that flows to the ocean, one should offer one hundred thousand lotuses; one sees a great treasure equal to a heap of lotuses, which never comes to an end. One should offer eight thousand white mustard seeds anointed with saffron; the king becomes submissive. One should offer one hundred thousand sesame seeds anointed with curd, honey, and ghee; one becomes a great householder who bestows everything. || 29.17 ||

Having made a mandala with cow dung that has not fallen to the ground, and having scattered loose flowers over it, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. Then, one should read a volume of the True Dharma (saddharma). Within a month, one becomes supremely intelligent. Having recited the *rocanā* (bezoar) one hundred and eight times, one should apply it as a forehead mark (*tilaka*); one will become beloved by all people. Having recited [the mantra] seven times over one's topknot (*śikhā*), one becomes invulnerable to all sentient beings. || 29.18 ||

One should offer ten thousand *kirimālā* flowers; one is liberated from all diseases. One should recite [the mantra] seven times every day; this exhausts karma that is destined to be experienced. Furthermore, by reciting it one hundred and eight times at the time of death, one beholds the noble Mañjuśrī in his entirety face-to-face. Thus ends the seventh ritual procedure for cloth-paintings (paṭakarma). 29.19.

Thus concludes the twenty-ninth chapter, the ritual procedure for the Mañjuśrī cloth-painting, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the *Bodhisattvapiṭakāvatamsaka*; it is the seventh section on ritual procedures.
{S325} {V251} Now begins the thirtieth chapter.
Chapter A30.
Then indeed the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince: 30.1.

Mañjuśrī, there are places for the accomplishment of all mantras—beginning with the Universal Monarchs among the Vidyārājas and headed by the Uṣṇīṣas of all the Tathāgatas—in your mantra-tantra. Briefly stated, in the northern region (Uttarāpatha), the Vidyārājas of the Tathāgatas everywhere attain accomplishment. 30.2.
In China and indeed in Mahācīna, Mañjughoṣa shall prevail;
and those mantras of his will indeed attain accomplishment there.
The success of the Uṣṇīṣa Kings is indeed seen everywhere there—in Kāviśa, Vakhala, and likewise in Udiyāna on all sides.

A being who has gone to another body is drawn forth by the application of mantras;

Then he will proclaim the entire account from beginning to end—
