These syllables, joined with ten vowels and being the causes of all phonemes,
are seen upon the surface of the earth as increasing tenfold.
From one hundred syllables down to twenty, and even unto a single syllable—woven together with these measures of phonemes is the perfection of mantra. (33.11)
Mantras joined with four feet accomplish all aims;
for those mantras spoken by the Jinas are the eldest, the most excellent, and the noblest.
At that time, there were [mantras] of superior, middling, and inferior [power].
But those taught by their sons, the sons of the Conquerors, are indeed the Middle Way.
Those mantras which are indeed spoken as being for all worldly purposes are the lowest;
those mantras which were spoken by the Nairṛtas are said to be inferior.
The measure of the mantras spoken by the Noble Ones and the Victors is thirty-three, ten, eight, seven, twenty-eight, or up to more than one hundred; however,
from the perspective of syllables, they may consist of one or two syllables up to five hundred.
To whatever extent the mantras have been revealed by the Bodhisattvas.
That application of mantras, arranged upon the syllables of the *ap* [mantra], has been illustrated;
it is adorned with the meters, the union of vowels, and the meanings of the verbal roots. 33.17
Even a well-employed statement, if endowed with the principles of systematics (tantrayukti), may sometimes achieve success; however, one that is deprived of the proper sound and accent will fail.
Accompanied by mudrās and sounds produced from the head down to the sibilants, the palate,
teeth, lips, and throat, the sound that has thus issued forth is the practice of the ritual means.
But that which is well-applied, having turned away from the unmanifest, is declared to be complete in its phrasing;
one who employs such a word will achieve success.
A mantra that deviates from the prescribed rules, is devoid of ritual action, and is separated from its words and meanings, will not be swiftly accomplished; it requires a long period of time.
The success of that reciter who does not perform his practice in vain is never fruitless;
even in another birth, the granting of boons through mantra-perfection is seen.
By the power of his mantra and because of the long duration of those who recite it,
the mantra makes the ritual action unfailing for people who know the mantra and possess the mantra.

Those mantras of all worldly beings, including humans, which are inferior among all mantras— those spoken by all spirits and those characterized by envy— their syllables are said to number one, two, or three. They are expressed in various Mleccha languages and those proclaimed in regional dialects.

Bound by *paṅkti* meters and always intermingled according to their phonemes, they range from one thousand, eight hundred, and eight down to a single syllable. That which consists of four quarters (*catuṣpāda*), half-quarters, prose (*gadya*), and verse (*padya*) is thus described.
But a *śloka* consisting of only *daṇḍaka* measures is called a *gādhaskandhaka*.
The introduction, the application of meaning, and the thousand-fold ornamentation of the sense—these are differentiated [as] Apabhraṃśa and Saṃskṛta words, or as being devoid of meaning. (33.27)

The unmanifest, though devoid of the manifest and lacking the [specific] measures, is joined [to it]. That which results from the disjunction of movement and location is called the accomplishment of mantra (mantrasiddhi).
This is the characteristic of all mantras:

those mantras that abound in the letter *śa*, are adorned with the meaning of the syllable *oṃ*, and abide within the system characterized by the letter *ta*— in them, success (*siddhi*) will certainly occur.
Those mantras beginning with the syllable Oṃ and ending with the letter Ma,
when joined with the letter Śa, are likewise unfailing and auspicious.

The syllable *apa* is square in shape and devoid of any final consonant of the *pratyāhāra*. Joined with the letter *ta* and the letter *ra*, it constitutes the mantra for the ritual of accomplishment (*sādhanakriyā*).
Its first part abounds in two *repha*s (the letter *r*) and arises from the quality of the syllable *huṃ*.
Within the square enclosure of the letter *pa*, the phonemes are capable of accomplishment.
[The mantra] consists of the letter *ka* joined with *ra*, ending in *ma* and mixed with a vowel measure (*mātrā*).
With *ma* and *na* as its beginning, that mantra is said to be supreme. (32–33)
That mantra in which the letter *pa* is seen to abound in all tantras is called "gentle" (*saumya*). That which is adorned with the syllable *huṃ* is said to belong to Yama.
And that which abounds in the letter *bha* is said to belong to Indra and Vāyu.
They say that the letter *ca* belongs to Varuṇa and is beneficial for prosperity in the world;
while a mantra in which the letter *va* predominates is seen to belong to Mahendra.
The first is the mantra for going for refuge to the Three Jewels;
by performing this salutation, it becomes a cause for peace and brings about happiness.
That other [mantra] is employed for the purpose of paying homage to all the gods.
One's own mantra, as well as the Lord of Mantras—that mantra performs all rites.
A mantra that abounds in the syllable *da*, ends with *phaṭ*, and is uttered with *huṃ*—these mantras are extremely fierce, radiant, and possessed of great power.
Because it immediately obstructs the vital breaths when employed against a cruel creature,
one should therefore not perform sinful deeds, especially such as these.
Therefore, the reciter should avoid that which has always been shunned by the sages;
for even in both matters, the mantras for pacification and nourishment are accomplished.
In an instant, one performs all the rites as many as have been spoken;
for these mantras, when well-recited, are radiant and possess great supernatural power.
One should perform pacifying rites with those spoken by the Jina;
however, one should perform all enriching rites within the Kokanada family.
All evil deeds whatsoever are employed in malevolent rites (*ābhicāra*). One should perform all malevolent rites by means of the Vajra family;
though forbidden by the Lords of the World, they were revealed by the Lord of Yakṣas.

The greatness of the mantra’s emergence for the sake of disciplining sentient beings has been explained in three ways throughout all the three families. (33.43) Those eight foremost families which were proclaimed by the Sage himself—in them, accomplishment proceeds in three ways, declared to be of three types. (33.44)
It is divided into three types: superior, middling, and inferior. || 33.44 ||
Pacifying (śāntika), enriching (pauṣṭika), and also the malevolent (ābhicāruka) rites are intended;
however, the application of mantra alone is declared to be the application of tantra.
The greatness of the efficacy of mantras is employed for malevolent purposes;
however, this action is base and is censured by the omniscient ones.
One should not perform an action that obstructs life, even when one has fallen into great distress.
However, this has been described here in brief solely for the purpose of illustrating the majesty of karma.
The procedure for the application of tantric methods, with its extensive expansion of ritual actions through mantras, is taught here in this *Karmarāja*; it is also seen in other tantras.
One who is skilled in the application of all mantras should never resort to a rite that is deficient in action.
49. As many as there are worldly mantras, both with parts and likewise without parts.
All of them are indeed supramundane, and their qualities are always [supramundane];
the accomplishment of mantra is immeasurable, and that is proclaimed to be immeasurable.
Although the section beginning with the number one up to twenty has thus been explained,
there is also the section of thirty in summary, and another of forty.
Then they say there are sixty-three, seventy-one, and likewise fifty-two; and another ten, and yet another eighty in number.
They say that ten times nine hundred is a full hundred followed by another ten;
the number one hundred is thus calculated, and ten times that is a thousand.
Ten thousand is a *sahasra*, while ten *ayutas* are an *ayuta*. Ten *lakṣas* are a *vilakṣa*, and ten *vilakṣas* are a *koṭi*.
Ten times ten million (koṭi) is an arbuda;
ten arbudas is said to be a nirbuda; ten times that is held to be a khaḍga.
Ten *daśa-khaḍgas* make one *nikhaḍga*; ten *nikhas* are held to be a *kharva*. Ten *kharvas* likewise make a *padma*, and ten *padmas* make a *mahāpadma*.
Ten *padmas* are a *vāha*, and ten *vāhas* are likewise another [unit], the *vivāha*. A *mahāvivāha* is seen to be ten times that, and it is called a *śaṅku*.

The tenth stage after that is Mahāmāyā; the tenth stage beyond Mahāmāyā is Samudrā, as designated by the Leaders of the World in their knowledge of calculation. Following that, the twentieth [stage] is Mahāsamudrā.
For it has been said that there are fifty-nine great oceans, and likewise the Sāgara [ocean] is equal to ten of them.
They say that a *mahāsāgara* is composed of twenty-five [units];
ten times a *mahāsāgara* is indeed called a *praghara*.
When it is said, "Let ten flow forth," that is proclaimed as *ghara*.
When it is said, "Let ten *gharas* [flow forth]," that is called by the name *Aśeṣa*.
{S344} *Aśeṣa* multiplied by half of twenty is *Mahāśeṣa*.
62. That measure is indeed called "incalculable" (asaṃkhyeya) by the Leaders of the World. || 33.62 ||
They say that ten times the number *saṅkhya* is *asaṅkhya*; when that *asaṅkhya* is multiplied [by itself], it becomes [the next stage]. Beyond that, it is likewise [multiplied]... ||33.63||
That world is proclaimed to be a thousandfold greater than Amita;
beyond that world is Mahāloka, which is multiplied [in extent] by Mahāloka.
Then, that which was called "darkness" is said to become light; having multiplied the mass of light by ten, that is called "great radiance. (33.65)
From a heap (*rāśi*) it is said to be a great heap (*mahārāśi*); from a heap, it is called profound (*gambhīra*).
They say that from the profound comes the stable (*sthira*); from the stable, one should proceed to what is even more stable.
Beyond that, by way of great esteem, a highly esteemed state is described:
"Those who are diligent in the knowledge of calculation say that this state is a state beyond all states. (33.67)
Then one should go to Mahāsthāna; Mahāsthāna is considered to be "Measured.
Having made that which is measured even more measured, it is proclaimed as being of great significance.
From Mahārtha, one should go to Suśrutasthāna, and from there to Mahārṇava;
they say that [Suśrutasthāna] is even more primary than the first [Mahārṇava], for it is indeed the most primary of all.

Regarding the first [vow], they say it is the most excellent; from the most excellent, it is called the "eldest" (jyeṣṭha). That which is named the "abode of the eldest" is proclaimed as inconceivable. (33.70)

The inconceivable is desired from the inconceivable, the terrible from the terrible, and the kingdom from the kingdom; beyond the kingdom is the secret place, and beyond the secret place is auspiciousness. 33.71.
Beyond the auspicious, there is the "great consciousness"; it is intended as the consciousness of the great consciousness.
(72) That which is without consciousness is the distraction of the mind; it is described as being expressible. 33.72.
But they are both expressible and inexpressible; it is also described as having sound.
Beyond the universe (viśva) is the Great Universe (mahāviśva); that is said to be soundless (asvara).

From *asvara* comes *mahāsvarasthāna*, and from *kharva* comes *adhigarvita*; these are called the stages leading to the peace of excellence by those who have mastered calculation. From *mahādhṛṣṭa* comes *dhṛṣṭa*; that is here called *odaka*.
75. Odakā, Cittavibhrānta, and another supreme place.
Beyond the highest [heaven], the Buddhas do not perceive the realm of lower stages;
indeed, it is impossible for humans to calculate the conception of the world.
Beyond that, it is held that there is no further range of the Buddhas;
indeed, the Buddha-field is said to be as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.

Having analyzed atoms, the Leaders spoke thus: "This is indeed made into an illustration; however, the domain of logical knowledge is established by means of a reason (hetu), whereas substance cannot be [fully] grasped by those who rely on mere calculation. (33.78)

In the past, I attended upon as many perfectly awakened Buddhas as there are atoms in this [universe]. Having propitiated them during this thoughtless eon, I existed for such an infinite length of time as a bodhisattva in former times.
For the sake of sentient beings, the Perfectly Awakened One enters into the state of Buddhahood; in various places, I have spoken tantras and extensive ritual manuals.
This is the supreme ritual manual, the most excellent, which has been spoken by the Buddhas;
this is the authoritative standard, as I, the Ancient One, have been proclaimed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones.
Now, O Kumāra, at this final time of birth,
I have proclaimed as many worldly mantras and beautiful *kalparāja*s as there are.
Supramundane, as well as divine and human— including those of the gods and asuras—
this application of the tantras has been proclaimed for all mantras.
But this king of rituals, of great supernatural power, is approved everywhere;
through the ritual procedure of those [tantras], the venerable Mañjuśrī attains accomplishment.
By this very method and procedure, Mañjubhāṣin,
the accomplishment of all of them has been declared by the Sovereign Lord.
Furthermore, in the world of humans, as well as those other mantra-deities—
whether they be supramundane mantras or mundane ones possessing great supernatural power—
all attain success through this application of ritual according to the King of Rituals (Kalparāja).
The mastery over all mantras has been proclaimed in every ritual manual;
indeed, Mañjuśrī is honored here in this supreme king of manuals.
Whatever worldly arts and sciences there may be, esteemed by the world; the knowledge of signs and omens, marked by the science of astrology;
the practice of interpreting signs, as well as the sounds [of creatures] that are auspicious or inauspicious;
and indeed the cries of all beings, which are characterized by their mental states—[all these he knows].
The element, the sense-field, and the substance... [are] ... || 33.89 ||
They say that bodily gestures and omens, as well as the extraction of minerals and their processing, constitute [these fields];
likewise, arithmetic, grammar, the sciences, weaponry, sequence, and ritual procedure.
The inner science (adhyātmavidyā), medicine—which brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings—and likewise other sciences such as logic and grammar were set forth [by him]. (33.91)

Furthermore, the varieties of meters, the science of music, and the application of perfumes have been proclaimed; these were spoken by me, as a Bodhisattva, for the benefit of sentient beings. (33.92)
Formerly, when I was a bodhisattva, for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings dwelling in this ocean of saṃsāra, I spoke these words to you.
For I have dwelt for a long time in the dense wilderness of saṃsāra;
indeed, I act therein according to the needs of those beings who are to be disciplined.
In whatever way sentient beings indeed undertake beneficial action,
in that very way I establish for them a foundation of auspicious deeds for the sake of their welfare.
Through various karmas, the states of sentient beings serve as sources of benefit;
indeed, their diversity is produced for diverse purposes by those corrupted by the womb.
Just as I have described in this treatise various purposes joined with diverse actions,
so too do I bring about for these beings a manifold perfection of form.
33.98. "I shall likewise assume various guises with diverse limbs, both my own and those of others; out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings, I manifest manifold forms. 33.99.
[I appear as] Maheśvara, Śakra, Brahmā, and the rest, as well as Viṣṇu, Kubera, and Nairṛta."
In that same way, in the past, I created various forms of the planets.
With minds permeated by great compassion, I shall gradually establish those beings, who range within the sphere of their own dispositions, in the auspicious state.
I have wandered through saṃsāra for a long time observing this;
the accomplishment of the welfare of sentient beings has been taught in the form of mantras.
The knowledge of mantras and the ritual manual of mantras have been set forth in due order; for a long time, as I wandered through births, I have remained established in the lineage of the Buddhas.
And yet, there exists for me no one who is either my creator or even my master;
having relied upon the fixed lineage, I have awakened to supreme enlightenment.
I have attained security—ageless, peaceful, sorrowless, stainless, and auspicious;
I have reached extinction and tranquility; I am liberated from the bond of birth.
Now the wheel has been set in motion, resting upon the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). I shall indeed reveal this ritual manual (*kalpa*) for the discourse on mantras in full detail.
The reciter (*jāpī*) must not perform the ritual procedures in vain; [I shall teach] the ritual manual of rites in full detail.

As many worldly mantras and ritual manuals as have been thus proclaimed—106—all of them are to be honored and respected; contempt for them must be avoided. Therefore, the practitioner of mantras should not hold in low esteem their extensive ritual procedures. 33.106.
One should not perform these signs and the application of knowledge proclaimed in the science of astrology in vain; they are declared for the sake of auspiciousness.
Thus, the substances for success and the like, as well as medicinal herbs, pertain to this very life;
since the eye is accompanied by worldly gain, success is therefore called auspicious.
Adorned with the verses of the Jina and verses of auspiciousness,
it was consecrated on excellent and preeminent days of the bright fortnight, clearly marked by favorable signs.
When conjoined with the most auspicious white planets, one should begin the practice of mantra-sādhana.
(110) Such favorable configurations as these should be employed, while one should avoid those that are inauspicious.

(110) This was previously taught by me alone; therefore, it must be accepted by those who recite mantras. (111) Whatever skill in the knowledge of astrology exists among anyone in this world, [it should be understood according to my teaching]. (111)
Or others there who were experts in policy, possessing the causes and reasons thereof,
well-versed in the treatises on logic, and acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
All that has been spoken by me alone is to be grasped by those who recite mantras;
this path, which is the cause of accomplishment, has been shown by the seers of reality.
For everything—the entirety of the established doctrine that is the cause of liberation—has been taught by me.
By means of that alone, one who seeks accomplishment should follow the path of mantras, which are the causes of success.
A practitioner of recitation should not perform the application of mantras in vain, for they are complete in every respect.
All worldly mantras are proclaimed as supreme. || 33.115 ||
One should employ all supramundane and likewise divine [mantras] in every situation;
one should not cause the mind to become false, nor should one ever corrupt the mental faculty therein.
Indeed, all mantras are to be honored; they are proclaimed as those who know the samaya.
In this teaching of the Tathāgata, there is equality for the Buddhas established in the welfare [of beings]. 33.117
The sons of the Victors have been established, drawn in, and caused to enter;
they are declared here as knowers of the *samaya* within the mandala of the Moon-like Sages.
They are never in vain with respect to the mantras, having been brought here with the intention of entering.
119. One should not bow down to the mantras of others, nor should one treat them with contempt;
for those mantras which are indeed ignoble are proclaimed to be fruitless.
However many worldly mantras there are— those arising from recitation that are inferior,
accompanied by afflictions, and ending with the path of vision— they are nonetheless fruitful for those who perform the recitation.

One should not pointlessly direct the mind toward one who is prone to anger or filled with resentment; nor should one offer praise or devotion to such a person, for their actions bear fruit in vain. Indeed, since the mind is dependent on that [anger], one should never yield to it.
But one who is established in reason, focused, and constantly performing the recitation (*japa*) with a single mantra,
obtains the entire fruit exactly as described by the rule of the ritual procedure.
Having made the mind steady, one should recite that single mantra.
123. For one whose mind is single-pointed, the mantras that accomplish all aims are perfected. || 33.123 ||
For one whose mind is distracted and whose self is deluded, success is not seen;
yet, by attaining the complete accomplishment of the fruit, one shall reach the vast state.
"He whose mind is eternally pure, who has faith in the teaching alone, and who is devoted to the Three Jewels—for such a person, the desired accomplishment is proclaimed. (33.125)

From the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, from the 126th Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra, the thirty-third chapter, the detailed exposition on the instruction of the knowledge of signs for the ritual procedures of action, is completed. {S350} {V272} Chapter A34.
Then indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon that abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince.

Listen, Mañjuśrī, to your mudrā-mantra together with its secret, which is most supremely hidden. It must not be revealed to those beings who lack faith, who have no devotion to the teaching of the Tathāgata, who are not authorized by the samaya, who do not act to ensure the non-interruption of the lineage of the Three Jewels; nor to those who are under the influence of evil friends, who have no desire for merit, who are mixed with wicked people, who are possessed by sinful associates, who have become distant from the Buddha-dharmas, who have become fruitless in this eon, who have received no instruction from a master, who have not been consecrated in your most supremely hidden maṇḍala, O Youth, who have not seen the samaya in the family of the Tathāgata, and who are not universal persons—this must not be revealed to any such beings, even if they follow your mantra.
One who lacks faith in the Buddha’s teachings is indeed far removed from awakening;
one should not cause such a person to receive the mudrās, nor should one show them the tantra.

If, out of negligence or deluded by ignorance, one causes [the ritual] to be performed out of greed and so forth, the tantras and mantras will certainly not succeed for such a practitioner who recites them perversely. 34.4
If one should otherwise employ the mudrās and mantras when [the deity] is not present, one will not swiftly attain accomplishment and will even be deprived of one's body. (34.5)

At the proper time, for those who are gentle, whose minds are intent on the śrāddha rite, who perceive reality, and who are engaged in the practice of tantras and mantras, one should reveal the Mudrā-tantra.
One should reveal the mudrās to those who worship the Three Jewels, who have faith in the teaching of the Jina, and who have observed the prescribed applications of the ritual.
One should reveal the mudrā to those who know the ritual of the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*), who are adorned with the awakening mind, and who always abide on the path to enlightenment.
For those who have seen the higher and lower [realities] at the time of application through the tantras and mantras, and who are intent upon great awakening, one should reveal their mudrās.
One should reveal the seal to those who are devoted to those sons of the Jina— the Śrāvakas and the Pratyekabuddhas— for whom there is the fruit visible in this very life.
One should reveal the seal of those who do not conceptualize phenomena, who possess faith, whose stinginess has departed, and who understand the logic of the Teacher’s words.
These have indeed been sealed with the seal; they stand at the measure of one hundred and eight.
Neither more nor less, they were revealed directly by the Buddhas.
In the ritual manual (*kalpa*) of Mañjuśrī, the mantras are indeed equal to that;
one hundred and eight mantras are said to be proclaimed as being of equal status.
Furthermore, one hundred and eight mudrās were taught in the past by the best of sages.
This is the measure for the emergence of mudrās and mantras within a kalpa. It is declared to be the treasury of all Buddhas, the treasury of mantras.
When mudrās are fully endowed with mantras, they are joined together as performers of swift action.
Just as no movement occurs in a chariot without a wheel, likewise no ritual action is performed by any mantra when devoid of its mudrā.
Mantras joined with their corresponding mudrās, being properly united, accomplish their tasks swiftly.
For these [mantras] cause everything to revolve, including the three worlds with their gods and asuras;
how much more so in the world of humans, regarding other conditioned activities?
For the fruit of this is seen in the present life within these mudrās and mantras;
when joined together on both sides, it is shown to be pure when practiced according to the prescribed rite.
The foremost of Jinas, together with their sons, cause the beings to turn back [from suffering];
the mantra, the mudrā, and the austerity likewise abide in three ways within the performance of ritual action.
Just as a practitioner of recitation may obtain the entirety of all desired accomplishments,
so too are the mudrās sealed by the mantras, and the mantras are likewise sealed by the mudrās.
A mantra devoid of mudrā is ineffective, and a mudrā bereft of mantra is likewise powerless;
however, when mudrā and mantra are joined together, they are fully empowered for all ritual actions.
For these are mutually the fruits of one another, arising from mutual fruition. The practitioner should apply the appropriate method; there is no ritual action that cannot be accomplished.
All mantras indeed succeed when joined with the mudrās of those possessing form; for when a mantra is employed according to the prescribed ritual and accompanied by its mudrā,
there is no place where one who has been summoned does not achieve success.
He traverses the world-systems from the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell.
Wherever he has entered, he cannot be drawn back; there is no one who is incurable. There exists no sentient being whatsoever who can turn him back.

Even Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*) are drawn in when the ritual is properly recited. Even Bodhisattvas who have attained the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are unable to break the protective arrangement or to obstruct the accomplishment of the rite. 34.25.
Invincible to all beings, they rely upon mantras and mudrās. For he who among all beings relies upon the mantra and is indeed engaged in the application of mudrās—these are the sources of protection.
The manifestation of all mantras is seen within all mantras;
from the mantra, all mudrās arise, being mutually dependent upon one another. (34.27) The procedure for form and recitation is employed on the path in the rite of fire-offering (homa). (34.28)
Therefore, success born from this is likewise seen in the mantras and mudrās.
For one who recites constantly, being ever-diligent and always established in those [practices], all mantras will indeed be accomplished; for the word of the Munis is never in vain.
Otherwise, they would have made the word of all the Buddhas false.
By those who have performed the ritual according to the principles of mantra and tantra, and who have applied the entire procedure together with the mantras and mudrās; 34.30.
O youth Mañjuśrī, I shall speak this again and again:
the application of all mantras without exception, as well as the mudrās therein, brings about the arising of benefit.
I pay homage to that which, in this King of Ritual Manuals (*kalparāja*), brings about the attainment of the fruit;
it is the most beneficial and most secret *mudrā-tantra* revealed for the world.

Then that glorious and wise youth, patient and possessing a slightly smiling face, was the Kumāra from whom the universe originates; he was a Bodhisattva of great heroism who had attained the ten stages. "O Best of Sages, grant me the Buddha, the kinsman of the sun—this very cause of mantras which has been described in the world, O Blessed One."

"In the past, that was also spoken by the perfectly awakened ones before me; why has it now been fully revealed by the Lion of the Śākyas? This doubt has arisen in me; explain this, O best of sages. (34.35)
The wise one, possessing the voice of a kalaviṅka bird and produced from the thundering of Brahmā,
spoke to the Bodhisattva who was established on the tenth stage.
In the past, as I wandered through many eons in saṃsāra,
I obtained this king of kalpas from the sage named Saṅkusumita.
In various places there, I performed many acts of benefit for sentient beings; having come under the power of compassion, I then made this vow:
"May I indeed become a Buddha, the foremost, during this most degenerate age."
Having indeed performed the turning of the Wheel of Dharma for the sake of the teaching, and when I am about to enter nirvāṇa on earth during this final age,
I shall set forth this King of Ritual Manuals before you.
"When the world has passed into extinction and the land called Jambudvīpa is empty,
when the Teacher has departed and the treasury of Dharma has become distant in the Kali age, this King of Kalpas shall act for the sake of the teaching and for the benefit of sentient beings. (34.40)
This king of rituals, in its full detail, has been entrusted to you alone;
at that time, he will be intent upon the welfare of sentient beings.
At that terrifying time, sentient beings will be most unrighteous;
kings, with wicked minds, will always remain unstable.
Both humans and non-humans alike, all those who hate my teaching,
will destroy my entire treasury of Dharma that I have proclaimed.
This treasury of mantras has been proclaimed for the sake of their discipline.
O youth, this vow of yours [is based on] inconceivable past eons.
As many Buddhas as there have been who have entered nirvāṇa, the kinsmen of the world—
For their instruction, I shall act in every age.
I shall wander everywhere in the form of a young child;
then, at various times, I will discipline sentient beings through the form of mantras.
"O youth, this very vow was indeed made by you in the past;
that has now been attained, O child, and I shall explain it to you."
"In a Buddha-field that is empty and when people are without refuge, you, though appearing as a mantra-form, shall instruct beings as one who is [seemingly] ignorant. (34.48)
You shall lead many beings, being the bestower of all perfections;
you are the granter of boons to all sentient beings at that time, in this most degenerate age.
For when I have passed away and the world has become empty upon the surface of the earth,
you yourself, in the form of a child, shall perform the work of a Buddha.
"Then, in the great and delightful forest arising from the lap of the Himalayas,
on the bank of the river Hiraṇyavatī, my final liberation (nirvāṇa) shall take place."

From the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra, the thirty-fourth chapter, the detailed section on the ritual for the invocation of mudrās as taught in response to the inquiry of Mañjuśrī, is completed. Chapter A35.

Then indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, entered the samādhi called "The Exhortation from the Treasury of the Tathāgata’s Great Seal. Immediately upon the Blessed One Śākyamuni’s entry into that state, a great ray of light issued forth from the circle of hair between his eyebrows (*ūrṇākośa*). That net of rays, accompanied by a retinue numbering many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rays, illuminated countless buddha-fields, exhorted all the Buddhas, and then vanished back into the circle of hair between the Blessed One Śākyamuni’s eyebrows.

Immediately after being thus exhorted, all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, entered the meditative absorption whose nature is space and stationed themselves in the expanse of the sky above the Śuddhāvāsa heaven. Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having honored all the Buddhas, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Listen, Mañjuśrī, to the ritual procedure for the chapter on the treasury of mudrās, which is empowered by all future Buddhas."
Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, paid homage to all the Buddhas, and addressed the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, as follows.

"May the Blessed One graciously explain that chapter on the treasury of the seals of all Tathāgatas, which is most supremely secret, whenever you deem it the right time. That shall be for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of a great multitude of people; it will result in the arising of happiness and the ripening of happiness for gods, humans, and all sentient beings."

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having been requested by the Blessed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, looked upon all the Buddhas, took hold of all sentient beings in his mind, gladdened all the bodhisattvas, pacified all the pratyekabuddhas and noble śrāvakas, incited all those whose minds were intent on the meaning of mantras, warded off all the wicked, comforted all who were afraid, and established all those in misfortune in the secure, auspicious state of nirvāṇa; for the sake of the happiness of all who suffer, he spoke this chapter on the ritual of mudrās.
Listen, O youth Mañjuśrī, I shall speak of the chapter that is sealed [with the mudrās]. First, there is the five-crested [mudrā]; it is considered the Great Mudrā (mahāmudrā). 35.6.
One should know the second to be Triśikha and the third Ekacīraka;
the Fully Awakened Ones, the supreme among bipeds, call the fourth Utpala.
The fifth is seen as Svastika, and the sixth is called Dhvaja.
Those well-adorned with the knowledge of mantras say that the seventh is "Full. || 35.8 ||
The eighth is designated as the staff by the Lords of the World who have conquered their enemies;
the ninth is designated as the parasol, and the tenth is called the spear.
The eleventh, however, the Fully Awakened Ones designate as Sampuṭa;
the twelfth is said to be Phara, and the thirteenth is likewise Gada.
The fourteenth is the sword as specified; likewise, the fifteenth is the bell.
The sixteenth is said to be the noose, and the hook is remembered as the seventeenth.
The eighteenth is the Bhadrapīṭha, while the nineteenth is the Pīṭhaka.
The twentieth is declared to be Mayūrāsana, and the twenty-first is Paṭṭiśa.
The twenty-second is Ekaliṅga, and the twenty-third is Dviliṅga.
Likewise, twenty-four is the *mālā*, and twenty-five is the *dhanus*.
It is declared that twenty-six plus sixty [arrows] are prescribed for the *nārāca* formation;
they say there are twenty-seven when applied to the *samaliṅga* formation.
Likewise, the twenty-eighth is the trident (śūla), and the twenty-ninth is the mallet (mudgara).
They say the thirtieth is the javelin (tomara), while the thirty-first is the tooth (daśana).
The thirty-second is the face, and the thirty-third is said to be the cloth;
likewise, the thirty-fourth is the jar, while the thirty-fifth is the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga).
The *kalaśa* is said to be for thirty-six [units], while for thirty-seven it is the *mauśala*. For thirty-eight it is the *paryaṅka*, and for thirty-nine it is the *paṭaha*. (35.17)
They say that the fortieth is declared to be the Dharma-conch; the forty-first is proclaimed as the Śaṅkalā. 35.18
The second is said to be highly esteemed; the third fulfills one's desires.
The fourth is seen as the Mother, the measured Prajñāpāramitā.

The fully awakened ones, the supreme among bipeds, say that the fifth is the vessel (*pātra*). The sixth is called the archway (*toraṇa*), while the seventh is the beautiful archway (*sutoraṇa*). The eighth is designated as the sound (*ghoṣa*), and the ninth is the sound of recitation (*japa*).
It is said that fifty [beings] are like a drum; however, the Drum of Dharma is superior to them.
They say that when the trunk is raised in three ways, it is the "Elephant" (Gaja), which is the fifty-second;
it should be known as the fifty-fourth, and the mudrā moving therein is called Tadgatacāriṇī.
They say the fifth is the *ketu*, and likewise the sixth is the *āpaśara*;
the seventh is designated as the *paraśu*, and the eighth is the one honored by the world.
Likewise, fifty-five [finger-breadths] should be known as the measure of the *bhiṇḍipāla* in brief;
and sixty [finger-breadths] should be properly joined for the *lāṅgala* in brief.
Sixty-one [years] after that was Padma; sixty-two is called Vajra.
Sixty-three is said in the world to be when the Wheel of Dharma was set in motion.
Likewise, the Puṇḍarīka should be known briefly as having sixty-four [fingers];
one should know that the supreme Varada-mudrā has sixty-five.
Likewise, the sixty-sixth is proclaimed as the Vajra-mudrā of the bride;
similarly, the sixty-seventh is called the Kunta in the world by the wise.
Likewise, one should fashion sixty-eight [fingers] as the vajradaṇḍa;
seventy minus two (sixty-eight) is thus proclaimed as the śataghnī.
Then, one should know that seventy [fingers] is, in brief, the nāvāmudrā.
29. "Seventy-one," they say, is the auspicious celestial palace (vimāna) Mudrāvara. 35.29.
In brief, this chariot is said here to consist of seventy-two [parts];
the bed of the Lords of the World consists of seventy-three in summary.
The seventy-fifth is called Ākhyāta, and likewise the seventy-fourth;
the half-moon and the lute—both of these are declared to be mudrās.
The seventy-sixth in the world is the mudrā Padmālayā;
the seventy-seventh, the most excellent, is the mudrā Kuvalayodbhavā;
and the seventy-eighth is declared to be the mudrā Namaskārā.
|| 35.34 The ninth is the number ninety; both are excellent and auspicious mudrās. {S358} The *sampuṭa* and the *yamala* mudrā constitute the ninety-first number. 35.35 ||
They say that the ninety-first is declared to be the Flower Mudrā (35). The second is the Bracelet Mudrā, while the third always performs the offering of incense (36).
The fourth is the Fragrance Mudrā, and the fifth is known as the Lamp Mudrā (35.36).
One should know the means [of accomplishment] by means of the sixth [case]; the seventh is traditionally taught as the seat.
The eighth is declared to be the invocation, while the ninth is the dismissal.
Likewise, one should know that a hundred plus three is the *mudrā* for all rites;
they say that one hundred plus eight is known as the *mahāmudrā*. 35.38.
The uṣṇīṣa of the Lords of the World is always that of the Cakravartin Guru;
that mudrā is declared first, while the second arises from the white one.
The third is seen as the root mudrā of Mañjughoṣa; the fourth, abiding in the treasury of Dharma, is characterized as the Dharma mudrā.
"The fifth is called 'the Sangha,' and that would also be the Mahāmudrā;
the sixth, however, is the 'Subduer of Beings,' arising from the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats."
The seventh [stage] belongs to the Bodhisattvas, while the tenth belongs to those who have entered [the path]. The seal known as the "Lotus Garland" is understood by the wise to be the Mahāmudrā.
The bestower of boons among all mudrās and mantras, including those of the worldly realm—
of great power, most excellent, the eldest, and worshipped by the three worlds.
One should employ the eighth [mudrā], the mudrā called Tribhuvanālayā.
The number of mudrās taught in this great and arisen tantra is thirty-four.
One hundred and eight is the number prescribed for the seals;
this measure was proclaimed of old by the Fully Awakened Ones on the surface of the earth.
When the Teacher’s instruction has perished, it shall circulate among embodied beings.

First, one places [the hands] upon the palms; then, with both tips resting on the hands, one interlaces and joins the fingers of each other. Then, both hands are joined together, marked by the sign of the five crests.
Thereafter, those fingers are reversed at their tips.
The five-crested mudrā is to be known, as well as the five locks of hair.
This is renowned as the Mahāmudrā, the head of the Bodhisattvas; this seal of great power, when applied, accomplishes all rites.
One should always employ the mantra of Mañjuśrī, or his heart-mantras, or indeed the mantra of Keśinī, or her root-mantra.
Or again, one should apply [this] among all mantras according to the prescribed rule;
one may perform all ritual actions, for this word of the Sage is never in vain.
In that same manner, one should place the two hands together to form a hollowed cup;
therein, with the fingers interlaced, one should form the three-pronged [mudrā].
When both hands have the thumbs shaped like needles and pressed together, and the middle and ring fingers likewise form two interlaced coils in opposite directions.
This should be known as the "Three-Pointed" (*triśikha*), and furthermore as having the form of the triple braid (*tricīrā*).
This is the Mahāmudrā of the wise Mañjughoṣa. (35.53)

One should perform all rites indeed as they are prescribed by rule; one should employ them with all the mantras of Mañjuśrī. For by means of these, the practitioner quickly accomplishes the goals desired in this life. (35.54)
One should likewise form that very same [mudrā] with the hands placed together as a single crest (ekaśikha).
When the middle fingers are joined together, it certainly becomes the "Single Crest" (Ekaśikhā) [mudrā].
This is the Great Mudrā (Mahāmudrā) revealed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones.
The mantras entrusted to Kumāra, as well as others belonging to the worldly realm,
when joined with this [practice], are accomplished and swiftly bring about the fulfillment of one's activities.
By this, the supreme mantras spoken by the Victors are likewise accomplished;
for one quickly achieves all aims through ritual action as prescribed by the rules.
That same [mudrā], with the hands joined and the fingers arranged closely together; 58. both index fingers bent, resembling a needle and the *añjali* gesture; 35.58.
with the pair of thumbs placed [at the base] and the two middle fingers extended.
Having encircled the ring finger, it is declared: "It arises" (utpale).
This is observed to be the root mantra of the Bodhisattva.
Whatever ritual action has been taught in the *Pañcacīraka*, all of that is [contained] in this very [mantra].
One should perform all that quickly; however, one should accomplish it with the *utpala*. This is the boon-granting mudrā, which swiftly brings about enjoyments;
when joined with the root mantra, it will quickly fulfill one's purpose.
One should always keep both hands joined with the palms facing upward;
having formed that very same *sampuṭa* (cavity) with the fingers on all sides,
it is placed so as to have a beautiful form arising in the shape of a *svastika*.
When the middle finger is placed in the middle and the little finger is made equal [to it],
with the pair of thumbs positioned [therein], this mudrā is called the Svastika.
This mudrā, which accomplishes all aims, is employed in rites of pacification (śāntika).
When joined with the six-syllable heart-mantras, it indeed performs all ritual actions.
When those very two hands are joined together with the fingers interlaced, those who have attained the excellence of the knowledge of gestures call it the *pūrṇamudrā*. 35.65
Placing the hands together in the *añjali* gesture with the fingers slightly spread apart from all sides,
the Fully Awakened Ones have declared this to be the "Full Mudrā" for those who recite mantras.
This [mantra], which pacifies everything, when impelled by the root mantra, quickly makes one who is afflicted by suffering and poverty rich in wealth.
Furthermore, those well-versed in worldly knowledge and skillful conduct call this the *apara-mudrā*.
Having positioned both hands in that manner, one rests upon the left index finger. (35.68)
Having placed the right hand upon it with the fingers positioned [therein],
when the index finger and the middle finger are extended, it is called the Banner (dhvaja).
This is known as the *dhvajamudrā* (banner mudrā); when raised, it is the *śakradhāraṇī*.
With this mudrā, one should perform the sequence of rites such as the *bali* offering and the *homa*.
For, impelled by the root mantra, this indeed accomplishes all activities.
Placing the two hands thus, with the fingers joined in a hollowed cup, that shall be the *sampuṭā* mudrā, which destroys all obstacles. (35.71)
One who knows the mantras performs the ritual action in sequence, united with mantra-knowledge;
indeed, mantras seen according to the prescribed rule quickly accomplish one's purpose.
When joined with the mantras of Mañjughoṣa arising from the heart-center,
it performs all activities marked by worldly signs without exception.

Placing the hands exactly thus, with the right hand resting upon the left, one should grasp the right index finger while extending the left index finger; this is known as the *yaṣṭi* mudrā, which wards off Śakra. 35.74.

It pacifies all obstacles, whether terrible or most fearsome. Prescribed for the purpose of slaying all malevolent beings, it shall quickly accomplish the aims of those who recite the mantra when joined with the root mantra. (35.75)

That very same hand, placed [on the head] and raised up in the shape of a staff—having made the right hand thus extended—it is called the "parasol" (chatra). With this mudrā, one should perform self-protection over the head. (35.76)
One should perform protective rites with all mantras;
one may, as desired, conceal the faces of enemies or paralyze them.
Or one may cause wicked beings, including humans, to act according to one's desire;
indeed, all obstacles perish upon seeing the mudrā together with the parasol.
One should form that very same hand-gesture, beautiful with its arranged shape;
the tips of the thumbs joined and extended along the middle fingers.
The ring finger, with its tip bent at the middle joint, while the middle finger remains as before—that very same [mudrā] is designated as Śakti, the warder-off of all malevolent beings.
This protection, which destroys the influence of the *grahas*, was proclaimed by the Lords of the World;
it was deposited by the wrathful King Yamāntaka. It would swiftly produce terrible evil arising from sin in the world—a deed that obstructs life and is shunned by all the Buddhas.
One should not perform such an action as this, which has been forbidden by the supreme ones in the world.

Therefore, one should employ the supreme power (śakti) by means of all-pervading mantras. Whatever worldly mantras there may be, as well as those spoken by the Jinas—one who is well-composed should apply them to this mudrā by means of the power.
Upon seeing the formidable and supreme mudrā, all the Nairṛtas, Piśācas, Tārakas, Pretas, Pūtanas, and the Mātṛs perish.
O Bālāgraha and Virūpākṣa, the torment of children shall cease;
indeed, all wicked ones who perform cruel deeds shall perish.
That very hand is placed [there], arising in the form of a spear;
it has the shape of an inverted casket, with the fingers of both hands interlaced.
The Buddhas, who are free from all enmity, call that very thing the "Casket" (sampuṭa). One should perform the ritual action with this single-syllable mantra;
one should seal all directions—this is called the "Binding of the Directions. (35.87)
This mudrā, the great protection, stands encased in a seal;
indeed, all malevolent beings and whatever other harmful things there may be are destroyed. 35.88.
It protects the entire body and the retinue within its range;
it protects the whole circle wherever the practitioner of recitation always dwells.
No sin whatsoever nor any harm shall befall him;
there will be security, abundance, and health—whence could there be fear of a foreign army? (35.90)
Having joined both hands together, one should make them cross;
placing the right hand below and always keeping the left palm facing upward—
these two hands thus interlaced are called the *pharaṃ* by the Supreme Victors.
It wards off the arising of evil from wicked enemies.
(92) Having been brought forth through syllables joined with prosperity (*ṛddhi*), it is endowed with...
(35.92). {S363} Joined with mantras of a single color, this indeed swiftly accomplishes its purpose; it performs various meaningful rites that eliminate the evils arising from enemies. (35.93)

When applied with the root mantra, it destroys the poison of those who consume it; it also eradicates other defects produced by [magical] applications for embodied beings. This supreme mudrā has been proclaimed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones, the best of bipeds. (35.94)
Placing the two hands together with the fingers joined, one should then form the shape of a mace (gadā), encircled at the base;
it is well-enveloped by the two little fingers placed between the two thumbs.
One should fashion a very beautiful needle-shaped form with six fingers. This mudrā is called the Mace (gada), which destroys all dānavas. 35.96.
Even those Daityas who are evil-minded become gentle-minded upon seeing [the deity];
they are destroyed when the mudrā is raised, or even by the well-worshipped mace.
When employed with the root mantra, it is auspicious and swiftly accomplishes one's purpose;
likewise, it is indicated by the sword-gesture formed by the tips of the ring fingers well-contracted.

In that same way, one should form the two hands with the tips extended and slightly curved; having made them equal in shape to a shallow bowl on all sides with the fingers, the Buddhas know this as the Bell mudrā, which they revealed for the sake of embodied beings.
Then, having joined both hands together and formed them into a hollow casket (*sampuṭa*), one should interlace the middle fingers with one another;

it should be made in the shape of a mandala, and that shall take the form of a noose (*pāśa*). Then, the index fingers are placed upon the middle joints, well-interlaced; this is known as the "Noose" (*pāśa*) mudrā, created by the Buddhas.
However, for the sake of those to be trained, he appeared as a being liberated from most terrible bondage. || 35.101 ||
And whatever malevolent planets there are, and whatever cruel rākṣasas,
when merely impelled, she binds here even with her mother.
Having been told, "Bind! Bind!", she binds even those who possess the power of Śakra; how much more so, then, the flesh-eating, meat-consuming demons in the world of men?
Then, having placed both hands together so that they are equal, one should likewise place the right hand upon the left hand. 35.104
That same [mudrā], with the middle and index fingers shaped like a hook—having pressed the middle phalanx of the middle finger, one should form the index finger into a hook. (35.105)
This goad, empowered by the root mantra and thus impelled,
swiftly causes practitioners of recitation to accomplish whatever deeds they desire in this very life.
One should quickly summon the lords of the gods, beginning with Brahmā and including Śakra. When employed, this excellent and auspicious supreme mudrā performs the drawing-in by means of a hook.
Then, having joined the two hands together so that their forms are inverted like a mass, one should bend the middle and ring fingers resting upon the left hand. (35.108)
The two index fingers and the little fingers [are joined]; both index fingers are directed to the right.
As indicated by the right hand, the middle and ring fingers are bent down. 35.109.
Then, with the hands inverted and placed down, the thumbs are joined together;
that very same gesture is called the Auspicious Seat (Bhadrapīṭha), a most excellent and auspicious mudrā.
This seat of all the Buddhas wards off even the enraged Śakra;
it is joined with all the mantras arising from the families of the foremost Jinas.
Established by all the Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power, it indeed renders the entire world, including the gods, completely motionless.

That very same *bhadrapīṭha* rests upon the middle fingers; with the middle and ring fingers placed above and extended, that is designated as the *pīṭha* by the lions among sages who have conquered their enemies. (35.113)
Then, with both hands thus joined together, one should intertwine the fingers;
thereafter, one should form the needle-like [tip] of the little finger into a braid.
Having contracted [the fingers] from the middle, one should quickly form [the hands] with the span of a lotus petal;
joining the two thumbs together, one should always maintain this steady posture.
This is declared by the Fully Awakened Ones, free from all hatred, to be the *mayūrāsana* (peacock posture). This belongs to the wise Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa.

This mudrā, which is always described by the best of sages as a child’s plaything, possesses great power; it was indeed taught of old by the Self-Existent Ones (*svayambhu*). Impelled by the charming mantra, it performs a variety of rites and destroys the wicked, the flesh-eaters, and the corpse-eaters.
Thus, twenty [mudrās] have been fully explained; beyond these, they were taught by the Perfectly Awakened Ones, the supreme among bipeds, who are the leaders of the world. 35.118
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the origin of the ritual procedure for the mudrās: with hands that are auspicious, pure, stainless, and cleansed by water. (35.119)
Having sipped water mixed with white sandalwood, camphor, saffron, and many other excellent fragrances, which has been dried by the wind; 35.120.
With pure hands, and with ointments and goads that are not dull, one should likewise bind that very mudrā, which is to be venerated, belonging to the Best of Bipeds. 35.121.
Apāyañjaha, Śāla, and Saṅkusumita; Amitābha and Ratnaketu;
Amitāyus, Jñānaviniścaya, Indra, Lokanātha, and Divaṅkara.
And Kṣema, Lokanātha, Sunetra, and Dharmaketu;
the one renowned as Prabhāmālī, the eldest, the most excellent, and the supreme.
Having paid homage to one of these Buddhas, the supreme among bipeds,
and having become pure in a pure place, one should bind the mudrā at the conclusion of the recitation.
But having seen that teacher by whom one is liberated from doubt regarding the meaning, one who is perfected in such conduct should, according to his pleasure, bind the mudrā with the bond. (35.125)
Having thoroughly purified [the site] and made it secluded, one should consecrate the location with mantras;
neither angry, nor impure from food remnants, nor reviled by another.
One should never bind the *mudrā* upon charcoal or in the midst of ashes. At that time, one should not be attached to the wives of others nor to the property of others.
One should not bind the *mudrā* that brings about bliss while standing or lying down;
nor should one do so facing south, nor rising with one's face toward the west.
One should not perform the binding of the mudrās above nor below;
rather, one should do so facing north, or toward the east, or indeed in those various intermediate directions.
The knower of mantras, having recollected the mantra of the Wielder of the Discus (Cakrin), should bind the mudrā.
This method is considered the most excellent among all mudrās for binding. Hereafter, I shall explain the twenty-first mudrā: one should join both hands together, with the fingers interlaced.
Then, one should indicate the middle finger with the fingers as being the needle.

The knower of mantras should always form the *paṭṭiśa* mudrā by placing the tips of the middle fingers upon the little fingers, with the thumbs resting on the curved [fingers] and joined in the shape of a triple needle; thus do the wise know it. (35.132)
This best of mudrās swiftly cuts through the mantras of others;
likewise, it shatters the supreme mudrās employed by wicked beings.
It shall terrify all beings—the grahas, mātṛs, and pūtanas;
it performs a variety of rites and swiftly brings about auspiciousness.
Those mantras which were spoken by Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā himself—the knower of mantras severed them through a rite prescribed by rule.
By means of this very mudrā, joined with the great-souled paṭṭiśa weapon,
and established in the mantra born from the mouth of the Jina.
It performs a variety of actions, such as cutting and piercing; likewise, it utterly destroys that evil [magic] performed by other beings. || 35.137 ||

Then, having curled both hands together with the middle fingers raised, the two hands joined so as to take the form of a linga, and measuring four finger-breadths [in width], is considered the Linga-mudrā. 35.138.
The divine son Maheśvara indeed spoke his own mantra and mudrā in this tantra for the purpose of summoning, as was previously taught by the Sage.
Furthermore, having been summoned during this supreme ritual manual (kalpa), he revealed in full detail the mantras and mudrās of others as well as his own.
Indeed, this excellent and foremost mudrā is proclaimed among worldly ones. (35.140)
Whatever mudrās have been proclaimed by Rudra upon the surface of the earth,
this single-liṅga mudrā is indeed their sovereign and foremost.
By the power of the wise Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa,
he who accomplishes the *hauma* rite has been brought into the maṇḍala.
Whatever evil beings there may be who roam upon the surface of the earth—
the seizing spirits (grahas), flesh-eaters, meat-devourers, mātṛs, and kaṭapūtanas— [all these are subdued].

For the purpose of warding them off when obstacles are created by Rudras, this excellent *mudrā* is indeed taught again for the *bali* rituals at night; through the miraculous power of the Buddha’s empowerment, it accomplishes all rites. (35.144)
Having performed it in that very same manner, it is designated as having two genders.
Likewise, when the *mālā* [mudrā] is formed with the fingers, it is proclaimed as *mālā*.
By contracting that same *mālā* so as to produce the shape of a casket (*sampuṭa*), [it becomes the *sampuṭa* mudrā].
Joining both index fingers together, one should form them like a bow;
pressing the two thumbs within the fist, that is recognized as the bow mudrā (dhanurmudrā). || 35.146 ||

One should form that very same finger [gesture] emerging from the right hand; pressing the left index finger against the joint within the fist is called the *nārāca* mudrā. Now I shall again describe the *samaliṅga*.
Then, having joined both hands together so that they are interlaced and pressed against one another,
those experts in this teaching and ritual manual know that the raised thumb of the right hand constitutes the *samaliṅga* (the equal-liṅga) born from the liṅga. 35.148.

Having joined both hands together with the fingers interlaced, one should join the two index fingers and form the shape of a trident. This is declared to be the "Trident," which subdues those beings who are wicked. (35.149)
Having extended those very hands and formed fists, then again making both thumbs stand upright, it is declared as the *mudgara* [mudrā]. (35.150)
That same *mudgara* [mudrā], slightly moved within the hollowed palms, is called *tomara*;
its tip is the *mudrā* that destroys Śakra. 35.151.

Then, having formed the *utpala* [mudrā] with the ring fingers, it is placed below the two thumbs in the middle, hidden from view. This is called *daṃṣṭra* (the fang); when opened, it is called *vaktra* (the mouth). || 35.152 ||
Having made them equal, then, having placed [the hand] upon the chest from all sides of those fingers, one should cast it to the left; this is called the *paṭa* [mudrā].

Having joined both hands together in a hollowed casket (*sampuṭa*) with the palms beautifully placed, and having interlocked the fingers so that their tips touch one another, one should contract the raised thumbs; this is declared to be the *kumbha-mudrā*.
Then, having joined the fists and again raised the two index fingers, one should form the shape of a *khakhara* and the appearance of a braid (*veṇikā*).
This mudrā is declared to be the *Khakhara*, O Destroyer of Enemies. (35.155)

That very same [mudrā] is called *khakhara*; it is beautiful when slightly bent downward. One should place the thumb [downward]; that is here called the *kalaśa* (vase) [mudrā]. (35.156) Furthermore, having raised [the hand], one should form the union of the index and middle fingers; with the other four fingers, one should form the shape of a pestle (*muśala*). (35.157)
Those endowed with the knowledge of mantras call this mudrā the pestle.
Having placed the middle and ring fingers of both hands downward,
one should always place [the thumb] upon them, encircled from right to left.
Having encircled [the hands], one places the little finger and the index finger upon the two thumbs; the Tathāgatas call this the *paryaṅka* (cross-legged) form of mudrā.

This is known throughout the world as the *paryaṅkamudrā*. When joined with this mudrā, and further conjoined with the mantras spoken by all the Jinas arising from the Vajra and Lotus families, [one attains success].
Employed with these mantras, this [rite] is auspicious and performs all actions.
And those mudrās which have been taught, such as the mallet and others originating from the trident—all these indeed belong to the Wrathful King Yamāntaka here in this teaching.
For these are indeed fierce weapons, manifested for the sake of disciplining sentient beings.
Then, by the power and supernatural might of the Bodhisattva, he performed [these acts];
thus were all the mudrās, such as the Kumbha and others, taught for those wicked ones who are to be disciplined.
That very hand, placed so as to take the form of a drum,
should be bound with all the fingers joined together like a bundle of reeds.
Having formed the *veṇikā* gesture and then placed the thumbs upon the hand, one should position the index finger in the middle and raise its tip;
this is the *paṭaha* mudrā, which is prescribed for warding off evil beings. 35.164.
Then, those very hands are placed together, well-applied as the añjali;
both index fingers are bent, beautiful in the form of a ring. || 35.165 ||

Having placed your thumb downward, both thumbs are bent and enter within the middle cavity; this becomes the beautiful Śaṅkha mudrā. This is indeed proclaimed as the excellent Dharma-Śaṅkha mudrā. || 35.166 ||

Endowed with the mantras spoken by the best of sages, it is effective for all rites. When employed with the root mantra, it performs a variety of actions and utterly destroys all the venomous fangs of serpents.
One should fill a conch shell with water over which the great-attained Kings of Knowledge (vidyārāja) have recited mantras;
by this, any creature who has fainted from poison will quickly become free of poison.
Thus, forty supreme and greatly powerful mudrās have been fully explained.
169. Henceforth, I shall explain the arising of the characteristics of the mudrās.
Placing the two hands exactly thus, with the tips of the fingers interlaced, one should further press them together with effort and turn them toward the left;
having positioned them below in every respect, this is declared to be the *śaṅkalā* [mudrā].

This most excellent and supreme mudrā binds all malevolent beings; when joined with these mantras spoken by the foremost of sages, it binds all spirits, planetary deities, mother-goddesses, and those possessed by demonic afflictions.

Having contracted the hands and released that very [mudrā], one should raise the braid. Having bound it according to that same rule, having pressed the middle joints of the thumbs against each other, one should again join the tips of both hands.
Having offered [oblations] facing the fire and being well-joined with the fire-mantra,
one should always invoke the crested Fire-god during fire-rites for the purpose of oblation.
When joined with this mudrā, the bearer [of oblations] is summoned swiftly;
one should dismiss him with this very mantra, using the tips of the index fingers interlaced.
When the thumb is constantly pressed [against the ring finger], one should release the fire-deity;
for this mudrā is highly esteemed as it accomplishes rites involving fire. 35.175.
When one recites the mantras of those who seek the gods,
this mudrā, which is highly esteemed by them and described as being empowered by the Buddhas,
brings about a variety of ritual actions when joined with the supreme mantras. (35.176)
Those very same hands, placed together with the fingers fully extended, should form a loose, rounded hollow by means of the añjali gesture. (35.177)
Then, having fully formed the bud born of the lotus,
one should know that desire to be the mudrā that accomplishes all aims.
This mudrā is excellent and supreme; it was sung by the Tathāgatas of old and has been entrusted to Mañjughoṣa for the sake of desiring the welfare of sentient beings. 35.179

Whatever mental aspiration a sentient being desires for the sake of their own welfare, they shall swiftly and quickly accomplish it through mantras endowed with great supernatural power. This supreme and most excellent mudrā is called "Manoratha" (The Wish-Fulfiller). 35.180. {S371}
This mudrā is excellent and supreme, accomplishing all rites;
it swiftly brings to fulfillment mantras and ritual substances in their full detail.
This [mudrā], radiant as the moon, was set forth by the Moon-like Sage.
The moon is the mantra in the Lotus family; thus, when well-employed, it performs a variety of rites, being born from the white-colored nectar.

Those very two hands, both thoroughly purified, rest upon the fingers. 183. With the six fingers joined together, they take the form of a book; having made them raised and rounded, the little fingers and thumbs are properly aligned. This mudrā is declared to be the excellent Prajñāpāramitā. She is the mother of all Buddhas, employed for the sake of liberation. 35.183. Ap35. She is the mother of all Buddhas, indeed appointed for the purpose of deliverance.
One should indeed accomplish all rites when joined with the purposes of pacification and nourishment.

Placing the two hands thus, with the right hand above the left, one should position them at the region of the navel, forming a hollow like the interior of a *kola* fruit; embracing both hands together in that manner, it is called the *pātra* mudrā.
The vessel is the mother and the mudrās are well-joined with the mantras of the Jinas;
they perform a variety of activities as desired by those skilled in mantras. (35.186)
Raising both hands, one should form that very [mudrā] with the index fingers extended;
the tips of the middle fingers should be slightly bent to form an arch. 35.187.
Having raised those very same [fingers] and joined them at the tips, it is called *sutoraṇa*.
Having bound those very same [fingers] together with one another as specified by the *ghoṣa*,
with the thumbs raised to the highest position, the wise know this to be the *japa-śabda* mudrā.

When the two hands are raised with the tips of the fingers well-curved, and all the fingers are released and spread apart like hair, the wise know that as the *bherī*; when raised, it is called the *dharmabherī*. 35.189.

That very palm [of the hand], with the right one raised and the left one elevated, having placed it below in a well-composed elephant-like form—190—one should make the right middle finger into the shape of a trunk. This is designated as the Elephant Mudrā by those who have gone beyond saṃsāra. 191.
This mudrā, the Great Mudrā (Mahāmudrā), has been revealed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones;
honored by the world, it performs all those various activities without exception. 35.192
Raising the right hand, one should form the gesture of granting fearlessness (abhayamudrā); having grasped it at the wrist with the raised left hand.

Having touched the middle finger with the index finger, and placing the thumb in the middle, resting upon the middle joint—this is called the *varahasta* (best hand) gesture. This most excellent and supreme mudrā was proclaimed by the primordial Buddhas; having bound this mudrā, the reciter bestows fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
When joined with mantras according to the teachings of the sages, it swiftly accomplishes one's purpose.
Those very hands joined together, beautiful in the form of a hollowed casket (sampuṭa), with the middle fingers raised—this is the mudrā known as Tadgatacāriṇī. 35.196.

Having thus encircled that very [object] with the fingers, with the two thumbs positioned on top and placed upon the surface of the joints—this they call the *ketu* mudrā. That same [mudrā], when the tips are raised upward, is designated as the auspicious *kaṃ* mudrā. || 35.197 ||

Both index fingers joined together with their tips interlaced, the thumbs bent at the joints, and the little fingers raised up—this very same [mudrā] is designated as the Axe (paraśu), the mudrā that accomplishes all aims. 35.198.

Having contracted them all again, that mudrā is indeed honored by the world. 199. One should then raise it up so that the tips of the index fingers form a needle; from that comes the bhiṇḍipāla mudrā, which proceeds from the plow and the discus. 35.199.
Having bent the two index fingers, this is the supreme *lāṅgala* mudrā;
thus has the sixty mudrās been described again according to the ritual rule.
All those weapons, when joined with mudrās and impelled by mantras,
[subdue] all the faults created by obstacles, the grahas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and mātṛs;
[and they subdue] all the chief rākṣasas who terrify all children.
It destroys all those mudrās that arise from weapons.
Thus, the characteristics of these sixty mudrās have been fully described.
Hereafter, I shall explain the origin of the ritual procedures for the mudrās.
Placing the two hands together with the fingers raised in the shape of a lotus, and extending all the fingers—this is known as the *padma* (lotus) mudrā. 35.204
This mudrā is known as the excellent one; when it is applied, it originates from the Lotus family (abjakula).
As many mantras as there are in the Lotus family, when joined with them, it brings about auspicious results.

Known as the performer of swift deeds, arising from the empowerment of the Buddha, she accomplishes all mantras whatsoever that originate from the Lotus Family. This lotus mudrā among all mudrās is declared to be the central one. (35.206)
Both hands joined together,
with the index fingers raised and joined with the middle fingers, forming the shape of a [lotus] bud;
having placed the two thumbs there upon the joints of the middle fingers.
That very [vajra] is called the inferior [vajra], while the mudrā is the supreme. || 35.208 ||
As many mantras as there are in the Vajra family, they are sealed by this [mudrā];
when employed according to the prescribed rite, they are quickly accomplished. (35.209)
For one who always accomplishes the task to be achieved through the application of these [mantras], there shall be constant success— whether superior, inferior, or middling—
and indeed all worldly mantras will be accomplished without exception.
Both hands joined together with the middle fingers raised;
having contracted the ring fingers and thumbs, the little fingers rest upon the needle.
Both index fingers are joined together with their tips bent at the middle joints;
the two middle fingers are placed like needles, giving rise to the form of a wheel.
This very Wheel of Dharma, the King of Mudrās, has been proclaimed here;
for it was likewise spoken by the Kings of Dharma that the Wheel of Dharma should be set in motion.
Then the seventh, Moon of Sages, chose the Wheel of Peace; it was joined with the King of Mudrās through the recitation that severs the three impurities.

Those who possess the wheel, as well as the Uṣṇīṣas, Locanā, and the supreme Vidyā; Bhrukuṭī in the Lotus family, Tārā, and Māmakī the wielder of the vajra—these are accomplished when joined with the King of Mudrās, the Wheel of Dharma.
All worldly mantras spoken by Viṣṇu and Īśāna, when seen by the reciter as being severed yet joined with the mudrās, [are effective]. (35.216)
This supreme and most excellent seal, issued from the Dharmadhātu,
indeed performs all activities for sentient beings according to their desires.

This mudrā was proclaimed by the Dharma King for the sake of peace; in this most excellent and supreme ritual manual, it accomplishes all rites. This is the mudrā known as the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra) within the teaching of Mañjughoṣa.
One should employ all the preceding mudrās in rites for pacification;
they are constantly perceived by practitioners as arising from the wheel of Śiva. 35.219.

Then, those same hands, placed together in the form of a hollowed casket (sampuṭa) and raised upward, with the fingers slightly spread and elongated, both beautiful and contracted—this should be known as the Puṇḍarīka mudrā, which accomplishes all aims. (35.220)
Placing that very hand down and releasing it from the fist with the fingers extended,
the palm spread out in the shape of a hand is called the Varada (Boon-granting) mudrā.
Again, having joined both hands together with the fingers on all sides...
Having bound it in the form of a braid, this mudrā is called the "rope. || 35.222 ||
Again, extend that single excellent right hand; one should form the shape of a needle with the middle and index fingers.
With the tips of the fingers slightly contracted and the [other] fingers bent at their joints, one should form the *sthitikā* mudrā there, with the index finger well-placed upon it.
When [the fingers] are joined there, one should place [the thumb] resting on the ring finger joint;
this is the mudrā designated as the "spear" (kunta) by the many leaders of the world.
Placing the two hands exactly thus, with both index fingers pointed,
and having made both [hands] equal like fists, and again with the fingers even—
this very mudrā is designated as the Vajradaṇḍa by the wise.
Having joined the two hands together in the form of a hollowed casket (sampuṭa),

with the fingers placed [within] in the gesture of reverential salutation (añjali) and resting upon one another’s embrace, and having both thumbs rest [upon them], it is called the Śataghni mudrā. || 35.227 ||
Then, having formed both hands so that they are hollowed out all around, one should then form the añjali gesture, resembling the shape of a boat.
This mudrā is known as Bherī by those who seek the welfare of the three worlds;
it delivers sentient beings from the great ocean of saṃsāra.
Then, releasing that very añjali gesture with both palms beautifully displayed,
those who follow the path of the upward-leading beings call this the Vimāna-mudrā.
Contracting the hands in that very manner, it is here called the chariot;
for those who follow the tradition have declared that the chariot is the supreme vehicle for traveling through the three worlds.
He leads all beings who recite mantras to the perfection of mantra; having relied upon the supreme vehicle, they go indeed to that state which has reached the Buddha.
Then, having released those very hands and joined both together once more, one should form the pure *citratala* [mudrā], which arises in the shape of a pedestal (*vedikā*). 35.233.
This supreme and most excellent mudrā is well-honored by the Lords of the World;
it is declared by the Sons of the Victors to be the bed of all Buddhas.

Wherein the past Perfectly Awakened Ones, having relied upon that, attained peace; wherein they were deposited in the realm of *nirvāṇa*, following their ascended intention—that is known as the *mudrā* called "the reclining of the Leader of the World. That very same [gesture], with the hands placed together and the fingers joined evenly, is arranged like a hollow casket; however, the right index finger is [extended].
For one should first make it curved; that is called the half-moon. || 35.236 ||
Having again brought both hands together, with the right thumb held in a fist and all the fingers of the left hand resting against it in a straight alignment,
one should form a fist at the tip of the hand, joined with the right thumb.
With those same right hands joined together and formed into a hollow cup, having extended the little fingers, this is declared to be the vīṇā mudrā. || 35.238 ||
Again, having formed both hands with the fingers spread apart like the sky, both middle fingers are placed between the two thumbs and both index fingers are joined;
this is the Padmālayā mudrā, as taught by the Perfectly Awakened Ones in the world.
O Kuvalayodbhava, when the thumbs are again constantly raised, this mudrā is described in the world by the perfectly awakened ones, the supreme among bipeds. (35.240)
Thus, having made the añjali gesture toward the Teacher of the World who appears in the form of prostration—
this is the mudrā of homage, renowned throughout all worlds.
Having fixed those very hands together in the *yamala* (twin) position, this is the *yamalamudrā*, renowned throughout the three worlds. (35.242)
With the hands slightly raised from the base and the two thumbs firmly pressed together, that shall be the *sampuṭa* mudrā, which destroys sorrow and fatigue. (35.243)
These mudrās have been described as all those arising from weapons; those called "Flower," those of "Reclining," those beginning with "Musical Instruments," and those named after the "Planets.
All of them, when joined with all the mantras as spoken, accomplish every purpose.
Neither the lunar day (tithi), nor the asterism (nakṣatra), nor fasting is prescribed;
yet when combined with mudrās and mantras, they swiftly accomplish all rites.
The wise practitioner of the *jāpa*, endowed with austerity, achieves success by merely reciting;
when the mudrās are employed in conjunction with the mantras, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished. 35.246.

Again, having joined both hands together in the *añjali* gesture with the fingers interlocked, the little fingers, ring fingers, and thumbs placed on the sides are declared to be the incense mudrā (*dhūpa-mudrā*). 247.
35.247 || {S377} By joining the palms as a support, one should slightly bend the two index fingers;
this is the general *bali* mudrā, which was manifested by the Protectors of the World. 35.593 ||
In the middle [of the hands], flowers are to be arranged with various [substances] as available;
this constitutes the offering for all the ritual services (*balikarma*) of the mantras.

(35.253) Having formed the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*) with the right hand, one should grasp the right hand by means of the left hand at the junction of the wrist (*maṇibandhana*). (35.254)
This has been declared to you as the scent-mudrā of all mantras. || 35.254 ||
