With the right hand in a fist, always [placing] those two thumbs and middle fingers; having then formed them in the shape of a needle, it is declared as the lamp mudrā (dīpamudrā). || 35.255 ||
From the ring finger and the thumb, [the beads] are held upon the rosary;
always extending the little finger, with the middle finger behind it, and placing the index finger in a curved position—this is called the *akṣamudrā*. (35.256)
Then, having placed the *garbhāñjali* [mudrā] there, the knower of mantras should recite the mantra as desired upon the rosary; this quickly bestows the boon of accomplishment.
This is always the prescribed method for all mantras that ensures auspiciousness.
With the right hand of the fire-god (Agni), one should form the tip of the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*);
having placed it facing the flame, one should always bend the index finger. (35.258)
Placing the thumb upon the hand and keeping it curved in the middle—this is prescribed as the *āvāhana* (invocation) mudrā for Jātavedas.
The tip of the index finger is bent and the two thumbs are joined together;
this mudrā of dismissal (visarjana) is prescribed for all rites during the fire ritual.
The wise one should perform the fire-offering (homa) rite for all mantras, joined with these mudrās and properly applying the mantra to the fire. 35.261.
The *praṇāmāñjali* (salutation-gesture) has the fingers interlaced on all sides;
one should perform that same gesture inverted, with the two thumbs joined together.
Having drawn back the two index fingers and resting them upon the middle fingers—this is declared the supreme mudrā, to be employed in rites of worship.
One should cause the prostration to the Lord of Mantras among all mantras, the Son of the Jinas;
one should provide the purification of all mantras and the seat.
Even in the absence of flowers, one should apply the mudrās after forming them; for these mantras, when worshipped according to the rule, accomplish all aims.
By means of the binding of mudrās, that which is performed for the sake of worship becomes beautiful. Second is the mental worship, which is just like that which arises from flowers.
This method of worship has been proclaimed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones, the supreme among bipeds.
However, due to the absence of flowers, worship is said to be of two kinds.
For the sake of accomplishing all mantras, one should employ [this] in all rites;
this mudrā, which performs all actions, was taught by all the Buddhas.
Whether on a seat, in bed, while bathing, or during drinking and eating, [one should use it].
In a beautiful place, illuminating, possessing mantras, and serving as the site for constructing a mandala. || 35.269 ||
This is the samaya of all mantras for the sake of empowering practitioners; it has been taught by the Lords of the World as this mudrā that accomplishes all rites.
This complete enumeration of one hundred mudrās has been declared according to the rule;
hereafter, I shall explain the mudrās that have attained the state of the eighth.
Then, having placed both hands together once more,
one should likewise position the index fingers so that they are joined with the tips of the middle fingers.

Below the nail, at the third part, they should be made joined together; having encircled the hollow [of the hand], one should make it in the shape of a needle. This is the mudrā of the Great-souled Cakrin, the Lord of Mantras.

These very same [fingers], with the index fingers moved together and the middle fingers level; the ring finger placed upon the tip of the nail and joined—this is indeed the Uṣṇīṣa mudrā proclaimed by the Lords of Jinas.
Placing the two hands together with the middle fingers interlaced and joined by the little fingers—
this is the mudrā arising from Sitā.
Having aligned the middle fingers together and joined the fingertips,
with the hands released [from the previous grip], that which is shaped like a coil is called the Mahāmudrā.

Then, having placed that same [ring-finger] at the tip of the index finger, slightly bent, with three joints [of the middle finger], one should then place it upon the middle needle with the hands joined below. 35.277.
The two thumbs are placed on the third joints of the ring fingers and pressed by the nails;
this is declared to be the excellent mudrā of the wise Mañjughoṣa. (35.278)
Then, those very two hands are placed together in the form of the *añjali* gesture (275). The middle fingers are positioned like the point of a needle and remain bent;
the two thumbs touch the middle finger at the three joints of its phalanges (35.279).
Having formed a needle with the little fingers, [the other fingers] are bent and raised;
this is the excellent and supreme mudrā, which has attained the state of being established in the treasury of Dharma.
That very [mudrā] has the two hands placed together according to the prescribed method;
thus, with all the fingers fully extended, it is held in the form of a sheath.
One should open both hands with the eight fingers covered.
Those who know the reality of the eightfold person, who have entered the fourfold union—that indeed the Perfectly Awakened Ones, the supreme among bipeds, call the Saṅgha. (35.282)
This very mudrā is called the Saṅgha in the abode of existence;
this supreme and most excellent mudrā accomplishes all ritual actions. 35.283.
Having joined both hands together in the form of a hollowed cup (añjali), one should extend a single index finger protruding from the right hand. (35.284)
This very one has been taught by the seers of reality as the pacifier of beings;
this mudrā is proclaimed as supreme, accomplishing the purpose of all rites.
That same [mudrā], with the hands placed together, the tips of the fingers bent down,

held as a single mass in the shape of a casket, with the thumbs raised and extended— this is that *padmamālā* (lotus garland), as taught by the Primordial Buddhas. That same [mudrā], with the hands turned upward, with the fingers on all sides...
With the thumbs and fingers slightly bent like blossoming flowers,
the two thumbs and both index fingers are placed upon the second joints;
this is known as the supreme mudrā by the perfectly awakened ones who dwell in the abode of the thirty-three gods.
These eight seals are the Great Seals; they perform the work of pacification.
Possessing equal radiance and great heroism, they have been fully revealed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones.

Sixty-five koṭis of Buddhas, together with eighty [others] who arose simultaneously—these innumerable supreme sages of the past have indeed revealed these mudrās. It is said that one hundred and eight mudrās arise according to their specific ritual procedures.
With all of these, however, one should accomplish all mantra-rites;
likewise, one shall successfully accomplish all mantras as well as all activities.
This hundred mudrās has been proclaimed by all the Buddhas of great supernatural power; for when applied according to the prescribed rite, these quickly accomplish one's purpose.
Having spoken thus, the foremost of sages, the Lion of the Śākyas, the supreme among men,
endowed with great supernatural power, then chose Mañjughoṣa as a bodhisattva.

This, Mañjuśrī, is the origin of the origin of the mudrās in the *Mañjuśrī-kalpa*. It has been entrusted by you yourself for the sake of protection within the teaching on this earth when the end of the age has arrived, even after I have entered final nirvāṇa.

For the sake of protection within my teaching, all this has been told by me: the characteristics of the mudrās have been declared, as well as the mantras in full detail; the secret of all the worlds and the hidden mystery have also been proclaimed. This has been extensively expanded with a wealth of virtues in this king of manuals, this sūtra.
And in many ways, there is the arising of the qualities, descriptions, and collections of the mantras.
The application of mantras in many ways and the application of tantras are thus brought forth;
[it explains] the power, qualities, and established tenets, as well as the causal origin for those who recite [mantras].
For it has been taught that the auspicious results arising from these are the destinies and wombs of sentient beings;
O Youth, they are applied as the causes for the accomplishment of your mantras.
Thus addressed, the youth Mañjuśrī, dwelling in the sky,
bowed his head to the Perfectly Awakened One, the Lord of the World, the Light-Maker.
Sighing deeply and drenched with compassion, he then wept aloud again;
having asked leave of the Giver of Boons, he stood once more near the Buddha.
When the Blessed One has passed away from the world, and the treasury of mantras has perished upon the earth, how will there be a noble destiny for sentient beings? (35.301)
Thus addressed, the Perfectly Awakened One then spoke to Mañjughoṣa:
"Listen, child Mañjuśrī, O youth, if you have a question."

For when I have passed away, when the world has become empty and the surface of the earth is desolate, and when the treasury of the Dharma has perished along with the disciples who have long since entered nirvāṇa— (35.302)
Having fashioned an image of the Teacher, Bimbisāra, that best of bipeds,
performed worship with due honor using incense, perfumes, and ointments.
Having prepared various offerings consisting of diverse excellent garments and other ornaments such as jeweled earrings, along with various kinds of foods and edibles,
he presented them to the one who can assume any form at will, who is endowed with manifold forms.
In that same way, having repeated the mantra, he brought about an auspicious rebirth among the wombs of sentient beings in an excellent city for the sake of a supreme state of existence;
finally, established in the inclination toward awakening, he attained peace in his last life.
Thus addressed by the Perfectly Awakened One, Mañjuśrī was pleased;
then that wise Bodhisattva of great supernatural power rejoiced.
All this was sung of old by him who dwells above the Śuddhāvāsa heaven;
in the presence of the Buddhas, the Buddha, the turner of the wheel of Dharma, then chose the wheel of mantras that has continued for a long time. Thus it is said.
Thus concludes the thirty-fifth chapter, the detailed exposition on the ritual of mudrās, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
{S382} {V298} Chapter A36.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Mañjuśrī, there exists your most supreme secret, the characteristic of the mudrās together with the root-mudrā and its retinue, which is to be employed in all rites, bestows all success, is fruitful, conforms to all mantras, and accomplishes the purpose of all activities; in brief, listen, Mañjuśrī! (36.1)

First of all, with the hands extended in the *prasṛta-añjali* gesture, the index, ring, and middle fingers are inserted individually into the middle joints [of their respective counterparts]. This, Mañjuśrī, is your root mudrā, renowned as being effective for all rites. 36.2.

In the same way, having restrained the two hands, with the ring fingers joined, the index and middle fingers likewise [joined], and the thumb placed upon the top of the little finger with its lines pointing upward—this, Mañjuśrī, is declared to be another facial mudrā of yours. 36.3.

Having formed a fist with the fingers interlocked, releasing the middle fingers and making them like a needle, one should place the pair of index fingers, bent at their sides, at the ends. Mañjuśrī, this is your mudrā; it is the fang. 36.4.

Regarding the mudrā: one should place the pair of thumbs on the two sides. This mudrā is you, Mañjuśrī, in person. In that place, within those joined palms, you abide through your commitment (samaya) by means of your presence. 36.5
With the fingers and fists joined together, having released the index fingers and placed the pair of thumbs in the middle—this, O Mañjuśrī, is that other mudrā of yours, the Cīraka-mudrā.

Having made the fingers extended with the palms joined, and placing the index finger between the ring and middle fingers with their tips meeting—this other mudrā, O Mañjuśrī, is declared to be you yourself, the Root Mudrā. (36.7)
Having extended the index finger of this very same mudrā, this, O Mañjuśrī, becomes your Eye Mudrā. || 36.8 ||

With the little and ring fingers joined like a braid held within the hollow of the palms, the middle fingers are positioned outside, their tips bent over the index fingers, and the tips of the thumbs touching [the sides of the middle fingers]. This other face-mudrā of yours, Mañjuśrī, is effective for all rites. 36.9

In this manner, by this sequence, one should release each finger one by one, then both [thumbs], and finally all the fingers together with the thumbs; by the joining of the fingers, one should extend them one by one, with the right thumb raised high. O Mañjuśrī, this is your Uṣṇīṣa-mudrā. 36.10.

Mañjuśrī, by contracting the right hand and raising the left, this is your forehead mudrā; upon seeing it, all malevolent grahas flee. {S383} Likewise, [one raises] the ears, neck, arms, heart, hands, throat, waist, navel, thighs, shanks, feet, eyes, face, and tongue. Thus, with the ten fingers raised in successive order, there is the characteristic of the sequential mudrā; and in this sequential manner, one performs the ritual actions.

By the *vaktramudrā* (mouth-mudrā), there is the binding of the mouth; by the *daṃṣṭramudrā* (fang-mudrā), the release from evil planets; by the *jihvāmudrā* (tongue-mudrā), the warding off of evil speech; and by the *hṛdayamudrā* (heart-mudrā), the destruction of a king’s anger. Furthermore, it serves to destroy the wrath of any other being—whether divine, asura, human, non-human, or those belonging to various other states of existence. In this manner, through this sequence, one performs all rites in every respect.

In this manner, there are incalculable mudrās; and you, Mañjuśrī, perform incalculable activities in every way. Indeed, all activities are contained within all mudrās. These great mudrās were bound by those immeasurable Great Heroes, the Tathāgatas—Great Heroes who have attained the great stages—who are beyond numbering, and who, in the world-transcending succession, are sixty nayutas in number, multiplied by nine, five, thirty-six, and eight. (36.14) {V299}
All [deities] are included within the mudrās, as are all other worldly activities; by means of any one of these mudrās, one should accomplish every purpose.
It should indeed be bound with both hands during the time of practice in the mandala, or again, by one intent upon prior service during fire-offerings and recitations.
Whether seated or standing, the observer of the vow should recite [the mantra] for as long as he desires.
By means of this great protective rite, one may protect oneself or another.
"One should perform all rites at all times within all mudrās. Thus [ends the verse]. 36.17.

Thus concludes the thirty-sixth chapter, the second detailed section on the ritual of mudrās, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
{S412} {V320} Chapter A37:
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī, the Youthful: 37.1.

"Mañjuśrī, in your *Mūlakalpa*, there is yet another mudrā that is most supremely secret. It is approved by all the mudrā-tantra procedures and by all mantras; it is to be employed in conjunction with all mantras. It accomplishes all rites, purifies the path to perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), and destroys the paths of all worldly existence (*bhava*). It is the sustenance for all beings, fulfilling longevity, health, sovereignty, and every aspiration. It fulfills all the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), brings satisfaction to all beings, and makes fruitful the hopes and desires of all beings. It performs all actions, assists in the realization of all mantras, and is accompanied by all mudrās and mantras. Listen, O Youthful Mañjuśrī! (37.2)

First, there is the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa*. With both hands extended and palms joined, place the ring fingers within the center of the palms, nail against nail. The little fingers are concealed by the tips of the thumbs and joined at their points like needles; likewise, the middle fingers have their nails and tips touching at the middle. The index fingers are shaped like needles. This is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) named "The Universal Radiance of the *Uṣṇīṣa*. And here is the mantra: ĀḤ MUḤ HAṂ. 37.3.

Moving those same two index fingers, one should touch nail to nail with needle-like [tips] in the shape of a circle; this is the Great Dharma-Wheel Mudrā, called "the burning away of the thorns of false views and perversions. And here is the mantra: Oṃ dhuna pātaya chinda cakre vajriṇi hūṃ. || 37.4 ||

† Samayiravo †; the index fingers are in the portion † nirgugugulyākātṛkam †. This is the Great Seal named Vajravīrā, the immovable great thunderbolt that devours the afflictions of the earth, the bed of the enemy of the four Māras. And here is the mantra: Oṃ vajrānane hūṃ phaṭ. 37.5.
But when the mudrās and mantras are joined together in all rites, all obstacles are indeed destroyed, just as clouds are by autumn.
Whatever obstacles created by the four Māras, as well as those involving gods and asuras, perish the very moment this supreme *mudrā* is seen. (37.7)
Pointing equally toward the other [hand], with the third finger extended and the tip [of the index] slightly contracted, this auspicious fist is known as the Tathāgati-mudrā.
By means of the three worlds, there is the great mudrā named Mahāmaheśvaragabhastimālinī. And here is the mantra: Oṃ vijaye haḥ. || 37.8 ||

And there is the Tathāgata-muṣṭi-mudrā. Having bound any one of these mudrās with both hands, at the time of practice or during the preliminary service, one should recite [the mantra] once and then chant it as much as desired, whether sitting or standing. In this way, all obstacles and impediments find no opportunity to enter, and accomplishment becomes manifest. 37.9

Having moved those same index fingers so that their tips are joined above the two middle fingers, one forms the Udgatoṣṇīṣa mudrā. And here is the mantra: Oṃ jvalojjvala dīptodgatoṣṇīṣa dhuna dhuna hūṃ. || 37.10 ||

Moving those same index fingers so that they are always touching the tips of the nails of the middle fingers, this mudrā, shaped like a ring with bent ankles, is the White Parasol Uṣṇīṣa. And the mantra for this is: Oṃ ma ma ma ma hūṃ niḥ. || 37.11 ||

Raising those same two index fingers equally further back and joining them with the middle fingers forming a needle, this is the Tejorāśi mudrā. And here is the mantra: Oṃ tathāgatoṣṇīṣa anavalokitamūrdhni tejorāśi hūṃ jvala jvala eka eka dara vidara cchinda bhinda hūṃ hūṃ sphaṭ sphaṭ svāhā. || 37.12 || {V321}

When those same [fingers] have their middle fingers joined at the tips of the index fingers in the shape of a circle, it is the Jayoṣṇīṣa mudrā. And here is the mantra: Oṃ jayoṣṇīṣa jvala jvala bandha bandha dama dama ṅraṃ ṅraṃ ṅraṃ haḥ hana hūṃ. This is the Jayoṣṇīṣa mantra. 37.13.

Moving the tips of those same index fingers so that they touch the third part above the nail of the middle-finger needles, this is the Cakravartin mudrā. Oṃ namaḥ | To the invincible Tathāgata-Uṣṇīṣa, the Cakravartin on the Unbeheld Summit: Hūṃ! Blaze, blaze! Burn, burn! Shake, shake! Tremble! Terrify! Slay! Destroy! Strike, strike! Aṃ aṃ aḥ aḥ kaḥ kaḥ! Proṃkhini proṃkhini! Kuṇḍalini! Wielder of the Invincible Weapon! Hūṃ phaṭ! Cakravartin! 37.14

Moving the tips of those very index fingers so that they are joined at the third part below the nail of the middle finger-tips is the mudrā of the Universal Monarch (cakravartin) of the Lord of Mantras. Moving the tips of those very index fingers so that they are joined below the nail of the [middle] finger-tips is the mudrā of the Lord of Mantras. || 37.15 ||

Moving those same tips of the index fingers so that they touch the space between the nail and the joint of the middle finger’s phalanx constitutes the mudrā for a Great Cakravartin. Moving those same tips of the index fingers so that they touch the third phalanx of the middle finger from below in a circular (kuṇḍala) shape constitutes the mudrā for a Great Cakravartin. Moving those same tips of the index fingers so that they touch the space between the joints of the third phalanx of the middle finger constitutes the mudrā for the Great Cakravartin who is the Lord of Mantras. 37.16.

Those same index fingers, with the ankles bent at the third joint, joined beneath the middle phalanges by the middle needle-like finger at its third joint—this is the heart mudrā of Aparājita-uṣṇīṣa-cakravartin. And here is the mantra: Oṃ aparājita dhik. By means of this same uṣṇīṣa-root mudrā, or by one of the others, when arranged with the appropriate ritual offerings, one should perform all rites. 37.17.

37.24. With the tips of the thumbs moving, one should stroke the ring fingers and perform the invocation (*āvāhana*). And here is the mantra for this: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya | ehi ehi bhagavan dharmarāja | pratīccheyam arghyaṃ gandhaṃ puṣpaṃ dhūpaṃ balyaṃ dīpaṃ ca | māṃ cābhirakṣa | apratihatabalaparākramāya svāhā*. The invocation is performed with white flowers. One should offer the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and the seat; then, while seated upon that seat, one should bind [the directions] in this very manner in the cardinal points, the intermediate directions, below, and above. 37.18.

One should wipe those very ring fingers with the tips of the thumbs and then bend them toward the middle joint; having touched [the face], one should lift them up. With the *visarjana-arghya* (offering for dismissal), one should rotate [the hands] counter-clockwise (*apasavya*) for one’s own deity. Thus, the *mudrās* for binding the directions become released. And here is the mantra: *Namo ’pratihatoṣṇīṣāya gaccha gaccha bhagavan dharmarāja pratīccha mayārghyaṃ gandhaṃ puṣpaṃ dhūpaṃ māṃ ca rakṣa | Apratihatabalaparākramāya svāhā.* [This is performed] with the *mudrā*, the mantra, and the *visarjana-arghya*. 37.19.

Those same two index fingers are joined at the third joint below the needle-like middle fingers. The thumbs and little fingers are pressed together, forming fists; the middle fingers remain like needles. And here is the mantra: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya oṃ oṃ hrauṃ bandha hūṃ phaṭ*. This mudrā and mantra of the Apratihatoṣṇīṣa Tejorāśi are employed for all bindings and so forth; it is effective for all rites. || 37.20 ||

Those same two index fingers, with their tips bent and slightly touching the third joint of the middle-finger needle, form the *vikaraṇoṣṇīṣa* mudrā. And here is the mantra: *namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya vikaraṇa dhuna dhuna hūṃ*. This *vikaraṇoṣṇīṣa*, the great king of vidyās belonging to the Blessed Lord, the Master of Vidyās, is employed in all rites within the *Uṣṇīṣa-tantra*: for the destruction of all obstacles and *vināyakas*, for consecrations, self-protection, the binding of the directions, the binding of the maṇḍala, and so forth. (37.21) {S415}

Those same two index fingers, with their tips opened and slightly bent, moved and drawn back, perform the invocation of Agni; subsequently, one performs the oblation (*homa*). This very same gesture, with the index fingers cast apart, is the dismissal. It is the *Jvālāmālinoṣṇīṣa* mudrā, unimpeded in all rites. And here is the mantra: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya ehy ehi tejomāline agnaye svāhā*. (37.22)

Those same two index fingers, with their tips bent, are joined at the third joint of the middle finger—between the joints of the middle finger—in the *Balotkaṭoṣṇīṣa* mudrā. And here is the mantra for this: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya | imaṃ gandhaṃ puṣpaṃ dhūpaṃ baliṃ dīpaṃ ca pratīccha hara hara sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite dharmarājāpratihātāya svāhā*. This is the mantra for the incense and other offerings. 37.23.

With the ring fingers inverted and the index fingers joined at the third joint of the thumbs, shaped like a needle—this is the Vajratejoṣṇīṣa mudrā. By means of this, one should effect the subjugation of all unimpeded Vināyakas, as well as their companions, directions, and times. Thus, with these mantras and mudrās, protection should be performed during recitation, during the practice of sādhana, and within the maṇḍala; all rites are to be carried out in this manner. And the mantra for this is: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya sarvavighnavidhvaṃsanakarāya troṭaya svāhā.* (37.24)

With the two ring fingers at the base of the thumbs in the shape of a coil, and likewise with the two index fingers in the shape of a needle—this is the *Aparājitoṣṇīṣa-mudrā*, which is everywhere unimpeded. And here is the mantra: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya sarvatrāparājitāya samaye śānte dānte dharmarājabhāṣite mahāvidye sarvārthasādhani svāhā.* One should perform rites for pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*) during oblations of ghee and the like. 37.25.

When the two ring fingers are bent at their tips against the two index fingers, this is the *apratihatoṣṇīṣa-mudrā*. And here is the mantra: *namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣa | oṃ śaṅkare svāhā*. It provides protection in all rites. 37.26.

The tips of the two thumbs are pressed against the third joints of the two ring fingers; likewise, the two index fingers form a needle. This is the Vajrāpratihatasamaya-uṣṇīṣa-mudrā, which is common to all samayas. And here is the mantra: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya | Oṃ śaṅkare samayaṃ svāhā* || 37.27 ||

The two thumbs at the tips [of the hands], the two index fingers bent at their tips and pressed against the middle joint of the ring fingers, joined with the needle-like middle fingers at the middle joint—this is the Unobstructed Great Samaya Uṣṇīṣa Mudrā. It is employed among gods and asuras when established in the samaya. And here is the mantra: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya | Oṃ śaṅkare mahāsamayaṃ svāhā* || 37.28 ||

Having performed the binding of the maṇḍala with this [mantra], one should recite: "O Cakravartin, abide, abide at my command! One thus overcomes other Cakravartins. Performing the recitation in that very place, one can, without obstruction, effect the mutual destruction of the power of the spells (vidyā) and the strength of all mundane and supramundane mantras among all those who recite in a single location. Such are the Uṣṇīṣa Kings; they are innumerable. The entire Tathāgata family should be treated in detail in this manner.

For here, Mañjuśrī, in this King of Rituals (Kalparāja), there are immeasurable mantras and likewise various forms of mudrās. I shall speak of them in brief; for if I were to explain them in detail, it would be impossible for all humans and non-humans to grasp or retain them, even in a period of time measuring a thousand kalpas. Therefore, Mañjuśrī, I will speak in brief. Comprehend this in summary. 37.30.
The supreme mudrā of the Sage of the Heart is taught here;
after that, indeed, is the mudrā of the Universal Monarch, the God beyond gods,
the wise Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvaracandra.
Then the mudrā of Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the yakṣas, is proclaimed. || 37.32 ||

Then, [he taught] all the other great mudrās of immeasurable power, as well as the entire host of male and female messengers (dūta-dūtī), and likewise the supreme male and female servants (ceṭa-ceṭī).
Yakṣas and yakṣīs, as well as gods and other nāgas and nāgīs, and the male servants and female servants, as well as the piśācas and piśācīs.
[He saw] the great supernatural powers of the rākṣasīs, as well as those of other celestial women, the wives of the daityas, and all the siddhas and vidyādharas. || 37.35 ||
The mudrās have been taught individually for all non-human beings, as well as for all human beings, and for all those born within the three realms of existence. (36) 37.36.
The mantras, moreover, are of various forms and are effective for diverse ritual actions;
in royal families and among the Maṇi clans as well, their mudrās are each distinct.
37. For the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, both seals bring about auspiciousness.
38. For all the Bodhisattvas established on the ten stages, {S417} the seal and the heart-mantra are each proclaimed individually.
And also in the divine Yakṣa clan, which is honored by ṛṣis and gandharvas.
In the seventh family, it is taught that the mudrā is based on the Gandharvas; likewise, in the eighth family, the mudrā is proclaimed from the families.
O Sugata, all the mudrās have been fully explained, as well as those that are other [than these],
both among the worldly mantras and within the teachings of the Sugata, each belonging to its respective mantra.
A mantra accompanied by a mudrā becomes radiant in ritual actions;
the Vināyakas do not follow after one who is skilled in the casting of mudrās and other such techniques. (37.42)
Now, furthermore, there is the definition of these [mudrās], beginning with the Mahāmudrā. It is the definition of the heart-mudrā of the Blessed Buddhas. 37.43.

With both hands, having interlaced the fingers with one another, one should show the two thumbs; this is the heart-mudrā of the Tathāgatas. This same [mudrā], when the right thumb is shown individually, becomes the mudrā of Padmadhara. Having first formed a fist with the left hand, one releases the pair of middle fingers and extends them together into the shape of a vajra; this is the mudrā of Vajradhara. 37.44.

Having bent down a single finger, this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Gandhahastin. Raising it once again, one should form a circular shape; this is the mudrā of Gajagandha. One should bend a single joint on both [fingers]; this is the mudrā for the Maṇi family. For all those who move within the Maṇi realm, such as Jambhala, Jalendra, and others, one should employ them with their respective mantras. (37.45)
The two index fingers, with two joints, bent and joined with their nails touching one another—this is the mudrā for the Yakṣa family, for the great-attained Yakṣas beginning with Pañcika.

One should hold the thumbs with their nails joined over the [other] nails. Likewise, having positioned the hands as before, one should raise the pair of middle fingers and form them into the shape of a needle; this is the mudrā for all the gods of the divine family, for the celestial dwellers beginning with Akaniṣṭha.
Again, in the same manner, having restrained the hands and formed a fist, one should display the two thumbs. This is the mudrā of the Pratyekabuddhas and the noble Śrāvakas. 37.47.
Thus, among these eight mudrās, the family is encompassed by eight;
however, one single mudrā for all the sons of the Victors shall now be described.
With the palms joined and extended, it is then slightly contracted again.
This is the mudrā described for the most exalted Bodhisattvas:

the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi), the mendicant’s staff (khakkhara), the patched robe (saṅghāṭī), the alms-bowl and monastic garment, and the fangs with the hand in the gesture of fearlessness—these are the seven mudrās of the Sage.
The Sugata stands with the web of light-rays from his eyes, his loving-kindness, and the tuft of hair between his brows; this too is another supreme seal born from the very body of the Victor.
These two groups of seven seals have been remembered by me;
together with those of the Sage’s Heart, twenty are said to have been taught by the Self-Existent Ones and others.
Indeed, these mudrās were previously taught by the primordial Jinas;
they are declared to be the twentyfold retinue of the Cakravartin.
These supreme mudrās and mantras are established according to their respective numbers.

Having raised [the hands] and coiled them, it is the *cintāmaṇi-mudrā*. Holding the fists at the shoulder region on the left and right in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*), it becomes the *khakharaka-mudrā*. With the palms joined facing each other, it is the *saṅghāṭī-mudrā*. || 37.54 ||

The bowl is held in the hollowed palm; the robe is held in the left hand. Regarding the fang, it is the left thumb raised from the heart mudrā. The hand of fearlessness is inclined in the gesture of granting fearlessness, with the robe hanging down from the left side; such is the hand of fearlessness. 37.55.

In the *sampuṭa* [mudrā], one should place the two middle fingers together, with the two index fingers bent outward and the two thumbs [at their base]. This is the *Buddhalocanā* mudrā. With this same [mudrā], if one bends the joints of the index fingers and brings them together on one side, it is *Buddhamaitrī*. Having formed the *añjali* with the fingers spread apart, one should conceal the index and ring fingers with the three [remaining] fingers like a needle. This is the *Māmakī* mudrā. || 37.56 ||

Having formed the *añjali* gesture, one should join the third joints of the index and middle fingers, bending them outward; the two thumbs should be held separately in the shape of fingers—this is the *Bhogavatī-mudrā*. With the left hand, one should hold the *Vijayā* with the index and middle fingers, while holding a three-finger-width *vajra* at the waist with the right hand.

In this very way, having bound the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of the King of Knowledge (vidyārāja) upon one’s own head with the eight [seals], one should perform all rites. One should scatter flowers at the assembly (samaya) or in the mandala; whether by the previously prescribed method or by this one, one may perform all rites according to one’s desire. The pledges (samaya) are those declared by the knowledge-mantras (vidyāmantra). The powers of the seals (mudrā) reside in the seals being well-impressed. If one should suddenly bind a seal in an improper place, that itself constitutes a breach of his pledge.

That which is the vajra is the trident (śūla); there is no difference between the trident and the vajra. That which is positioned above becomes the mudrā of Vajradhara; that which is below belongs to Maheśvara; and the one in the middle belongs to the preceptor, the guru, those worthy of offerings, and all human beings. 37.59.

When raised with one finger, it is the mudrā for all humans—beings established within the three realms of existence, whether two-footed, four-footed, many-footed, or footless. When raised with two fingers, it is the mudrā for all yakṣas and yakṣiṇīs. When raised with three fingers...
This is the mudrā of all the vidyādharas and vidyādharīs. With the four fingers raised and the palms placed evenly together, this is the mudrā of the women of the gods and asuras.

The two hands placed with palms joined and positioned in an auspicious form constitute the mudrā for all the gods belonging to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). Those same hands [in that position] constitute the mudrā for the gods belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). || 37.61 ||

That very same [mudrā], with the hands formed into hollowed cups and bound into fists, is the mudrā of all beings dwelling in the desire realm, beginning with the Lord of the Desire Realm (Kāmadhātveśvara), including humans, animals, pretas, and those belonging to the world of Yama. || 37.62 ||

That same mudrā, with one finger extended, becomes the mudrā for all male and female piśācas. With two fingers extended, it is for the rākṣasas and rākṣasīs. With three fingers extended, it is for all flesh-eaters such as the kravyādas, the grahas, mātṛs, kūṣmāṇḍas, and so forth; and for all ḍākinīs, vyantaras, and others, together with the kaśmalas. With four fingers contracted, it becomes the mudrā for all kaśmalas. || 37.63 ||

Attraction is performed with mudrās that are drawn in; dismissal is performed with mudrās that are raised upward. One should perform all rites by means of one’s own mind. With these very mudrās, one should employ each respective mantra according to one’s desire. One should not employ the mantras of others, nor should one perform other rites. One should employ whichever mantra pertains to whichever specific rite.
For these mudrās are not to be transgressed, being empowered by all the Buddhas; indeed, no sentient beings whatsoever are able to provoke anger even upon seeing a mudrā.

By transgressing the mudrās, they meet with destruction. From the destruction of the mudrās comes the violation of the *samaya* and the neglect of all vidyās; in the end, those who create obstacles attain an even more intense rebirth in the Raurava or Avīci great hells. However, for those who abide by the *mudrā-samaya*, there is long-lasting and no small measure of happiness, and they are reborn among the great gods; at the conclusion of their course, they will certainly be destined for awakening.

In brief, many kinds of mudrās have been revealed by the primordial Buddhas and by the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power. It is not possible for anyone to reach their limit, nor to calculate their number, nor for all sentient beings to grasp them. (37.67)

In brief, within the family of the Victor, there is a single-syllable Vidyārāja-Cakravartin for the purpose of protection; its mudrā is as follows: {S420} Having first formed fists with both hands, one should release the pair of middle fingers and extend them together. One should bend a single joint on both [fingers]. The pair of index fingers should be bent at two joints and held joined against each other's nails upon the tips of the thumbs. This Cakravartin-mudrā, effective for all rites and the most excellent of all mudrās, has been taught by the Protectors of the World. 37.68.

When conjoined with the previously described One-Syllable Universal Monarch (*ekākṣaracakravartin*), it becomes effective for all rites. When this [mantra] has been accomplished, the entire family of the Tathāgatas and all mundane and supramundane mantras become perfected. By reciting this, all mantras are recited. || 37.69 ||

Furthermore, before this supreme mantra has been enjoined in this King of Rituals (kalparāja), the practitioner must necessarily perform eight thousand recitations (*jāpa*). In this way, all these vidyās become manifest; they swiftly bestow accomplishment and quickly grant boons. One will certainly be destined for awakening.

When joined with the single-syllable heart-mantra of Avalokiteśvara, the mudrā of Padmadhara performs all rites. Alternatively, when joined with the vidyā or mudrā of Pāṇḍaravāsinī, it likewise performs all rites. When joined with the single-syllable heart-mantra of that same Vajradhara, his mudrā likewise performs all rites; or [it may be performed] with the great vidyā of Māmakī. (37.71)

Thus, in the royal family, one should perform all rites with the single-syllable heart-mantra of the Bodhisattva Rājagandha and with its corresponding mudrā. Likewise, in the Jewel family, the Yakṣa family, the divine, and the noble families—herein, all rites are to be performed with their respective single-syllable heart-mantras and their corresponding mudrās. Thus, everywhere, all rites are to be performed with all mudrās and all mantras. One should apply the empowerment of the power of the vidyā-mantras according to the proper method; rites are not to be performed otherwise. 37.72. {V326}

Thus, for the Brāhmaṇa Sahāmpati, the mudrā is with the right hand raised in the gesture of granting auspiciousness (*svasti*). For Maheśvara, it is the *ekaliṅga* mudrā. For Viṣṇu, it is the *cakra* mudrā. For Garuḍa, it is the *añjali* mudrā with the fingers slightly spread and open. Likewise, for the Ṛṣis, it is the mudrā of hands raised in the gesture of pronouncing a curse. Likewise, for the Gandharvas, along with the Suras and Asuras, it is the fist-position with the left thumb placed inside the palm. The mudrā of the Four Maidens is performed with that same mantra. (37.73)

Thus [are] the *mudrās* of Kārttikeya’s spear; thus [are] the *mudrās* of Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Mahoragas, and so forth—of all beings dwelling in the three worlds, included within all states of existence, and dependent upon the realm of sentient beings—and of all beings such as the grahas, mātṛs, kravyādas, kaśmalas, and others. All their *mudrās* have been taught, as well as their mantras, everywhere. When applied in due order and succession, everything comes about from them and not otherwise. (37.74) {S421}

First of all, the practitioner, relying upon the auspicious *mahāmudrā* of the Tathāgata’s gait and the mantras which are its limbs within this King of Rituals (*kalparāja*), [should practice]. O Mañjuśrī, the *utpala-mudrā* belonging to you—namely those of the Noble Samantabhadra, Mahāsthānaprāpta, and Vimalagati—and the *mudrās* of these Bodhisattvas must necessarily be performed by the practitioner. Rising at dawn, pure and situated in a clean place, facing the east and toward the sun, he should bind one of these *mudrās* and cast it upward above his own head. (37.75)

One should recite one of these mantras eight hundred times; one becomes liberated from all diseases, gains long life, and is not overcome by any obstacles. One becomes invincible to all beings, and all mantras become manifest before one. They swiftly bestow accomplishment (*siddhi*), and one becomes empowered by all the Buddhas. One is destined for enlightenment and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta becomes one’s spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) until reaching the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*). And what are those mudrās and mantras? 37.76.

First, the Mahāvīra-mudrā shall be described. Having joined the two hands together in a hollowed gesture (*sampuṭa*), the thumbs and the inner fingers are raised and bent at the third joint like a mountain peak. This is the Mahāvīra-mudrā, proclaimed by all the Tathāgatas. And here is the mantra: *Āḥ vīra hūṃ khaṃ*. When conjoined with this mantra, this mudrā performs all rites. (37.77)

Having joined those same two hands in the hollowed-cup gesture (*sampuṭa*), one should again open them so that the fingers are spread wide on all sides, forming the shape of a vajra. This is the excellent mudrā called *Vikāsinī*, revealed by the primordial Buddhas. And here is the mantra: Oṃ gaganasambhave dīpta dīpta jvālaya jvālaya buddhādhiṣṭhite vikāsaya vikāsaya sarvabuddhān | hūṃ hūṃ vikāsini phaṭ phaṭ svāhā || 37.78 ||

This blossoming mantra, when joined with this mudrā, becomes effective for all rites. It causes those possessed by spirits to speak and causes those seized by spirits, those afflicted by flesh-eating demons (*kravyāda*), those seized by impurities (*kaśmala*), or those unconscious from poison to speak. In whatever manner it is employed, it accomplishes all that accordingly. This vidyā, which briefly accomplishes all aims, when joined with the blossoming mudrā, quickly effects its purpose even if it has not yet been mastered. (37.79)

Having formed a hollowed cup with both hands, one should make the fingers level within. This is the *hṛdayamudrā*. Having consecrated the heart [mantra] seven times over the heart, it should be released. It is the same for all [mudrās]. And here is the mantra: *oṃ godare vīra svāhā*. This is the *Tathāgata-hṛdaya*.

{S422} That same hand-cup, with the fingers interlaced and a hollow space between the tips and middle of all the fingers, is the *uṣṇīṣamudrā*. And here is the mantra: *oṃ droṃ bandha svāhā*. This is effective for all rites. {37.81}

Having formed a fist with the right hand while leaving the thumb free, this is the *khakharaka* mudrā. And here is the mantra: *oṃ dhuna ajitaraṇa hūṃ*. This *khakharaka* mantra is effective for all rites. {V327}

Having joined this very mudrā and placed the left hand holding the robe against the robe, it becomes the *cīvara-mudrā*. And here is the mantra: *Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhitātmacīvara svāhā*. This is the Tathāgata’s robe. By means of this very mudrā, one performs all rites. Having consecrated the robe with this mantra, one should wear it; one becomes fortunate. Great protection is thereby established. All grahas, mātṛs, piśitāśinas, kravyādas, śakaśmalas, and all obstacles flee upon merely being seen. 37.83.

Having interlocked the left thumb with the right little finger and placed them below, supporting them with hollowed palms, this is the bowl mudrā (*pātramudrā*). And here is the mantra: *oṃ lokapālādhiṣṭhita dhara dhāraya mahānubhāva buddhapātra svāhā*. This mantra, when joined with this very mudrā, is effective for all rites. It should be recollected at the time of eating; then no poisons or venomous substances will have power over one. (37.84)

With the two hands joined in fists, the two index fingers are bent at the middle joints. This is the Cintāmaṇi mudrā. And here is the mantra: Oṃ tejo jvala sarvārthasādhaka sidhya sidhya cintāmaṇiratna hūṃ. [This is] the Cintāmaṇiratna. Joined with this very mudrā, it is auspicious and performs all rites. (37.85)

Having consecrated all varieties of ornaments and decorations with this [mantra], one should bind them on oneself; thus a great protection is established. One becomes supremely fortunate. Having adorned oneself and consecrated one's armor with it, one may enter into battle; no weapon shall fall upon one’s body. One becomes invincible to all enemies. One protects one’s own army and overcomes the enemy host. Such and other immeasurable deeds he accomplishes even while not yet fully perfected. 37.86.

Having taken any one of the specific jewels, such as ruby or emerald, and having consecrated it one hundred and eight times with mantras, one should place it at the top of a banner, upon one’s own head, or on the shoulder of an elephant when descending into the front line of battle; it must not be bound [otherwise]. Upon merely seeing it, the enemy army will certainly suffer a rout without even fighting, or it will become utterly paralyzed, or their leader will cause the broken ranks to flee. {S423}

Having formed fists with the fingers interlocked, and having bent the two index fingers at their middle joints—the third phalanges—at the position of the middle fingers, this is the Dharmacakra-mudrā. And the mantra for this is: Oṃ chinda bhinda hana daha dīptacakra hūṃ | Dharmacakra || 37.88 ||

With the left foot extended and the right knee resting on the ground, and with the left hand stretched back while the right hand, making the sound *huṃ*, strikes with force—this is the Aparājitā mudrā. And here is the mantra: *oṃ hulu hulu caṇḍāli mātaṅgi svāhā*. This is the Aparājitā Dharmacakra Aparājita mantra. When joined with these very mudrās, it becomes effective for all rites. In brief, it cuts through all sufferings. In whatever way it is employed, in that way it performs all activities. (37.89)

Placing the hand in the same manner upon the lap of the braid (*veṇī*), with the right hand in the gesture of teaching the Dharma (*dharmadeśanāhasta*), there arises the Tathāgata-Śakti-mudrā. And here is the mantra: *oṃ vijaye mahāśakti durdhari hūṃ phaṭ vijayini phaṭ maṅgale phaṭ*. This is the Tathāgata-Śakti. When joined with this very mudrā, it becomes effective for all rites (*sarvakarmikā*). It paralyzes all obstacles, all malevolent beings, all enemies, and even all gods. Its virtues are limitless; in whatever way it is employed, in that way it accomplishes all activities. (37.90)

In the same manner, with both hands turned upward, the fingers interlaced, and the tips of the two index fingers joined in the shape of a needle, one should place them inverted and facing downward upon the forehead. This is the *ūrṇā-mudrā* of the Blessed Buddhas, revealed by the Primordial Buddhas. And here is the mantra: *Namaḥ sarvatathāgatebhyo ’rhadbhyaḥ samyaksambuddhebhyaḥ | he he bandha bandha tiṣṭha tiṣṭha dhāraya dhāraya nirundha nirundha ūrṇāmaṇi svāhā*. This is the *tathāgatorṇā-mantra*. When conjoined with this very mudrā, it becomes effective for all rites. 37.91.

Having made a tilaka on the forehead with *gorocanā* while reciting the mantra, one may enter into the midst of enemies; one becomes invincible and is not harmed by any wicked beings. Or, one may enter the midst of battle; upon seeing it, one brings about the rout of the enemy army, and not without seeing it. One performs immeasurable deeds, and these have been spoken by immeasurable Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. (37.92)

Having formed a continuous añjali with the fingers mutually interlocked, the two index fingers are bent into the middle of each other, and the two thumbs are likewise [bent]. This is the Tathāgatalocanā mudrā. And here is the mantra: Oṃ ru ru sphuru jvala tiṣṭha siddhalocane sarvārthasādhani svāhā.
This is the Tathāgatalocanā mantra; when joined with this very mudrā, it becomes effective for all rites. || 37.93 ||

Having consecrated one's eyes with mantras, one may enter into the midst of enemies; upon merely being seen, they become free from anger, develop a mind of loving-kindness, desire one's welfare, and attain friendship. Or, at the head of a battle, having consecrated one's eyes, one should gaze upon the enemy army; they will become gentle-minded, incapable of striking back, and will retreat without fighting, even offering assistance. || 37.94 ||

Both hands are likewise formed with the fingers shaped like a book, with their tips joined to one another and held crosswise. This is the *mudrā* of the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). And here is the mantra: *namo bhagavati cārudarśane oṃ tha*. This Blessed Lady, the Perfection of Wisdom, when joined with this very *mudrā*, becomes effective for all rites. 37.95.

By reciting the mantra while touching the heart, one becomes possessed of mindfulness. Reciting it in the midst of wicked enemies, one steals away their minds. Or, in the midst of battle, one causes two-footed or four-footed beings and adversaries to become bewildered, or causes their minds to be distracted. In brief, in whatever way this Blessed Lady is employed, in that very way she accomplishes all rites. In brief, her qualities are limitless, and her ritual application (*kalpa*) is likewise limitless. 37.96.

The mudrās and mantras of the Tathāgatas are infinite. Just as it was stated in the *Saṃnipātaparivarta*, all those retinues of the Tathāgatas—the mudrās and mantras—are to be employed here. Furthermore, there are incalculable [mudrās and mantras] belonging to other [kalpas]; these mudrās and mantras are to be applied in this King of Rituals (*Kalparāja*). 37.97.

Thus, in the Lotus family (*padmakula*), it is accompanied by the lotus mudrā. The mantra is: *oṃ jiḥ jiḥ jināṅgabhṛdbhayabhedine svāhā*. This mantra of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, when joined with the lotus mudrā, is effective for all rites (*sarvakarmika*). By reciting this, the entire Lotus family is recited; by mastering this, the entire Lotus family is mastered. || 37.98 ||

Or one may use the Mahāvidyā of Paṇḍaravāsinī. And the mantra for this is: Oṃ kaṭe vikaṭe nikaṭe kaṭaṅkaṭe kaṭavikaṭakaṭaṅkaṭe svāhā. One should employ it with a mudrā, either with the lotus-mudrā; it becomes effective for all rites. Furthermore, protection must be performed by one who has gone to any cremation ground. 37.99.

In this way, Tārā, Bhrukuṭī, Candrā, and Hayagrīva—as described in the chapter on the Assembly of the Vidyārājas—all these and the entire immeasurable Lotus Family (Padmakula) should be employed with their mudrās, mantras, and extensive ritual manuals. || 37.100 ||

Thus, in the Vajra family, there is the mantra accompanied by the double-vajra mudrā. And here the mantra is: HŪṂ. This is the direct [mantra] of Vajrapāṇi; when this has been accomplished, the entire Vajra family becomes accomplished. By reciting this, everything is recited. When joined with the previously described double-vajra mudrā, it performs all rites according to the practitioner’s will—even those that are contrary to the supreme Victors—by virtue of the necessity of disciplining sentient beings. This great yakṣa is exceedingly fierce. 37.101.

By means of the great vidyā Māmakī or Kulaṃdhārī, one performs all rites. And here is the mantra: Oṃ kulaṃdhari bandha bandha hūṃ phaṭ. This great vidyā named Māmakī, which accomplishes all rites, has been taught by all the Buddhas. When joined with the previously employed mudrā of the great vidyā Māmakī, it becomes effective for all rites according to the practitioner’s wish. In the introductory chapter previously described, the entire Vajra family, including its retinue of Vajrapāṇi, should be employed here through the combinations of mudrās and mantras. 37.102.

Thus is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Gajagandha in the Elephant Family: Oṃ gajāhvaye hūṃ khacare svāhā. When joined with the previously described mudrā, it is effective for all rites. In this manner, as before, the entire Elephant Family becomes accomplished. 37.103.

Thus is the mantra of Samantabhadra: Oṃ samāsama jinasuta mā vilamba hūṃ phaṭ. The mantra of Mahāsthānaprāpta: Tiṣṭha tiṣṭha mahāsthāne gatabodhaḥ samayam anusmara hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. The mantra of Vimalagati: Oṃ vimale vimale vimalamūrte dhaka dhaka samayam anusmara svāhā. (37.104)

The mantra of Gaganagañja, when conjoined with the mudrā of all bodhisattvas, becomes effective for all rites. Likewise, there are innumerable mudrās and mantras belonging to the countless great bodhisattvas who have attained the ten stages, such as Apāyajaha, Sadāprarudita, Kṣitigarbha, Ratnapāṇi, Maitreya, and others; these are to be employed in this King of Ritual Manuals (Kalparāja). 37.105.

The extensive nature, the superiority over all mundane and supramundane realms, and the detailed exposition of all mundane mantra-mudrās and rituals; the great commitments (mahāsamaya) that have entered into the commitment—these conceptualizations of all rituals are here proclaimed, and all these mantras are to be accomplished here.

In this same way, they should also be applied to the Maṇikula, Yakṣakula, Divyakula, and Āryakula. All mantras and mudrās of all tantras, though residing in the three times, constitute only one family and no other; that is to say, the Tathāgatakula. And you, Mañjuśrī Kumāra, are to be seen as belonging to the Tathāgatakula.

"Understand, Mañjuśrī, that all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as all mundane and supramundane mantras—whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—and all mudrās and conceptualizations have entered the Tathāgata family. Mañjuśrī, there exists no secret of any mudrā-tantra or mantra that has not entered the Tathāgata family and the Tathāgata’s samaya. Mañjuśrī, young man, understand that it has indeed been entered. (37.108)

Because the Tathāgata is declared to be supreme, therefore the family of the Tathāgata is declared to be supreme. In this way, Mañjuśrī, this king of manuals and this jewel that is the foremost of families has been revealed, taught, established, and expounded by the Buddhas of the past. 37.109.

The Blessed One [has] proclaimed it by the Blessed One Saṃkusumitarāja, the Blessed One Śālarājendra, the Blessed One Saṃkusumitagandhottamarāja, the Blessed One Ratnaketu, the Blessed One Amitābha, the Blessed One Puṇyābha, Kusumottama, Saṅkusuma, Supuṣpa, Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, and by me, Śākyamuni, now at this time; they have proclaimed it and they shall proclaim it.

Thus it is; this King of Rituals (kalparāja), Mañjuśrī Kumāra, has come down through the succession of Buddhas. It is the foremost jewel of the Tathāgata family, possessing great benefits, certain, and dependent upon the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu). It is not possible to describe its benefits even in a thousand eons, nor can its vast expansion of great qualities be told in detail, whether by all sentient beings or by those like you, to speak of or hear [them], for they are to be experienced in this very life and lead toward awakening in future lives.
Thus, for him, there arises an immeasurable manifestation of the fruit of the expansion of great qualities.

They bring about benefits both in this present life and in future lives. Then the Yakṣa general, enraged at these words of defeat,

"Why was this King of Wrath revealed by the Sons of the Jina in the past? It was for the purpose of disciplining sentient beings, even though it is seemingly devoid of purpose. (50.35)
"The power of the King of Wrath has been proclaimed as it was in the past. Having spoken thus, the Wielder of the Vajra then set down his vajra and stood still.
Then, having laughed, the wise Mañjughoṣa Kumāra, possessing great supernatural power and appearing in the form of a youth, indeed uttered these words: || 50.37 ||
Do not be corrupted, O great yakṣa Vajrapāṇi of great supernatural power!
For this King of Wrath of great supernatural power has indeed been revealed by me. 50.38
I shall give you the mantra; reveal it as you wish.
It is not possible for you to fully describe the power of anger.
Indeed, this [being] residing within the body is perceived here by you alone;
it has been drawn toward you by him, if you ask about your heart.
O Lord, it is indeed impossible to turn back one who is possessed by anger here;
therefore, having abandoned your own rule, please permit me to manifest as I wish.

[The mantra] is always abandoned by all the supreme mantras in one who does not bathe, who is fast asleep, who indulges in vulgar conduct, who has anointed himself with oil, who is unprotected, or whose mind is wicked;
and [it is abandoned] in those who lack faith in the teaching.

Likewise, a mortal who is full of doubt, one who is faithless toward those in a state of suffering, one who rejects the Sangha of the jewel of the True Dharma, and one who is unconcentrated; one who belongs to the naked sect, who is always impure with leftovers, and whose conduct and sphere of activity are unclean—[these are the ones who do not see the Buddha].
For [he who is] unprotected, devoid of mantra, constantly impure, and merciless, [should not enter] the dwellings of the gods, the shrines, or the courtyards and mandalas of monasteries. 45.45.
There, those who delight in sexual intercourse will have their [attainment] destroyed by anger;
they have fallen from the samaya, are devoid of faith, and are ignorant of the application of mantras.
Their gait and conduct may falter due to intoxication, and anger may fall upon them;
among all humans in the world, heedfulness is not found.
Those who delight in negligence and fail to guard against the breach of their commitments are slain by the King of Wrath, even if they have not been employed as practitioners of mantra. 50.48.
In every way, all fools are subject to the power of negligence,
with the exception of those free from passion— the Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and Śrāvakas.
"Indeed, all are to be slain and punished in every way by the King of Wrath.
Thus was it said, O Mañjuśrī, by one whose mind was permeated with compassion.
"The conduct of the Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power is inconceivable. Having spoken thus, they all then remained silent.
Then the glorious Vajradhara again grasped the vajra;
having taken up the vajra, he was satisfied and, having received permission, spoke thus. (50.52)

Thus concludes the fiftieth chapter, the detailed exposition on the rules for the majesty of the mantras and the description of Yamāntaka, the Wrathful King, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Chapter A51.

Then Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Guhyakas, having surveyed the entire great circle of the assembly, addressed all those hosts of beings seated above the Pure Abodes: ap51.1 Then indeed Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Guhyakas, having looked upon the entire great circle of the assembly, addressed all those hosts of beings seated above the Pure Abodes.

Listen, worthy sirs, to the procedure for the cloth-painting (paṭavidhāna) at the outset, as spoken by the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī—[the rite] of Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, who possesses immeasurable strength and prowess, the tamer of the untamable, the ender of Vaivasvata’s life, and who is intent upon the subjugation of wicked beings. 51.2.
Neither a specific lunar day nor a constellation is prescribed, nor is fasting enjoined;
when fear of enemies has arisen, one should have this painting executed.
Having taken [it] on the fourteenth or eighth lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kṛṣṇa,
one should obtain a corpse in a cremation ground and the garment of a Brāhmaṇa.
Having taken it, one should then dye it with blood during the night;
thereafter, one should thoroughly wash it with water and dry it well.
One should have a cruel, fierce, and angry figure painted in a terrifying place; in a cremation ground during the dark fortnight, one should complete it in just three nights.
On the eighth and fourteenth nights, illuminated by lamps of human fat, the painter remained there, always facing the south.
When seated upon a human skull, having performed the protection ritual and being composed in meditation,
the mantra-practitioner himself should draw [the mandala], even if he is afflicted by the suffering and fear of enemies.
When the first watch of the night has begun, there is great fear for enemies; in the second, they are seized by a high fever and the enemy faints.
In the third [case], he releases his life-breaths and passes to the next world;
how could there be peace for him when the mantra-practitioner is displeased? (51.10)
The body of the enemy indeed withers away, and the destruction of his house occurs;
such is the result from painting the cloth of Yamāntaka during a time of great terror.
One should draw the six-faced one with six legs, black in color and pot-bellied;
he wears a garland of skulls, is wrathful, and is clothed in a tiger skin.
{S553} He brandishes various terrible weapons, with a staff in his hand, fearsome, with blood-red eyes, full of wrath, and marked by the movement of the three-eyed one. 51.13
With hair standing erect, blazing, and of a smoky hue in some places,
it was as terrible as black collyrium, possessing a luster like a monsoon cloud.
One should depict him resembling the very form of Kṛtānta (the Ender), mounted upon a buffalo, performing cruel deeds, most terrifying, fierce like Rudra,
and a destroyer; indeed, he is the one who seizes the life of Yama himself, rising up as the slayer of sentient beings.
Cruel, exceedingly active, terrifying, and most dreadful.
This supreme wrathful deity, who strikes terror even into fear itself and brings death to all embodied beings, should be drawn with pigments made from one's own blood. 51.17
One should write with bright substances mixed with great quantities of animal fat and cow products,
using skull-bowls fashioned from human bone.
Provided with wicks made from hair derived from a corpse,
one should then draw [the deity], either fasting oneself or having a painter do so.

One should first cause the excellent cloth [painting] to be adorned with abundant offerings of food and flowers, red garlands, and choice sandalwood; it should be decorated with incense of human flesh and fat, and lamps of fat, at the beginning, the end, and the middle of the worship.
Having had the cloth-painting made clearly visible and having given wealth to the artisan— indeed, even a great price by which he is always satisfied—
one must ensure that his labor is not in vain, and one must also perform virtuous deeds out of great fear.
One should provide him with whatever he desires as the hero’s fee in brief;
the work for the artisan should be fruitful, and one should avoid that which is without reward.
One should employ [the ritual] in such a way that he becomes fully satisfied;
furthermore, great protection must be provided, for otherwise he will indeed die.
The practitioner together with his family perishes; therefore, he should protect himself.
(24) This rite is to be performed by one who has recited the vidyā; it is not said to be for others.
Having made the cloth-painting clearly manifest, or having seen it as desired in the mind, (51.24) {A14v} {S554}
And one should cause all fierce rites that destroy enemies to be performed.
Taking a superior garment, one should go wherever one desires,
even to those of great factions, great kings, or those who are proud of their vast wealth.
[It is for those] with great pride and arrogance, the cruel and those who perform cruel deeds; for those who harm the Three Jewels, the nihilists, and those devoid of mantra;
for those who do not worship mantras, and those who revile its devotees and dependents.
Those who revile the reciters of the *jāpa* and their defeat—against them this application must be performed by means of the ritual action seen in the injunctions. 51.28.
Furthermore, against those who are most unrighteous and who constantly cause suffering to all sentient beings,
one should employ a rite that immediately obstructs their life-force.
Having taken the *ariṣṭa* fruit, leaf, bark, and even the root, [one should proceed].
30. Sour gruel mixed with acid and powdered human bone.
Pungent oil and poison, sour vetasa, and fresh ginger;
black mustard and blood produced from human origin.
Having taken all the necessary materials and placed the cloth in a secluded place,
he should face south while the cloth faces north.

Having prepared a fire-pit as desired with dry wood produced from bitter trees, one should kindle it with branches while remaining composed; then, fully equipped, one should offer into that pit the oblations prescribed by the ritual rules.
Having again invoked the fire with the mantras of the King of Wrath (Krodharāja),
one should then bind the trident-mudrā (śūlamudrā) for all rites here.
One should offer eight thousand oblations into the fire-pit with wrath;
when the first joint [of the year] arrives, there will be the death of a son.
In the second [recitation], his wife, the assembly members, and the leaders will indeed [be affected];
in the third, death will come to him for whose sake that rite was performed.
When the recitation is performed at midnight in the presence of the cloth-painting, [the result follows].
And for the sake of slaying enemies, it follows that very same course.
There will be the collapse of his kingdom and the emergence of strife within his army; fire, great winds, and heavy rains shall arise.
The entire wheel [of his kingdom] is struck down on all sides by the wheel of an enemy;
he is beset by various calamities and overwhelmed by great diseases.
The entire body of that king will surely wither away; of this there is no doubt.
His entire house will be crowded and filled with non-human beings.
He finds no peace upon his bed nor on the surface of the earth;
his home is surrounded by *rākṣasas*, *pretas*, and flesh-eating demons.
Afflicted and deeply distressed by intense sufferings, he fears everywhere;
the great lords and other deities on earth are powerless to protect him.
Brahmā and the other world-protectors, Śakra and the other lords of the thirty-three gods,
all mantras, all deities, and all those born in the mundane worlds.

For one who is wicked, arrogant, and enraged, his life shall end there. When the practitioner recites [the mantra] at midnight or at midday, Yama, the King of Death, appears in person as Vaivasvata in a state of fury.
Having established the cloth-painting on the surface of the earth during the dark fortnight according to one’s desire—
Having performed a great worship and an offering (bali) produced from a cremation ground or a forest.
Likewise, under a solitary tree, at a sacred site (liṅga), on a mountain, in a remote area, or in caves, one should always undertake one's practice alone and without a companion. 51.46.
In the great forest, in a secluded place, in empty temples, in an empty mansion, by a river, or resorting to the shore of the ocean; || 51.47 ||
In that region or its vicinity, whether staying there himself or otherwise, he may always cause rituals to be performed as desired within a range of up to one hundred yojanas.
One should always have these ritual actions performed by a pure person; or else, one who abides in the immeasurable, having gone beyond the limits of space, remains pure.

Regarding the inconceivable domain of mantras: the sphere of mantras is inconceivable. The supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of mantras is inconceivable; the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of those who recite them is inconceivable.
The karmic fruit is seen to be inconceivable, and indeed, it is beyond thought.

Inconceivable is the activity, the domain of supernatural power, and the magnificent manifestation of the great-souled Yamāntaka, King of Wrath. Inconceivable is the accomplishment seen upon this earth for those who recite [his mantra].
All bodhisattvas of great supernatural power are unable to protect [it],
let alone worldly mantras, along with the grahas and those mātṛs.

Īśāna, Viṣṇu, Skanda, and Purandara— even they, along with the Jinas and the sons of the Jinas, were supported by you at the time of the waters. So too were the great-souled Bodhisattvas who abide on the ten stages, as well as the Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, those free from passion, and those of great supernatural power.
They too were unable to maintain the agreement that had been made by them in the past.
I shall speak in brief; listen, you who desire prosperity! No one else is capable of turning back a reciter who is not pleased.
How could there be peace for him here in this world when the supreme mantra is dissatisfied?
Whenever the practitioner of the mantra of the great-souled Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, becomes clear-minded or moistened with compassion,
then he attains peace, fortitude, or the preservation of life.
Apāmārga, picumarda, pungent oil (kaṭutaila), sour gruel (kāñjika), and the five poisons;
human blood, human flesh, salt, and again the three pungents (trikaṭuka);
black mustard (rājika), conch powder, amlavetasa, and fresh ginger.
58. Furthermore, the roots of dhurdhūraka and likewise those of kośātakī; || 51.58 ||
Castor root, barley-alkali, safflower, and thorn-apple;
the root of the Madana tree, garlic, and likewise the Gṛñjanaka;
Palāśa, Śākhoṭaka, onion, along with wine and spirits.
Having made all these equal, one should offer them into the fire in the presence of the cloth-painting.
When eight thousand five hundred [recitations] have been completed, there is the destruction of enemies along with their very roots;
he shall slay all water-dwellers, the courtiers, and the sons and grandsons.

By offering oblations during the second junction of the day, one uproots that [affliction] along with its very root; and when the third junction has arrived, by offering oblations while reciting mantras, [the same is achieved].
There will be famine for him, as well as among the people and the merchant guilds; there will be drought and great pestilence, with the land everywhere swarming with rākṣasas.
Fire, burning, falling stones, thunderbolts, and lightning strikes will occur in that kingdom or region under that ruler.
(51.64) There will likewise be a convergence of many calamities and the arrival of enemy armies; moreover, various and manifold afflictions shall arise in his land. (51.65)
Various forms arise through the destruction of great fortune.
If one offers an oblation of the root of *dhurdhūraka*, madness arises for that person. By constantly offering *kaṭuka*, one is seized by a great burning fever.
By offering extremely sour substances into the fire, a great fever accompanied by cold chills occurs.

For one who dwells within the body of such [a king], there shall arise [misfortune] from wicked kings who are arrogant in their power— those who possess great factions, are strong, cruel, and rely upon vast armies. His life will end in two nights or seven nights.
Whichever deity or lunar mansion (nakṣatra) someone is devoted to, one should write its name;
having fashioned an effigy from the charcoal of a cremation ground and placed it on the ground before the cloth painting,
one should perform the recitation while standing upon its head with one's foot, filled with wrath.
Suddenly, O lord of men, that king is seized by various kinds of sharp pains;
overcome by a great disease, he may even die at that very moment.
He is struck with an axe and becomes maimed once again;
he is devoured by cruel *rākṣasas* born of foul and non-human origins,
as well as by *kravyādas*, *pūtanas*, *piśācas*, *pretas*, and *mātṛs*.
At that very moment, he was also slain by his own servants.
Then the glorious Vajradhara, having spoken thus to the assembly,
paid homage to all the Buddhas and thereafter remained silent and steadfast.
Desiring the welfare of the worlds, he once again released the mantra for all the hosts of yakṣas and for all the yakṣiṇīs from every side.
Then the Bodhisattva, the general of the yakṣas, spoke:
"I shall choose a chapter of yakṣīs that encompasses all rites—
bringing about the summoning of all, the subjugation of all, and the extraction of every thorn."
When a practitioner of mantra is desirous of sexual union, blinded by passion, or of deluded intellect, he cannot be restrained by antidotes or by the commands of the Sugata.
In this beginningless, vast saṃsāra, those who have long been tormented by suffering have been told by the Tathāgatas that their destination is from suffering to even greater suffering.
The celibate student who has conquered his senses attains a beautiful rebirth; what is auspicious and propitious has been taught, and in the end he shall obtain peace.
Having ascended to the equality of the three vehicles, he shall attain final, perfect nirvāṇa.
Those ascetics who are perverted, seized by evil intellect, and blinded by passion,
wander in the five states of existence within the terrible thicket of saṃsāra.

"For the sake of those who are suffering, the enjoyment of sensual pleasures is indeed described. Having been freed from all evils and having turned back from the threefold faults, those who are permeated by the Teacher’s command are liberated from all bonds. (51.79)

The fifty-first chapter, the second detailed exposition on the ritual procedure for the sorcery of the wrathful king Yamāntaka, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, is completed.
{S559} {V437} Chapter A52:

Now, at that very assembly, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati was present and seated. Rising from his seat, he paid homage to all the Buddhas, stood in the midst of the circle of the assembly, circumambulated the Blessed One Śākyamuni three times, and prostrating at his feet, he looked toward Vajrapāṇi, the great general of the yakṣas, and uttered these words: 52.1.

"O Vajrapāṇi, you are exceedingly cruel, in that you proclaim mantra-tantras associated with sensual desires and harmful to all beings. Indeed, O Son of the Conqueror, this is not the way of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas. For the great Bodhisattvas practice the conduct of a Bodhisattva as manifested by great compassion; they have set out with the resolute intention for the welfare and benefit of all beings, yet they do not release themselves from the bonds of existence. || 52.2 ||

Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones do not preach a teaching of the Dharma that harms sentient beings for the sake of all beings; rather, because they are endowed with great compassion, they act with the resolute intention to benefit all sentient beings. 52.3.
Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:

"In this very way, Śāntamati, a bodhisattva should train; in this way should he practice—just as you speak and just as you proclaim, so shall all the Buddhas and the bodhisattvas of great supernatural power, and I myself, explain it according to the ultimate truth."
Relying upon the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), one is liberated at the limit of phenomena (dharmakoṭi); indeed, the inconceivable limit of sentient beings is brought to inconceivable maturity.
The qualities of a Buddha are indeed inconceivable, and their conduct for awakening is inconceivable; for, having regard for the beings to be trained, they perform an inconceivable course of action.
The conduct of the bodhisattvas is proclaimed to be inconceivable;
because of its power, this tantra among all mantras is also inconceivable. (52.7)
The sphere of supernatural power and the greatness of the movement of the great-souled Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, and his mantra are inconceivable and beyond thought.

Śāntamati, the conduct of bodhisattva mahāsattvas, which brings about the accomplishment of the realm of sentient beings, is indeed inconceivable. Śāntamati, a bodhisattva who recites mantras should generate the following thought: "Even if for the sake of this sentient being I should produce much demerit and be reborn in the great hells, let it be so; yet this sentient being shall not produce a greater mass of demerit. May it not be that this sentient being becomes incapable of the three types of enlightenment."

Thus, Śāntamati, a bodhisattva who recites mantras should establish the mind and apply skillful means as well as the rites of *abhicāruka*. In all ritual actions, he should be one who perceives the signs and not one who perceives the unwholesome. Taking the conversion of sentient beings as his objective, he should train himself with a mind permeated by compassion. 52.10.

Moreover, O Son of the Victor, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, realize the non-abandonment of the greatness of the paths of dharma and adharma, the auspicious and the inauspicious, the wholesome and the unwholesome, and the means for training sentient beings; they also realize the non-abandonment of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Indeed, all of them realize the ripening of sentient beings through the means of teaching the Dharma. 52.11.

In the same way, O sons of the Conqueror, we must train ourselves for the sake of disciplining, maturing, and instructing sentient beings. In this regard, O sons of the Conqueror, all of you who are seated here in this great assembly of the maṇḍala should listen with one accord and have faith; you should become seekers of what is wholesome and unwholesome, that is to say, you should become those who delight in the Dharma teachings of the Tathāgata. 52.12 {V438}

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati, having looked toward Vajrapāṇi, the general of the yakṣas, remained silent and sat upon his own seat, reflecting that the qualities of a Buddha are inconceivable, while gazing at the Buddha, the Blessed One.

Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Guhyakas, having gazed upon that entire circle of the assembly, spoke again the ritual manual of the Wrathful King: "Listen, O hosts of gods, and all you multitudes of spirits who dwell within the realm of sentient beings! (52.14)

First, having performed the protection ritual (*rakṣā*) and taken up that cloth-painting (*paṭa*) of the Wrathful King (*krodharāja*), one should go to a secluded place. At a site with a single linga, such as a temple of Maheśvara, one should smear that linga with poison, blood, black mustard seeds (*rājikā*), and sour gruel (*kāñjika*). One should worship it with *picumarda* leaves, make a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) for oneself from human intestines and sinews, and hold a human skull-cup in the right hand.
