Striking [the linga] with the left hand, threatening the linga with the index finger, and overcome by supreme wrath—having been insulted by wicked kings who have treated him with great contempt, or by other rogues, those with great factions, those with great wealth, the extremely fierce, or great leaders—one should close the door. Naked and with hair disheveled, treading upon the linga of Maheśvara with the left foot, one should recite the wrathful mantra until the linga of Maheśvara bursts asunder in the middle. 52.15.

When it splits into two parts, a great *hūṃ* sound is heard; at that time, one must not be afraid. On that very day, whether it be an evil king or anyone else who possesses a great faction and is an enemy, he will be seized by fever at that very moment, or by a non-human spirit.

One is seized by *rākṣasa*s and other such beings. One should recite [the mantra] at that very spot for a moment until, in an instant, the life of the enemy comes to its end in death. If one recites until the end of the night, his entire family perishes. (52.16)

There is another rite as well. At midday, having gone likewise to a temple of Maheśvara, one should worship with nimba leaves, offer incense of *mahāmāṃsa*, and recite the mantra. As soon as the enemy’s house is consumed by fire, the enemy suffers from a great fever and trembling. If he does not abandon the recitation, or if he remains enraged while standing before the *dakṣiṇamūrti* [image], that enemy dies; his lineage is destroyed. Now, for the restoration: having washed the *liṅga* again with water, one should bathe it with very cold milk, and then again with cow’s milk. He becomes healthy once more. (52.17)

There is yet another rite: having kindled a fire with *madanakaṇṭaka* wood at the southern face of the *liṅga* of Maheśvara, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *vaikaṅkata* fuel-sticks smeared with poison, blood, and black mustard seeds. All enemies will be seized by a great disease; they become incapable of all their activities. On the second day, they will be seized by a great fever or a great colic, or by various diseases, or by non-human afflictions leading to death. On the third day, at the three junctions of the day, they will completely abandon their lives. To bring them back, one should offer milk; peace will prevail, and all enemies in all lands will become healthy. 52.18.

In this way, one may perform rites by stepping upon whichever deity among all the gods and all beings a person is devoted to. Having stepped with the left foot upon that [deity’s] constellation-mantra, one should perform the rite—except for the *vidyā* of the Tathāgatas. For all [other deities], one should perform the rite after grasping them by the middle of the big toes; one should never perform it by stepping on them or by leaping over them. One may also perform rites by stepping upon all worldly mantras.

The King of Wrath is indeed accomplished even by mere recitation; he performs all rites. He destroys all mantras, slays all enemies, and causes all magical devices (*yantra*) to fall. In brief, however he is employed—even according to the ritual procedures of all mundane and supramundane mantras—he accomplishes all that. He brings all that to fruition. By mere recitation, he fulfills all hopes. This King of Wrath is accomplished through simple recitation; he bestows the supreme accomplishment. By the mere wish of the mind, he slays the enemy. When joined with the Great Trident Mudrā (*mahāśūlamudrā*), he performs all activities. 52.20. {S562}

There is yet another ritual: having gone to a cremation ground at midday and stayed for one night on a funeral pyre, one should kindle a fire with wood from the cremation ground on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and offer as oblation *rājikā* seeds smeared with poison and blood. Then all the *preta*s arrive making cries of "Hā! Hā! One must not be afraid. Then one should say, "Kill my enemy. Having said, "So be it," they vanish. Then, in a mere moment, even after traveling a thousand *yojanas*, they kill the enemy and destroy his lineage. Such are the rituals they perform. 52.21.

There is another rite as well: in a secluded and clean place, having entered an empty house while clothed in clean garments, one should offer eight thousand oblations of cotton seeds (*karpāsāsthi*). Then, taking that ash with both hands, [one should place it] upon a clean piece of cloth.

One should bind them. Having made two separate small packets and placed them in a casket of earthenware bowls, and having performed great protective rites for oneself, one's materials, and the house, one should go to a great cremation ground. On the night of the fourteenth or the eighth day of the dark fortnight, standing upon a funeral pyre and facing south, holding the casket of earthenware bowls, naked, with hair disheveled, and remaining fearless and enraged, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times. That ash becomes perfected. 52.22.

If some non-human being requests wealth, it should not be given. If he acts with violence, one should recollect the King of Wrath (*krodharāja*). The syllable *hūṃ* should be employed; at that very moment, [the obstacle] perishes. This is the procedure for all obstacles. One should cause the mark of ashes to be held in the left and right hands. 52.23.

Having ensured protection while remaining vigilant, one should return at dawn; having bathed at sunrise, being pure and clothed in clean garments, one should enter one's own home or proceed to whatever place one desires. || 52.24 ||

Then, with the ashes held in the right hand, one should strike the heads of all living beings—humans, bipeds, quadrupeds, along with gods, nāgas, and yakṣas; they become submissive. Or, with the ashes held in the left hand, one should strike the heads of all humans and non-humans, and of all women; they become submissive. || 52.25 ||

If one takes the ashes with the right hand and strikes them on the navel region of men, they become eunuchs; or, if one pulverizes the region of the genitals, they become incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse.

If one sprinkles ashes upon the private parts—the secret region—of whichever woman he is attached to, she becomes incapable of serving another man; her wound is destroyed. Only when she encounters that very same man again does that opening of her wound reappear. Thus, she is rendered unable to engage in sexual misconduct. 52.27.

The same applies to a man. One should sprinkle the male organ with ashes from the right hand; it too becomes incapable of approaching another’s wife. His member remains as if withered. It reappears again only through the power of the giver. Whether it belongs to a woman or a man, it functions or does not function according to the will of the one to whom those ashes were given, or he may act with it as he desires. || 52.28 ||

If they perform it by force, however, worms will appear in the secret parts of those to whom it was given, and being devoured by them, they are deprived of life. Within a month, they become putrid, resembling foul-smelling corpses; men are seized by male diseases such as the great discharge (mahāpradara) and other ailments, and a great swelling arises, by which they meet their end through that very affliction. Or, at the will of the giver, they become incapable of enjoying [sexual pleasure]. Merely by being touched, he causes all of this to happen according to his desire. 52.29.

If one does not obtain physical contact, whether standing within the range of sight or out of sight, or when facing a following wind, one should scatter ashes so that he is slightly dusted by them. Having formed an intention in the mind, the donor should scatter the ashes; whatever he has intended, all those actions he performs, either through another's hand or by his own self. Just as desired, he performs all those actions, and it is never otherwise, nor does it ever prove fruitless. || 52.30 || {V440}
Then, there were various kinds of beds, seats, and so forth, as well as coverlets, robes, and so forth.

One should sprinkle with ashes all the various ornaments, diverse garments, or all the specific implements such as vehicles, carriages, sandals, umbrellas, and so forth; all the vessels and utensils used for the body, such as food, drink, and edibles; and all things including flowers, betel, fruits, perfumes, and incense. The bodies of enemies will become completely infested on all sides with lice, bedbugs, and worms, and they shall be devoured. Stricken by manifold sufferings, they die within seven nights. No physicians nor any gods are able to prevent this; no mantras whatsoever are able to protect them—except for that person by whom [the rite] was bestowed.

Now follows the method for bringing [the patient] back [to life]: having combined liquorice, blue lotus, and white sandalwood, one should grind them with cold water and anoint that body, starting from the head down to the soles of the feet, while reciting the root mantra of Noble Mañjuśrī. He becomes restored to health. 52.32.

There is yet another rite: having gone downwind from women, one should employ this where one desires it against all wicked *ḍākinīs* and arrogant women, but not against others. Standing downwind, one should scatter ashes while visualizing in the mind that all their vulvas and breasts are seized; thus the male organ, beard, body hair, and breasts of even a man appear. In this way, he performs many various and diverse rites, or causes them to be performed by another, or causes them to be performed by whomever pleasure arises—whether by a woman or a man. 52.33.

Or, wherever the cessation of the mind arises, having applied ashes to that [spot], one causes whatever is desired to be done; and one should instruct [the practitioner] regarding the application. In this way, one causes them to be seized by great diseases. Having thought it in the mind, by touching the head, a headache arises; by touching the mouth, an inflammation of the mouth arises. In this sequence, it continues until heartache or stomachache arises in the heart. Likewise, one causes them to be seized by diseases arising from the feet and shanks, such as those involving corrupted blood and other ailments.

In brief, it kills, withers, causes to ripen, attracts, and brings under control. In whatever manner it is employed, it performs all those things accordingly. Whether causing harm or performing acts of attraction and subjugation, it carries out these rites even when situated at a great distance.

Having gone near a very difficult wall and standing downwind, one should cast that very ash while grasping both hands; the rampart, the gateway, and the watchtowers will collapse. A great conflagration shall arise in the residence of the governor, and a rout of the army occurs. He becomes afflicted by great calamities, and having abandoned everything, he either flees or falls into captivity. (52.36)

In the same way, one should cast ashes against the enemy force with the wind at one's back; the great army will be broken, or it will be seized by a great fever of burning. A collapse of the elephants, horses, chariots, banners, and so forth, as well as of the commander-in-chief, will occur, or they will fall into captivity.

In this way, he performs various kinds of rites according to his desire for the destruction of enemies, as well as great protection for himself, for his own army, or for his friends. Then, he effects a counter-measure against all of them from every side. He should offer a thousand oblations of milk before the cloth painting (*paṭa*); they will become healthy and invincible. 52.38.
Now, for one desiring to accomplish the practice of a yakṣiṇī:
Naṭī, Naṭṭā, as well as Bhaṭṭā, and the renowned Revatī;
Tamasundarī, Thālokā, Mekhalā, and also Sumekhalā.
Thus, these eight yakṣiṇīs are the accomplishers of all desires.

The mantra of Naṭikā: Oṃ naṭi mahānaṭi, come, come, O you of divine form, svāhā! The ritual procedure for this is as follows: having drawn her on a wooden board or a cloth, the vidyā should be recited eight thousand times by one subsisting on meat or milk. She should be depicted adorned with all ornaments, dark-complexioned yet radiant, leaning against a tree, wearing a single garment, with loose hair and blood-red eyes, her face slightly smiling as she threatens the practitioner with her right hand, while her left hand clings to a branch of the tree; she is beautiful in every limb and dressed in variegated silk.

In front of that very cloth-painting of the Wrathful King (*krodharāja*), one who is free from mental distraction (*unmanā*) should stand facing north, kindle a fire with *palāśa* wood, and offer eight thousand pellets of *guggulu* resin smeared with curd, honey, and clarified butter at the three junctions of the day for seven days. Then, on the seventh day, having prepared a grand sacrificial offering (*bali*) and lit lamps of clarified butter, one should remain reciting the mantra until midnight. Thereupon, that *yakṣiṇī* herself, having produced a great radiance, will come in her own form.

Having arrived, she asks, "What must I do? Then the practitioner should say, "Become my wife. Having said, "So be it," she vanishes. From that time forth, she becomes his wife; she grants all desires and leads him to her own abode. She bestows an elixir (*rasāyana*) which, when drunk, makes one possess a divine form, rivaling even the great *yakṣas*. If she does not come, he should recite the mantra together with the King of Wrath (*krodharāja*) on the second occasion. She will certainly come; otherwise, he will wither away and die. 52.42.
The mantra for Naṭṭā is: Oṃ naṭṭe, you who wear white garments and garlands, you who delight in sexual union, svāhā! This is her very ritual procedure. 52.43.

The mantra of Bhaṭṭā is as follows: Oṃ bhaṭṭe bhaṭṭe, O illuminator, why do you delay? Come, come! Approach, approach! Accomplish my task, svāhā! This [vidyā] succeeds even without a painted cloth. Having prepared a small maṇḍala at the head of one’s bed and burning guggulu incense, one should recite the vidyā eight thousand times while remaining silent, alone, and pure, having closed the door. Within one month, she will certainly arrive at night. 52.44.

When she has arrived, she should be desired; she becomes a wife who grants all desires. If she enters his house, he lives for five thousand years. If she does not, he lives for five hundred years in this very Jambudvīpa. He sports with her; she fulfills all his commands. Together with him, she goes wherever he wishes. She bestows an elixir (*rasāyana*) upon him and, like a beloved wife, acts with a beneficial intention.
The mantra for Revatī: Homage to all yakṣiṇīs! Oṃ, O red one, you who possess a red radiance, you who are anointed with red unguents, svāhā!
The Yakṣiṇī Revatī is the most excellent; Lalantī is fond of sexual union.
She has dark, curly hair and wears a slightly reddish garment.
The Yakṣī, beautiful in all her limbs, is always devoted to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures; she constantly bestows desires and wealth—one should designate her as the granter of boons. 52.47.
Having painted the cloth as before, this is its specific distinction: she is dressed in a red silk garment, wears a red silk upper robe, and is red in complexion. (52.48)
The mantra of Mekhalā: Oṃ Mekhalā, great yakṣiṇī, accomplish my purpose, svāhā! 52.49.

The mantra of Sumekhalā: Oṃ mekhale sumekhale mahāyakṣiṇi sarvārthasādhani hūṃ | samayam anusmara svāhā || 52.50 || The mantra of Ālokinī: Oṃ lokini lokavati svāhā | For these [deities], the ritual procedure is exactly the same as that for these [preceding ones]. || 52.51 ||

The mantra of Tamasundarī is: Oṃ ghuṇu guhyake ghuṇu ghuṇu guhye, ehy ehi guhyake svāhā. Regarding its ritual service (*upacāra*): there is no procedure involving a cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*) for this one. First, being pure and dressed in clean garments, on the full moon day, in a secluded place with the door closed, in darkness devoid of light, one should recite the vidyā ten thousand times. Thus the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished. || 52.52 ||

Then one should begin the practice. Starting from the full moon until the next full moon—in this interval the ritual is performed. At night, at the time of going to bed, having ascended the couch in a secluded and hidden place, alone, having closed the door, in the darkness devoid of light, having mixed *saṅkucitakarṇikā* and forest flowers with pungent oil, having washed both hands and feet, and having consecrated the right arm one hundred and eight times, one should sleep in silence. Thus, day after day, until the full moon. Then, at midnight, she certainly arrives. 52.53.

When she has arrived, one must not speak with her; she should be desired through silence alone. When she speaks after six months have passed, then one may converse with her. From that time forward, she becomes perfected; she becomes a wife who grants all desires. She provides him with divine and pleasant tactile sensations, and even without being seen, she accomplishes all tasks. She bestows elixirs and alchemical potions. 52.54.

Mounting him upon one's back, one may carry even Mount Sumeru; at night, one causes one to traverse Jambūdvīpa; one may cause even an enemy situated a hundred *yojanas* away to be slain. Whatever is commanded, all that is accomplished—except for approaching another’s wife. This is the procedure for all [mantras]. One must not approach another’s wife; one should dwell together with her [only] as permitted by the mantra. If one does approach her, they will bring about death or madness. (52.55)

This is the yakṣiṇī named Andhārasundarī, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of yakṣīs. Once she has been mastered, she dispatches one yakṣī servant every day for the sake of all practitioners. She is accompanied by a retinue of many mantras and possesses great supernatural power (*maharddhika*) among all yakṣīs; she is surrounded by them. This very same procedure applies to all of them. However, while they may be seen, she herself cannot be seen. || 52.56 ||
The yakṣiṇī named Andhāravāsinī possesses great supernatural power;
she dwells in caves, is a hero among men, and is renowned throughout the world as a maiden.
Apāyajahā, Vadhūyakṣī, Manojñā, and Saptamā Surasundarī—
these seven yakṣiṇīs bring benefit to sentient beings.
They wander through this world and indeed across the entire earth; in just a moment, they fly up to the abode of the gods.
In the battle between the gods and the daityas, those of great supernatural power fought; they were most righteous, filled with compassion, desirous of the welfare of beings, and very affectionate.
They wander upon the surface of the earth for the sake of desiring the welfare of sentient beings.
Nothing is difficult for them to accomplish; these auspicious ones perform all activities.
They were spoken of by the Bodhisattva for the purpose of the enjoyment of sentient beings.

The mantra of Guhāvāsinī: Oṃ guhile guhāmati guhāvāsini, bring [her] here, O Blessed One, to my presence; remember the pledge! Svāhā! Having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *priyaṅgu* flowers smeared with ghee.

For one month, at the three junctions of the day, the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished. Thereafter, one should begin the ritual practice (*sādhana*). On a wooden board, a cloth, or a wall, using non-sticky pigments and new vessels and brushes, one should first have King Sumeru drawn; it should be square, with four peaks rising upward, and encircled by a range of seven mountains. At the edge of those mountains, a cave situated on the mountain should be depicted.

Therein, one should have painted a Yakṣiṇī named Guhāvāsinī, who dwells there, possessing a divine form, adorned with all ornaments, and alone. She is clothed in silk garments, wears a silken upper robe, is golden-hued, and has a most wonderful and beautiful appearance. Having had such a cloth-painting (paṭa) executed, one who is pure, subsisting on a diet of milk, should recite the vidyā ten thousand times in a clean place. Having performed a great worship according to one's ability, at the conclusion of the recitation, the Yakṣiṇī, emitting a great radiance and possessing a divine form, will herself come forth. 52.64.

When she has arrived, an offering (argha) should be presented with jasmine flowers mixed with white sandalwood water. Then she says: "Child, what must be done? One should say: "Please be my mother. Having said, "So be it," she vanishes. One must not corrupt one's mind toward her, nor should one pray for anything connected with sensual desire; for she is a noble lady of great supernatural power (maharddhika), and if one prays for sensual pleasure, it will not be accomplished. From that time forward, she performs all duties like a mother. || 52.65 ||

She provides food and clothing for a retinue of eight hundred. She protects one who is in distress. Even for one situated atop a great mountain range, she accomplishes all tasks. She grants desired food and bestows all things such as elixirs and alchemical potions. She acts according to one’s wishes and manifests dwellings such as huts and cottages.
He bestows a thousand pieces of gold day after day; all of it must be spent on that very same day. If he does not do so, his [merit] is severed; it does not remain at all. (52.66)

There is another rite for this [deity]: having kindled a fire before this very painting with *khadira* wood, using embers from which the flames and smoke have vanished, one should draw an image on the palm of the right hand with red arsenic (*manaḥśilā*) and the name of either a man or a woman on the palm of the left hand; then, while reciting the mantra, one should heat it over that same heap of embers. She brings [the person] even from a hundred leagues away and causes everything that is commanded to be done. This rite is for the night, not by day.

The mantra of Naravīrā is: Oṃ naravīre svāhā. Likewise, having painted her image on a cloth, one should have it depicted as resting against an Aśoka tree, excluding the cave-dwelling. This is her specific distinction: all the ritual procedures are exactly the same as those for the Cave-Dweller (Guhyakālī). Furthermore, this [mantra] should be recited: "Become my sister. 52.68.

She has another rite: during a lunar eclipse, one should wrap gold ochre with birch bark, place it in the mouth, and recite the mantra as long as the moon remains eclipsed. Then, by writing the name of a man or a woman with that gold ochre, one brings them even if they are situated a hundred *yojanas* away; at dawn, one leads them back to that very place. She performs tasks like a sister and provides great protection in times of distress. By the mere recitation of the mantra, she brings all women under one's control. This is the procedure for Naravīrā. 52.69.

The mantra of the Yakṣakumārikā is: Oṃ yakṣakumārike svāhā. This is her ritual procedure: she should be caused to be drawn with yellow orpiment on birch bark. She is a maiden with half-curled hair, adorned with all ornaments, wearing a single garment; in her right hand she holds a citron fruit, and with her left hand she clings to a branch of an Aśoka tree. 52.70. {A22v}

Such a birch-bark leaf should be placed above the location of the head. One should sleep alone in a secret place. Having prepared a mandala with white sandalwood and having scattered *jātī* flowers at the three junctions of the day while burning *guggulu* incense, one should recite the vidyā eight thousand times for the duration of one month.

Then, on the full moon day, having performed a great worship with *jātī* flowers and having offered lamps of ghee and sacrificial oblations, one should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass and recite the mantra throughout the night until the maiden, the daughter of Vaiśravaṇa, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred, arrives in her own form. Having surveyed that entire region of the sky, she stands in the air in her own form. She says this: "What must I do? Then the practitioner should say: "One of these three boons should be requested: [to be my] mother, sister, or wife. (52.72)

If she becomes one's mother, her mind must not be corrupted; for one who corrupts her, ruin ensues. One should behave toward her as toward a mother. And that mother provides food, clothing, and various exquisite ornaments for a retinue of five hundred at every moment, by mere thought alone. She gives a thousand *dīnāras* day after day, providing everything for those wandering right here in Jambudvīpa.

If she becomes a sister, then even from a distance of a hundred *yojanas*, she brings that woman [to the practitioner]; she leads her right there and accomplishes all tasks just like a sister. If she becomes a wife, she leads him to her own abode; he lives for a thousand divine years. When he dies, he is reborn into a wealthy family. Like a wife, she carries out every command. (52.74)

The mantra for Vadhūyakṣiṇī: Oṃ niḥ! This is Vadhūyakṣiṇī. The ritual service (*upacāra*) for her is as follows: having smeared the right arm with white sandalwood paste and the left with saffron, and having empowered [the latter] one thousand times, one should, alone and observing silence at night in a secluded place, close the door and cook five or eight *vibhītaka* fruits in sesame oil. 52.75.

Having taken that oil and discarded the *vibhītaka* fruits, one should place it in a new vessel—whether of gold, silver, copper, or clay—and set it at the foot of the bed after consecrating it a thousand times with this very mantra of the One-Syllable Yakṣiṇī. Then, one should sleep on a bed strewn with flowers in a secluded, dark place. || 52.76 ||

And having arrived, a non-human woman massages his feet; her palms are soft with a divine and pleasant touch, by the mere touch of which a divine, pleasant sleep arises, such that even at sunrise, at the end of the night, he awakens with difficulty. Even when awakened, he should think only of that. She must neither be desired nor spoken to. In six months, she becomes accomplished. 52.77.

Then she, possessing a divine form, like a newlywed bride, filled with joy, surrounded by female attendants, holding a lamp in her hand, illuminating the surroundings with her own radiance, carrying a bed and seat, and resplendent with various ornaments, arrives and speaks with him. Carrying the requisites for sensual enjoyment, she arrives and embraces the practitioner around the neck. || 52.78 ||

From that time forward, she attends upon him like a beloved wife. When she arrives, she is to be desired; having been served at night, she disappears at dawn. Leaving a pearl necklace worth a thousand pieces of gold upon the bed, she departs day after day. All of it must be spent without remainder; if one keeps anything back, she does not appear again. It must not be told to anyone; if one tells someone, she will not come again, or she will cause harm ending even in death. For these are supreme *guhyakas*, most secret; they do not tolerate the disclosure [of their presence] to a second being. (52.79)

One must not disclose this even to one's mother, father, friends, masters, or kinsmen; nor should it be entrusted even to animals or beings of the animal realm. This is the supreme secret. This very same rule applies to all *guhyakas* and all *yakṣiṇīs*. Even those who have attained accomplishment (*siddha*) become unaccomplished if they reveal it. Furthermore, one should always avoid sexual intercourse with other women and [excessive intimacy] even with one's own wife. (52.80)

The mantra of Manoñjā is: Oṃ manohare madonmādakari vicitrarūpiṇi maithunāpriye svāhā. The ritual procedure for this is as follows: having caused a well-constructed hut to be built beneath an Aśoka tree in a garden grove.
Having made it very well-guarded with raised walls and artificial doors and bolts, one who is pure should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.

Then one should begin the ritual action. Having taken human fat and made a wick with a cloth from a cemetery, one should close the door and light the lamp. One should place a fresh garment, free of hair, outside the door. At night, she comes naked, puts on that garment, and enters, having assumed the form of a human woman. Then the practitioner enjoys himself with her as long as the lamp burns. 52.82.

When the lamp has gone out, she disappears. Having tied a single piece of gold to that garment, she leaves the bed, casting off the garment. Then the practitioner seizes her by the hand; she slips away, dropping a single ring from her finger. Then [she drops] a divine pearl necklace from her neck; then a bracelet from her arm; a girdle from her waist; anklets from her feet; and a jewel from her head. In this manner, whichever divine ornament is grasped here or there, she bestows it upon him.

It goes and returns unfailingly. In this manner, it should be expended entirely every day. When she has thus conferred counsel for six months, then one should take counsel with her; she becomes a wife. Constantly present, she bestows an elixir (*rasāyana*) by drinking which one lives for a long time. Having meditated in the mind, one should drive a stake of *khadira* wood into the ground; a divine celestial chariot (*vimāna*) appears. Once it is pulled out, it vanishes. 52.84.

Its second mantra is: *Oṃ mahānagni nagnije svāhā*. Having lit a lamp with that very [substance] and having consecrated it one hundred and eight times with this mantra, one should employ it; she will certainly come. Furthermore, having consecrated a ritual stake (*kīlaka*) and driven it into the ground, when the lamp is extinguished and the [stake] is pulled out, there is invisibility (*antardhāna*). One should carry the ritual stake, human fat, oil, and a wick made of cloth from a cemetery to another place—either in a cow-horn, a *gavala* horn, or a buffalo horn—to wherever one desires, or one may do it oneself. However, the mantras must not be given away; if one gives them, one’s mastery of the vidyā is severed. 52.85.

Whatever one gives, that very thing accrues to him. Or, wherever he desires, or in whatever secret place he performs this, this accomplishment becomes unfailing. Or he causes others to rejoice, yet he does not converse with them. Whatever another woman’s sight he finds pleasing and desires in his mind, a corresponding form approaches him, for it occurs through the power of the unprecedented practitioner. || 52.86 ||

The mantra of Surasundarī is: *oṃ surasundari svāhā*. Regarding this, the ritual procedure is as follows: having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter at the three junctions of the day for one month. Then, on the full moon of the bright fortnight, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass in a clean place, being pure oneself, one should recite the mantra in secret until, at midnight, she certainly arrives. Thereafter, whether she is a mother, a sister, or a wife, she performs everything exactly as before; and all of this should be explained in detail. (52.87) {S572}
Thus, these seven yakṣiṇīs, by the command of Vajrapāṇi,
roam throughout the entire earth and the three worlds, including the gods and asuras.
They wandered about among the compassionate mortals, fond of sexual union;
some were noble, while others were childish, deluded, and female yakṣas.
Likewise, at night, other female lions also roam about;
greedy for meat-eating, they seek to destroy the lives of young children. (52.90)
Likewise, drawn by the scent of blood, she came indeed to Jambūdvīpa;
that yakṣī, who constantly takes life, is ever fond of blood.
They roam through all the houses that are unprotected and defiled by death or birth;
this time for their suppression has been proclaimed. 52.92.

Just as the attachment for gathering [disciples] and the binding of the foolish in this world, so has all this been taught for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings. (52.93) When a practitioner of mantra, blinded by passion and deluded in mind, desires sexual union, he may, having summoned her with mantras, enjoy a yakṣī or a rākṣasī. (52.94)
And then a Nāga woman, a Gandharva woman, a Daitya woman, and then a Kinnara woman. || 52.94 ||
The wise practitioner of mantra should enter the delightful Pātālabhavana, the supreme city of the asuras, where there are countless women;
having gone there, the knower of mantra who recites the mantra may dwell for an eon.
When he becomes a perfectly awakened Buddha named Maitreya, then he will hear the true Dharma; having heard it, he will be liberated.
Having summoned a celestial maiden, a goddess, or even the excellent wife of a Vidyadhara by means of mantras, he should then enjoy the delight of divine bliss.
The minister, having gone to Jambūdvīpa, always brings [the substance] right there;
at that time, he should remain in a pure and secret place, constantly devoted to the practice of purification.
For the deluded, the supreme accomplishment never arises;
[their bodies] are always a place of impurity consisting of feces and urine, foul-smelling and putrid.
Likewise, they are vessels of suffering, containing the pain of disease, sorrow, and ending in death.
One should not touch a human woman who is joined with sexual pleasure if it results in separation.
Impermanent, suffering, likewise empty, void, hollow, and non-eternal; it is a deception for the foolish, arising from conceptual construction.
The mantra-practitioner should not pursue all desires born of beginningless time out of passion;
the cessation of these is called liberation, and within them lies the state of accomplishment.
Indeed, his mantras are accomplished if he is detached from sensual desire;
[even] that which is smeared with feces, urine, and blood is worshipped as if it were anointed with nectar.
One should not touch a human body that is subject to old age, death, grief, and suffering.
One should not indulge in sexual intercourse there with those whose minds are blinded by delusion and possessed by passion;
for the practitioner of mantra who always serves such [beings] and remains impure shall not attain accomplishment. 52.104.
One who knows the mantras and recites them, possessed of wisdom and with senses subdued, devoted to purity and right conduct, and steadfast— such a person is always successful in all mantras.
Padmoccā and Pramodā, as well as Ajitā and Jayā always;
Śyāmāvatī and likewise Yakṣī—these are the yakṣīs of great supernatural power (maharddhika). 52.106.

The mantra for Padmoccā: Oṃ padmocce svāhā. The ritual procedure (kalpa) for this is as follows: On the bank of the Gaṅgā or on the shore of the ocean, in the middle of a garden or flower grove, having constructed a raised platform (uḍaya), and having become exceedingly pure oneself, one should fashion a stone-slab-like form out of clay. Having closed the door there at night and gathered all necessary articles for enjoyment according to one's desires, one should prepare a bed for the Yakṣiṇī right there near oneself. Then, one should recite the vidyā ten thousand times. 52.107.

Thus, until she certainly arrives within a month, once she has arrived, she becomes a wife who may be enjoyed for pleasure. Having left a divine pearl necklace upon the bed, she departs at dawn. In this way, day by day, she becomes permanently present after six months. That pearl necklace must not be taken; if one takes it, she will vanish right then and there. That necklace is adorned with jewels and gems, and is worth a hundred thousand dīnāras. (52.108)

When six months have passed, she becomes a constant companion as a wife who grants all desires. Having assumed whatever form is desired, she attends upon him; she manifests herself in whatever way is pleasing according to the wish of the practitioner. This is the procedure for all Yakṣīs mentioned here and elsewhere. (52.109) The mantra of Jayā is: Oṃ jaye sujaye jayamati, perform all my tasks, svāhā. (110)
The goddess has the luster of gold, variegated limbs, and dark, curly hair; she is beautiful in all her limbs, gentle, fortunate, and auspicious.

Priyaṃvadā is the best of women, beautiful and lovely to behold; Śukra is praised for his form and is highly honored by all the world. One should point out Jayā by means of a slightly reddish garment. (52.111)

The ritual procedure for this [deity] is as follows: First, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; thus the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished. Then, having entered a great forest and subsisting on fruit, one should recite until she appears in her own form. When she has arrived, she asks, "What shall I do? If she becomes a mother, she fulfills all hopes like a mother; she bestows a kingdom, makes one a lord of great wealth, and grants long life. || 52.112 ||

Then, as a sister, she brings a woman according to one's desire, even if she resides a thousand *yojanas* away. She gives a hundred thousand *dīnāra*s day after day, and that [wealth] must be spent. Then she becomes his wife;
he leads her to his own abode and sports with her for a long time, mounted upon a divine celestial chariot (*vimāna*). He wanders at will for thirty thousand years.
He becomes like a great yakṣa. || 52.113 ||

The mantra of Pramodā: Oṃ ṣṭhrīḥ hrīḥ mahānagni hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. (114) The ritual procedure for this: At midnight, an immeasurable number of recitations (*jāpa*) must be performed; one must not fall asleep again. Within a month, she will certainly arrive. She becomes a wife who grants all desires; day by day she bestows twenty-five *dīnāra*s and provides sexual union herself. Furthermore, she causes one to live for a long time. (52.114)

In this way, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yakṣiṇīs; likewise, piśācīs, nāgakanyās, asurakanyās, apsarases, surayoṣits, and daityakanyās—all possessing great supernatural powers (maharddhika). In this manner, there are incantations (mantras) for all the vidyādharīs from every direction, as well as for human and non-human women, numbering in the incalculable. Likewise, there are mantras for the yakṣas, devas, nāgas, ṛṣis, gandharvas, asuras, pretas, and rākṣasas. There are also mantras for Mahābrahmā, Maheśvara, Viṣṇu, and the Mothers headed by Aindrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍī, and Vārāhī. All of them, individually, having been summoned here by the Wrathful King Yamāntaka, were brought, seized, established in their pledge (samaya), and presented to Mañjughoṣa together with their retinues.
The attendant stood in succession.

In brief, for all [these purposes], having made an image or a likeness oneself, one should recite the mantra of Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, until the reflection trembles, moves, or perspires. Then he will come in his own form and accomplish everything that is commanded. 52.116. {V448}

In the same way, for those four young women who are great yakṣiṇīs, accompanied by their brother Tumburu—possessing divine forms, dwelling upon the ocean, mounted upon a boat, highly honored by all the world, and acting for the benefit of sentient beings—the procedure is exactly this, namely: || 52.117 ||
Whether carved in relief upon a cloth, a wall, or a wooden panel, or even painted,
she is depicted as having embarked upon a boat, following her elder brother.
Ap 52. A maiden residing within the ocean, accompanied by four companions, remains there in concealment; having established their wrath, one should begin the recitation of the mantra. 52.119.
Trembling, shaking, and likewise perspiration arise in them on all sides.
Then, knowing that they have been mastered, the reciter of the mantra should cease the recitation. 52.120.
At the end of the night, they announce auspicious and inauspicious matters by their very own forms; indeed, they become the accomplishers of all goals for the practitioner of recitation.
Commanded, drawn forth by wrath, and rendered unconscious [by power], they perform everything, along with the foremost of planets such as Soma, the sages, and likewise the rākṣasas. (52.122)
Those of great supernatural power were well-honored by both piśācas and garuḍas;
likewise, those of great supernatural power were honored by Maheśvara and others of such a kind.
And these eons of spoken mantra-tantras in their full detail—124. all of them, together with their ritual manuals and extensive procedures, should be employed;
they all abide effortlessly under the power of the King of Wrath. 52.124.
Whatever mantras there may be that arise from withered or despondent states, they are all enjoined by and revealed through the King of Wrath.
O noble one, those mantras which are indeed distinguished and all-pervading—
excellent, preeminent, and foremost, spoken by the supreme Victors as well as by me, the holder of mantras— have been thus proclaimed. (52.126)
Furthermore, those other chief mantras belonging specifically to the five families,
which were spoken by the sons of the Victors, as well as the worldly ones possessed of great supernatural power— 127.127.
Having drawn them all together, the King of Wrath, possessed of great supernatural power,
bound all their mantras and tantras within this teaching.
Whichever procedure has been prescribed for those [deities], by that very one this Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, is enjoined; he is supreme and effective for all ritual actions.
Tārā and Bhṛkuṭī, as well as Pāṇḍaravāsinī; Mahāśvetā, the Vidyā, Māmakī, and she who is born from the vajra;
all those born from the uṣṇīṣa, and the goddess Locanā.
The entire Vidyā of the Tathāgatas and the wise Mañjughoṣa.
[He saw] Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Samantabhadra, and likewise the Lord Padmadhara;
and I too [saw] the Bodhisattva Yakṣeśa, who possesses great supernatural power, in the world.
As for what was said regarding the Son of the Victor, renowned throughout the world in all his limbs— Vajrasena, Suṣeṇa, and my wise sons as well— 52.133.
The reciter should not treat with contempt those mantras which have been spoken by me;
one should always honor them all, for what has been spoken therein is inviolable.
The reciter should not employ the well-worshipped King of Wrath there;
one should never effect the severance of the vidyā-mantras within those mantras.

And all the worldly mantra-deities according to their respective functions, such as Umā, Śaṅkara, Brahmā, and others, as well as Hari who was well-worshipped—just as it has been done for all mantras in the tantras, so too [was it done] here. (52.136)
One should undertake every mantra from every source; indeed, the activity of all mantras is seen to arise from the Wrathful One.
This mantra is the Great Wrathful One, known by the name Yamāntaka;
having drawn [the victim] forth, it can swiftly cause even the great-souled Yama to be slain.
This mantra, a great mantra, has been proclaimed by Mañjubhāṣin;
it performs all rites, is fierce, and accomplishes all mantras.
Having spoken thus, the glorious Vajrapāṇi, possessed of great supernatural power,
bowed to the Buddha, the Great Hero, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Supreme among Men; then the Vajra-holder, relying upon the wheel of mantras, spoke this mantra of great power.
May all sentient beings indeed listen, as well as all the auspicious hosts of spirits;
I, the presiding lord of all the assemblies of mantras, shall speak this supreme mantra.
This was spoken by the wise Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa:
it is a formidable subduer of the difficult-to-tame and a warder-off of all that is evil.
However, for the sake of those to be trained, the Bodhisattva has spoken [thus] to sentient beings;
and I too shall speak here in the midst of this assembly something most terrible.

Homage to all Buddhas, who have arisen from the nature of non-existence. Homage to the Pratyekabuddhas and the noble Śrāvakas. Homage to the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, the lords established on the ten stages. It is as follows:
Oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi, O tamer of wicked beings! You who hold a sword, a mace, a noose, and an axe in your hands—four-armed, four-faced, six-legged—go!

Go, O Destroyer of Great Obstacles! O You of Deformed Face! O Terrifier of All Beings! O You who Utter the Aṭṭahāsa Laughter! O You Clothed in Tiger Skin! Perform, perform all rites! Cut, cut all mantras! Pierce, pierce the supreme mudrā! Summon, summon all beings! Grind, grind all the wicked! Enter, enter into the center of the maṇḍala! O End-maker of the Life of Vaivasvata! Accomplish, accomplish my purpose! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Do not delay, do not delay! Remember your vow! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! Shatter, shatter all obstacles! O Fulfilled One of All Desires! O Blessed One, why do you tarry? Accomplish all my aims! Svāhā!

O worthy ones, this is that King of Wrath named Yamāntaka, who brings even the King of Death himself, slays him, withers him, cooks him, and subdues him. In this way, he [subdues] all mantras and all gods; how much more so a miserable human being? He brings even Bodhisattvas established on the ten stages; how much more so worldly mantras?
Thus, this King of Wrath possesses immeasurable strength and prowess. In this way, even among all that is spoken in the mantras and tantras, he performs all rites for all mantras.
Just as he is applied, so does he act; he is accomplished through mere recitation. This King of Wrath named Yamāntaka is thus completed. 52.148.
Śakra too [attained] mastery over the high-souled Vaivasvata Kṛtānta; he is the terrible lord, the subduer of the unsubdued, who draws all things under his control.

From the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra, the fifty-second [chapter], the third detailed section concerning the regulations for all rites of the wrathful king Yamāntaka, is hereby completed. Homage to the Buddha! The ritual manual (*kalpa*) of the wrathful king Yamāntaka is finished.
Chapter A53. {S579} {V451} ap53. Chapter A53.

Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having arisen from that samādhi, while teaching the Dharma to the ocean-like assembly circle, sat before all beings and all hosts of spirits. There he addressed the many thousands of incalculable bodhisattvas headed by Vajrapāṇi; the many thousands of incalculable arhats headed by Śāriputra; the incalculable sons of the gods of the Four Great Kings headed by Vaiśravaṇa; the incalculable sons of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven headed by Śakra; and the gods of Suyāma, Santuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahma, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, up to Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, and Akaniṣṭha. Thus he addressed them.
"Listen, O assemblies of gods, all bodhisattvas, and noble śrāvakas:
all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, subject to the nature of arising and passing away.
Having arisen, they indeed cease; their complete stilling is bliss."
All [phenomena] arise with causes, originating from ignorance;
for the aggregates, together with their origin, are said to be the root of suffering along with its cause.
The knowledge that brings about their cessation—the cause of happiness and the activity of happiness—is called, in brief, the abandonment of suffering and its prevention.
That very threefold vehicle has been taught by me here: that all conditioned things are impermanent, suffering, selfless, and momentary.
It has been taught that the entire bond of existence is always and at all times empty; those beings who have emerged from their spiritual lineage proceed toward dispassion for it in three ways.
At that time, there were Bodhisattvas who had attained the enlightenment of Pratyekabuddhas, as well as others who were Arhats, free from passion, and possessed of great supernatural powers.
Relying on the awakening of the śrāvakas, they have indeed attained the threefold peace.
This Dharma, both auspicious and inauspicious, has been taught by me in brief.
One should always avoid what is unwholesome and always practice what is wholesome, according to the Dharma as it has been revealed: non-violence toward all living beings.
There is but a single path for the dharmas within the five destinies— namely,
that dharma which is untainted and rests upon the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). This very path was taught by the ancient primordial Buddhas.
I too have related everything that leads to peace and nirvāṇa.
By relying upon the limit of phenomena (dharmakoṭi), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is attained; the limit of all phenomena is declared to be the limit of reality, which is itself without limit.
This Dharma has been revealed in brief as being of two kinds.
Let all the gods and the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power listen!
O Arhats and Śrāvakas, when my Nirvāṇa occurs upon the earth...
He was born in the midst of a Sāla grove, produced from the womb of the Himalayas.
In the river Hiraṇyavatī, in the territory of the Mallas,
in the midst of the Yamaka-śālavana grove, my parinirvāṇa will take place.
In the city of Pāvā, at the Makuṭabandhana shrine, and always on the delightful bank of the river—there, upon this earth, my final nirvāṇa shall take place.
Indeed, all the bodhisattvas and the śrāvakas of great supernatural power,
as well as the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and the world-protectors of great supernatural power— 53.17.
Śakra, Brahmā, Suyāma, and others such as those from Akaniṣṭha—
indeed, the assemblies of all of them will gather in that place.
In the Yamakasāla grove, in that vicinity of the Mallas,
on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā and likewise on the other side of the Mahī river.
On the southern side of the Snowy Mountains, in the Sāla grove forest, there my final bed shall be; in that place my last resting place will come to pass.
Then, on the delightful bank of the river, on the auspicious shore named Hiraṇya,
there will be a gathering of all the hosts of gods.
Then, by all men, the best of kings, and those born of both human and non-human origins; likewise by all beings, mortals, whether ignorant or wise.
I gathered there at that place with great enthusiasm for a magnificent festival; I performed a divine sacrifice there while my body was still possessed of flesh.
But having then established it as being free from flesh, one attains peace and liberation.
Having relinquished the twenty-four categories of phenomena (dharmakoṭi), one should enter into the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Then my birth was not the last; it occurred in the city of Kapilavastu.
I was born into the preeminent clan of the Śākyas within this prison of existence.
Then, having abandoned my miserable self, I likewise departed from my home;
yet even after attending many sacred fords, I did not attain immortality once again.
And difficult practices were performed by me, having tormented this body;
for six years I dwelt there, even until my frame was withered away.
And yet, nothing was obtained by me whereby my knowledge might have been obscured. Then, having risen there, I took food consisting of auspicious rice.
Having followed the path indicated by the deities, I arrived there at that spot upon the earth—
on the beautiful king of trees on the bank of the Nairañjanā River,
in that forest on the ground strewn with various flowers.
[He dwelt] in that place endowed with the fruits of the great forest, where various trees grew.
Then, having encircled the Mahānadī river, I stayed at the foot of a tree;
for upon seeing even that small portion of ground which was my own, I attained steadfastness.
In the same way, having seen that tree— adorned with leaves and branches,
a great tree with vast shade, and beautified by its hidden roots— I [approached].

Having sat down at the foot of the Aśvattha tree, he indeed attained the state of an Aśvattha; there he found steadfastness, as well as meditation and supreme concentration. There he attained freedom from desire, which brings an end to birth at the close of that night.
Māra had employed many obstacles of various kinds;
having his army shattered, he turned back and went again to his own abode.
Furthermore, for that purpose, mantras and tantras have been taught in many ways;
various applications, meditations, and forms of knowledge have also been taught.
Furthermore, there is a threefold vehicle therein, practiced and cultivated by all; for the remedies against the faults have indeed been revealed in three ways. (53.36)
Then, having risen and gone back again to Urubilvā, which possessed auspicious waters,
he bathed there in the water and approached the seer together with his disciples.
Having performed various deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, I then departed from there;
subsequently, I entered the beautiful city of Kāśī in due course.
Having gone to that place in the past, those Buddhas of great supernatural power remained there; I myself stayed in that region among the people, among the people of Kāśī.

Having set in motion the wheel of the True Dharma that brings about peace and Nirvana, for the sake of the happiness of all beings, he revealed the Dharma there— the destination of the worlds including the gods and asuras, which is not dependent upon the five [sensual] pleasures.
In the past, the primordial Buddhas turned the wheel of Dharma there;
by me, too, the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma has been taught there.
For the sake of the bliss of liberation from existence and for the removal of the faults of sentient beings,
he indeed set in motion the Brahma-wheel, which is secure and leads to ultimate peace.
For the sake of destroying the path of existence, he [attained] the Noble Eightfold Path born from the meditative concentration on the Four Truths, adorned with the four sublime abodes.
[The wheel] of dependent origination, consisting of twelve aspects,
is joined with the cessation of ignorance and is born from the rim of the production of knowledge.
It revolves toward the limit of reality, which is indeed born from the excellent limit of the limit of existence.
45. [He attained] the state born of the majesty of movement through both forward and reverse orders. 53.45.
The wheel of Śiva’s instruction shall liberate many beings;
having released [them] in the delightful city of Kāśī, I shall then go to Śrāvastī.
Then, having subdued the heretics through miracles and transformations at Śaṅkasya, he likewise displayed his supernatural power throughout the countryside.
Then, having again brought satisfaction to those staying at many sacred fords and shrines,
he performed the auspicious descent of the gods by means of a vessel of fire among the people;
and among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, he established Śakra in the nature of Dharma.
Likewise, [he saw] the gods beginning with Akaniṣṭha, as well as Brahmā, Īśa, and Purandara.
He [honored] Vaiśravaṇa, lord of the yakṣas, and the gods of the Four Great Kings;
the Sadāmattas, the Karoṭapāṇis, the Trivīṇas, and the Māladharins.
[He addressed] all the gods, the hosts of yakṣas— those of the earth, those of heaven, and those of the intermediate space—
as well as the noble ones, the leaders of the yakṣa hosts, and indeed all the gods and asuras.
Having made them devoted to the fruits of the Dharma and inclined toward Nirvana in three ways, he then united many beings who were free from mental afflictions with that very excellence.
The number of those who have reached the end of saṃsāra is incalculable;
they have entered the meditative absorptions within the realms of thousands of great world-systems, remaining there without thought.
Having indeed established many beings in the truth of the ultimate reality, I have come here; I am stationed above the Śuddhāvāsa heaven.

Having set in motion the true Dharma of mantras, which accords with the three vehicles, and having brought about the discipline of sentient beings, he then proclaimed this King of Rituals (Kalparāja) in many ways throughout the world and bestowed it upon Mañjughoṣa. When I have entered parinirvāṇa and the surface of the earth has become empty, Mañjuśrī will then perform the Buddha’s work for the sake of sentient beings.
However, for the purpose of manifesting the power of mantras, this extensive ritual manual (kalpa) has been taught;
indeed, at that time, during the end of the age (yugānta), which is truly great, terrible, and most dreadful.
In that lowest age, O lords of men, kings will be exceedingly cruel, delighting in killing one another; they will be evildoers of wicked conduct with meager enjoyments.
Of this there is no doubt at that time in that debased age.
And it was for the sake of worshipping me that [the tree] appeared in the Sāla forest.
Having seen that very deed of mine, my own wondrous performance,
I myself, through the discipline of taming, performed the act of taming those to be converted by a Buddha.
Remembering that auspicious and wondrous life-story, all the lords of men, together with the gods, asuras, and humans, will all perform worship.
Then all the kings, having assembled, will undoubtedly perform a great festival of worship in my presence at that time.

When the body has been placed upon the funeral pyre, with its flesh partially consumed and its qualities having arisen, at the end of the impure there is indeed the pure; all these are devoid of merit. Furthermore, the peaks of existence are empty within the arising of the five aggregates.

But many beings, having seen him, were engaged for the sake of great merit; the great śrāvakas, the high-souled ones, free from passion and possessed of great supernatural powers, and all the bodhisattvas who had indeed attained the ten stages.
All of them stood surrounding him, compassionate toward all sentient beings— indeed,
all the hosts of gods, both the noble ones and ordinary worldlings.
And all of them, having taken refuge together in this place of great merit,
attained clarity of mind as a basis for the realization of impermanence and suffering.
All the hosts of spirits stood nearby at the edge of the shrine;
they performed a great worship, wailing and weeping aloud.
They shed teardrops with their eyes full of tears, moved by compassion;
and thus they all cried out, [proclaiming] impermanence, suffering, and emptiness.
For the sake of protecting the true Dharma of the Lords of Jinas after their final nirvana, Mañjughoṣa will be its constant and eternal guardian.

The Buddha has taught the Dharma now upon this earth; he is that very same excellent and most eminent Sage, the seventh among the bull-like seers, the Śākya-born one, the foremost of all beings—this is my final sight of him.

This Blessed One lies here, speaking of impermanence and suffering; he proclaims the ultimate truth of emptiness and speaks of the meaning of primordial peace. O hosts of gods, for what reason do you not awaken that Lord? (53.72)
All these sons of the Buddha have indeed come here, possessing great supernatural powers;
they are seekers of the Dharma, great heroes, and disciples endowed with great supernatural power.
All sentient beings, as well as humans, gods, and asuras, are indeed suffering.
For the time has indeed come here for the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
May the Blessed One arise quickly to conform to the Buddha’s time;
for when the great ocean is stirred, O Sage, it must be crossed by those who have set out upon it.

Nor could the Sage, disregarding many beings for a long time, truly establish the path to peaceful Nirvana—consisting of meditation, liberation, and concentration—born of meditative absorption. (53.76)

Having thus uttered many such words of lamentation and much idle chatter, all those hosts of gods of great supernatural power became silent; having raised an incomparable cry, they then stood there with their palms joined in reverence.
Having cried out for a long time with choked throats and faltering voices,
Brahmā and the other gods, along with the asuras, were filled with grief and their minds were distraught.

All those human lords of men were seated there upon the surface of the earth. Another Śākya-born one was liberated—free from passion and possessed of great supernatural power—a knower of the Great-Souled Buddha, the God of gods.

The monk named Aniruddha was his younger brother, a noble and auspicious man; he was subtle, skillful, discerning, and an expert in the rules of song, surrounded by many eminent Arhats and even by numerous lords of men.
With hearts moistened by compassion, they spoke sweet words with gentle breaths, directed toward the wrestlers and the king, who were themselves filled with grief.
"Friends, do not set fire to the funeral pyre here until the Blessed One’s son, who has arisen from the nature of reality (dharmatā), [arrives].
This disciple named Mahākāśyapa is one of great supernatural power (maharddhika)."
O Great Sage of supreme intellect, he was born as a Brahmin, free from worldly desire.
Born among the people of Magadha, he remains concentrated there on Mount Gūhapippala in the excellent city of Rājagṛha.
He himself will indeed come quickly, and not otherwise;
whatever deity there is who is devoted shall ward off that Deholkā.
Do not, for now, vainly exert yourselves to create an illumination for the funeral pyre,
as long as that one of great supernatural power remains— the foremost disciple, the true son of the Sage.
Having circumambulated the Buddha, the Teacher honored by the three worlds, and having bowed his head to the feet of the World-Honored One which are revered by the world, [he said:
"Then you all must perform this for the sake of the funeral lamp; at that time, these [remains] shall become a blazing shrine."
"O people, do not all of you here labor in vain for nothing but food."
Thus addressed by the wise Aniruddha,
all those wrestlers, along with the men and the king, sat down.
I was born among humans and was nurtured by humans with various enjoyments and other auspicious accomplishments in the arts and crafts.
I attained awakening among humans at the foot of a tree upon the earth;
I have taught the Dharma for humans, which is beneficial to all sentient beings.
For this very reason, the funeral pyres of humans are prepared for the purpose of lighting lamps:
"I am a human, and I have attained the state of preeminence among all beings;
in the world of humans my peace has been realized, and my parinirvāṇa is thus conceived. (53.93)
Whatever Buddhas there may be, indeed, whether belonging to the past, the future, or the present,
they are all, in this world of humans, men born from human bodies.

Having likewise awakened to the [four] truths, turned the wheel, and practiced the auspicious path of similarity, all the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats entered the threefold peace; having relied upon a human body, they attained unsurpassed tranquility. (53.95)

I have performed beneficial service for them throughout inconceivable eons. Now, when I have become peaceful, cooled, and ceased, and the surface of the earth has become empty, my relics have been established there.
For the benefit of human beings, and out of a desire to bestow honor and grace upon the worlds of gods and asuras, as well as upon the ṛṣis, yakṣas, and garuḍas.
The rākṣasas, pretas, kūśmāṇḍas, and piśācas of great supernatural power;
indeed, all beings, along with the grahas and the mātṛs.
And all the worlds, as well as inconceivable and innumerable relics, were established by you at that time for the sake of honoring all living beings,
when the surface of the earth had become empty.
Some mortals possessing material wealth, other kings of the gods, others dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla), great and powerful lords of the dānavas,
as well as the kings of the nāgas and the daityas— each of them [offered] minerals to me individually.

Having taken away [the relics], those who possess virtue and great supernatural power (maharddhika) will then perform worship and carry them back to their own abodes. There is no doubt that they will all become Buddhas of great supernatural power, categorized as superior, inferior, or middling according to the threefold clarity of their minds.
They will appear in the world in three ways: as Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats.
Thus, the vehicle is proclaimed in the world as being of three kinds.

At that time, there will arise in the world those who have emerged from the path described in the Mahāyāna and its associated practices, as well as those who have set out toward the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha.
And there will be other disciples there, free from passion and possessed of great supernatural power;
at that time, they shall appear in the world, adorned with the threefold lineage.
Those great protectors of the earth, possessing vast enjoyments and great gentleness, as well as the wielders of the wheel—
having long experienced divine and human prosperities,
they finally reached the threefold peace at the end of their time.
By those of former times who possessed primordial wisdom, by those of the present, and indeed by all those of the future—
this very path has been clearly revealed just as it is.
There, all the deities were seated upon the ground of Nirvana;
with their minds divided and agitated, they spoke with faltering voices.
When he spoke thus, they all then said: "Alas, how painful is impermanence!
Even those Buddhas of great supernatural power in the world have resorted to final nirvana. (53.109)
Thus addressed, all those kings of the gods, possessed of great supernatural power, remained silent and stood still.
In the excellent people of Magadha, who dwell in Kuśāgrapura,
there is a mountain near that place known by the name Vārāha.
There, that monk meditates, hidden in a cave beneath a peepal tree.
My disciple is indeed my foremost son, born of my own breast and arisen from the Dharma; he who is named Mahākāśyapa was then seated in that excellent cave.
Then, having eaten that alms-food, he sat down and thought to himself: "For a long time I have paid homage to this Buddha, the Great Sage;
now I wish to go to that Self-Existent One, the Supreme among Men. (53.113)
"Where does the Blessed One, the Śākya, the best of sages, reside? Does he, while staying there, keep the great Kāśyapa, the king of brahmins, in his thoughts?"
Thus, with his mind alone, the Sage contemplated the Sage;
with the divine eye, he surveyed the world and all the worlds.
Having illuminated the world-systems beginning with Akaniṣṭha, [he beheld] the worlds.
All those known as complete beings, who have arisen from the Great Trichiliocosm.
With his divine eye, he perceives as far as the sphere of the disciples—
the teaching that is extinguished, peaceful, cooled, and free from worldly taints.

He was surrounded on all sides by hosts of gods of great supernatural power, as well as by humans, lords of men, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and all the multitudes of bhūtas, and by bodhisattvas of great supernatural power. (53.118)

Then there were also śrāvakas of great renown who had attained preeminence in wisdom—both those still possessed of passion and those free from passion, as well as divine beings, noble ones, and humans.
Then [he saw] the hero, the Buddha, the kinsman of the sun, who had ascended the funeral pyre—
the god of gods, the most excellent, the lord, and the best among sages.
He was surrounded on all sides by the kings dwelling in the islands,
who held grass torches in their hands, as well as by the wrestlers and the lords of men.
They were unable to set it on fire, as they were restrained by the deities;
thus it was said by the monk Aniruddha, who was observing his vow.
With a throat choked with tears, he heard the earth resound with loud cries, a terrible clamor of "Alas!
Alas! and the booming of kettledrums.
That divine forest was crowded with hosts of ṛṣis, praised by celestial nymphs,
and resounded with the songs of siddhas and vidyādharīs, as well as the high-sounding chants of kinnaras.
The auspicious crying of birds resounded with sweet warbling;
there was a wonderful and charming music, filled with the sounds of both divine and human beings.
The Sāl forest became a place where the songs of Apsaras were heard, frequented by Siddhas and Vidyādharas, and filled on all sides with yogins.
Then, sighing deeply, he who was once free from sorrow became indeed filled with grief as he gazed upon that best of sages, the preeminent among ascetics, lying there surrounded on all sides.
Then the śramaṇa Kāśyapa, shedding a single tear, was at that time rolling upon the earth as my foremost disciple.
And he quickly utters these words: "Alas, what a tragedy unfolds!
For even those Buddhas who have passed into final nirvana and are free from outflows [are no longer present]. (53.129)
"Furthermore, it was taught by him here that [the world] is impermanent, suffering, and empty;
I have not seen anything eternal that persists through other births. (53.130)
Then, having risen from there, he should quickly go to the King of Magadha, Ajātaśatru, who is afflicted by suffering and overwhelmed by grief for his father. (53.131)
Then, having gone to his house, he spoke to that lord of men:
"O Great King, that perfectly awakened one, the supreme among bipeds, has passed into final nirvāṇa."

Quickly prepare the vehicle; let us go into the presence of the Teacher—to him who lies upon the earth, free from fever, his consciousness departed, having transcended all enmity and fear, the most excellent of embodied beings worthy of veneration.
Having heard those cruel words, that king became deeply distressed; then, O King, the monarch spoke these words of inner lamentation while weeping.
I have fallen away from both the Teacher and my father;
abandoned by all my kinsmen, I am likewise untrustworthy among people.
I have fallen into a terrible hell; whom shall I choose as my refuge?
"Save me, O Great Hero, foremost disciple of the Teacher!
Mahākāśyapa of great majesty, there is no life left for me here. (53.136)
Having spoken thus, the king, the preeminent lord of men among the Māgadhas, fell at that very moment to the earth at the feet of the foremost disciple;
motionless and fainted, he suddenly lay upon the ground.
At that time, O Kumāra Mañjughoṣa of great supernatural power,
you wander everywhere throughout the worlds with the desire to benefit sentient beings.
When my body had been placed upon the funeral pyre in that forest grove,
you, O Mantra, sat there surrounded by a host of Bodhisattvas.
For you have made this body here upon the surface of the earth for the sake of worship;
look all around at living beings—who is suffering, and who can deliver whom? (53.140)
Thus I, the prince of profound and true intellect, fell to the ground;
then Mañjuśrī, you must [act] for the sake of the king who is in extreme distress.

Even though he was staying there, you alone were able to discipline him; for that state is accessible only to a Bodhisattva, and cannot be attained by those of great supernatural power, nor by gods, sages, or others—neither Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, nor Śrāvakas.
Remaining there, the lord of men shall see Mañjughoṣa as if in a dream; that king, overcome by grief, will be possessed by you with supernatural power.
Then he beholds in a dream, and as if before his very eyes, Bāli—
the youth who is the soul of the universe, Mañjughoṣa of great supernatural power.
O Mañjuśrī, by your grace, I have witnessed the Bodhisattva, together with all the children, manifesting such a Dharma and displaying various inconceivable miraculous powers.
The king’s descent into Avīci and his swift emergence, as well as various aspects of the nature of reality (dharmatā), the destruction of the miserable states (apāya) which is auspicious,
and the qualities of the greatness of his destiny— all of which are beyond the reach of all the śrāvakas.
Then, having related in detail the destruction of King Ajātaśatru’s remorse regarding the Sūtra, as well as his extensive recreation, [the Blessed One spoke].

In brief, this has been proclaimed, adorned with the meaning of its extensive significance: the speech of all Buddhas, who abide in the beginning, the middle, and the end. This detailed ritual manual (kalpavistara) was spoken for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings. 53.148.
At that time, O Youthful Mañjuśrī,
you shall everywhere subdue the rulers of the earth who follow after evil deeds.
Your range of supernatural power (ṛddhi) will be inconceivable, and those to be converted (vineya) will likewise be beyond thought;
you shall indeed become the converter of all hosts of living beings.

Having spoken thus to Mañjughoṣa, who possesses the great splendor of the Buddhas and was then stationed above the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, the Great Hero— the Perfectly Awakened One, the best of speakers, and the supreme among bipeds— addressed him at that time.

After many eons have passed— inconceivable, beyond calculation, and beyond the numbering of human reckonings— you shall become a perfectly awakened Buddha named Mañjudhvaja in the world. Having then performed the deeds of a Buddha, you shall always proceed in due succession.
You shall liberate many beings, and you will attain parinirvāṇa.
When this had been said, the prince, who was indeed a youth of great supernatural power, sighed deeply; agitated and with a heart overcome by compassion, he spoke.
Having gazed upon the Perfectly Awakened One for a long time, he shed teardrops from his eyes;
then, with palms joined in salutation and without bowing, he sat down once more. Then, standing upon the surface of the earth, the supreme king named Ajātaśatru [remained there].
Having bowed his head to the wonderful Brahmin Mahākāśyapa, [he spoke].
Having awakened and regained consciousness, he prostrated at his feet before him;
then, sighing for a long time, he related the matter in detail.
Seated there was the king’s son, named Ajātaśatru, a great lord.
Then he chose Mahākāśyapa, saying: "Let us go to that cremation ground, to the honored image situated in the shrine, who is worthy of the offerings of men."

Remaining there, that foremost disciple indeed approached by means of his supernatural power. His mind was thus inclined: "It is not fitting for me to go to the great shrine by means of my supernatural power; I wish to go on foot to the assembly."
"This is the Teacher’s final journey; it is for the sake of seeing him that I have come. Then, at the halfway point, that observer of vows stood in the Saṅghārāma.
There he saw a resident of the monastery,
an elderly monk who was a novice, an evil being, and utterly deluded.
Having seen him approach—long departed, of great renown, highly fortunate, pure in being, and free from affliction—the elder [approached]. (53.162)
Having approached and then bowed at the feet of that brahmin, he said to that illustrious man, "Welcome; for what purpose have you come?"
"Where will you go so quickly, or why do you stand here so agitated?
He said to that young seer: "O long-lived one, have you not heard?
The Teacher of the entire world, the Perfectly Awakened One, the supreme among bipeds—"
My father, the Buddha of supreme wisdom, has entered parinirvāṇa like the flame of a lamp.
The Great Hero has set; the earth has indeed become empty.
All the worlds are likewise empty, and the quarters have become empty for me.
Then that delighted Mahalla, perverse and of childish intellect, laughed and spoke these words, being at ease in his great length: || 53.167 ||
With long, hanging arms and a head shaped like a very high umbrella,
our leader is indeed foremost among those who perfectly abide by the training and what is beyond training.
"Now that he has passed away, I shall wander according to my will.
Thus addressed by the elder, that man of great supernatural power was filled with joy.
Then, knitting his brows and making a face, he should employ the syllable *huṃ*.
At that very moment, the brahmin became enraged, as did the ascetic who was conditioned by latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
There, upon the surface of the earth, he would strike with his big toe at that very moment;
the entire earth trembled, and the lofty mountains made a great roar.
All the oceans were agitated, as were all the trees and mountains;
the caves and mountain recesses, along with the serpent kings and deities, were likewise shaken.
At that time, the earth lost its light, as did the moon and the sun;
the winds ceased to blow, and meteors fell from the sky.
Then there arose this mantra, renowned among the Śrāvakas, born of their lineage: it is the single-syllable mantra accompanied by *huṃ*, auspicious and capable of performing all rites.
Even if not yet perfected, this king of mantras effects [its results] by mere recitation:
it likewise paralyzes all weapons and both stationary and mobile poisons.
By the mere recitation [of this mantra], it paralyzes all wicked beings;
it performs a variety of rites, and especially others as well. (53.176)
Lamenting and being elderly, he remained silent there and departed from that place.
Having been won over by his supernatural power and disciplined at that very moment,
he was then led by that foremost disciple to the vicinity of the funeral pyre.
For that monk, free from passion and possessed of great supernatural power, traveled on foot.
Having gone there, he saw the funeral pyre upon which the Sage’s body rested,
where a great worship was being performed in many ways by hosts of deities.
The body of the Sage Gautama was indeed placed upon the funeral pyre, endowed with various excellent forms and beautifully adorned in every way.
But having seen that illustrious and wonderful Mahākāśyapa,
all those monks, free from faults and possessed of great supernatural power, [were amazed].
All the hosts of gods and spirits let out cries of "Alas!
and raised a great sound of lamentation, uttering a roar born of profound sorrow.
Then all the gods and nāgas of great supernatural power went out to meet him and said to that illustrious one: "Pay homage to the Supreme among Men."

Your consecration alone is [the true one], O God; all the hosts of deities, along with human beings, all the multitudes of spirits, sages, yakṣas, and lords of men—though intent upon lighting the pyre—are unable to kindle it. (53.184)
Then, freed from all faults, possessing great enjoyments and great supernatural power,
he circumambulated the Tathāgata many times and called him to mind repeatedly.
At the end of the funeral pyre, in its final portion, that one of great supernatural power pays homage.
Then, having broken through the iron trough, his two feet emerged;
bowing his head at the feet, he touched them again and again.
Having gazed many times there at the excellent feet of the best of sages,
they entered further into that place, taking refuge in an iron trough.

Then that one, free from passion and possessed of great supernatural power, rose up from his seat; and his retinue, consisting of Arhats who were free from passion and possessed of great supernatural powers, likewise arose. Then the chief King of Magadha approached the vicinity of the funeral pyre.
In due order, by means of various vehicles— elephants, horses, chariots, and mounts—
all the kings with their great armies, forces,
and conveyances arrived there at that time to pay homage to the Sage Śākyamuni.
He was lying on the ground in a peaceful, remote forest,
by the bank of the river Hiraṇyavatī at the Makuṭabandhana shrine,
entered into the state of peace and established in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
There, the Magadhan king, accompanied by a vast army,
also beheld that divine being with its various forms and movements.
