It possesses great merit and power, a wondrous ornament upon the earth; there, the Sage was placed upon the funeral pyre, having emerged from the body of the shrine.
The monk named Ānanda was a devoted attendant to the Well-Trained One;
he who was always affectionately intent upon that most excellent of men will, at that time, be distressed with a troubled mind. (53.194)
Then, having gone to Mahākāśyapa, he fell at his feet upon the ground;
afflicted by suffering, trembling and with a faltering voice, he spoke thus.
Today my Teacher has passed into nirvāṇa; I am now without a protector. You alone have been proclaimed by him to be my shelter and my refuge.
By that very same Muni-candra, I was prophesied in your presence:
"The abandonment of all afflictions, the state of Arhatship, shall be attained by you in his presence. (53.197)
On the night, during the final watch, it was indeed taught by that Jina:
"Even after I have entered parinirvāṇa, I shall always choose you. (53.198)
For the sake of the Buddha's work, that well-wisher indeed acted for you;
even I, having abandoned my suffering, have gone to peace, O Great Sage.
The wise one named Aniruddha comforted that ascetic:
"Do not weep, do not grieve; do not be overcome by sorrow.
Do not go anywhere else; take refuge in this very place."
He alone shall be the Teacher after the Eye of the World has passed into nirvāṇa.
For he was prophesied here by the Sage that he would perform the work of a Buddha;
and we, together with you, shall follow Kāśyapa.

Possessing supernatural power, highly fortunate, radiant, and of great splendor— like a second Teacher, he was a reflection upon the surface of the earth. Indeed, he was Mahākāśyapa, the foremost among the disciples, endowed with great supernatural power.
While he is indeed staying and remaining present, do not give way to grief.
Thus speaking, all of them— filled with compassion, possessed of great supernatural powers,
free from passion, great yogins, sons of the Sage— sat down.
Then that funeral pyre was set ablaze by those Mallas and the lords of men;
indeed, once it was fully ignited on all sides, the pyre was reduced to ashes.
Seeing him, the hosts of gods and the majestic Mahoragas sprinkled that site of his funeral pyre with sandalwood water for the sake of pacification.
Then, at that very moment, they stood once more releasing a great rain; and again, upon the surface of the earth, they released a vast shower of flowers.
At that very moment, they all arrived to pay excellent homage to the relics of the Jina;
at that very moment, they all began to engage in mutual combat.
Brahmā and the others, as well as Śakra, Yama, and all the hosts of gods,
were likewise warded off by the disciples who were free from passion and possessed of great supernatural powers.
Mahākāśyapa, having divided the relics born from the body of the Jina, distributed them in small portions everywhere for the sake of worship,
on account of the threefold turning of the vehicles and ultimate peace.
Then the great Kaśyapa, a yogi free from passion and possessed of great supernatural power,
reflected upon that which was spoken by the elder regarding enlightenment.
"Indeed, let not the entire teaching—the twelvefold word that brings about happiness, namely the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—become like smoke;
for when the Great Hero has passed away, there will be a total disappearance.
Therefore, this entire speech spoken by the Buddha must be preserved. Let us all go together, we who are free from passion and possess great supernatural power."
The excellent city of the Māgadhas, the auspicious town known as Rājagṛha.
In the delightful city of Kuśāgrapura, on a mountain of well-formed peaks;
and in the auspicious region of Vaiśālī, at a most beautiful site for a caitya.
Indeed, for the sake of the teaching, all those Mallas of great supernatural power made many such utterances of various kinds. (53.216)

At that time, indeed at the end of the eon, when I have passed into parinirvāṇa, there will be rulers of the earth who delight in killing one another. (53.217) At the end of the eon, monks will be engaged in many worldly occupations, and sentient beings will be overwhelmed by greed; likewise, the male and female lay followers will be devoid of faith. (53.218)
Addicted to killing one another, they were intent on seeking each other out.
In that age when the Sage has passed away, the monks will be unrestrained, constantly attacking the vulnerabilities of others, full of wounds, and likewise corrupting the [spiritual] humors.
At that time, eight of great supernatural power, free from passion and without outflows, were established by me upon the earth for the sake of protecting my teaching.
At that time, the Arhats such as Rāhula and others will be proclaimed as the elders;
however, in that lowest of ages, there will be no vision of them.
The sight of them is unfailing for practitioners at the time of their accomplishment.
53.222 All the mantras of supernatural power and great majesty have been established here by me. 53.222
O you of great renown, I have resolved upon the infliction of punishment for those who transgress my command, even if they are disciples. (53.223)
"Remain as long as the True Dharma, the limit of reality, and the unconditioned endure;
remain as long as this meritorious word of mine resounds upon the earth."
Then, being peaceful, selfless, and free from outflows, you shall enter final nirvana at that time when the Sage’s teaching has disappeared. At that time,
all monks will be seekers of alms, and the nuns will be full of envy.
In that age, the logicians were constantly despised and held in contempt.

At that time, those seeking wives and children will be firmly established in my teaching; and the lay followers (upāsakas) will always remain faithful to their own wives and never to the wives of others.
At that time, there will be nothing but the mere signs of the fourfold caste system as a residual convention;
all will be devoted to the practice of enmity and will mutually harass one another.
At that time, the earth will be mostly overrun by heretics and inhabited by gods; people will be devoted to the twice-born caste.
Men who are of wrong conduct, likewise deluded, and devoted to harming living beings—
this Apāmārga has been prophesied to attain final nirvāṇa in the Kali age.
There will be many women and men who are constantly devoted to the wives of others.
All are delighted in unwholesome things and are devoid of the aim of the wholesome.
When I have passed into peace upon this earth, there will be many beings;
indeed, the hosts of gods of great splendor shall perform worship to this body of mine.
And likewise the high-souled humans, as well as hosts of yakṣas and bhūtas;
the asuras, gandharvas, and kinnaras of great supernatural power.
Then the Garuḍas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, and likewise the Ṛṣis, as well as the Siddhas and Yogins of great luster... 53.234.
Sentient beings of various forms, born from diverse destinies and wombs, are bound by the thread of existence; yet they are liberated by the wise one who has severed their bonds.
Then they will perform worship to this body, now free from fever, on the bank of the river Hiraṇyavatī in the grove of twin Śāla trees.
At the Makuṭabandhana shrine in the vicinity of the Mallas,
when I have passed into final nirvāṇa, may I attain peace, free from all fear.

Having gathered these elements of mine while they were being carried away by others— by gods, asuras, and likewise by all the hosts of beings— he divided them into separate portions and caused them to be distributed.
At that time, the king of men named Ajātaśatru, the ruler of Magadha, possessed of a great army,
sought out all the disciples who possessed great supernatural powers.
"O great-souled ones, please rescue me as well— I who have performed no merit, who caused my father's death, and who am now fallen and suffering."
Then there was the foremost disciple, wise and the legitimate son of the Buddha,
renowned as Mahākāśyapa, who acted for the welfare of all beings.
Then, seeing that distress of the wise one named Ajātaśatru,
he focused his attention at that moment and empowered him through his supernatural power (ṛddhi).
He took a single portion of the relics belonging to the Victor;
the others were carried away by other powerful serpents.
Having caused mutual agitation through their reciprocal passion,
they took the constituent element through the skies and remained in their own abode.
Then the monk Mahākāśyapa, the foremost disciple, reflected upon the Sage.
Alas, what a pity! Among humans on this earth, this realm is empty of Buddhas,
Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas of great supernatural power.
Those beings who wander in the prison of existence, deprived of light,
will for a long time experience various intense sufferings. But by honoring the relic of the Protector of the World, the Savior, [they shall find relief].
They will experience no small amount of happiness in the world of the gods.
And they shall obtain sovereignty, as well as enjoyments and the very rare accomplishment of mantras, in various forms and with diverse movements and activities.
Having worshipped the relics— the foremost wealth of the world, desired by all, and adorned with the threefold liberation— one shall attain the supreme accomplishment.
Having reflected thus, the world-renowned brahmin,
the foremost disciple of the Sage, known by the name Kāśyapa, [spoke].
Then, having taken up that relic,
he carefully enshrines it upon the earth at the place called Ajātā, specifically with the effort of the Māgadha king.
Thus, even when all those kings had perished, that disciple of the Great-Souled One, possessing great splendor, bestowed [the teachings] upon everyone from every side.
Once again Bhava remained there, perceiving existence as impermanent; with a mind possessed by compassion, he took pity upon sentient beings.
Sentient beings will weep for a long time, for many kinds of eons, when the world has lost the True Dharma of the Teacher, the Bull of the Śākyas.
This statement must be remembered; do not let it become like smoke [vanishing] in an instant.
Then the hero, whose mind was intent upon his spiritual power,
rose up and addressed the lord of men, the king named Ajātaśatru.
"Let us go to the city of Rājagṛha to honor the teaching of the Teacher;
having carefully enshrined the relic set within a vessel of refined gold."
Then they arrived quickly at Rājagṛha by way of the eastern road;
having reached the Bamboo Grove, they established the offspring of the Jina there.
Having constructed a most wonderful stūpa for the Protector of the World, the Savior, he honored that stūpa with various kinds of ornaments.
With garlands, robes, and parasols, with powdered incense and perfumes; with various colorful umbrellas and banners, with bells, garlands, and ointments;
and with many kinds of diverse rows of lamps and wreaths.
Having performed worship, O protector of the earth, with their minds intent on prostration,
they bowed their heads to that stūpa and then made a solemn vow.
"By whatever great merit I have gained from worshipping Loka-agra, may I attain inconceivable worship of many Tathāgatas.
(53.262) Then the king, rising up, wiped away his tears with eyes clouded by weeping, and spoke to Mahākāśyapa. (53.263)
Then, with a heart filled with compassion, he should remember his father.
O noble one of great wisdom, be my witness regarding the sin that I have committed,
which will surely lead me to the Avīci hell.

Having caused the death of such a Dharmarāja, who stood upon the path of the Teacher’s word—that father of mine—I am unable to find any solace. Noble one, my spiritual friend, you ought to teach me for the sake of the Dharma.
Thus addressed by the Jina, that great-souled one, the foremost disciple named Kāśyapa, wise, uttered these words: || 53.266 ||
"Do not fear, O Great King; you have performed much that is wholesome.
You possess the practice of being born [in this state] from many hundreds of previous lives."
In the absence of Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas appear. At that time, there was a son of a merchant in the city of Vārāṇasī;
out of ignorance and childish impulsiveness, he then went out onto the street. (53.268)
Then, O Blessed One, that very Pratyekabuddha arrived there;
seeking alms, he wandered about with the desire to benefit the world.
Seeing that the youth’s mind was serene and his gait composed, he fell at his feet and asked: "O monk, what will you do?"
The Blessed One, the Unborn, remained silent as if he were a sword; then that boy seized hold of his robe.
"Go, go to this excellent palace adorned with banners! This is our dwelling; having washed your feet, you shall eat.
Eat quickly according to your desire, and we shall play as we please."

Then, free from all defects and having destroyed the three stains, he, intent upon benefiting others, proceeded there in due order. Having arrived at the entrance of this [city], the one of great splendor stood right there.
Then, having entered by means of that boy, he said, "Mother!"
"O Mother, give me food; give me many various kinds of alms."

"Indeed, my friend has come here; after a long time, he who used to play in the dust has arrived. You shall rejoice for a long time with him; he stands at the door. (53.275) Then, she, hurrying, went out to the door at that very moment.
He beheld that illustrious one, peaceful in appearance and possessed of great supernatural power.
Then she quickly returned, took a beautiful vessel, and having thoroughly washed her hands, [she proceeded]. || 53.277 ||
Having taken pure rice adorned with many flavors, and having placed various kinds of foods in the vessel, it shines brilliantly. (53.278)
Having arrived there quickly and having offered it into the bowl,
she, who was devoted to the Dharma, fell at his feet together with her son.
Having taken up that alms-food, he ascended into the sky; then, blazing like a row of lamps, he was seen.
For those who move like rhinoceroses, no verbal dharma exists;
these great-souled ones display their power and supernatural transformations to sentient beings.
Those most compassionate ones, having abandoned all stinginess toward sentient beings,
display their supernatural powers for the sake of sentient beings in order to benefit them in the next world.
By the ripening of that karma, the boy, together with his mother,
shall experience divinity for five thousand births.
Among the gods, he was that very king of the gods;
among humans, O Lord of Men, he then became a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Having experienced happiness here for a long time, the son of Bimbisāra then drew the Blessed One toward him and took hold of him by the edge of his robe.

Formerly, when I was urged with the words "Become a plaything in the dust for me," having spoken such ill-spoken words and addressed him as a "monk," [I have now experienced] the intense suffering of the Great Torment (Pratāpana) hell for a long time and for much,
as the result of that speech which was undesirable and bitter.
Having fallen into a terrible hell, he experiences unbearable suffering against his will.
But beings bound by the snares of karma go to an evil destiny;
karma is performed by those laughing, yet it is experienced by those weeping.
Formerly, out of foolishness, I uttered wicked words toward one who was a Pratyekabuddha; such is the result of that karma.
Having emerged from the hells and come here to the human state,
O lord of men, his consciousness was indeed born of karmic maturation.
"For that very reason, exercise the sovereignty here.
Thus they conversed with one another on the ground in the Veṇu forest.
"And my one foremost disciple, O lord of men, he was the second;
having bowed down a hundred times to the stupa, he then departed by way of his own home. (53.293)
Then that foremost disciple of mine, who dwells in the cave of Pippalāguha,
having assembled all the sages who were free from passion and possessed of great supernatural power—
Thus he recited the entire twelvefold teaching and the Vinaya; that Dharma was previously taught by me just as it was by the supreme Victors.
Therefore, that foremost of disciples should instruct in three ways:
through the arrangement [of the Sūtras], by means of the analysis of the Sūtras, and according to the Vinaya and the Abhidharma.
He shall liberate beings from the three bonds and dry up the three defilements;
having freed them from the three sufferings, the steadfast one shall then establish them in the three vehicles.
The one of supreme intelligence shall cause [the stūpa] to be built for the sake of the teaching of the Buddhas.
He will be renowned as a great king, a lord of men in Magadha. As far as the boundaries of Magadha and Aṅga, and beyond Vārāṇasī, that king of great power will rule to the north of Vaiśālī.
"He will exist, there is no doubt; he will carry out the purpose of the teaching.
O Prince, you have pointed him out and prophesied his supreme peace."
His son also will be a king celebrated by the name beginning with the letter *U*;
at that time, he will swiftly become intent upon the purpose of the teaching.
He will cause this teaching of the Teacher to be written out in detail;
and having performed great worship, he will carry it to the ends of the quarters.
He shall not fall into an evil rebirth, but will be reborn among the gods;
for thirty and twenty years, he shall dwell together with his ancestors.
Then, at the hour of the fifth watch, at midnight, he will pass away;
at that time, he will be overcome by a disease originating from his own kinsmen.
Afflicted by suffering for twenty-six days due to a great disease,
he was seized by every kind of ailment and fell into various states of unconsciousness.
Because of that intense rage, you were nearly deprived of your life.
Recalling his former latent predispositions for the conduct of a Pratyekabuddha, the Buddha appeared before him; thus he was honored and made to perform worship.
Having passed away from there, that lord of men will quickly be reborn among the gods;
through diligent effort, he will certainly attain awakening in due course.
These and many others, both those who have passed away and those yet to come, having performed various services for the Pratyekabuddhas, [attained their goal]. (53.307)
They proceed in due order toward peace and the perfection of freedom from decay— attaining both divine and human prosperity, as well as desired and distinguished wealth.
In the first age, inferior, superior, and middling kings were described, such as Nahuṣa and others, beginning with Pārthiva.
Kings who are masters of mantras will always experience the rising of Mercury and Venus;
Śāntanu, Citra, Sucitra, and the Pāṇḍavas shall likewise be lords of men.
Then the curses of the sages were warded off and came to an end. In former times, there were Kārtavīrya Ārjuna, Daśaratha, and Dāśarathi Rāma.

Arjuna, however, was one whose mantras were perfected; the other, Aśvatthāman, the son of the twice-born Droṇa, was another counselor who mastered that king of mantras. Then, by means of powerful mantra-weapons, he would exercise sovereign rule over the three continents throughout their entirety, as they were situated within Jambūdvīpa.
And the kings and others who performed temples and recited mantras—
they too, having rejoiced in the worship of the Tathāgata, went to heaven.
Some of them are destined for Buddhahood, while others belong to the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas;
some are destined for the state of a Śrāvaka—all of them are ultimately intent upon liberation.
In accordance with the established duration of time, the lifespan is differentiated:
the highest [lifespan] belongs to those of long life, and likewise, the middle [lifespan] belongs to those of middling [life]. 53.316.
But in the final age, the wretched Kali-yuga, the lowest of eras,
the kings will be fond of strife.
Addicted to mutual enmity and harming one another,
they have fallen into low births, suffering the pain of being struck by weapons.
At that time, there will be no doubt that kings, who are contemptible to the world, will be intent on the use of weapons and devoted to the wives of others. (53.319)
At that time, in the interval between the Dvāpara and Kali ages, people will be deceitful, performers of base deeds, ignoble, and likewise envious.

I shall speak in brief; listen, O Kumāra, to that which concerns the kings who will exist upon the circle of the earth during the present age. Listen now to their physical characteristics, their emblems, and their complexions.
Prasenajit, the king of Kośala, and likewise Bimbisāra.
Apāyana, the best of Kṣatriyas, born from Śatānīka;
Subāhu, the one known as Sudhana, who was equal to Mahendra and Candra.
Likewise, there was born among the Licchavis a lion originating from Vaiśālī; Udāyin, Vidyota, Pradyota, and Mahāsena are also mentioned.
In Ujjayinī there was likewise King Caṇḍa, and in the city named Kapila,
King Śuddhodana, as well as the very powerful one called Vairāṭa.
Thus have these Kṣatriya rulers been described as worshippers of the Teacher.
They behold the Buddha, the Lion of the Śākyas, the supreme among men, face to face.
Having heard the Dharma, they too shall thereafter attain prosperity for a long time;
and those who are surely desirous of liberation shall likewise attain that peace.
These kings, world-renowned upon the circle of the earth, were declared by their caste to be Kṣatriyas, identified by their insignia and their names. (53.328)
He will honor on earth the words spoken by me; you yourself have prophesied in the world that this youth in the form of a child, named Ajāta, is destined for supreme enlightenment.
When I have passed into final nirvana a hundred years hence, on this earth within the mandala— devoid of light, devoid of joy, and shrouded in the darkness of ignorance—
the earth will then become empty, bereft of the Victors.
At that time, in that most terrible city called Kusumapura, there was a king known on earth by the name Aśoka, a protector of the world;
at that time, he would be fierce in action, full of wrath, and merciless.
Having approached a spiritual friend who is free from passion, possessed of great supernatural power,
a monk endowed with ethical discipline, free from feverish affliction, and whose mind has reached tranquility.

And because of the cause of his former latent impressions (vāsanā)—the gift of dust which possessed great supernatural power—this king is destined for a perfect field [of rebirth] and is immensely wealthy;
he is a deliberator of dharma and adharma, compassionate and indeed merciful.
The one free from passion and possessed of great supernatural power revealed the cause:
"O King, it was indeed by you in the past, out of ignorance and childish fickleness..."
Then, with a handful of dust from beneath the feet of the Lion of the Śākyas, he placed it in his bowl; having done so, divine riches were obtained in heaven.
Having passed away from the world of the gods, he has now come here to the world of the ancestors.
"Enjoy the kingdom, O protector of the earth, including Jambūdvīpa with its forests.
Having propitiated the mantra of the great-souled Yakṣa Jambhala,
Bhūtaratha then became a perfected one (*siddha*) and a sovereign of the earth."
Yakṣas stand before him, their minds intent on receiving his commands;
and likewise, noble nāgas stand ready as his servants.
Thus, at that time, he became a righteous wheel-turning monarch of great supernatural power;
his movement was according to his will, and there was no one anywhere who could obstruct him.
But as for the task previously established by the Jinas on this earth— the most excellent relics—
[they were placed] then in the city of Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana).
Taking up relics from the relic-holder with a mind focused on the virtuous object,
he worshipped that stūpa according to the ancient tradition.
Having taken that jar of relics and divided it again into a hundred parts,
the wise one shall, in a single moment, issue commands to the yakṣas.
"O sirs, let you indeed cause this entire Jambūdvīpa to be adorned with the ornament of stūpas, making the earth itself a repository for the relics."
At midnight, the Yakṣas,
having diligently executed this superhuman feat, erected a stone pillar upon the ground for the one who had received the command.
At that time, he planted many thousands of pillars for the purpose of honoring the caityas and as a sign for embodied beings.
Having constructed various stūpas for the Protectors of the World,
those yakṣas arrived in the presence of the king in a single instant.
Then, having prostrated with his head, he uttered these secret words:
"Everything has been done exactly as commanded; do you not see it, O Bhūta?"
Then that king quickly ascended the chariot,
which was adorned in many ways for the sake of various forms of worship.
Then the king quickly filled that chariot of living beings with gold, silver, copper, and various ornaments for the stūpas;
in a single moment, he reached that place where those Jinas, the holders of the relics, were located.

The lord of men should worship with diverse forms of offerings. (53.350) Then, having beautified the entire earth with reliquaries of the Jina, the high-souled King Dharmāśoka made this aspiration: "By means of this root of merit, may I become an unsurpassed Buddha. (53.351)
Having understood this, that great-souled Dharmāśoka, the lord of men,
who is destined for enlightenment, will certainly go to the state of a deity after death.
For eighty-seven years he shall worship the most excellent relics on earth;
having ruled a kingdom free from thorns, he shall live for one hundred and fifty years.
A disease produced by his own karma arises within his body;
afflicted by that very disease and suffering, he dies and becomes one who goes to heaven.
Having attained great prosperity and experienced the pleasures of the celestial dwellers,
the wise one will, in due course, attain the enlightenment that is so difficult to find.
At that time, the mantras of both the Vajra and Padma families will be effective.
Likewise, Jambhala and other yakṣas who abide by this teaching,
as well as the renowned yakṣiṇīs such as Hārītī and others of great supernatural power, [will be present].

When a wheel-turning monarch appears, the mantras of the Wheel-Bearer are accomplished. Those mantras spoken by the Victors—the kings of vidyās of great supernatural power, beginning with Uṣṇīṣa, and all others spoken by the Victors—[are likewise accomplished].
At that most auspicious time, one should perform the supreme practice (sādhanā).
This supreme goal is to be accomplished by those who are noble and not base, who have taken refuge in the highest state—
just as Dilīpa, Nahuṣa, Māndhātṛ, and Sagara did.
Having mastered those mantras of the wheel-bearers spoken by the Jina,
the mass of splendor was then accomplished for the high-souled Nahuṣa.
The *Sitātapatra* was indeed perfected by King Sagara;
likewise, the single-syllable mantra was perfected by Dilīpa. Furthermore, in this world, the *Unnatoṣṇīṣa* was perfected by Māndhātṛ.
Likewise, Jayoṣṇīṣa was accomplished as a Siddha under Dhundhumāra, the best of kings.
Likewise, the victory-uṣṇīṣa of King Kandarpa is proclaimed;
Prajāpati was indeed his son, and his son on earth was Locanā.
The son of Prajāpati was Nābhi, and his son was called Ūrṇa.
Nābhi’s son was indeed Ṛṣabha, who had accomplished his tasks and was firm in his vows.
For him as well, the yakṣa Māṇicara was perfected on the Himavat mountain.

Bharata was the son of Ṛṣabha; he too then recited the mantras. He, in due course, became perfected as Mahāvīra on earth at that time. These and many other kings, world-renowned, [attained perfection].
Having accomplished the mantras and ruled over kingdoms, they have gone to heaven.
Those kings of knowledge (*vidyārāja*) of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*) who were spoken by the Lords of Jinas—
all of them [flourished] in the auspicious time, during the age of eighty thousand years.
The perfected ones, who are skilled in the meaning of mantra and tantra, will accomplish [the goal].
These and many other world-renowned kings, having ruled for eighty thousand or even a hundred years, will then go to heaven, being destined for supreme enlightenment.

At that time, during the middle period, the mantras— possessing divine, marvelous, and great supernatural powers, and proclaimed by the one who holds a lotus in his hand— attained accomplishment through the practitioners,
the foremost of men, the kings, and the sovereign rulers of the entire earth.
And King Brahmadatta in the great city of Vārāṇasī was indeed a perfected one;
he was the Lord of the World, Abjapāṇi, renowned throughout the world.
That great-souled one of great heroism, the exceedingly compassionate Great Being,
taught the Dharma to sentient beings by means of the form of mantras.
King Brahmadatta experienced human happiness;
then, having perfected his mantras, he entered heaven in his own body.
His son was likewise wise, of meritorious deeds, and firm in his vows.
His son also was accomplished, of great heroism, and renowned as Hayagrīva.
By the power of that mantra, Śakra was then defeated.
At that time, his son, the king named Śveta, became the giver of everything to all.
The mantras that grant boons for him are known by the name Mahāśvetā;
having mastered that mantra, one shall live for three hundred years.
By the power of that mantra, he goes to Sukhāvatī;
his awakening is certain, as is that of others who have been prophesied by me.

At that time, during the intermediate period, one should accomplish the intermediate mantras. In this most wretched final age, when I have attained Buddhahood, the mantras of even the Vajra and Lotus families will attain accomplishment.
O Kumāra, those mantras which were previously spoken by you on earth shall indeed attain accomplishment; for these mantras possess the quality of being a portion [of the supreme reality].
But the other mantras are worldly and various;
they are degrading, of distorted form, and belong to the intermediate space, moving through the sky.
And likewise the yakṣiṇīs of the earth, as well as various piśācīs,
garuḍas, kinnaras, pretas, and those spoken of as rākṣasas.
In this difficult age, this lowest of ages, the mantras of the piśācas, uragas, and rakṣasas, as well as those of the highly powerful nāginīs, will attain accomplishment.
The mantras indeed take the form of youths, while those in the form of maidens always [attain success];
they too shall achieve accomplishment during that terrifying time.

Mantras are likewise threefold, and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) are of three kinds; indeed, the threefold success (*siddhi*) is intended according to the three types of time. I shall speak of this, which is being told in great detail, in brief.

Behind King Aśokamukhya there shall be a king renowned in the world as Viśoka, a follower of the Dharma. (53.383) These mantras were mastered by him; having accomplished them, the goddess Pāṇḍaravāsinī bestowed [the power] upon Viśoka for the sake of the gods. (53.384)
Having experienced happiness for a long time on the back of the celestial vault, that great king,
being virtuous and wise, returns once again to the human state.
Having experienced sovereignty and various forms of prosperity for seventy-six years, that illustrious one of great splendor worshipped the supreme relics;
thereafter, overcome by fever, his body dissolved and he went to heaven.
Immediately after him, King Śūrasena is proclaimed;
he was renowned as a practitioner of dharma and was always devoted to this teaching.

By him also, the goddess Mahāśrī was propitiated through the power of mantras; by him also, a very great monument for the Teacher was then caused to be built, so that the entire earth, as far as the edge of the ocean, was adorned with stūpas.
Through the ripening of that karma, a disease born of his body will arise;
after wasting away for one fortnight, he will pass away from this life.
Having ruled the kingdom for seventeen years, that man, destined for enlightenment, passed away and ascended to heaven. (53.390)
After him, there will be a king named Nanda,
glorious, possessing a great army and great strength, in the city called Puṣpa.
By him also the mantra known as Piśāca-pīlu was accomplished;
through the power of that mantra, he will possess great wealth and will become renowned in the world as both a low-born person and a leader.
Having obtained that wealth, the minister attained the status of a king in this world.
At that time, there will arise on earth Brahmins who are mere logicians;
dwelling in the city of Magadha, they will be greedy and possessed by the pride of having attained supernatural powers.
There is no doubt that they will become those who are falsely proud and conceited.
Surrounded by them, that king—
though naturally righteous and virtuous in soul— will bestow that wealth upon them.
Having encountered a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), he shall worship the most excellent relics.
But then, through that practice and by means of the cause of unimpeded generosity,
sixteen and eight monasteries were built by that wise one.
At that time, in the city named Puṣpa,
there will be a high-souled chief minister who is compassionate, virtuous, and likewise a twice-born brahmin.
That king will be a righteous soul, surpassing all others;
he too shall have a perfected mantra, and the yakṣiṇī Vīramatī shall be upon the earth.
By him also was constructed on earth an excellent reliquary for the Jinas; for he was exceedingly wise, yet remained concealed through the power of a yakṣiṇī.
Impelled by that karma of habitual tendencies and driven by former impressions,
the wise one will, in due course, attain the enlightenment that is so difficult to find.
Young men will meet their death through the fault committed by women. At that time, there was one renowned as Vararuci, who was excessively passionate.
The illustrious King Nanda, too, due to the transgression of his past karma,
caused his ministers to become disaffected within the city named Pāṭala.
But Viraktamantravargin, though true to his word and possessed of great strength,
will become afflicted with a grave illness due to the transgression of his past karma.
Afflicted by suffering from a great fever, he will die at midnight. The lifespan of that king shall indeed be sixty-six years;
furthermore, that king will certainly attain the awakening of a śrāvaka.
Furthermore, one of his friends, a young man named Pāṇini, will certainly be prophesied by me as being destined for the state of a Śrāvaka.

Furthermore, O twice-born one, having perfected the mantra of the great-souled Lokīśa, he who desires wisdom shall accomplish the Hālāhala wrathful deity. Another king of that [lineage], known as Candragupta, will arise.
But one who is a *siddha* under the *yakṣa* Jalendra shall cause a kingdom free from thorns to be established.
That lord of the earth was possessed of great wealth, true to his word, and righteous in soul;
yet, having encountered an evil friend, he committed many killings of living beings. Due to the ripening of that karma, he fainted from poisonous eruptions.
Having wept at midnight, he shall establish his son upon the earth—
one known as Bindusāra, a boy who will be a wicked minister.

Then he, having fallen from the state of Candragupta and passed away upon the earth, at that time attained the world of the departed, a destiny devoid of human beings. However, through the practice of mantras, he was then joined [with the divine]; casting off that destiny, he went to heaven.
O Lord of Men, through the arising of the cause of mantras and through volition directed toward wholesome objects, he gradually attains individual enlightenment.
Formerly, this caitya was caused to be built by King Bindusāra, while he was still a youth with an unrefined mind, during his previous existence as Siṃhadatta.
By the power of that karma, he indeed went to heaven, blameless;
for five thousand births, he enjoyed happiness among the immortals.
Having descended from the heavenly realm, he was reborn as a lord of men;
born into the royal family of the wise Candragupta.
Then, while still a youth, the king attained no small amount of happiness;
he became mature, bold, and eloquent, speaking kindly.
He ruled that kingdom under his own authority for seventy years.
O lord of men, when the mantra named Keśinī has been mastered by you,
then those mantras of yours, O Kumāra, will attain success.
At that time, the mantra-siddhi spoken by you will come to pass;
the Soul of the Universe, the Lord of the worlds, will manifest in the form of a youth.
There is no doubt that it will exist for embodied beings in the form of mantras;
out of a desire for their welfare,
at that time, the recitations will always achieve success upon this earth.
The minister of that wise King Bindusāra was the one renowned as Cāṇakya, a young man who had mastered the wrathful deity;
indeed, the wrathful deity named Yamāntaka was mastered by that evil-minded man.
Overcome by anger, he deprived living beings of their lives;
having committed that intense evil deed, he then indeed ruled over three kingdoms.
That contemptible twice-born shall live for a long time;
by the power of that mantra, he shall inhabit an asura body while still in his own flesh.
Having entered an asuric body, he shall live there for a long time;
thereafter, when his body is destroyed, he departs from the hells.
Then that evil-minded one, having experienced the suffering of hell here,
undergoes various undesirable and painful hells born of his own karma.
Having exhausted one kalpa impelled by the mantras of anger,
he falls from that suffering hell and is reborn among the animals.
Having entered the womb of a nāga, he will become one of terrifying form—
a nāga king of great wrath, possessing vast coils and arrogant with poison.
And he who performed cruel deeds...
having passed away, that evildoer went to the world of Yama.
Born from that [state], he became Yama, the King of Death, the Lord of Pretas, possessed of great supernatural power;
having thus experienced thousands of sufferings again and again.
In due course, that dull-witted youth will come to the earth; having attained a human birth, he will be of fearsome appearance. He will be poor, prone to anger, and one who has few friends.
Those Pratyekabuddhas in the world who are free from desire and wander like rhinoceroses, who move about the surface of the earth out of compassion for the lowly and the wretched,
and who enter upon the practice of begging for alms for the sake of wishing for the welfare of sentient beings—
they, being knowers of the minds of others, then beheld that evil-minded one.
But they remained attached to him there out of compassion, and for no other reason.
Then, those pieces of boiled grain were taken by him for the purpose of eating;
however, overcome by the mantra of anger, he revealed his motive at that time.
He offered alms-food there to one of those great-souled ones, saying:
"O all you renunciants, eat this as you please. Out of compassion for him, he then displayed his supernatural power before the Buddhas.
Then, overcome with wonder and his mind uplifted by that power,
he prostrated himself with his head toward all the Buddhas who were like swords.
All those free from faults traveled through the sky as they pleased.

By that same wholesome purpose, he thought of individual enlightenment: "May I become such a great being in this world—possessing a peaceful appearance and great supernormal power—neither suffering nor falling into an evil rebirth."
But having exhausted the remainder of his karma, he will always depart from this world to go to heaven;
in due course, that righteous-souled one shall attain the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha.
Therefore, one should not perform malevolent rites for the sake of mantras.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have prohibited malevolent magic (*ābhicāruka*). However, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who possess great compassion and great supernatural power (*maharddhika*), have demonstrated all ritual actions (*sarvakarmin*) for the sake of the efficacy of mantras.
The Tathāgatas have indeed proclaimed mantras that are like wish-fulfilling gems;
yet those who are of childish form and deluded mind, overcome by anger and greed,
employ against one another those mantras intended for malevolent rites.
Thus, it has been prohibited by the Buddhas and the wise Bodhisattvas in every respect for the mantras to increase the enjoyments of sentient beings.

Now, rising up, one should indeed perform the great protection for the sake of prosperity; however, the mantras are to be accomplished by attracting beings who have taken various forms of birth, but never by obstructing their lives.

At that time, there will be monks of mine who are deeply learned; one named Mātṛceṭa, having composed a hymn of praise for me alone, spoke according to my true qualities and in accordance with my form.
Having everywhere propitiated the mind and delighting in the teaching of the Buddhas, you, Mañjughoṣa, are indeed one whose mantra-attainment is difficult to perceive;
you are virtuous, perfected in ethical conduct, a speaker of Dharma, and profoundly learned.
Formerly, while still in the state of an animal, he spoke this hymn:
"In a delightful city named Nṛpa, in a forest called Khaṇḍa, I wandered at my ease together with a multitude of disciples. (53.442)
A crow dwelling there caused my mind to become serene;
having serenely fixed my mind upon me, he departed for heaven when his body perished.
Having passed away from among the gods, he will be reborn among humans;
having been reborn among humans, he shall go forth into homelessness within my teaching.
Having gone forth into homelessness, that great-souled one, observing his vows and known by the name Mātṛceṭa, will at that time praise me as I truly am.
He will compose a sublime hymn of praise, truthful and endowed with various illustrations and reasons, for the very benefit of all living beings.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he will be intent on exhorting them with hymns of praise at that time, at the end of the age when the world is reviled.

By the ripening of that karma, his body having dissolved, he went to heaven. That wise one, having experienced various pleasures in due course, shall attain awakening—the omniscience, the supreme goal, and the inconceivable.

When four hundred years have passed after I, the Tathāgata, have entered parinirvāṇa, there will be a monk named Nāga who delights in the welfare of this teaching; having attained the stage of *muditā*, he shall live for six hundred years. (53.449)
The *māyūrī* spell was mastered by that great-souled one;
he understood the meaning of various scriptures, the meaning of verbal roots, and the reality of the naturelessness of all things.
And when he has cast off his body, he shall be reborn in Sukhāvatī;
in due course, he will certainly attain the state of Buddhahood.
At that time, there was a monk named Asaṅga, who was skilled in the true meaning of the treatises;
he further analyzed the definitive and interpretable meanings of the sūtras in many ways.
One whose soul is disciplined will become a speaker of the worlds and one of non-trivial character; for such a person, it is said that Śāladūtī is accomplished.

Through the power of that mantra, a superior wisdom arose in him. By compiling the essential meaning of the Sūtras for the long endurance of the Teaching, he lived for one hundred and fifty years; then, having cast off his body, he went to heaven.
Having experienced happiness for a long time while wandering through the long cycle of existence,
this very self will, in due course, attain awakening.
"O monks, in this way, during that era, there will be many kinds of practitioners within my teaching; however, those who possess wisdom and are virtuous in their conduct shall be rare."
Then, at that later time, there was one named Nandana;
he too was one whose soul was joined with the meaning of mantras, a knower of tantras, and very learned.
His *bhadraghaṭa* (auspicious jar) was accomplished through the incantation of a yakṣa.
But in the Mahāyānāgra-sūtra, it was previously told by me that at that time,
the one of great asceticism drew [the child] out from within that jar.
53.459. Because he had previously seen this book in that place, which contained the form of the mantra, no protection was provided there for this jar accomplished by the yakṣa. 53.460.
Due to a lapse in mindfulness from lack of vigilance, the jar was stolen at Mūrdhaṭaka.
Then that monk, a reciter of mantras, became one whose mantra was perfected.
He had the jar inspected, yet he did not see [the snake] therein.
Then, his limbs red with rage, he spoke while trembling:
"From the realm of Brahmā down to a blade of grass, including Śakra and the rest, up to Maheśvara—"
"Though one might be drawn and brought by means of mantras, I am neither a practitioner of mantras nor a king of mantras."

Those mantras which were spoken by the sons of the Buddha, as well as by the supreme Victors, for the purpose of subduing or for taming those who are difficult to tame— if all of those do not exist upon this earth, then I shall not draw out these thieves.

Then, having arisen from that state, the mantra-master, firm in his vows and whose ritual actions were accomplished, being intent on swift summoning, employed that mantra— which serves as the cause for drawing [the deity] through its application— into the various directions.
Indeed, by merely recollecting this in an instant, one performs swift action;
with a single utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*, one can bring Brahmā and the other gods down to earth.
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā and including Śakra, were drawn forth; uttering cries of "Alas! Alas!", they were distressed and made a terrifying noise, crying:
"What shall we do? Why have we been brought here? This is not the fault of the mantra!"
Then the wise and confident monk, acting with haste and speed, addressed the celestial dwellers: "Return the water-jar from here to that place."
Then all the gods spoke to one another, and that monk addressed them: "Quickly tell me—may you be blessed—who has stolen the jar?
Those gods searched everywhere, but they would not give it up.
The Lord of Gods reflected: "By whom has this water-jar been stolen?
Then the glorious Bodhisattva of great splendor beheld the wielder of the thunderbolt.
He had a son who was terrible, exceedingly wrathful, and very cruel;
created in the form of an obstacle, he wandered everywhere throughout the world.
"By that [means], O Lord of Gods, he brought the jar; it was thus addressed:
'There is an obstacle in the Vajra family who sports with ease upon the earth.'"
"Thinking, 'I have been honored by this one,' he took that water-jar.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Gods returned once more to heaven.
Then all the gods were dismissed by him with their respective mantras.
In a mere instant, and even more quickly than a moment, he then brought that obstacle there by force, together with its jar. Then,
by means of that obstacle, he took possession of the jar of the hungry ghosts (pretas).
Then, when Vighna had been led away, he spoke these words:
"The jar was taken to the world of the pretas; we are not at fault in this matter."
Enraged, that great minister addressed the obstacle:
"Go! Go, O great obstacle! Do not act in this manner ever again!"
Then, at that very moment, those hungry ghosts were brought by him;
their minds were agitated and overwhelmed, and they were wretched, for they had needle-like mouths.
They cried out with piteous voices, for they were indeed most terrible; they uttered a mournful cry: "Save us, O Great-Souled One!"
"O Ghaṭa, bring [the vessel] here for us; we shall do as we wish.
Let trembling arise in the Great Compassionate One, the Mantrin."
With a mind moistened by compassion, he spoke these words:
"What suffering do you have in this world? Speak it without delay. (53.480)
With dejected minds, they said: "O Great-souled One, hunger assails us; we have been thirsty in this world of pretas for a long time."
The monk Mahākāruṇika gave that very jar to them. Then, with joyful minds, those beings went quickly to their home;
by the mere thought of them, food and drink appeared in the jar.
In this world, during that wretched time when it has arrived, there will be a monk named Nandaka, a scion of the Candana lineage; he shall live for three hundred years.
A great-souled one who is inclined toward awakening, he will swiftly attain that which is difficult to obtain.
There will be no doubt that in that lowest of ages,
the king Gomimukhya shall cause my teaching to disappear.
Taking the eastern direction as his starting point, he shall even reach the very gateway of Kaśmīra.
Then that fool will destroy the monasteries as well as the reliquaries containing the relics.
That evil-minded one will cause those monks who are perfected in virtue to be slain;
taking his stand in the northern direction, death shall come to him.
Overcome by a wrathful non-human being, that evil-minded one, along with his kingdom, cattle, and kinsmen,
will be seized by a fragment of the mountain and go to the netherworld.
Then his destination below will be from hell to a hell even more terrible;
he shall fall into a fierce and dreadful state, from suffering to a greater suffering,
in the well-known hell of Avīci for those who commit evil deeds.
That evil-minded Gomiṣaṇḍa shall be released after a great eon (mahākalpa).

Having encountered an unwholesome friend, you have committed most dreadful evil deeds. Therefore, with every effort, having gladdened your entire mind toward this teaching of the Tathāgata, you shall enjoy all prosperity. You shall all forever travel upon the path leading to Buddhahood, the eightfold way, to the city that is free from sorrow and decay.

Immediately following him, there will be a protector of the earth known as Buddhapakṣa; he will possess a great faction, be a great renouncer, and delight in the teaching of the Buddhas. There is no doubt that this will happen at that time, in that debased age.
For the king was exceedingly delighted and devoted to the teaching of the Teacher;
he [constructed] monasteries, groves, and shrines, as well as unsurpassed images of the Teacher.
Having caused various ponds, tanks, wells, and lakes to be constructed, a great king, even when his life has reached its end, shall go to heaven.
His son, the accomplished and most heroic Abjaketu, shall rule the earth on this surface of the world for the sake of protecting it for that great-souled Bodhisattva.
By the power of that mantra, he shall live for three hundred years;
through the remainder of that karma, he shall swiftly attain awakening.
Moreover, his son shall be a king of great army and great strength.
Renowned for his profound side, he traversed the entire earth that had arisen.
At that time, King Apañcaka too will be disciplined in soul;
that king of great splendor will, without a doubt, cause many monasteries, dwellings, shrines, as well as ponds and wells to be constructed in various ways.
By him also was accomplished the mantra of the wise Mañjughoṣa,
that six-syllabled utterance which is of great significance and increases enjoyments.
By the power of that mantra, he shall indeed become one of great enjoyment; in due course, being wise, he will swiftly be intent upon awakening.
He shall perform various kinds of deeds within this teaching of the Tathāgata.
At that time, there will be one who dwells in the northern direction,
in the renowned region of Nepal situated within the lap of the Snowy Mountains;
he will be King Mānavadeva, born of the Licchavi lineage.
Even though he was a pauper, having accomplished the purpose of the mantra, he will become one of great enjoyment. O lord of men, the vidyā named Bhogavatī will be mastered by him;
having ruled for eighty years, his kingdom will be free from thieves.
Then, O King, at the risk of his life, he went to the heavenly world;
at that time, the mantras for pacification and nourishment of Śītalā were quickly accomplished.
And the goddess Tārā, world-renowned, and Pāṇḍaravāsinī,
Mahāśvetā, who is ever intent on the welfare of others with an untiring mind.
Apas, Apsaras, and others such as these were then proclaimed as kings in many ways;
they were described in manifold and diverse forms and colors.
Those Mleccha kings who worship the Teacher are as follows:
Vaviṣa, Suvṛṣa, Bhūbhāsa, Subhūbhāsa, Bhākrama, Padakrama, and Kamala is likewise proclaimed.

Apagupta, Vatsaka, and Bhāsvān shall be the last; at the end, there will be Udaya and Jihnu, as well as various Mlecchas. Beyond that, people will have fallen from the bounds of propriety and will serve other men.
Then, destroyed by the falling of weapons, the lords of Nepal will have their knowledge lost and their kingdoms ruined, serving barbarians and thieves. (53.508)
Many kings will be proclaimed, various and dear to the twice-born;
at that time, they shall appear everywhere, having reached China.
But King Hiraṇyagarbha was possessed of a great army and great strength;
he was extensive and well-organized, with abundant people and kinsmen.
Subdued by the Mlecchas yet victorious, he was devoted to the teaching of the Teacher;
by him also the mantra was mastered, just like that of the Greatly Resplendent Kumāra.
Endowed with great power, it is the eight-syllable king of vidyās,
renowned by the name Mahāvīra, the great abode of all attainments.
Therefore, the king of dull intellect was composed for the sake of the kingdom,
by the mere recollection of whom the state of Buddhahood is a certain goal.
O Lord of Men, if you, desiring this unsurpassed boon, appoint me to minor tasks for the sake of the kingdom, [then grant it]. (53.514)
He always commands the entire host of deities beginning with Brahmā;
how much more so, then, the humans in the world and other contemptible beings?
Having lived for a hundred and fifty years, that great king shall go to heaven;
in due course, that righteous soul shall attain supreme enlightenment.
These spells were spoken by the prince in that region.
Even those [beings] possessing passion will achieve success, but others will never succeed in the vidyā-mantra.
The Bodhisattva Mahāvīra, Mañjughoṣa of great splendor, will indeed dwell visibly in that region in the form of a youth.

That supreme, divine field of accomplishment will then be realized by human beings. A king named Turuṣka, possessing a great army and great heroism, will appear in that place, residing in the northern region.
As far as the gateway of Kaśmīra, including Baṣkala, Udyāna, and Kāpiśī.
Then that king shall enjoy the surface of the earth for seven hundred and fifty *yojanas*. That monarch will have two hundred and seventy-seven thousand [subjects];
of this there is no doubt during that lowest age (*yugādhama*).
One who has mastered the mantra shall live for three hundred years;
the wise Keśinī-vidyā was accomplished by the intelligent Narādhyakṣa.
For the sake of his own ultimate welfare, he should cause many monasteries to be built;
likewise, he should construct eighty-six thousand excellent stūpas.
Furthermore, the Perfection of Wisdom, the mother of the Buddhas and the supreme dharma of the Mahāyāna, is established in that region in this world.
When the king's body has perished, he will go to the heavenly realm;
in due course, that lord of the earth will attain supreme enlightenment.
In the meantime, there was a king of that land known by the name Mahāturuṣka. He was wise, highly esteemed, renowned, and devoted to honoring his gurus.
He was indeed accomplishing the mantra of the goddess Tārā, who possesses great supernatural power.
Moreover, on this earth, there will be a king named Apasvāmin, renowned for his mantras;
he will possess a great faction, a vast army, and be known as a lord of great power.
He will also become a king, esteemed by his circle of kinsmen;
at that time, there will be eight thousand monasteries.

By the power of that mantra, he shall live for two hundred years. When his body has perished, he is reborn among the Tuṣita gods as a highly accomplished Bodhisattva, esteemed by the sons of the gods.

In due course, that righteous one, having fully perfected the factors of enlightenment, shall through gradual effort attain incomparable awakening. In that place, the extensive teaching always remains— the teaching previously proclaimed by the Victors, and now likewise proclaimed by me.
It was frequented by those free from passion and also by nāgas of great supernatural power.
At that time, the world-protectors as well as the yakṣas who guard the Teacher’s instruction will become protectors of the true Dharma on earth.
Thus have been proclaimed the many kinds of kings renowned throughout the world;
they have been described, and they will also be described during that most dreadful time.
Beyond that, as far as the border of the region in Ujjayinī, and further still,
as far as the edge of the ocean along the coastal region of Lāḍa.
A king named Śīlāhva, devoted to the teaching of the Buddhas,
will arrive at the city of Valabhī and become a Dharma King.

That king, whose soul is disciplined and who is devoted to the Dharma, will likewise cause to be built monasteries that hold the relics and are variegated, for the sake of the welfare of living beings.

One should perform various kinds of worship of beautiful images of the Jinas and offer them to the most eminent holders of the relics among the illustrious Lords of the World. Such a person is not a master of mantra, but is merely one who has attained excellence through ritual action.
In that region, there was a well-known monk who lived on alms;
he was virtuous, endowed with wisdom, and devoted to the teaching of the Buddhas.
That great-souled one, moving at the proper time, entered for alms;
he beheld the excellent royal palace, vast and crowded with people.
Having entered there seeking alms, he was overcome by hunger;
thirsty and weary in mind, he did not obtain any food at that time.
Having been seized by men, he quickly departed from that house; then, with an anxious mind, he was guarded by the king's soldiers.
They departed from that city and returned to their own abodes at that very moment;
hungry, thirsty, and miserable, they fell into a state of dejection.
Then, when midnight had arrived, that ascetic of feeble mind, his food having been cut off, gave up his life.
At that time, he made this aspiration: "May I become the sovereign of the Lāḍas."
Then, after passing away, that monk shall be reborn into the royal family of a king named Dharā; that great-souled one will be a worshiper of the Teacher’s dispensation.
Having ruled a kingdom free from thorns for thirty years—ten and twenty—he will [attain his goal].
Through the practice of his greedy kinsmen, he becomes faint from indigestion.
Then, his body having perished, the king passed away and went to heaven,
to where the excellent Tuṣita gods dwell and Maitreya resides.
That great-souled one, a listener to the Dharma, will be reborn there;

he will listen to the Dharma with reverence from Maitreya, who possesses great splendor, and in due course, he will attain the enlightenment that is so difficult to find. When King Śīla has passed away, he will become restless there.
Having ruled for half a year, one fortnight, and likewise five months,
he was killed by various weapon-wielding men who lived by the sword.
But because of a fault committed by a woman, he was pierced by a weapon and went to the lower regions;
his younger brother, named Dhruva, likewise attained the state of a fixed star.
A servant, miserly, and foolish shall become the lord of the Lāḍas; all other kings, however, shall have their origins among the servants.
And when Śīlāhva has passed away, their ancestral lineages will then all become kings at Ambhoja on the banks of the river.
Nṛpendra, Sucandra, Dhanu, and likewise Ketu—
these were proclaimed as the names of the sons born in the city of Vāravatī.
Having come to the city of Valabhī, he first performed his preliminary rites; then there were thousands named Prabha and likewise thousands named Viṣṇu.
"An infinite number of kings born in the lineage of the Yādavas have been proclaimed;
the last of them will be a king named Viṣṇu.
Overcome by the curse of a ṛṣi, that wise king, along with his citizens, people, and kinsmen, will see his city submerged in water when the sun has set."
At that time, his [city] Dvāravatī was situated upon the great ocean.

In the northern direction, everywhere upon various peaks and slopes, infinite kings are said to reside, belonging to various castes. Then, thirty lords of men from the Śaka lineage shall arise; learn of them now.
Fifty-three, ten, and eight kings were renowned as rulers of the entire earth; at the end, however, the Nāgasena dynasty was eclipsed, and those others then perished.
Then Viṣṇu, Hara, and the unconquered one named Kunta; then Īśāna, Śarva, Paṅkti, Graha, and another, Suvrata.
Then those kings were deprived of their sovereignty, and they always transgressed the bounds of proper conduct.
At that time, there were two wealthy men of great enjoyment there, born from Viṣṇu.
Then those two chief ministers, beginning with the letter *bha*, were both wealthy, illustrious, renowned, and devoted to the welfare of this teaching.
Thus, while you were reciting the king of mantras, Kumāra became the mantra-king within you; thereafter, two supreme kings arose as lords of men.
At that time, there were seven hundred and eight Śrīkaṇṭhāvāsins;
and the Vaiśyas named Ādityas were residents of Sthāṇvīśvara.
There will be no doubt that at the end, in every place, there shall be a lord of the earth;
he is proclaimed by name as one called with the letter *ha*, a sovereign ruler of all lands.
In that place, these mantras shall indeed attain success;
they are the vidyās for pacification and nourishment proclaimed by Dharmarāja.

In that time of the lowest age, there will indeed be those who have attained accomplishment there: various kinds of wealth consisting of objects of enjoyment, as well as various yakṣiṇīs of great supernatural power who assume diverse forms.
Residing in the southern direction over the earth together with its oceans, there was King Śvetasucandra, who was indeed Sātavāhana.
Mahendra, Śaṅkara, Vallabha, and Mahīpati; Sukeśin and Keśin are renowned in the southern direction. Maṅgala is declared to be Vallabha, and Govinda is Vṛṣaketu.
Mahāpota, Pota, Mahendra, and Candra; Gopendra, Indrasena, Pradyumna, and Mādhava—these were they then.
Gaṇaśaṅkara, Vyāghra, Siṃha, and likewise Budha;
Budha, Śuddha, as well as Kumbha and Nikumbha are celebrated.
Apasmathita and Sumitha,
Bala, Pulina, Sukeśin, and likewise Keśin.
Innumerable and many kings are renowned in the southern direction; understand that they include those of the past, the future, and the present.
Indeed, in this world of manifold death, these beings are overwhelmed by various diseases;
some, having died by the falling of weapons or through famine, have gone to heaven.

Thus have all these kings been described as being turned away [from the Dharma]. Then, the king named Mahendrānta, as well as Sahati, and others—these shall come to be at that time; thus it has occurred.
At that time and in that place, for those who desire the accomplishment of mantras, these mantras—beginning with the Wrathful ones and appropriate for the Vajra [family]—are to be practiced;
they are beneficial for rites of sorcery as well as for the purpose of subjugation.
The great majesty of Mañjuśrī is indeed that of the Youth in the form of a child;
he attains accomplishment in that land when the Kali age has arrived.
Residing on Mount Vindhya by the salt-water ocean,
he is celebrated as Kārttikeya, the bestower of boons upon all beings.
"O, by the wise Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa, [this] command was given:
'For the sake of desiring the welfare of sentient beings, you shall dwell in the southern direction.
(53.576) Those mantras of Kārttikeya which were spoken by the sweet-voiced one—success in that region shall then come to pass, without a doubt. (53.577)
Then, in the region of Śrīparvata, on the slopes and ridges of the Vindhya mountains.

And throughout all the continents, he is celebrated among the Kaliṅgas and the Udras; in the lands of the Mlecchas, he is renowned everywhere due to his triple qualities. From the interior to the shores of the ocean, kings of infinite number are proclaimed.
Indeed, those known as the Kāmarūpa-kula dwell within the interior of the Himalayas;
many kings are said to always reside among the joints of the Udra regions.
The leaders of various non-Aryan tribes were devoted to the worship of the Teacher;
O King, Indra, Sucandra, Mahendra, and others were rulers dwelling among the Mlecchas.
Both kings there, devoted to the teaching for sixteen and a half [years], will be worshippers of the images of the Teacher through your grace... (53.581)

There is no doubt that many excellent kings who have resided in the eastern direction— those of the past, the future, and those who exist at all times— will become clear in their faith toward the teaching of the Jina. 582.53.582.
I shall now describe the first of the excellent kings born in the lineage of the Gauḍas on this earth; he was born in the beautiful city of Vardhamāna to a renowned father.
A king named Lokākhyo, the increaser of Gauḍa, will arise;
in this world yet to be born, he shall be a contemplator of the Dharma.

Many kings have passed away, engaged in various worldly activities; in the intermediate period, there were those who found solace, being middling and possessing middling qualities. Now hear in truth, O lord of men, concerning the kings in the final Kali age.
The king named Samudra and Vikrama are also celebrated;
thereafter follows Mahendra, the preeminent and chief of kings, whose name begins with the letter Sa.
In that lowest of ages, there will be a king named Devarāja;
he will be a preeminent ruler known by various names, wise, and devoted to dharma.
He also had a younger brother named Bala, who was devoted to the teachings and to what is beneficial;
he beautified the eastern region as far as the ocean with the splendor of stūpas.
He will undoubtedly then [govern] the entire earth;
he will always establish monasteries, groves, ponds, parks, and pavilions.
Then the illustrious one, the builder of bridges, will construct crossings;
at that time he shall worship the images of the Teacher and worship those who are devoted to him.
Having ruled a kingdom free from rivals and thorns, a protector of the earth should live for thirty-six years; at the age of thirty, the king should go forth into the religious life.
Then the king, brooding and utterly bewildered, tormented by grief for his son, took up the conduct of an ascetic and brought about his own death.
Then, his body having been destroyed, he was reborn from the hells;
after dwelling for four days in that hellish state, he departed.

Having cast off his body in hell, the king shall always go to heaven; in the world of the virtuous gods, he is known as Śuddhāvāsa. There, with a purified soul and inclined toward awakening, he shall become a king of the gods.

Having experienced happiness in heaven by the hundreds and thousands, they once again attain human birth and subsequently become Buddhas in another existence; for it is by that very same karma that embodied beings are led through various births.
At that time, in the city of Ujjayinī, which was famous among the people as Kālavāṇā,
there lived a preeminent merchant named Ayanī, who possessed great wealth.
In a time when Buddhas are absent, in a world that is empty and without refuge,
Pratyekabuddhas of great supernatural power dwell in this world.
Desiring the welfare of sentient beings, they wander upon the surface of the earth;
having reached the city of Ujjayinī, they entered it for alms.
The great-souled ones, traveling in a group, were descending onto the street;
then Vāṇijeya, seeing that very sage directly before him, [stood there].
Then he invited them to a meal and led them to his own home;
having brought the best of sages there, he quickly invited them to take their seats.
"Come together as a saṅgha; the time for the meal has arrived. Yet those great-souled ones remained silent at that time and did not utter a word.
And he caused the bowl to be given to a merchant,
for a merchant is always one who understands hints and is possessed of intelligence.
He filled the bowl with various kinds of food and then,
with his own hand, carefully offered it to them.
Having taken hold [of him], they all then departed through the sky in every direction;
appearing like a row of lamps, they were seen resting upon the form of the firmament.
Then, his hair standing on end and filled with intense spiritual fervor, he—
And having fallen there upon the ground, his mind was captivated by supernatural power.
Then he made this vow, speaking these words: "By this root of merit which I have acquired from today, may I become the foremost among the best of sages, indeed an unsurpassed Buddha."
Then, for ten thousand births, he was a universal monarch (cakravartin) on earth;
thereafter, having cast off that body, he became a denizen of the heavens for sixty million [lives].
Having experienced happiness for a long time and having abandoned birth among the denizens of heaven,
they then obtain human birth here, subject to the power of others.
His birth shall always be within a royal family here;
that king shall be named Bāla, and he will rule over the eastern region.
For thousands of births, the illustrious king shall attain long-lasting, unobstructed happiness,
and finally, he shall attain omniscience.

Having thus reflected in many ways upon such vast riches, who indeed would then perform worship and entreaties for the Teacher, as well as meritorious deeds suited to the application of the path to enlightenment?
Subsequently, there was a king, a sovereign of the Gauḍas.
He was proclaimed by the name Kumāra, and he too was exceedingly devoted to the Dharma.
Beyond that is the glorious one known as Ukāra;
beyond that, their mutual separation is intended.
For these Gaudas are indeed great separatists and fierce-minded;
therefore, the king known as Deva is remembered as the ruler of Magadha.
Apaso too, though surrounded on all sides by enemies who had destroyed his transport,
will then exercise sovereignty under another named Candra;
yet he too shall be pierced by weapons due to karma previously impelled.
His son, the twelfth, shall live for a succession of twelve months.
At that time, even the boy Apāṅga was killed by a different weapon while still a child.
Thus it was for those fierce ones, whose minds were intent on mutual harm and who delighted in what is unbeneficial.
At that time, there will arise a preeminent king named Bhaka,
the leader of the Gauḍa people, who will be afflicted by a great malady.
Afflicted by that very same disease, he passed away and went to the lower realms. For several days thereafter, one known as Dakāra ruled over him.
In this land of Gauḍa, there will be one named Bhavitā, residing on the banks of the Gaṅgā;
after him, one called Bhaka shall rule for three days.
Then, at that time, Gopālaka will become the king for all time;
that king will be pleasant-spoken, compassionate, and indeed possessed of great strength.
One who is under the sway of women is wretched and foolish; yet a youth may become a conqueror of enemies. By approaching a virtuous friend, he will then become one of great renunciation.
At that time, he saw monasteries, excellent and beautiful shrines, various groves,
as well as ponds abounding with water and magnificent almshouses.
Many who served him were elevated by his fame and renown;
they constructed delightful mountain caves as temples for the gods.
[The land] was overrun by heretics and inhabited by various sectarians.
He has pervaded all directions, reaching even to the shores of the ocean.
Kṛpī will be a ruler who enjoys pleasures, is vigilant, a sovereign, and a lover of dharma;
he will be powerful in the eastern direction, of this there is no doubt.
Afflicted by acute dysentery in his old age, he then resorted to the banks of the Gaṅgā and ruled the kingdom;
having lived for twenty-seven years, he died at eighty.
Then, having cast off that body, he was reborn even among the animals;
thereafter, he became a glorious Naga king, righteous in soul and devoted to the Dharma.
By whomsoever a beautiful caitya and an image of the Teacher were caused to be made for him,
and by whom monasteries were likewise caused to be built there on earth at that time for the sake of the Saṅgha— [by him this merit was acquired].
By the ripening of that karma, when his final existence has been reached,
he shall attain the path to Buddhahood, the unshakable state.

Beyond that, on this earth, lies the city of the Gauḍas, which has been overrun by heretics. In this eastern region, in the city known as Tīrthikasamāhvaya, there was a king renowned as Bhagavat, who was the sovereign lord of the Gauḍas.
Having been consecrated by the powerful Vratina standing to his right,
he ruled there and subsequently proceeded toward the western direction.
Having entered the beautiful city of Sāketa as he desired, he returns once again, humiliated by his enemy.
Having been surrounded by bandits across the eastern ocean as far as its shore, he was struck down by blows from weapons; having died, he has gone to the state of a preta.
Having ruled that small kingdom for three years,
that king was then seized by bandits; having died, he became a preta of great supernatural power (*mahardhika*),
and for three years he exercised sovereignty over the pretas in that very place.
Then, having abandoned that body, he goes to the most dreadful world of the hungry ghosts (preta);
from there, once liberated from birth, he shall always go to the celestial realm (svarloka).
After him, the king known by the name Samudra is proclaimed; that dull-witted and evil-minded one shall obtain the kingdom for three days.
His younger brother, famous by the name Bhasman, shall follow him.
The Lord is free from taking life; he does not commit even the most blameworthy acts. He is compassionate and vigilant, exerting himself with care even regarding his own body.
Although he was seeking the sake of the next world, he did not do so with the body of a living being as an offering;
rather, having encountered an unwholesome friend, he committed much evil karma.
That kingdom was overrun by twice-born brahmins as well as by wretched logicians; likewise, that king obtained various forms of enjoyments for humans and ancestors, as well as manifold prosperity.
Having traveled by stages in that manner, that lord of the earth reached the western direction and took his stand in the northern direction as far as the gateway of Kaśmīra.
There too, having conquered in battle and ruled the kingdom at that time,
he reigned for twelve years and fifteen months everywhere.
On earth, afflicted by disease, he faints again and again;
overcome by great suffering, his body shattered, he goes downward.

When those greedy men, for the sake of the kingdom, harbor mutual hatred toward one another, they will bring about a great clash of weapons against each other. Having then consecrated a young boy named Sakara to the kingship, and having made him a mere figurehead, they will turn back once again.
By them even those who were the foremost among the twice-born were divided from one another.
Having reached the Magadhan country in the city named Udumbara,
he himself consecrated two boys and a preeminent brahmin upon the earth.
Then, proceeding by stages, he reached the eastern direction;
having arrived at the Gauḍa country, he was indeed then without rivals.
Those two chief ministers of Kaliṅga had been slain by that evil-minded one.
Having encountered an unwholesome friend, one commits much killing of living beings.
But those who had previously been honored by kings proud of their martial prowess,
he caused all of them among the inhabitants of Gauḍa to be slain.
Then King Soma by name will become a peerless hero;
his domain shall extend as far as the banks of the Gaṅgā, and beyond that, Vārāṇasī.
That one of dull intellect will destroy the beautiful images of the Teacher,
as well as the vast bridge of Dharma previously proclaimed by the Jinas.
The one of dull intellect, delighting in the words of the heretics, causes [the stūpa] to be burned;
then, being angry, greedy, falsely proud, and indeed disreputable, he [perishes]. (53.652)
At that time, he will destroy monasteries, groves, and shrines, as well as the dwellings of the Nirgranthas on the earth; he will cause the obstruction of all means of livelihood.
And at that time, in the Middle Country, there will be an excellent king named beginning with the letter 'Ra', one whose soul is disciplined and who is steadfast in the livelihood of a Vaiśya.
In this teaching, the king named Soma, who was likewise capable and equal to him,
was also indeed struck down by that king of the naked caste.
He too will have a younger brother named Hakāra, a solitary hero,
accompanied by a great army, valiant and of surpassing prowess.
One known by the letter *Dha* shall designate a king renowned as Soma; thereafter, that king will follow the conduct of a Vaiśya, possessing a great army and great strength.
Then they went to the eastern region, to that excellent city named Puṇḍra; there, relying on the duty of the Kṣatriyas, they were devoid of pride and anger, yet lacking in virtuous conduct.
Compassionate, devoted to the goals of dharma, and wise, he may commit the slaughter of many living beings;
he is intent solely upon the subjugation of others for the sake of not afflicting sentient beings.
He utterly defeated the one named Soma, who followed a course of evil deeds.
660. Then, having been forbidden, he named Soma remained in his own country. {S635} He named Hakāra, who was honored in the kingdom of the Mlecchas, did not turn him back.
661. King Hakāra, whose deeds were pleasing, [endowed] the one devoted to wealth and dharma with prosperity.
Whether he departed by his own power or by means of one who could travel at will,
the deed was performed by those very [beings] filled with joy for the kingdom.
Now he has obtained enjoyments based on his royal livelihood;
previously, he gave food and clothing to a Pratyekabuddha. (53.663)
Then he was given two sandals adorned with a parasol and fly-whisks;
by the power of his merit, these two became the great kings and gods among men.
Having enjoyed the abundance of pleasures at all times among gods and humans,
he shall indeed become a twice-born named Soma, a possessor of great enjoyments.
Having bestowed enjoyments upon the twice-born and having indeed ruled the kingdom at that time, together with [them], he likewise [reigned for] the seventh [year].
Afflicted by diseases of the mouth, he will remain so for fifty-three years, one month, and another seven days and eight nights.
Being devoured by worms, he met his death and went to a downward rebirth;
at that time, that city was overrun and destroyed by non-human beings.
Afflicted by fever and overcome by disease through a purely human fault,
that king then died and passed away by means of the application of a mantra.
