There is a hell renowned by the name Avīci for evildoers;
there that person who has practiced the culmination of evil deeds will be reborn.
Then that one of evil mind is cooked in hell for a great kalpa;
thereafter, he goes to Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Sañjīva, and Kālasūtra.
Having repeatedly experienced the terrible Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana), as well as the worlds of animals and hungry ghosts, and likewise the world of Yama once again; || 53.672 ||

Thus, as one wanders again and again through thousands of births in saṃsāra, one does not find happiness; rather, one shall always be a partaker of suffering. Therefore, with every effort, [one should apply oneself] to this teaching of the Tathāgata.
Purify your entire mind and proceed toward the state of freedom from feverish distress.
675. Toward the Buddha, benefit and harm result in infinite karma. One should construct a temple for the Buddha, and likewise for the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
In this world, those kings who worship the Three Jewels become supreme;
they are renowned for their great power, possess great kingdoms, enjoy great wealth, and are lords of riches.
O King, having worshipped the foremost of the worlds, one shall obtain various kinds of happiness and abundant prosperity; indeed, one shall attain lordship over the world.
They attain the state of Śakra, then the state of Yama, and again and again the state of Brahmā; they become Pratyekabuddhas, Buddhas, and indeed Śrāvakas on this earth.
Having attained the preeminence of the three vehicles, two have gone to a state free from desire.
For thus the Buddhas are inconceivable, and the Buddha-knowledge is also inconceivable;
for their fruit is inconceivable, and their maturation is inconceivable.
After this, when the king named Soma has also passed away from the earth, the Gauḍa realm will become characterized by mutual conflict;
its people will always have their weapons raised and will show no regard for one another.

For fifty-three days, and likewise for seven months, and then for another month, the rule of a collective kingship (gaṇarājya) shall then prevail forever on this earth within that monastery situated on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
After that, the son of that man named Soma was born;
he passed away after eight months and five and a half days.
Then, a child of the Vaiśya caste named Nāgarāja will become the king of Gauḍa.
While that king was seated at the end [of the assembly], Jayā and the others stood there; the twice-born were surrounded by Vaiśyas, and the one named Nāga was surrounded on all sides by Vaiśyas.
Then there will be calamities of famine and they will be oppressed by foreign armies. Their kingdom will not endure; it will be crowded with great thieves.
Having fallen away from moral boundaries, they will... [53.685]
For five years during the rainy season, he indeed lived in great distress;
they then brought about his death by committing many acts of killing living beings.
Due to the transgression of their past karma, those people will indeed adopt the livelihood of Vaiśyas;
at that time, they will become prone to mutual agitation. Thus it occurred. 53.687.
Then, in the Gauḍatantra, that powerful lord of men will undoubtedly resort to the conduct of a Kṣatriya. (53.688)
Some were pierced by weapons, while others were overwhelmed by diseases;
having met their end, those lords of men then departed for the hells.
There, O lord of men, a child who was the primary object of women's affection became once again a sovereign ruler.
Likewise, one who has been pierced by a weapon and killed shall remain there for exactly one fortnight.
Amidst the onset of a great famine and the turmoil of foreign armies,
the people of the eastern lands were scattered, terrified, and despondent.

There will be no doubt that there will be lords of men in that region. Born in Apāmādhurā, a merchant formerly known as Vaiśya, he will be an excellent king; even he, whose form is honored, shall become the king of the Māgadhas.
His younger brother, named Bhaka, settled in the eastern direction. His son, named Paka, was also born in the eastern lands;
he is declared to be a preeminent Kṣatriya who follows the lineage of Bālabandha.
For seventeen years he remained confined in prison;
bound by the king named Gopa, that Blessed One was released in the city called Bhagavatī.
Later, a great king named Aka came from the western region and established himself on the banks of the Gaṅgā as far as the eastern horizon.

The great king of the Śūdra caste, possessing a vast army and great strength, takes his stand upon that shore, remaining there on all sides. Having seized the city renowned among the Gauḍas as the famous Tīrthāhva, that mighty king remains in occupation.
And there a young kṣatriya arrived together with a merchant;
he entered there at night and was honored at the end of the night.
A king of the Śūdra caste, renowned as Nanda, shall once again establish [the law] throughout the city named Nandapura, extending as far as the banks of the Gaṅgā.
Then he established that infant on the throne of the Magadhas;
having reached the city of Vārāṇasī in the Kāśi region, [he was installed] in the inner palace.
Then the mighty king of the Śūdra caste entered [the city], afflicted with suffering by a great disease; he then consecrated his son.
Then, having consecrated the boy named Grahākhya as king,
he was indeed overwhelmed by a great disease and rolled upon the ground.
Then, having sighed deeply, even though his body was broken by effort, he crossed over from the animal realm;
at that time, he dwelt among the animals for fifteen months.
Then, having been liberated from birth, he will be reborn among the gods;

for twenty lifetimes, he will indeed experience various divine prosperities. (53.704) Then, in due course, that righteous-souled one shall attain the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha, owing to the very karma he had accumulated in previous births. (53.705)

The great-souled Pratyekabuddha was indeed completely covered with garments; they offered him sandals for the sake of [providing for] elephants, horses, and chariots, and those of resolute intellect then gave him food as well.

By the ripening of that karma, he will become Śatakratu, the king of the gods, in this world of the gods for thirty koṭis of births; then, having come to earth, he will become a king in this present life.
He will become the enjoyer of a kingdom acquired by others;
moreover, his son will be established as king in Vārāṇasī,
yet his kingdom will be utterly destroyed, ruined, and plundered on all sides.
At that time, that kingdom was for the most part overrun by twice-born men and enemies.
That king, heedless and acting according to his own desires, was marked by the planets;
indeed, in his final hour, he died later struck down by an enemy.
When King Soma had passed away, the Māgadha king became their ruler over the entire eastern region, though they were mutually opposed to one another.
Beyond that, in Vārāṇasī as far as the banks of the Gaṅgā,
there will then be a Kṣatriya king named with the letter *pa*. He will be one who was honored by that person of the Śūdra caste named with the letter *a*.
In a city named Nanda, situated on the bank of the Gaṅgā, there will be a Kṣatriya king impelled by his past actions;
he himself performed that deed, and it was also approved by him.
In the past, at that time when the Teacher named Kanaka had appeared,
there was a very wealthy guild-president in the great city of Vārāṇasī.
That merchant’s young son, surrounded by other children,
went out onto the street for the purpose of playing in the dust.
Having seen that excellent stūpa in my own home, worshipped by my father and mother,
I turned my mind toward that very stūpa and constructed one out of dust.
Then he performed worship with the remains of offered flowers;
with mindfulness directed toward faith in the Buddha, he praised that stūpa.
There, a boy, surrounded by children, plays;
at that time, he alone was the foremost disciple of the Jina, the Teacher Kanaka.
Free from faults, disciplined in self, his mind liberated from the three realms.
Then, being free from all faults, he wandered for alms.
Then he entered the most beautiful city of Vārāṇasī;
at that time, free from passion, he went to the region where those fools were on earth,
where all those children were gathered together on every side.
"Come, monk! Come here! Pay homage to the Teacher’s caitya.
We have constructed it with great effort; do you not see how beautiful it is? (53.721)
Then the merchant’s young son, having taken a roll of grass,
playfully bound the one who was free from passion and possessed of great supernatural power.

There, that one who was free from passion and possessed of great supernatural power took heed; standing there on the earth, he beheld the stupa that had been built by them. Placing his hand upon the head of the fool, the one of noble mind spoke thus: [53.723]
"Release the boy; let us go where the work you commissioned is located.
Then they all arrived at the place on earth where the receptacle for the relics was situated.
Having paid homage, that great-souled hero, free from passion, set out once again for alms as he desired, together with those children of his own age.
Then the young son of the merchant, taking hold of the edge of the robe,
led him to his own home and had food prepared for him to eat.
Then that chief of merchants, seeing that foolish man...
having seized by the hem of his robe the one who was free from passion and possessed of great supernatural power.
Terrified and with his hair standing on end, my elder brother came to my house;
falling at my feet, he quickly caused the boy to be released.
Having taken hold of his son, he diligently sought his forgiveness;
indeed, taking up the vessel before the Victorious One, the foremost Conqueror, the Benefactor.
He filled that bowl with rice, sauces, and solid foods; then he addressed his son, saying, "Take this bowl and give it [to him], sir."
Then the child, now possessing wisdom, having diligently washed his hands and taken a bowl full [of food], should offer it to the one free from passion.
Having bowed down to him, he quickly prostrated himself on the ground at his feet.
Vītarāga, having taken hold of him, reached the monastery and ate;
for Vītarāga was then truly at ease and attained a state of pleasant contact.

Furthermore, another fool there, his mind possessed by envy, on the following day, with a heart full of anger, took a great quantity of solid and soft food and gave it to that one who was free from passion.
"If there is any merit whatsoever in you, by giving this alms-food,
may I become the wealthiest man on earth through this son of a merchant."
Then all those heretics and the wives of the twice-born gathered together; having assembled, they all engaged in a quarrel, reviling him:
"You are a fool! You do not know what the destiny of the shaven-headed ones is!"
Since these do not exist by way of their own nature, how could there be liberation for others?
Such hatred as had arisen in that young being was destroyed by the Teacher, who described these [qualities] to them.
He shall cause the construction of the Dharmasetu monastery, the Vihāra of Sadākīrti, and the excellent Caitya on earth; indeed, he shall have them built for the son of the preeminent merchant chief.
Having given gifts to these beggars, what will be their destination?
For those whose minds are seized by evil destinies, I shall effect their deliverance.
That very child who was the most wicked, even he who was the king named Soma—
having experienced suffering for a long time, this is his ultimate retribution.
This son of the chief merchant, his body having perished, went to heaven;
there he experienced the happiness of the celestial dwellers for a long time, from time to time.
Having passed away from here, he will be reborn in this world of the gods;
then, in his final birth, he shall forever sever all bonds.
Having undergone three births, that mortal shall again become a lord of the earth; and then, by the power of karma, he shall fall again and again in various places at various times.
He who, out of childish fickleness, offers a discarded flower at a stūpa shall be born in this world as a king ruling over the earth.
Therefore, his enjoyments were indeed afflicted; that was the fruit of his afflicted giving.
Having obtained those enjoyments with great suffering, that king was like one whose joints have been shattered.
Because of instability, foolishness, and constant fickleness of mind,
one should always perform great worship upon the earth where the relics of the Teacher are enshrined.
By the ripening of that karma, one’s royal sovereignty may become unstable;
having been a king, one becomes [otherwise], and having not been [a king], one returns [to that state].
He shall exercise lordship as a ruler over the northern, western, and central regions of the earth.
That one whose intellect is liberated is a bound person, while that child is liberated again.
Bound by that ripening of karma, the fool was liberated;
for five hundred births indeed, the fool was bound and liberated.
Then, in his final birth, he will forever sever all bonds. At fifty-five or seventy-seven years of age,
he will become a king upon the earth, ruling as far as the eastern ocean.
But all those forest-dwelling barbarians and thieves settled in the interior of the Vindhya range shall remain subject to the king known by the name Pa on this earth.
Residing in the lap of the Himalaya mountains and taking refuge in the northern direction,
that Kṣatriya king then enjoys all the provinces.
Having built a stūpa out of dust out of ignorance and in a state of childishness, he shall become a king among the Māgadhas, without rivals and free from thorns,
ruling as far as this forested border and reaching the eastern ocean.
To the west of Lauhitya is the wise one, and likewise Himavat to the north; to the west is the beautiful city of Kāśī, or indeed the city called Śṛṅga.
In this interval, there shall be a protector of the earth who bestows the teachings of the Teacher.
Having conquered those two kings named Pañcakesarins, he ruled his own kingdom;
and all those sons of Siṃhaja were likewise then destroyed and uprooted.
O King, when the ten regions (daśānūpa) take refuge on the eastern shore of the Himalayan slopes,
that Kṣatriya king shall then enjoy all the inhabited lands;
and as his birth increases, so too shall his enjoyments increase.
And when the seventy-fifth year has been declared, one's enjoyments shall attain stability.
They shall live for eighty years, and likewise for seven times seven more;
then, overcome by old age, he will pass away and go to heaven.
Having thus experienced long-lasting happiness in this world of the gods, the king, however, falls again due to his previously accumulated karma;
he dwells for a month among the animals as a powerful Naga king.
Then, after his body has perished, he will be reborn among humans;
born as a wise Kṣatriya, he will become a skilled merchant living by trade.
Having encountered a spiritual friend, he will be one who enjoys the teaching of the Jina.
One should accomplish the Queen of Vidyās, the goddess Tārā of great supernatural power.
But that Jina, who has accomplished the mantras and moves according to his will,
will then become the Sugata, the king of the Vidyādharas.
At that time, he was renowned as a universal monarch (cakravartin) by the name Citraketu;
likewise, that wise one was famous for his deeds among the Vidyādharas.
For eighty-nine and seven [i.e., ninety-six] times ten million years,
he shall possess divine and human happiness as a universal monarch (cakravartin).
His retinue of sixty times ten million maidens was born to him.
Then, after his body has been cast off, urged on by the goddess Tārā,
he shall go to the lord of the gods and there teach the Dharma;
O protector of the earth, he will gradually and swiftly become intent upon awakening.
When King Pakāra had passed away during that time of the debased age, his servants, having resorted to mutual discord and great conflict,
exercised the sovereignty of the kingdom for seven days.
Then, after seven days, the king named Va will likewise be destroyed by a thunderbolt and depart for the various directions.
When that king named Pa has passed away, another known as Bha shall be regarded as the successor; he too shall exercise the sovereignty of the kingdom for three years.
His younger brother, known by the name Vakāra and consecrated by the ascetic,
shall be Rājyavardhana for four years.
53.770–773. Both of these, having suffered from indigestion and being overcome by sudden dysentery and fainting, passed away in this world and were reborn among the yakṣas.
Thereafter, those righteous ones attained the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha in due course.
His younger brother, a Kṣatriya named Dhaka who is devoted to righteousness, will also become king for three years...
he will be the lord of men... || 53.774 ||
His younger brother, the renowned king named Vaka,
will then become the sovereign ruler of the entire earth in this land.
He possesses elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles, as well as boats on all sides;
he is the conqueror of all enemies encountered in battle.
He [will rule] over all these provinces and the entire earth, adorning it with images of the Teacher, monasteries, and reliquaries of the Jinas.
It truly beautifies the entire earth in its totality.
Likewise, his [son] was Nṛpapūrvī, and then a twice-born Śākyaja;
he was proud, sharp-witted, wise, inclined toward awakening, and possessed of a mind that honors [the Dharma].

In that lowest of ages (*yugādhama*), at that time, she alone attains a state of happiness for him. The Kṣatriya is declared to be of foremost intellect, a king indeed devoted to righteousness (*dharmavatsala*).
He shall live for one hundred and twenty years, and with effort, for seven and eight more. Through the very fault committed by a woman, he will pass away and go to heaven.
The wise one, by following this gradual sequence, shall attain supreme enlightenment.
In the preeminent city of the Gauḍas, among the great people beginning with the letter *ba*, he who has conquered his enemies shall indeed exercise sovereignty there in every direction.
He had seven and eight monasteries constructed there;
indeed, they were occupied by the foremost of the twice-born, who were devoted to the practice of eating only vegetables.
Having obtained his assistance, he shall rule the kingdom on all sides; there, that lord of men shall live for eighty-one years.
Through the fault of his servants, that righteous-souled one died and went to heaven;
in due course, he likewise ruled over the kingdom even of the gods.
Then, having cast off this body, he shall go from heaven to the most excellent of heavens,
having fulfilled the wholesome dharmas that are the causes of his awakening.
The king, indeed, shall be his servant and shall rule a kingdom free from thorns; he will be a protector of the earth whose name begins with the letter *ya*.
Then, in that age, he shall rule the kingdom for eight years;
yet he himself will be slain by women, and having been killed, he will go to the lower realms.
Furthermore, there will be a Kṣatriya king of the Pakāra lineage;
by him, that entire class of servants will be slaughtered without interval.
Having encountered an unwholesome friend, he committed the slaughter of many living beings;
in this entire world, he shall become one who is intoxicated by the intensity of his power.
Quick-acting yet fickle, a drunkard fond of deceivers,
he was then utterly deluded by the intoxication of liquor as he lay upon the ground.
He was pierced by the blows of weapons from his enemies who had risen up against him.
789. Then, his body having been shattered, he passed away and went downward.
He too had a certain brother, known by a name beginning with the letter *ra*,
who ruled the kingdom on earth for forty-eight days.
Having given wealth to the twice-born, he shall meet his end; of this there is no doubt.
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, he will become a dog-eater and the like.
He himself will then belong to the Śūdra caste, deformed and indeed despised.
Abounding in unrighteousness, immoral, and always delighting in conflict.
After him, there will be a famous lord of the earth named Śrī,
a great king devoted to righteousness, who will rule according to the Gauḍa Tantra.
He will [deal with] the groups of the twice-born, the vassals, as well as the self-restrained and those who have gone forth into the religious life.
He indeed causes all [virtues] to perish, being always intent upon suppression.
He is the enforcer of severe punishments, as well as the slayer of thieves;
he is the restrainer of all the wicked who have taken refuge in heretical vows.
When he is liberated from the sin, having indeed ruled the kingdom at that time,
the king shall live there for seventeen years.
But having been overcome by the suffering of leprosy, he passed away and was reborn as an animal; from among animals, he became a wise Naga king with a great hood.
Then, having assumed a physical form that was most loathsome and full of swelling arrogance,
he experienced suffering for a long time as a consequence of his own ultimate transgression of dharma.
Such kings, who increase the world, have been described;
they are known throughout this entire world as those who abide in their former bodies.
Then, from the lineage of the king known as Pakāra, another Kṣatriya was born,
a hero of great prowess who became the sovereign of the three oceans.
In this eastern land, there will arise one of great army and great power,
[adorned] with divine monasteries, dwellings, and temples containing the relics of the Teacher.
With various gardens, ponds, wells, pavilions, and bridges, as well as perpetual almshouses, he constantly beautifies the earth.
That devotee, having relied upon the supreme vehicle, the most excellent sound of the Jina, was indeed brought to final consummation at that time by one who had gone forth as a Śākya monk.
He shall avoid all unfavorable conditions and cultivate favorable conditions;
renowned by the name beginning with the letter *Ka*, he will be possessed of mindfulness and be highly learned.
Having ruled the kingdom for twenty-one years,
that protector of the earth then met his end through cholera and ascended to heaven.
That wise one, in due course, swiftly became destined for enlightenment.
But his remaining descendants lived in dependence on others, their dwellings and livelihoods being subject to the will of others. || 53.808 ||
Beyond that time, O King, there will be rulers who live like cowherds and servants;
there is no doubt that people will become as wretched as the twice-born.
At that time, when the most unrighteous era has arrived and the Teacher’s dispensation has perished,
one should engage sentient beings in the welfare of virtue by means of the discourse on mantras.

However, those mantras for increasing enjoyment which were taught by Kumāra should then be practiced at that time for the sake of royal sovereignty; yet, the supreme accomplishment (uttamā siddhiḥ) was not to be achieved in that region at that time.
Likewise at the delightful Dharmacakra [temple], and likewise in the Mahābodhi forest, where that Blessed One entered into peace and the state beyond substrate—
there these two mantras are to be accomplished, namely the deities Tārā and Bhṛkuṭī.
Likewise, on the shore of the ocean, and always at Visphūrjī, the best of rivers;
and everywhere along the banks of the Gaṅgā, the practice originating from the lotus is to be accomplished.
That Bodhisattva who was renowned by the name Candra is indeed proclaimed as the Tārā, the queen of vidyās of great supernatural power.
Assuming the form of women, the goddesses wandered everywhere throughout the world with hearts moistened by compassion, desiring the welfare of sentient beings. 53.815 ||
And [the term] "one called a woman" applies to those residing in the Sahā world-system.
However, a Bodhisattva of great supernatural power (maharddhika) is a master immediately following the tenth stage (bhūmi).
The goddess Tārā is proclaimed as the one to be disciplined by all sentient beings; she provides effortless accomplishment for his protection, defense, and concealment.
The Goddess, who increases enjoyment and sovereignty, is accomplished through effort; she is also the cause for the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment.
Then the Goddess, filled with compassion for embodied beings, followed them;
in the form of a mantra, she became the cause for the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment for all sentient beings.
For the sake of the satisfaction and nourishment of all, she took her place in the eastern direction.
Furthermore, having again made himself five hundred thousandfold, he then manifested himself in many ways once more.
He wanders over the entire earth, bounded by the four oceans; thereafter, his success will come either in the east at Vārāṇasī or further beyond.
The eastern region of that goddess is proclaimed as his own field;
there, the king of the yakṣas, Jambhala of great splendor, attains success.
At that time, during this most degenerate age, he is sought by beings who desire enjoyments.
The Yakṣa King and Tārā Devī are to be accomplished for the sake of one who desires nourishment.
Furthermore, wrathful mantras should be accomplished in the southern region,
or among the Mlecchas, thieves, and islands, or even in the midst of the ocean.
And then Tārā is accomplished, as well as the King of Yakṣas of great power,
in Harikeṭa, Karmaraṅga, Kāmarūpa, and the place called Kalaśa.
All the various hosts of female messengers and the yakṣiṇīs of great supernatural power— those mantras for the sake of enjoyment which were sung by Mañjughoṣa—
will achieve accomplishment in that region as they would not in other places.
In the eastern direction and in the intermediate directions, various mantras with diverse causes were taught at that time; they are to be accomplished by embodied beings.
Likewise, in the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa), there were various ministers and kings;
understand that they possessed limited intelligence and a weakness of spirit regarding the vastness [of the teachings].
A summary of the principal monarchs is now declared, along with their number.
The one beginning with *ma*, the one beginning with *na*, and the one beginning with *pa* are proclaimed;
likewise the one beginning with *da*, the one beginning with *i*, the one beginning with *sa*, and the one beginning with *a*. (53.829)
That which is called *graha* and that which is called *kīrti*, and that which begins with the letter *ha* is proclaimed; and when it begins with the letter *śa*, then it occurs. 53.830.
That which begins with *ja*, that which begins with *ba*, that which begins with *la* marked by the moon,
and likewise that which is renowned as beginning with *ha*, and furthermore that which begins with *a*;
{S649} the letter *sa* and that which begins with *la* are called "female" (*stryākhyā*) and are hated by the world.
Beginning with the letter *sa* and ending with the one called *ma*, they are the sovereign lords of the worlds.

In due course, the marks of the karmic agents will be such that even Brāhmaṇas will adopt the livelihood of Vaiśyas; they will be mostly engaged in unrighteous acts, hateful, and lustful toward women.
At that time, during the lowest of ages, there will undoubtedly be kings who possess vast retinues; these lords of men will rule over the Middle Country.
In that lowest of ages, the lifespan of humans will be exactly one hundred and twenty years;
at that time, this is proclaimed as a long life.
Among those who were otherwise preeminent, there will be fluctuations of high and low status;
indeed, it is said that at that time, in that age, all kings will be short-lived.
Likewise, on the banks of the river Gaṅgā and on the slopes of the Himalayas,
as well as in the land of Kāmarūpa, there will be kings.
It is said that [these kings] will appear at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end, in the regions of Aṅga.
The first is Vṛtsudhāna, and he is proclaimed as Karmarāja.
At Apāpā were Aṅgapati, Tadaṅga, Subhūti, and Bhūti;
at Sadaha was Bhavadatta; and these were the ones born in Kāmarūpa.
From Apāṅga down to Subhūmi, Mṛga, and Kumāra, these were the sites of the two brothers in Vaiśālī; and there, in that supreme city named Kapila, this Sage was born.

The Śākyas born of the inner apartments are declared to be kings descended from the Sun and the Ikṣvāku lineage; they are renowned as ending with Śuddhodana, and [the lineages] known as Śākya and Śākyavardhana.
However, the mantras taught by the preeminent ones of the world are said to be of little power;
likewise, those mantras proclaimed by the Jinas and all the hosts of servants [are so].

Likewise, all the various hosts of female messengers belonging to both the Vajra and Lotus families are accomplished when they are being practiced by those who are skilled in the meaning of mantra and tantra. 53.843.
All those worldly mantras are accomplished here in this central region; specifically,
those spoken by the Jina should be practiced in the Middle Country through various types of signs and various types of causes.
But for embodied beings, various accomplishments arise from the application of various practices.

Likewise, in the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa), mantras are indeed to be accomplished for the increase of enjoyments, for protection, for rescue, and for the subjugation and attraction of embodied beings.
The past and future kings of the Middle Country have been described according to their various forms and signs, as well as their diverse lifespans and lineages.

All kings are said to be of three types—superior, inferior, and middling; likewise, one should apply the threefold accomplishment according to the three times. Furthermore, the best of sages have declared that mantras are likewise of three kinds.
Infinite kings are said to exist in the Middle Country, as well as in the west, the north, the southwest, the east, and likewise in all the intermediate directions;
they are found throughout all the outer continents, distinguished in four ways.
Infinite are the lords of the earth who have been proclaimed; infinite are the means for accomplishing mantras.
Taking refuge in the infinite directions, infinite are the accomplishments of mantra.
When the Sage’s teaching had disappeared for the sake of both punishment and favor,
at that time, Mañjughoṣa indeed spoke these mantras to the kings.
The practice of the [proper] time is taught for the purpose of playful protection and transformation;
it concerns the majesty of mantra and the destinies and wombs of sentient beings, O King. This has been fully explained according to place and time for those who desire to accomplish the mantra.
850. Eight hundred kings have been mentioned when the path [of the teachings] had vanished;
at the end, they were awakened to the greatness of the qualities of the mantras and their fruit. 53.853.

Two other vehicles have been described; O King, those who were previously instructed are established [in them] at that time of the lowest age, without a doubt. All the kings who have been mentioned are those who have taken refuge in their respective directions.
Having firmly established themselves in the renunciant life within the teaching of the Śākyas,
they will then carry out the purpose of the instruction, always delighting in the practice of mantra.
When the Best of Sages, the sole supreme eye of the world, has set, [they shall do so].
O Prince, I shall speak of them; listen then with a one-pointed mind.
At the end of the age, when the world has become corrupt and the teaching of the Teacher has declined on earth,
there will undoubtedly be ascetics who live by the ways of kings.
For example, there is the one known as Mātṛceṭa and the renowned Kusuma;
in the [place] called by the letter *ma*, there is the one called by the letter *ku*, who is exceedingly devoted to the Dharma.
And he who is known as Nāgāhva is named Ratnasambhava; he who is designated by the letter Ga is called Kumāra, and he who is designated by the letter Va is the contemplator of Dharma.
That great-souled one named A is difficult to master in the Teacher’s instruction;
the wise one named La is proclaimed as being honored for his virtues.
One whose name begins with the letter *ra* and is proclaimed to begin with the letter *na* will be a king on the side of the Buddha, an illuminator of the Teacher’s dispensation. (53.861)
The twice-born ascetic known as Ākāra was likewise renowned;
he resided in the city of Sāketa and was eighty years of age.
Likewise, there will be a monk beginning with the letter A who possesses passion; he will dwell in the southern direction, live for sixty years, be wise, and reside in the city named Kāśyā.
The ascetic whose name begins with the letter *Tha* is renowned in the southern direction;
he is a refuter of the doctrines of others and an ascetic who has attained mastery over mantras.
Another excellent renunciant, a resident of the city of Saihnika, was an ignoble man who perceived himself as noble; he lived on the island of Siṃhala. (53.862–865)
He will be a refuter of the proponents of other doctrines and a critic of the views of the heretics; indeed, he will exist at that terrible time at the end of the age.
One whose name begins with the letter *va* is declared a *yati*, and one beginning with *la* is celebrated as such;
likewise, one beginning with *ra* or *vi* will be a *bhikṣu* who has gone forth.
There is no doubt that he will be devoted to the teaching of the Teacher.
When King Bālāka is renowned, there will likewise be an ascetic whose name begins with the letter *sa*.
He will always construct monasteries, groves, and shrines, as well as ponds, wells,
statues of the Teacher, and various emblems, as well as bridges and causeways.
There will be no doubt; he is remembered as one who transcends the scriptures and ascends upward.
Beyond that, the one beginning with the letter *ma* and the one beginning with the letter *ka* have been proclaimed.
Apāṅga, Nakārādya, Sudatta, Suṣeṇa, and Senakīrtita; Dattaka and Dinaka, who indeed reviles the doctrines of others.

One was formerly a merchant and the other formerly a physician; both were concerned for the poor and the needy. The first became a renowned ascetic beginning with the letter *ca*, and after him came one beginning with the letter *ra*.
One whose name begins with the letter *bha* will be renowned for his faith and will commission the making of images of the Teacher;
likewise, one whose name begins with the letter *ma* will be born as an intelligent ascetic and similarly possessed of faith.
Various ascetics will be proclaimed, and they shall be infinite;
all those ascetics will be renowned as illuminators of the Teacher’s dispensation.
And when this teaching has perished and is without light upon the earth at that time, they will undoubtedly fashion beautiful images of the Teacher. 53.875.

All of them have indeed been prophesied for enlightenment; they are always foremost among my [disciples]. They are worthy of offerings in the world, as well as bringers of an end to the three realms of existence.
Through their application to mantra and tantra, they are renowned and remembered as makers of glory.

Now, however, I shall describe how, in that most dreadful time, there will be those among the twice-born who are virtuous in nature, yet who resort to the conduct of kings through their application of mantras and tantras throughout this entire world.
There was an excellent brahmin named Vakāra, wealthy and a master of the Vedas;
he wandered throughout this entire earth for the sake of debate. (53.878)
He who is devoted to the destruction of rival sects throughout the earth bounded by the three oceans,
yet remains intent on the recitation of the six-syllable mantra, shall indeed be face-to-face with me through his speech.

The prince Gītavāhya lived out many eons for the sake of desiring the welfare of sentient beings; he was honored and possessed of unwearied intelligence. Then there were Jaya, Sujaya, Kīrtimān, and after him Śubhamat.
Noble by birth and truly righteous, he was diligent, virtuous, and gentle.
Madhu and Sumadhu were then perfected; homage to them! Then there were the Raghus of the Śūdra caste, as well as others born of the Śaka lineage.
All of them, too, became reciters of mantras here through the word of Kumāra.
And all those virtuous men were wise and highly learned;
they were brought face-to-face with the ministers and established in the administration of the kingdom.
To the west of that place, there will be a renowned twice-born man named Vikāra;
in the city known as Puṣpa, he will become a Krodhasiddhaka.
Indeed, due to poverty and humiliation, he will exercise suppression over kings.
Mañjughoṣa, he who is proclaimed here as Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath,
is indeed the tamer of those beings who are wicked and difficult to subdue.
For the purpose of warding off what is harmful, for the sake of what is beneficial, and for the sake of increasing [virtue],
it was solely for the benefit of sentient beings, even though it obstructed his own body and life.
For that young brahmin was foolish, poor, and incited by anger;
he provoked that wrath which threatened the life of the king. (53.887)
Beyond him was another renowned twice-born man whose name began with the letter 'Sa';
he was skilled in the meaning of mantras and possessed a disciplined mind.
Then the Lord became widely renowned as a great reciter of mantras;
he accomplished that mantra solely for the purpose of subjugation and for no other reason.
Once all beings were brought under his control, he thereafter became possessed of wealth.
Beyond that, there will be a renowned twice-born man, a contemplator of dharma and artha, whose name begins with the letter *śa* and ends with *ta*. He will appear among the people of Mālava;
for he will be foremost in the teaching, gracious, and a reciter of mantras upon this earth.

Vetālas, grahas, and evil spirits; brahmarākṣasas and rākṣasas; all pūtanās and bhūtas, as well as various kinds of flesh-eaters—all those without exception, whether stationary or moving, were under her control.
Indeed, all those who possess self-control are likewise beneficial to him who bears the marks of a twice-born.
Beyond that, there will be a renowned twice-born man in the southern region,
known as one whose name begins with the letter *va*, who is devoted to the teaching of the Teacher.
In monasteries, groves, and sacred shrines, and before delightful images of the Teacher,
he indeed adorns the entire earth as far as the two oceans.
To the west of that [place] was renowned another, a most excellent twice-born man of great wealth;
likewise known as one whose name begins with the letter *Bha*, he resided in the southern direction.
The noble-souled one, reciting mantras, was indeed firmly intent upon awakening. In the Middle Country, there was a renowned brahmin named Pūrṇa;
he was both disciplined and well-disciplined, a resident of Madhurā.
One whose name begins with the letter *bha* will be a lord of wealth and a minister who performs the king's counsel and worship.
Thus have these twice-born ones been described, who honor the teaching of the Teacher;
they are the foremost among those of middle, final, and initial [stages], born of various lineages and shrines.
Those other twice-born ones are worshippers of the twice-born from various lands; they belong to various lineages and clans, and their spheres of conduct are diverse.

They are declared to be ascetics from all quarters and young brahmins (*māṇava*) of great learning. The Self-Existent One (*Svayambhū*), the King of Dharma, who accomplishes the welfare of all sentient beings, is proclaimed as the one for all living beings and for the three gods.
The four great kings are renowned throughout all worlds:
Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra the king of the yakṣas, and Śakra; and the lifespan of the gods is declared to be fixed.
Suyāma, the son of the gods, and Sunirmita, the Vaśavartin;
Santuṣita is declared to be the king, another lord of the desire realm.

Śakra and the others, who possess a single name, are likewise the lords of the desire realm; they always share a single basis, are of one form, and possess great supernatural power. Though they are said to be infinite, those gods also assume various forms.
901. Therefore, from that point upward, they are all equal and possess great supernatural powers (maharddhika). || 53.904 ||
Thus, O best of gods, those who possess perception are proclaimed to be "non-perceptive" (asaṃjñātāḥ).
For them, there can be no sovereign power, as they rely upon an identical mode of conduct.
Below, down to the limit of Avīci, no king is found there.
The eight hells, along with their sixteen secondary hells and their peripheries, have also been proclaimed.
The kings of karma are the non-rulers; Yama, the king, is the sovereign of the departed spirits.
Suvarṇa is the king of birds; Garuḍa possesses great supernatural power.
Among the kinnaras, Drumu is renowned; among the bhūtas, Rudra is said to be the leader.
Among the vidyādharas, King Vidyācitraketu is possessed of great supernatural power.
Likewise, among the Asuras, Vemacitrin was the supreme;
among the Ṛṣis, he is called Vyāsa; and among the Siddhas, he is Mahāratha.
Soma is designated as the lord of the constellations, and likewise Bhāskara of the planets; similarly, Īśāna is proclaimed to be the king of the Mothers.

The day is said to be the counterpart of the months; Kanyā is said to be the counterpart of the zodiac signs. The ocean is said to be the counterpart of rivers; Supuṣkara is the counterpart of clouds.
Airāvata is the counterpart of elephants; likewise, Harivara is the counterpart of horses.
Then, Prahlāda is proclaimed everywhere as the king of the animals. || 53.912 ||
Infinite are the destinies said to exist, and kings are likewise infinite;
yet among them all, everywhere, the Buddha is the supreme being in the world.
In those [continents] such as Uttarakuru and the others, there is no sovereign lord;
for among the other continents, such as Pūrva and Aparagodānīya, it is likewise so.
912. It is taught that for those dwelling in Jambūdvīpa, there are infinite wheel-turning kings (cakravartin) in the east, including the lords of men over the four continents. 53.915.
These lords of beings upon the earth, born among the three classes of gods and asuras, have been described here in brief, for they would be too extensive to recount in full detail.
914. Those dwelling in infinite world-systems, with infinite expansions of virtues, have indeed been described as infinite inhabitants of this earth within this eon. 53.917.
These have been taught for the sake of attaining success in mantra, due to the lapse of place and time;
thus the kings of mantras and various hosts of messengers are accomplished.
This Dharma has been briefly explained by the preeminent sages;
indeed, it has now been proclaimed by those residing above the Śuddhāvāsa heaven.
The great hero Mañjuśrī questioned the Leader of the World: "What is this Dharma that has been taught, and how should I uphold it? [The Buddha replied:
"The activities of all kings should be set forth in detail through a series of verses. 53.920.
918 His own Jātaka, the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra, [and that] of Mañjuśrī Kumāra, O Best of Sages. 919 [Ap53.]—
920. The activity of mantras for nine hundred and twenty kalpas; the lifespans of beings on earth; 921. likewise, the proclamation of the time and the lifespan of kings. 53.922.

"The Piṭaka named *Dharmasaṅgrahaṇa*, which is directed toward awakening, has been taught through the application of mantra and tantra; it flows toward awakening. You, O wise one, should always uphold this, which fulfills the purpose of mantra and tantra. (53.923)
Thus concludes the fifty-third chapter, the Prophecy of the Fifty-three Kings, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
{S657} {V515} Chapter A54.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī, the Youthful Prince.

"Mañjuśrī, wherever this Dharma-discourse shall circulate in this place, there I myself should be known to be present. Surrounded by a host of all bodhisattvas, honored by the community of śrāvakas, and attended by all gods, nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, siddhas, vidyādharas, humans, and non-humans—I should be known to dwell there. One should know that the Tathāgata stands there for the sake of protection, shielding, and guarding. || 54.2 ||
He spoke at length on the mantras for the sake of the Bodhisattvas; for the purpose of awakening to the meaning of the path to enlightenment, it is known as the *Dharmasūtra*.

Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, ten benefits are to be known in that place where this treasury of the Dharma of the Tathāgatas—whether in the form of a book or written down—is caused to be written, recited, or maintained; where it is honored, attended to with mindfulness, and worshipped with various yak-tail whisks, powders, parasols, banners, flags, bells, musical instruments, garlands, ointments, incense, and fragrant perfumes; where it is revered, respected, and honored, or where one holds the mind with one-pointed attention. What are these ten? 54.3.

Furthermore, he shall have no fear of enemy armies or famine; nor shall there be for him any affliction from a great plague or any fear of non-human beings (*amānuṣa*). He shall have no fear of fire or any fear of adversaries. There shall be no fear of drought or excessive rain for him there. He shall have no fear of great whirlwinds or any fear of flesh-eating demons (*kravyāda*). He shall have no fear of Śakra or any fear of rogues and thieves. He shall have no fear of death or any fear brought about by King Yama. He shall have no fear of the *asuras*, nor any fear of all the gods, *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, *gandharvas*, and *asuras*. He shall have no fear of spells (*mantra*) or any fear of poisons and venomous toxins. He shall have no fear of disease, nor any fear of fever, dysentery, or ailments of the limbs and minor members. These ten benefits are to be known as occurring where this treasury of the Dharma of the Tathāgatas, contained in this *Mahākalpavisara*, remains in the form of a book, or where we perform its writing, reading, worship, preservation, and recitation. (54.4)

This treasury of Dharma of the Tathāgatas is most secret, because it follows the mantras in every respect. It must not be revealed to those who have entered the commitments (*samaya*) of the master but do not know the commitments. For what reason? This is a secret; this is a secret teaching; this is the word of the Omniscient One. Lest beings indeed reject it and treat it with contempt. 54.5

They will not honor or revere [them], and they will produce great demerit. They will perform secret obstructive acts that harm sentient beings, reveal [the secrets of] kings, and cause the destruction of the lifespan and the infliction of calamities; this must not be disclosed to others. However, it should be disclosed to those beings who have entered the practice of the secret mantras of the *samaya* and the secret [teachings], who are well-trained and well-established in the training of the Tathāgata’s instruction, who are skilled in the meaning of the Dharma, who abide in the Dharma through their entry into the *samaya* of the sense-bases and elements, who are true to their word, who have attained firm vows, and who are compassionate beings having entered the path of conduct for sentient beings—to these beings it should be disclosed, and not to others. Thus [ends section 54.6].

Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, the bodhisattva, rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is the name of this Dharma discourse? And how should I remember it? The Blessed One said: [54.7]

"Memorize it as 'The Bodhisattva Basket of the Thundering Roar of All Bodhisattvas. Memorize it as 'The Chapter on the Teaching of Marvelous and Extraordinary Dharmas. Memorize it as 'The Instruction for Bodhisattvas Entered into the Practice of the Treasury of All Mantras. Memorize it as 'The Marvelous Instruction of the Vaipulya of the Mahāyāna.'"
"Also remember it as the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*. Also remember it as the *Sarvadharmārthapūraṇanirdeśa*. Thus [ends section] 54.8.
You, who as a Bodhisattva of great supernatural power have roamed everywhere throughout all the worlds in their entirety, investigating both dharma and adharma—
yet you do not perceive this supreme, most excellent secret of the Dharma.
The tenth [chapter] concerns the destination and the teaching on the absence of fault regarding the meaning of the sūtras of mantra and tantra.
O Hero, do you not see the supreme Dharma that is directed toward awakening—this very Guhyasūtra, which is adorned with the sense that requires interpretation? (54.11)
The meanings of the sūtras in their various forms and the practice of the mantra-tantras—there is no such thing as a *kalpavisara* here that does not exist [within them]. 54.12
One shall obtain the great enjoyments and the riches of the great kings, as well as those of the celestial dwellers;
likewise, one shall attain abundant fame, both divine and human.
One should avoid the eight faults of the senses and cultivate the eight favorable moments;
for such a person, Buddhahood is certain, as is rebirth in the three higher realms.
By upholding this sūtra, there shall be merit and these benefits:
neither poison nor fire shall affect his entire body;
nor indeed shall vetālas, grahas, pūtanās, or mātṛs, nor thieves or rākṣasas, [harm him].
Furthermore, no piśācas shall harm him who recites this sūtra, or who retains it, or who worships it again and again in various ways. (54.17)
Whether one is skilled in playing musical instruments or in honoring those worthy of worship,
that mortal who performs such acts obtains these benefits proclaimed here in this world.
The sick are freed from disease, and the miserable shall become happy;
the poor obtain wealth, and the bound are released from their bonds.
Having fallen into this suffering of saṃsāra, which is joined with the five destinies,
may he attain the secure, auspicious, and immovable state of nirvāṇa.
Having recited this sutra, one attains the state of a Buddha, as well as the ultimate awakening of a Pratyekabuddha and the state of a Śrāvaka. (54.21)
O Supreme Victors, by reciting this sutra here, one obtains all that merit which is gained from worshipping the infinite white sands of the Ganges. 54.22
However many inconceivable millions of fields there may be in this world,
one should always worship as many Buddhas as there are atoms in them.
They should always and in every way provide various kinds of food and drink, as well as medicines for the occasion of illness, and diverse seats and beds.
With various kinds of robes, as well as with powders, garments, and ornaments;
with parasols, sandals, and cloths, with fragrant garlands and ointments;
and with various incenses and lamps on all sides.
A living being shall obtain that merit by retaining or reciting this.
The Pratyekabuddhas who are in the world, the Śrāvakas of great supernatural power, and the noble Bodhisattvas of great soul established in the ten stages—[all these are surpassed by him]. 54.27.
By that same measure, all those [merits] and likewise their worship shall belong to that mortal who has the book in his hand; he shall obtain that merit. 54.28.
As many beings as are spoken of in the world, residing within the world-systems— all those are declared to be entirely free from the fever of suffering.
And whatever wise being, having honored them with devotion, should repeatedly perform worship of this supreme Dharma, that person would obtain that same merit.
It is not possible, even with jewels, to constantly worship this supreme treasury of Dharma of the Lords of the World for ten million eons.
And for the sake of jewels, this supreme Dharma shall be like a wish-fulfilling gem;
by reciting and retaining the mantras in this ritual manual spoken by Mañjughoṣa, [these results are attained]. 54.32.
He who, with an untiring mind, should accomplish these on earth, shall possess a wish-fulfilling cow that provides the wealth and abundance of great enjoyments.
The mantras spoken by the Sages, which possess the definitive meaning, the interpretable meaning, and their respective fruits,
shall accomplish the state of a Vidyadhara on earth through the proper application of ritual action and timing.
All his directions were renowned as being filled with an abundance of jewels;
through the greatness of his conduct, they became fruitful and were rightly praised by the virtuous.
O King, whoever among us shall uphold even a single mantra from this excellent ritual manual (kalpavara), his royal prosperity shall be fruitful, and he shall possess the wealth of long life.
Or he may attain supreme and manifold enjoyments as the best of kings;
nor is he harmed by weapons, nor by poisons, whether stationary or mobile.

And even by those who have performed the rites of the *paravidyā* mantras for the accomplishment of *vetāḍas*, [the world] is corrupted in this realm of the earth, being intent upon the magical operations (*parakṛtya*) of others.
For him there is no fear of fire, nor of enemies, spirits, or others;
neither the body of that king nor even that of a common being is destroyed. (54.39) This applies to whoever should uphold or recite this supreme and foremost of sūtras.
And he who, when battle has approached, places his head at [the enemy's] disposal, is a king.
Having placed the parasol upon his head, one should pay homage again and again;
neither bandits nor those with various raised weapons shall slay him.
Mounted upon the neck of an elephant, appearing in the form of a youth and well-seated upon a peacock-throne, one should cause him to descend into battle.
Seeing him in the form of a child, adorned with divine ornaments like those of a celestial youth, all his enemies and other people would turn back.
Having approached the flagstaff made of either gold or silver, he hoisted the flags and banners upon it, well-placed and perfectly aligned.
At that time, one should indeed cause the entire battle— filled with enemies and prepared with various weapons— to descend upon the battlefield.
Upon merely being seen, they indeed perish or become utterly bewildered on all sides—whether they be humans, non-humans, kings, or even the lords of the gods.
Even the perfected Vidyādharas who rely upon mantras and tantras,
as well as the powerful Rākṣasas and the Kaṭapūtana mothers.
Even the various kinds of flesh-eating beings, as well as the yakṣas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and pūtanas,
are not able [to harm] one merely upon seeing the raised banner standing there.
To the youth Viśvakarman, who possesses manifold forms and appearances;
to the high-souled Mañjughoṣa, the sovereign lord of the ten stages.
The great king, a Kṣatriya, was a protector of the earth for those dwelling upon it;
he was faithful, free from misapprehension and doubt, and a lover of the Dharma.
Having generated faith in the Sugata and with minds filled with compassion,
they indeed proceeded with this rite described here, desiring reconciliation.
For these have been taught in the scriptures by the Victors who have entered the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),
as the application of mantras for an eon and the method of the tantras upon the surface of the earth.
In the past, by countless supreme Victors who were established in the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), this treasury of Dharma was indeed taught to human beings upon the earth.
Formerly, during a terrifying war between the gods and the asuras,
the city was then indeed left with its armies destroyed by the enemies. (54.54) {S662} 54.40
Then, alone on the surface of the earth, deprived of his chariot and without attendants,
he questioned that best of sages, Kāśyapa, the supreme Jina.
"What should be done? the Lord of Śacī uttered these words:
"I have been defeated by the terrible asuras and have taken refuge here."
Having spoken thus to the dwellers of heaven, Maghavan, the performer of a hundred sacrifices,
then bowed his head at the feet of that best of sages;
for previously, he who was Kauśika, the thousand-eyed one, had sat down.
Thus addressed, the best of sages, Kāśyapa, became a brahmin.
Then the prince, the source of the universe, uttered a voice with the melody of a kalaviṅka bird,
which had been sung previously by the best of Jinas.
Mañjuśrī, he is a great being, difficult to encounter, endowed with a hundred thousandfold vigor; he is proclaimed as the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and the teacher of the profound meaning.

He taught the Dharma and other truths to sentient beings as being free from conceptual proliferation, formless, devoid of intrinsic nature, and without a substratum; remember that, O Lord of the Gods.

Then, being thus remembered by him, that son of Viśvarūpa, who had attained the state of reality, arrived there at that very moment as a youth. He came to where the Blessed One was standing, together with Maghavan, the lord of the gods.
Having arrived, she then spoke the mantras after bowing to the Supreme Victor;
having prostrated before all the Supreme Victors and the greatly radiant Kāśyapa,
she then recited these mantras, having received the permission of the Sage.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas whose teachings are unimpeded! Oṃ hana hana all fears! Destroy! Annihilate! Terrify! Crush! Cut! Split! Blaze! Blaze!
Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!

As soon as these mantra words were spoken by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, this great earth, together with its mountains and oceans, shook in six ways; and all the Blessed Buddhas, throughout infinite and boundless fields and the limits of every world-system and direction, empowered these mantra words.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, his fear and horripilation vanished, struck with wonder and amazement, his eyes wide open, rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times, and having looked upon Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta face-to-face, took up those mantra-words and fixed them in his mind. He then mounted his chariot once more and fled toward where those asuras were. All the asuras set out toward their own city, which was situated in the great ocean at the base of Pātāla.

With their minds struck down and shattered, their pride vanished from their faces as they sat huddled, overwhelmed and agitated by fear of the army, they beheld that Lord of the Gods blazing like a fire; having cast aside their weapons, they turned back and went to their own abode.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Trāyastriṃśa gods: "Do not fear, sirs! Do not fear! By the power of the Buddha, we have conquered the asuras. Let us go to our own city. Come, sirs; having gone to your respective excellent palaces and your own abodes, play, enjoy yourselves, and amuse yourselves. Then those gods, with joyful minds, turned back from there and went once more to their own abodes.

Then it occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "What if I were to fashion an image of that boy in the form of a bimba fruit and place it upon the tip of my banner? Then I would have no fear of the asuras. Thereupon, Śakra, the lord of the gods, took a great jewel-gem named *dyotigarbhaprabhodyotana* (Illumination of the Radiance of the Inner Light), had an image made in the likeness of the boy, and having erected and properly fixed it upon the top of his palace in the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods, in the midst of the great city of Sudarśana, he established it there.

Then those asuras, headed by Prahrāda and Vemacitrin, did not go upward to Pātāla, nor did they attack the gods, nor were they able to display their supernatural powers or advance toward the battlefield. This continued for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of years by human calculation; and thus, there was no fear of the asuras.

Thus has this, which proclaims immeasurable qualities and benefits, which increases longevity and health, been proclaimed by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, in the past. Thus has this detailed expansion of immeasurable qualities and benefits, which is infinite and boundless, been [proclaimed] in the past. || 54.70 ||

And immeasurable demerit is produced for one who slanders this Dharma-discourse, who discriminates against it, or who attacks it with a corrupted mind; or those who would say, "This is not the word of the Buddha," or "It is neither mantra nor medicine"; or those who, thinking, "The extensive majesty, the miraculous transformations, or even the detailed descriptions of the Bodhisattvas are spoken by non-noble ones," reject, abandon, and disregard them, or are unable to hear them, and depart from that place—for such persons there will be great demerit. Thus he said. (54.71)
Those men of deluded minds who shall indeed reject this supreme Dharma sung by the best of sages and by the wise sons of the Conquerors. (54.72)
Because of that, they go to hell, including its elevated regions and the animal realm: Kālasūtra, Sañjīva, Kṣuradhārā, and Gūthamṛttika.
Then one must endure the corpse-pit, the river of caustic liquid, and the torrent of fever; furthermore, the terrible Forest of Sword-leaves, as well as the Avava and Hahava hells.

The hell known as Aṭaṭa is famous in the world for those who have committed evil deeds; people go there who are men that corrupt the Dharma. That terrible place named Avīci is renowned and celebrated throughout the world.
A dwelling of evildoers, filled with loathsome things and strewn with broken walls.
Those people who would violate this Dharma are cooked in that [hell],
extending as far as Avīci— entirely, with its heights and its very foundations.
Having gone to the very end of the infinite realms of hell,
this person of wrong views will always be one who rejects this extensive sūtra, the entirety of the Dharma.
They go to the contempt of the world,
and then, having fallen under the power of others, they go helplessly to the hells ending in Avīci.

For he who relies upon the unobscured limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), which is adorned with mantras and tantras and known as the *Saṃsūtrakalpa*, and which is supported by hundreds of various supernatural powers (siddhi); 54.80.

The body, which has the dharma-realm as its object, is a cultivation without objective support; it is extensive, the most excellent of chapters, conceptual yet beyond the span of thought. It was well-composed by Mañjughoṣa and is rightly honored by the illustrious Mañjuśrīmati.
This extensive *Mūlakalpa* has indeed been taught in great detail.
It is free from the extremes of eternalism and nihilism, as well as the middle; it is devoid of both [extremes] and their objects.
Its transition is taught through a sequence, and it is raised high in the form of mantra.
Fire, wind, space, and the well-spoken teaching on emptiness—
whosoever always rejects these shall go downward, having fallen into the lower realms.
Then, having fully accomplished awakening through many various kinds of eons, I acquired merit earned over incalculable aeons from that most excellent Victor.
The meaning of the mantra-tantras has been spoken, which reveals the states of rebirth and is free from fault;
this Root Ritual Manual is indeed purifying, auspicious, and the destroyer of evil.
The fifty-fourth chapter has been proclaimed in full detail, beautified by the conclusion of the Nīlasūtra;
it describes the greatness of the qualities of kings as applied according to time and place.
Then, on this earth, for those born as human beings, the sons of the Conquerors were taught the True Dharma;
the seventh thought of the Sage was proclaimed by the Jina to the leaders of the world.
The detailed exposition of the ritual manual has been spoken, which increases glorious prosperity;
it is titled "The Chapter on the Root and the Spreading Mass," and is honored by the mantra-tantras.

Those mortals on earth who reject this supreme, foremost sutra— the treasury of Dharma empowered by the Jina— will dwell in the Avīci hell until the end of time for many great eons, as has been described.
When, at some time or other,
it may happen that mortals are born as outcasts (mleccha), they are born poor, diseased, and foolish;
they incur contempt in the world and suffer from leprosy.
Foul-smelling, loathsome, and deformed, he is indeed blind;
possessing a terrifying form and always appearing with a harsh countenance, he is seen on earth like a hungry ghost (preta).
Incapable, low-spirited, with deformed nails and likewise despised;
being devoured by worms and distressed by ringworm and itching.

One who rejects the treasury of the Dharma of the Victors, which is honored by their relics, becomes extremely loathsome, unfit for conversation, and is reborn [in such states]. With a mind seized [by delusion], that one of poor intellect wanders on again and again. (54.94) {S666}
95. He was accompanied by many who were suffering and weary, friends without kin, and those who were destitute. || 54.95 ||

The mortal is born in many ways, overwhelmed by grief and suffering; wherever his course goes, there the one of evil intellect is born. It is because of rejecting this sutra that he is reborn in those very places. Thus [ends verse 54.96]. {V522}

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, rising from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, his eyes wide open and gazing without blinking, perceived all those sons of the gods in the Śuddhāvāsa heaven and the many hosts of beings assembled to hear the Dharma; having understood this, he addressed the Blessed One Śākyamuni as follows.
"O Blessed One, it is marvelous how well-spoken this Dharma-discourse is! Therefore, O Blessed One, in the future time, there will be beings overcome by excessive greed."

Sentient beings whose minds are overwhelmed by the five degenerations—those who lack faith, who are deceitful, harsh, and of immoral conduct—will have no faith in the course, majesty, and worship of mantras, nor in the rules regarding time and place, nor in the ritual manuals and expansions concerning mantra practice, fire offerings, recitation, and observances. Thinking, "This is not the word of the Buddha," they will reject them. With afflicted minds, they will pass away and, having been reborn in the great hells, they will experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations. O Blessed One, how should one act toward those suffering sentient beings? For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are possessed of great compassion.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having touched Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta on the head, addressed him: "Excellent, excellent indeed, Mañjuśrī, that you have set out for the sake and welfare of all sentient beings! Excellent, Mañjuśrī, that you ask the Tathāgata about this matter. Therefore, Mañjuśrī, listen well and attend thoroughly; I shall speak to you for the sake, welfare, and happiness of all sentient beings, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake of gods and humans—[this] Dharmadhātu which enjoins the path to awakening for those who have entered into the practice of all mantras."

O Kumāra, this King of Vidyās, which is the supreme secret within the extensive chapter of your own Root Ritual Manual, should be recollected at the time of death by those who desire to take refuge in the Supreme Form. And what is that? {S667}

Homage to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones! Oṃ! To you who possess the form of a youth, source of the universe! Come, come! Quickly, quickly! Bhrūṃ bhrūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! O Conqueror of the Conquerors, Mañjuśrī, the one of beautiful glory! Deliver me from all sufferings, phaṭ phaṭ! Pacify, pacify! Destroy my sins arising from the non-arising of the nectar of immortality, svāhā!

"Mañjuśrī, this is your supreme heart-mantra (*paramahṛdaya*), which brings about all peace, destroys all evil, and liberates from all suffering; it generates longevity, health, sovereignty, supreme good fortune, and eloquence, and it awakens all the kings of vidyās. As soon as these words were spoken by the Buddha, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, this great earth—with its mountains, oceans, and the entire collection of the world-receptacle and its sentient beings—trembled in six ways. Furthermore, all states of existence, including the sufferings of all beings in the realms of hungry ghosts, animals, and the world of Yama, were completely stilled.

And this King of Vidyās, Mañjuśrī, should be brought to mind. At that time, their minds shall not be inclined toward the rejection of the True Dharma, nor shall the wicked Māras find an opportunity to enter. All obstacles and impediments shall depart. And one should generate this thought: "How could I possibly conceive or reject the inconceivable awakening and the qualities of awakening of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones? The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will know [this]. || 54.102 ||

Thus concludes the fifty-fourth chapter, the detailed section on the benefits, censures, and powers, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is a pinnacle of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
And thus concludes the *Āryamañjuśrīkalpa* as it has been obtained.
